<meta>This page serves as the formal dedication of the volume. ## TO THE MOST REVEREND LORD
# NARCISSUS MARSH
### Bishop of Ferns

->EDWARD BERNARD sends greetings.<-

Indeed, venerable sir, I have preferred to relate the passing of our dear Guise <note>original: "GUISII"; referring to William Guise (1653–1683), a brilliant Oxford specialist in Oriental languages who died at the age of 30.</note> to you while in mourning. For you, above all others, know how to value that loss; indeed, insofar as your heavy responsibility for the churches permits, you strive to restore that same level of scholarship to this age through your own similar studies. We are therefore deprived—even as heaven is enriched—of a man who was flourishing and most distinguished in his youth, his lineage, his means, his piety, his wisdom, his learning, and in every single gift of intellect. 

From the historians, whom our friend followed through every age of human affairs, he gained wisdom and the light of moral conduct; but the strength and perfection of his reason—for such is its certainty—he acquired from the mathematical sciences, most learned Prelate, following your own example. Furthermore, how much he excelled in philosophy, two of the famous Colleges of this place <note>Oxford University, where Bernard and Guise were based.</note> are always ready to testify. And how much such a great talent was able to achieve in Theology in a short time, the whole of Oxford <note>original: "Oxonia"</note> felt and marveled at when he spoke once and then again from the pulpit of divine eloquence. 

Yet even these were not enough for such a rare nature. Almost the dialects of all nations, which you yourself have mastered or I would wish to learn—whether they be soft or harsh, from nearby or remote in the furthest reaches of Asia—he made familiar to himself <note>The text ends here with the catchword "sibi" (to himself), transitioning to the next page.</note> as if they were the gateways to a rare and profound knowledge...

<summary>This dedication by Edward Bernard to Narcissus Marsh serves as a poignant eulogy for the Orientalist William Guise, praising his polymathic mastery of mathematics, theology, and global languages.</summary>
<keywords>Narcissus Marsh, Edward Bernard, William Guise, Oxford University, linguistics, mathematics, theology, 17th-century scholarship, Bishop of Ferns</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dedication by Edward Bernard to Narcissus Marsh, moving from William Guise’s general education to his specific mastery of Oriental languages and his work on Armenian and Mishnaic texts. ...and rendered them almost as his native tongues with incredible labor. I shall therefore pass over the European languages—which even fashionable men desire to master, being more eager for polite conversation than for true knowledge. Instead, he applied himself with great effort to those languages from which the phrasing of the Divine writers and the meaning of their words might be explained with greater certainty and clarity. For this reason, he diligently consulted the Arabic philologists and especially their poets—masters of an ancient eloquence untainted by any enemy.

Then a most vast field of study opened to our friend—one no less fruitful than all Greek literature (who would believe it?) but even more extensive. Next, this admirable man delved into the wisdom of the Armenians, in whose land is the final resting place of Noah’s Ark and the first origins of the English tongue. <note>A 17th-century linguistic theory, often associated with scholars like Goropius Becanus or later Raphelenghi, which attempted to find the "primeval" language or link Germanic/English roots to the Caucasus.</note> He thoroughly examined their Holy Bibles, Liturgies, Lexicons, Histories, and other works of that most obscure language. From these, he hoped the more common edition of the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>original: "LXX."; the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> might be restored in many places, and the faith of the Christians throughout Armenia might be declared more sincerely and faithfully than Greek writers are wont to do. From these studies, many other things might have been taught, had not a premature death snatched them away from that man and his age.

It would indeed be far too long and tedious to recount or describe all that man’s learning in foreign tongues: <term>Hebrew</term>, <term>Samaritan</term>, <term>Chaldean</term> <note>original: "Chaldaicam"; typically referring to Aramaic in this period.</note>, <term>Syriac</term>, <term>Egyptian</term> <note>original: "Ægyptiacam"; referring to the Coptic language.</note>, and <term>Ethiopic</term>. Therefore, I shall turn myself to that which this <term>Mishnaic</term> <note>original: "Misnicus"; referring to the Mishna, the primary collection of Jewish oral law.</note> booklet suggests and indicates—which the <term>Selden</term> <note>original: "Seldonii"; referring to the printing types or the scholarly legacy of John Selden (1584–1654), whose collection was vital to Oxford's Oriental studies.</note> types now prevent from perishing, even though barely a fragment of the intended work survives. For this wise man, most devoted to the study of Divine science, knew that for the <term>Holy Bible</term> of both Testaments, the diction, rituals, customs, and precepts...

...languages might be rightly understood, he saw that the body of <term>Pharisaic Law</term> <note>original: "Juris Pharisaici"</note>—which is called the <term>Mishna</term> <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions, organized into six "orders."</note> or *Deuterosis* <note>original: "Deuterosis"; a Greek term meaning "repetition" or "second law," often used by early Christian fathers like Jerome to refer to the Mishna.</note>—contributed a great deal. He had also seen this demonstrated with great praise by <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Hebraist who used Rabbinic literature to provide context for the New Testament.</note> Lightfoot in his work on the Holy Gospels. For this reason, he decided that this work—which had been promised by many and published in parts by various authors in varying styles—should be translated anew into the Latin language (which he mastered as thoroughly as Greek, alongside the most learned men). In this way, it could be presented to the Schools of Theology with a uniform appearance and polish, providing a great benefit.

It seemed good to him, furthermore, to adorn these "responses of the wise" among the Jews with a new commentary, following in the footsteps of <term>Jarchi</term> <note>Solomon ben Isaac (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French rabbi known as Rashi.</note>, <term>Maimonides</term> <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the Sephardic philosopher and jurist.</note>, and <term>Bartenora</term> <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro (c. 1445–1515), a famous commentator on the Mishna.</note>, so as not to add the overwhelming bulk of the double <term>Gemara</term> <note>The "Gemara" refers to the extensive rabbinic analysis and commentary that, combined with the Mishna, forms the Talmud. There are two versions: the Babylonian and the Jerusalem.</note>. He did this especially because that famous Moses Maimonides and all other Rabbis of a later age had committed many, even ridiculous, errors regarding the Mishna due to their total ignorance of <term>Hellenism</term> <note>The influence of Greek language, culture, and technical terminology on the ancient world.</note>. Furthermore, they had left quite a few points to be illustrated from the learning of the Arabs and Syrians.

Nevertheless, from this fragment of a grand work that now comes forth, we have heavy cause for grief. For in the very spring of his life and his writing, he was snatched away from such a noble study, for which very few in this age seemed as well-suited as he. For whatever rare and, to Christian men, almost unheard-of things our <note>The author refers here to Saint Jerome (c. 342–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate Bible, who studied Hebrew under Jewish teachers.</note> Jerome once learned from the lips of Rabbis in "twilight and stolen hours"—which form the subject of the work he calls his *Hebrew Questions*—I indeed find all of that among the doctors of the Mishna and the Gemaras, or among the Aramaic interpreters. Indeed, the <note>original: "rector Bethleemiticus"; literally "the Ruler of Bethlehem," a poetic title for St. Jerome, who lived and worked in a monastery in Bethlehem.</note> Leader of Bethlehem had at one time seen that Mishnaic work; he thought it a volume somewhat smaller than the Testament of our faith. But because of the difficulty of the subject matter...

...so that these matters might be correctly understood, the body of Pharisaic Law, which is called the **Mishnah** <note>original: "Misna"; the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions</note> or the **Second Law** <note>original: "Deuterosis"; a Greek term for the Mishnah</note>, contributes a great deal. He had seen this also demonstrated with great praise by <term>Lightfoot</term> <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English cleric and scholar who used Rabbinic studies to provide context for the New Testament.</note> in his works on the Holy Gospels. 

Therefore, he decided to translate this work from scratch into the Latin language—for he was as skilled in this and in Greek as the most learned men—and to present it to the schools of theologians with a uniform appearance and polish for their great benefit. This was a task that had been promised by many and published only in part by various authors in different styles. Furthermore, it seemed good to him to adorn these "responses of the wise" among the Jews with a new commentary, following <term>Jarchi</term> <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Talmud.</note>, **Maimonides**, and **Bartenora** <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro (c. 1445–1515), a famous commentator on the Mishnah.</note>, so as not to add the further massive weight of the twin **Gemara** <note>The "twin" Gemaras refer to the two versions of the Talmud: the Babylonian and the Jerusalem.</note>. 

He felt this was necessary especially because, due to a supreme ignorance of <term>Hellenism</term> <note>The influence of Greek language and culture on Jewish thought during the Second Temple period.</note>, the famous **Moses Maimonides** and all other Rabbis of a later age had committed many, and indeed ridiculous, errors regarding the Mishnah; furthermore, they had left quite a few things needing illustration from the learning of the Arabs and Syrians. 

Nevertheless, from that fragment of the great work which is now being published, we have a heavy cause for grief: that he was snatched away by death itself in the very prime of his living and writing, taken from such a noble pursuit for which very few in this time seemed fit. For whatever rare and, to Christians, almost unheard-of things our **Jerome** <note>original: "Hieronymus"; the 4th-century scholar and translator of the Bible into Latin, who lived in Bethlehem to study with Jewish teachers.</note> once learned from the lips of the Rabbis in his twilight and spare hours—the subject matter of what he calls his *Hebrew Questions*—I truly find all of that among the teachers of the Mishnah and the Gemara, or among the Aramaic interpreters. Indeed, that **Master of Bethlehem** <note>Referring again to St. Jerome.</note> had at one time seen that Mishnaic work; a volume slightly smaller—as he fairly judged it—than the Testament of our faith. But because of the difficulty of the subject matter...

<meta>This page continues the eulogy and academic appraisal of the scholar William Guise, specifically mourning his untimely death which left several major translation projects unfinished. ...he abstained from all translation. However, it was life that failed our dear **Guise**—not his talent, nor the fire of his spirit, nor his worthy and wonderfully broad learning—preventing him from giving as much to Latin ears as he might have. Therefore, amidst this wound to literature, it is pleasing to call upon **Allix** <note>Pierre Allix (1641–1717), a prominent French Protestant scholar and pastor who fled to England after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes.</note>, a man most well-versed in the books of the Rabbis and in others which even the Rabbis do not know, the glory and pinnacle of Reformed France. I call on him so that he might finally choose to set forth in Latin for Christian teachers the complete body of the **Second Law** <note>original: "δευτερώσεων" (deuterōseōn); a Greek term for the Mishnah used by early Church Fathers.</note>, which long ago in the time of the Emperor **Antoninus Caracalla**, the patriarch of that miserable nation <note>A standard, though harsh, 17th-century scholarly reference to the Jewish people in exile.</note>, **Judah** <note>Judah ha-Nasi (c. 135–217 AD), the chief redactor and editor of the Mishnah.</note>, had collected from the decrees of the Pharisees into various tracts or titles. In doing so, Allix might soothe the grief over Guise’s passing with such timely labor, especially while the ancient versions of the **Mishnah** remain hidden: both the Greek version that circulated in the time of **Justinian the Great**, and the Arabic one from another century.

Furthermore, I refrain from speaking of the piety and distinguished character of **William Guise**, a man most dear to us. Indeed, his great—nay, his greatest—glory, in my judgment, lay in those virtues, though they were of a more private nature: perhaps the admiration and example of his close friends and of a single University. Yet, with his great mind, he was looking much further ahead, seeking to be of service to future generations. 

Therefore, lest he publish for our benefit and that of posterity the **Armenian Lexicon**, the **Geographical Works** <note>original: "Geographumena"</note> of Prince **Abulfeda** <note>Ismail Abu'l-Fida (1273–1331), a Syrian Kurdish historian and geographer.</note>, and the **Pharisaic Pandects** <note>original: "Pharisaeorum Pandectas"; here referring to the Mishnah as a complete legal digest.</note>, a better hope intervened—eternity itself. When our earthly studies are compared to that eternity, they must seem but trifles and jests, closer to folly than to wisdom. Nevertheless, as long as this heart remains and breathes, the memory of so learned and sweet a friend will always endure. I shall often look back upon that face; I shall establish him as an example for myself and my own before [the rest...] <note>The Latin text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword "tera," suggests the next word is "ceteris" (others/the rest).</note>

->**Nay, rather**<-

<meta>This page concludes the dedication and eulogy for William Guise, shifting from his intellectual projects to his personal character. It highlights his esteemed reputation at Oxford and his friendships with the leading scholars of the era.</meta>

*...other [virtues], so that we may please God and the better sort of men: so excellent was his conduct, so great the grace and reverence of his life. Certainly, no one among the thousands at **Oxford** <note>original: "Oxoniæ"</note> lived with a more upright reputation: without stain, without a detractor, most abundantly praised for both his virtues and his learning. For this reason, he was dear, if anyone ever was, to eminent men of eternal renown: to **John Fell**, Bishop of Oxford <note>John Fell (1625–1686) was a hugely influential academic and cleric who oversaw the development of the Oxford University Press.</note>; to **Thomas Marshall**, Dean of **Gloucester** <note>Thomas Marshall (1621–1685) was an expert in Germanic and Oriental languages and Rector of Lincoln College, Oxford.</note>; and to the peaceful and venerable old age of **Edward Pococke** <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691) was the foremost English Orientalist of the 17th century and the first professor of Arabic at Oxford.</note> (in whom, as you know, all the learning of the East resides). Moreover, in your own mind—certainly a most impartial judge—he always appeared beloved and honorable.*

*Farewell, blessed man, you who wonderfully excel in all that **Guise**-like learning <note>original: "doctrina Guisiana"</note>, yet prefer that your other glory be surpassed by the holiness of your life; and in the presence of God, be mindful of us.*

<meta>This page continues the tribute to William Guise, transitioning from his personal virtues to the scholarly legacy he left behind. It discusses the "wound to literature" caused by his early death and mentions his unfinished projects, including his work on the Mishnah, which the author hopes another scholar, Alexius, will now complete.</meta>

he abstained from every translation. However, life failed our **Guise** <note>William Guise (1653–1683) was an English Orientalist and Fellow of All Souls College, Oxford.</note> before he could grant as much as he wished to Latin ears; it was not his talent that failed, nor his mental fire, nor his worthy and wonderfully vast erudition. Therefore, in this wound to literature, it is pleasing to call upon **Alexius** <note>Étienne Le Moine (1624–1689), also known as Stephanus Alexius, was a French Protestant theologian and scholar who eventually published Guise’s work.</note>, a man most versed in the books of the Rabbis and in others which the Rabbis do not know—the glory and pinnacle of **Reformed France**. 

We call upon him so that he might wish to explain the entire body of the **traditions** <note>original Greek: "δευτερώσεων" (deuterōseōn) – a term used by early Church Fathers to refer to the Mishnah, meaning "repetitions" or "secondary laws."</note> in Latin at last for Christian teachers. This is the work which long ago, in the time of **Antoninus Caracalla**, **Judah the Patriarch** <note>Judah ha-Nasi (2nd century AD), the chief redactor and editor of the Mishnah.</note> of that wretched nation had collected from the decrees of the Pharisees into various **tractates** <note>original: "massictis," a Latinized form of the Hebrew "masekhtot" (sections or volumes of the Mishnah).</note> or titles. In doing so, Alexius might soften the grief for Guise with such timely labor, especially while the ancient versions of the **Mishnah** <note>original: "Misnæ"</note> remain hidden: both the Greek one that was in use in the time of **Justinian the Great**, and the Arabic one from another century.

Furthermore, I refrain from speaking of the piety and excellent character of **William Guise**, a man most dear to us. Indeed, his great—nay, his greatest—glory, if I am any judge, lay in those qualities, but they were of a more private nature: perhaps only the admiration and example for his close friends and the University alone. 

Yet he, with his great mind, was thinking further ahead, wishing to deserve well of future generations. He intended to publish for our benefit and that of our descendants an **Armenian Lexicon**, the **Geographical Works** of Prince **Abulpheda** <note>Abu'l-Fida (1273–1331) was a celebrated Kurdish historian and geographer from Syria.</note>, and the **Pandects of the Pharisees** <note>original: "Pharisæorum Pandectas" – a reference to the Mishnah, using a Roman legal term ("Pandects") to describe the Jewish legal code.</note>. # Rabbi MOSES MAIMONIDES’
## *Preface to the Order of Seeds*; in which an account of the *Mishnah* and the entire *Talmudic* work is given.

->Translated by the illustrious EDWARD POCOCKE.<-

KNOW that all the precepts of the law which were sent down from God to *Moses* our teacher <note>original: "Mosen magistrum nostrum," a Latin rendering of the Hebrew "Moshe Rabbenu."</note> were sent down to him together with their interpretation. God first spoke the text to him, and then gave its explanation and interpretation, including everything that the authentic text comprised. Moreover, the method of teaching these things to Israel was in the manner I am about to describe to you. When [*Moses*] withdrew into his tent, *Aaron* was the first to meet him; [Moses] recited the text sent down to him <insert>from heaven</insert> once, and taught him its interpretation. Then, as Aaron rose and stood at the right hand of *Moses*, *Eleazar* and *Ithamar* his sons entered, to whom *Moses* dictated the same thing he had dictated to *Aaron*. Then, as they rose—one moving to the left of *Moses* our teacher, and the other to the right of *Aaron*—there entered the seventy Elders, whom *Moses* taught in the same manner as he had taught *Aaron* and his sons. Afterward, the general assembly of the people entered—namely, everyone seeking the Lord—and he recited the same to them, until everyone had heard [it] from him.

Thus, *Aaron* had now heard that text from *Moses* four times, his sons three times, the Elders twice, and the rest of the assembly once. Then, as *Moses* departed from them, *Aaron* repeated that text (which he held in his memory from hearing it four times from *Moses*, as we described) to everyone who was present. Then *Aaron* also departed. By this point, the two sons of *Aaron* had also heard [that which was spoken] four times: three times from *Moses* and once from *Aaron*. Therefore, after *Aaron's* departure, *Eleazar* and *Ithamar* repeated the same text, which they had heard four times as we explained, before the entire assembly of those present, and then they rose from teaching. By this method it happened that the seventy elders had now also heard that text four times: twice from *Moses*, once from *Aaron*, and also once from *Eleazar* and *Ithamar*. The seventy Elders then recited that text to the people once, so that everyone would hear it four times: first from *Moses*, second from

...by **Aaron**, a third time by his sons, and a fourth time by the seventy Elders, so that as they departed, they taught one another that which they had received from the messenger of God, while they inscribed the text in volumes. Then the leaders of the people were dispersed throughout all Israel to teach and instruct them until they held that text in memory and became skilled in its reading. Then they also taught them the interpretation of that text sent down from God, which contained all its universal meanings. They committed the text to writing, but the tradition to memory; and so say the sages (on whom be peace): "The Law which is written, and the Law which is handed down by mouth." <note>This refers to the "Torah she-bi-khtav" (Written Law) and the "Torah she-be-al peh" (Oral Law).</note>

They also said in the *Baraita* <note>original: "Baraitha"; a collection of Jewish traditions not included in the primary Mishnah.</note>, "And the Lord spoke to **Moses** on Mount **Sinai**." What does it mean when it says "On Mount **Sinai**"? Was not the whole law given from **Sinai**? But this was said to show you that just as the commandment of the year of release <note>Referring to the Sabbatical year or *Shmita*.</note>, with its general rules, particulars, and the minutiae pertaining to it, was given from **Sinai**, so too the rest of the commandments with their general rules, particulars, and minutiae were given from **Sinai**. For example: I tell you that the Lord said to him, "*In Tabernacles* <note>Referring to the festival of Sukkot.</note> *you shall dwell for seven days*," and then He taught him that these tabernacles are necessary for men, not for women, nor are the sick or travelers bound to them; nor should the roofs [be made] for them from other things than those which grow from the earth; for they are not to be covered with wool, or silk, or vessels, even if [fashioned] from those things which the earth produces, such as mats or garments. Furthermore, eating, drinking, and sleeping must be done in them for seven full days, and they ought to contain no less than seven palms <note>original: "palmas"; referring to the "tefach" or handbreadth unit of measurement.</note> in length and the same in width, and in height no less than ten palms. The Messenger of God (on whom be peace) therefore coming brought with him this commandment along with its interpretation; and in the same manner, the **613 commandments** together with their interpretations. The commandments were inscribed in volumes, but the expositions were handed down by mouth.

In the end of the fortieth year, at the beginning of the month of **Shebat**, **Moses** (on whom be peace) called them together, saying: "The time of my death has now approached; if anyone has forgotten any tradition received from me, let him come and ask that I may declare it to him, and if any question seems difficult for anyone to understand, let him come so that I may explain it to him." <margin>Deut. 1. 3.</margin> This is what the Scripture says: "*Moses desired to explain this law, saying, etc.*" and so the sages said in the book ***Sifre*** <note>An early legal commentary on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy.</note>, "*If anyone has forgotten any statute, let him come and hear it a second time, and if anyone has need of an explanation, let him come so that it may be explained to him.*" Therefore, they learned the truth of the traditions from him and received explanations during that whole span of time which falls between the beginning of the month of **Shebat** and the seventh day of **Adar**.

...applying himself to the copying of books, he drafted thirteen copies of the Law, all on parchment, from the letter *B* of the word *Bereshith* <note>original: "Bereſhith"; meaning "In the beginning," the first word of Genesis and the start of the Torah.</note> to the letter *L* of the word *Israel* <note>The final letter of the final word of the Torah.</note> [with which the Law concludes]. He distributed one of these to each of the twelve tribes for their use, but the thirteenth he gave to the Levites, saying to them: *Take this book of the Law, etc.* Then, around noon on the seventh of **Adar** (as is accepted by true tradition), he ascended the mountain. This was *his death* in respect to us, because we were deprived of him; but in respect to him, it was *life*, because of the level to which he was raised. And so the masters (on whom be peace) said: "**Moses** our Teacher did not die, but truly ascended to serve [God] on high." <note>This reflects a traditional Jewish view that Moses' "death" was a transition to a higher spiritual existence rather than a common passing.</note>

Truly, the discourse on these matters is very lengthy and not suited for this place. Therefore, after **Moses** died, since he had left **Joshua** instructed in the explanations that had been sent down to him, **Joshua** and the men of his generation gave judgment according to them. Whatever was received from **Moses**, whether by **Joshua** himself or by one of the elders, no controversy or disagreement ever arose regarding it. However, if there was some detail among the "branches" <note>The "branches" (*derashot*) refer to specific applications or secondary laws derived from the primary commandments.</note> about which nothing had been received from **Moses**, the decision on what should be established was drawn out by comparison, using the thirteen rules that were handed down to [Moses] at **Sinai**. These are the thirteen modes of reasoning by which the meaning of the Law is extracted. <note>These are the thirteen *middot*, or logical principles, used by the Rabbis to interpret the Torah.</note>

Of those things that were extracted in this manner, there were some about which no disagreement at all arose, as they were received by the unanimous consent of all. There were others, however, where a discrepancy occurred between two different interpretations, with one person's opinion prevailing or another's reasoning being preferred. For this is what usually happens among opinions drawn from logical arguments. When such a disagreement occurred, they followed the opinion of the majority, according to the command of **God** which bids us to incline toward the majority. <note>original: "juxta Dei mandatum quo ad plures inclinare jubet"; referring to the legal principle in Exodus 23:2 that the majority rules in a court of law.</note>

You should know, however, that prophecy contributes nothing to the investigation of explaining the Law or to the drawing of conclusions by the help of the thirteen modes. What **Joshua** and **Phineas** <note>The grandson of Aaron the High Priest.</note> did in terms of investigation and reasoning is exactly the same as what **Rabina** and **Rav Ashi** <note>The 5th-century scholars who compiled the Babylonian Talmud.</note> did. As for the excellence of a Prophet and what he might have done regarding the Law, of whatever kind it might be, that is certainly a foundation of great importance among the principles upon which religion is based. Furthermore, it seems to me that this is the place to explain that foundation, though it cannot be done without first making a distinction between the ways in which Prophets claim prophecy for themselves, and by what means a prophecy is proven true. Since this is also a great foundation about which not only the common crowd of men err, but even many of higher repute—thinking, namely, that one should not believe a person claiming prophecy for himself unless he has performed a miracle equal to those of **Moses** our Teacher, and that it is necessary...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of prophecy, moving from the historical transition of authority under Joshua to the legal criteria used to distinguish true prophets from false ones. ...so that he might break the ordinary course of things, as *Elijah* did in raising the widow's son, or as happened in the celebrated miracles of *Elisha*. However, this rule is not at all true, since everything that *Elijah*, *Elisha*, and the other Prophets performed, they did not do for the purpose of confirming their Prophecy; for it was already certainly established beforehand. Instead, they performed them because necessity demanded it, and because of the closeness they had with God, He fulfilled their will, according to
<margin>Job 22:28.</margin> that promise made to the pious: *And when you decide a matter, it shall be established for you.* True prophecy, however, is proven in the manner which I am about to describe to you in this discourse I have begun. I say, therefore, first, that the rules handed down in our law concerning prophets are as follows: namely, those who claim the office of prophecy for themselves are divided into two kinds—those who prophesy in the name of an Idol, and those who prophesy in the name of the Lord. Prophecy in the name of an Idol is, in turn, of two kinds. The first is when a rising Prophet says, "A certain star, having sent down its spiritual influence into me, said: 'Worship me in this way,' or 'Invoke me in this way'"; or when he invites people to the worship of some Idol or <term>Talisman</term> <note>original: "Telesmatis"; in this context, it refers to a physical object or image believed to be imbued with celestial or magical power.</note> saying, "This thing showed this to me, it announced this to me, or it commanded me to order it to be worshipped in such a way," just as the Prophets of *Baal* and the Prophets of the *Groves* <note>original: "Luci"; referring to the sacred groves (Asherot) frequently mentioned in the Old Testament as sites of pagan worship.</note> used to do. The second is when someone says, "A revelation came to me from God that such an Idol should be worshipped, or that a spiritual influence of this kind should be drawn out in such a way" (meanwhile describing some method of worship and certain actions used by those devoted to such worship, as is handed down among the foundations of our law). This man also must be counted among the Idolatrous Prophets, since this name includes not only those who say the Idol itself ordered it to be worshipped or commanded something, but also those who say the Lord commanded the worship of some creature. Therefore, when we hear someone boasting that he is a Prophet in any of these ways, and this has been clearly proven against him, he must be
<margin>Deuteronomy 13:5.</margin> removed from our midst by strangulation, as God says: *But that prophet, or dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death*; no account will be taken of the office he claims, nor will a sign be required from him; indeed, even if he performs miracles to confirm that profession, miracles more wondrous than anything we have ever heard of, he shall nevertheless be strangled, without any regard for those miracles. For the reason why those miracles were allowed to happen is that which the Scripture assigns, saying:

> <margin>Deuteronomy 13:3.</margin> *For the Lord your God is testing you, etc.*

...it has been proven with certainty that no one should be magnified or worshipped except the One who created all things and is distinguished from all by the highest perfection. Furthermore, those who prophesy in the name of the Lord are also of two kinds. 

1. When someone, prophesying in the name of the Lord, draws men to Him and incites them to worship Him, yet claims that God has added some commandment to His commandments, or has taken away some commandment from the number of those contained in the **book of the law**. And it makes no difference whether he has added or taken away something, whether from the written text of the law itself, or from the explanation received through **tradition** <note>The "tradition" refers to the Oral Law (Torah She-be'al Peh), which explains how the written commandments are to be performed.</note>. For example, if he should add or subtract from what is in the text in this manner: "God said to me, 'The period for which fruits are to be considered uncircumcised <note>Refers to *Orlah*, the biblical prohibition against eating fruit from a tree for its first three years.</note> is only two years, after which it is permitted to eat the cultivated fruits'"; or by saying, "The Lord said to me, 'For four years it will be unlawful to eat them,'" instead of what the Lord said: *For three years they shall be uncircumcised for you, etc.* <note>original: "Tribus annis incircumcisi erunt vobis," citing Leviticus 19:23</note> and so in other similar matters. 

Likewise, he is a false prophet if he should make any change whatsoever in the tradition, even if it seems to be supported by the literal wording of the text. For example, if he says that what is stated in the law—*And you shall cut off her hand, your eye shall not pity her* <note>original: "Et abscindes manum ejus, non parcet oculus tuus," citing Deuteronomy 25:12</note>—is to be understood as literal amputation, and not as a monetary fine imposed for causing shame to another, as has been received through tradition; and if he attributes this to a prophecy, saying, "The Lord spoke His word to me, '*And you shall cut off her hand*,' to be understood just as it sounds": even here he must be put to death by **strangulation**, since he is a **false prophet**, falsely attributing to God that which God did not say to him. 

No account shall be taken of him on account of a sign or miracle performed by him; for that Prophet [Moses] who drove the whole world to amazement with his miracles, and whom God fixed in our hearts so that we might believe and have faith in him (as God Himself asserted when He said, *And they shall believe in you forever* <note>original: "Et tibi credent in seculum," citing Exodus 19:9</note>), has already previously declared to us that no other law-giving would come from God than this one. And this is what is said: *It is not in heaven, that you should say, "Who will go up to heaven for us," etc.* <note>original: "Non est in cœlis ipsa ut dicas, Quis ascendet pro nobis in cœlum," citing Deuteronomy 30:12</note> and what is said, *In your heart, and in your mouth* <note>original: "In corde tuo, & in ore tuo," citing Deuteronomy 30:14</note>, implying either the opinions that are handed down or the conclusions drawn through speculation (one of the powers originating from the heart), to which He also forbade anything to be added or taken away, saying, *You shall not add to it, nor shall you diminish from it.* <note>original: "Non addes illi, neque minues de eo," citing Deuteronomy 12:32</note> 

Therefore, the **Sages** <term>Majores</term> <note>Latin "Majores" (Elders/Ancestors), referring to the Talmudic Sages; the accompanying phrase "quibus pax" translates the Hebrew "peace be upon them."</note>, upon whom be peace, have said: *It is not permitted for a Prophet to change anything from this time forward.* Since, therefore, we know that in what he claims for himself he is a liar against God, and falsely attributes to Him what was not said to him by Him, it is necessary that we put him to death, as the **Scripture** declares when it says, *The prophet who shall presume [to speak a word in my name which I have not commanded him]... that prophet shall die.* <note>original: "Propheta qui addiderit, &c. morietur Propheta ille," citing Deuteronomy 18:20</note>

Secondly, when [someone] invites men [to worship] God, yet—

The truth of the calling [of Prophets] will be established in the manner which I am about to describe. Namely, when someone has claimed prophecy for himself as we have declared, and has been suitable for it; inasmuch as he has been learned, religious, self-controlled, endowed with intellect and all integrity of character, according to that rule among us: *Prophecy does not rest except upon the wise, the strong, and the wealthy.* <note>This is a famous Rabbinic dictum from the Talmud (Nedarim 38a). "Wealthy" in this context often refers to being content with one's portion, and "strong" to self-control over one's impulses.</note> There are many signs regarding this matter, all of which we cannot encompass here; to try to prove each one in a formal discourse, citing texts from the Holy Scripture and the sayings of the Sages, would require a whole book in itself. Perhaps [we shall compose such a work one day], with all that pertains to it, if God provides help. 

When therefore he is suitable for this office as is proper, and has claimed it for himself, we shall say to him: *Perform promises for us, and report to us some of those things which the Lord has made known to you;* and when he reports them, if all his promises turn out true, we shall then perceive the truth of his prophecy. But if in any of them, even the most minute, he should be a liar, we shall know from this that he is a liar; and this is the express judgment of the law regarding this kind of trial—

fact): *And all Israel from Dan even to Beersheba knew that Samuel was confirmed as a Prophet to the Lord.* <note>original: "fidelis esset Samuel in Prophetam Domino"</note> Nor did any business occur to them about which they did not consult the Prophets. As 
<margin>1 Samuel 9:9</margin>
it says: *For he who is now called a Prophet was formerly called a Seer.*

But perhaps someone might think to himself and say: "Will the true Prophecy of those who claim it for themselves be judged then solely by the truth of their predictions of things to come?" If the matter stands thus, then Soothsayers, Astrologers, and those endowed with all manner of animal powers could claim prophecy for themselves, since we see with our own eyes that they predict the future daily. But (God knows) this point is of great importance, and we must explain it so that the difference may appear between what the Prophet reports from God and the predictions of those who are merely endowed with those other powers.

I say, therefore, that Soothsayers, Astrologers, and men of that sect do indeed predict future things, but in such a way that they are necessarily partly true and partly false; this we see constantly, and even those who profess these arts confirm it. They cannot deny it while they seek glory from the fact that one man's lies were fewer than another's. But for any of them to speak the truth in every single instance—this is impossible. Nor do those endowed with such powers claim this for themselves. But when someone says, "There will be a drought this year," and no rain falls because of it, or if it rains only a little; or when he says, "Tomorrow it will rain," and it rains the next day, etc., he is held to be quite...

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological argument concerning how to identify a true prophet. The previous page established that while God's threats may be averted by repentance, His promises of good are absolute markers of a prophet's legitimacy. This page transitions into the specific legal authority granted to a proven prophet to temporarily suspend religious laws.</meta>

<page-num>( 10 )</page-num>

...they have threatened, whether they have claimed the gift of prophecy for themselves truly or falsely; the true proof of their veracity is when the good which they promised has been fulfilled.

When the calling of a Prophet has been certainly established according to the previously stated foundations, and his reputation is well-known—as in the cases of **Samuel**, **Elijah**, and others—this Prophet is permitted to do that in the Law which is allowed to no one else. Specifically, that which I am about to describe: namely, when he commands any affirmative commandment to be omitted, or any prohibited act to be committed, it is necessary to obey his word in all things. Whoever transgresses his command becomes liable to death inflicted by Heaven, with the exception of the case of Idolatry. And this is the opinion of the <term>Sages</term> <note>The Rabbinic scholars of the Jewish tradition.</note> in the *Talmud*, where they say: *In all things, if a Prophet says to you: "Transgress the words of the Law," you should listen to him, except in the case of Idolatry.* <note>original Latin: "In omnibus, Si dicat tibi Propheta, transgredere verba Legis, auscultes ipsi, excepta Idololatria"</note> This is allowed, however, on the condition that he does not intend this command to be perpetual—claiming that the Lord commanded this thing to be done thus forever—but only commands it for a specific occasion and only for a designated time. Indeed, the Prophet himself will be questioned whenever he commands a transgression of any commandment that the Lord commanded through **Moses**. If, upon being questioned, he answers that this transgression will not be perpetual, but is to be committed only for the present moment—just as the <term>Senate</term> <note>Referring to the Sanhedrin, the high court of ancient Israel.</note> is accustomed to doing in a ruling that is valid for a short time—[he must be obeyed].

Just as **Elijah** did on Mount **Carmel** when he offered a sacrifice outside of **Jerusalem**, even after the Sanctuary had been built there; which was an act that would have made the perpetrator liable to <term>excision</term> <note>A divine punishment of being "cut off" from the people, known in Hebrew as *karet*.</note> without a Prophetic command, as it was forbidden by God in the text of the Law, where it says:

<margin>Deut. 12:13</margin>

But if he <note>Elijah (peace be upon him).</note> had been asked while offering on Mount **Carmel**, "What would you say if we were to do this perpetually, just like this act?" he would have said that this is by no means permitted, and that anyone who offers outside of **Jerusalem** is held by the penalty of excision. Likewise, just as **Elisha** did when he commanded **Israel**, during the conquest of **Moab**, to cut down the fruit-bearing trees, saying:

<margin>2 Kings 3:19</margin>
> *And you shall fell every good tree,* <note>original Latin: "Et omnem arborem pulchram dejicietis"</note> although God had forbidden this by saying: *You shall not destroy the tree by wielding an axe against it.* If **Elisha** had been asked whether this commandment had been abolished, and if it would be permitted for us in the future to cut down fruit trees when we besiege any places, he would certainly have said it is not permitted, but that this [was only for] the present...

<meta>The previous page concluded with the mention of Simeon the Just and the transition to "Our Holy Teacher" (Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi), who is the subject of the opening of this page as the compiler of the Mishnah.</meta>

from his teacher, and **Baruch** son of **Neriah** from **Jeremiah**, just as **Jeremiah** had without doubt received it from the Prophets, who received it from one another until the Elders, who passed down to **Joshua** what he himself had received from **Moses**. Having therefore collected these opinions and sayings, he <note>Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, the compiler of the Mishnah.</note> set his hand to composing the **Mishnah**, which would contain the explanation of all the commandments written in the **Law** <note>The Torah or Pentateuch.</note>, partly by traditions received orally from **Moses** (peace be upon him), partly by logical deductions drawn from arguments about which there is no lasting disagreement, and partly by conclusions regarding which there was disagreement between two methods of reasoning. Specifically, someone might say: "Since the explanations of the Law were (as we have established) received orally from **Moses** (according to their saying which we reported: *The entire Law with its general rules, its particulars, and its fine details was spoken from Sinai*), what then are these specific rulings that are called the 'Laws of Moses from Sinai'?" <note>The author is distinguishing between the general Oral Law and a specific category of laws called "Halakhah le-Moshe mi-Sinai," which are traditions with no biblical source.</note> This then is the fundamental rule that must be held: namely, that regarding the explanations received from **Moses**, there is no controversy at all. For example, though someone might say— <margin>Exodus 21:24</margin> "If someone puts out another's eye, his own eye must be put out," because the Lord says, *An eye for an eye*—while another argues that he is only bound to pay a monetary price, we do not find that the Sages actually differed on the Law itself. Nor do we find them differing in opinion regarding what the Lord said <margin>Leviticus 23:40</margin>: *The fruit of a beautiful tree*, as if one contended it was a citron, while another thought it meant a quince, a pomegranate, or something similar. Likewise, they do not disagree that the "leafy tree" means the **Myrtle**. Nor do we find any controversy regarding God’s saying, *And you shall cut off her hand*, but that it must be understood as a monetary fine. Nor regarding His saying <margin>Leviticus 21:9</margin>, *And the daughter of any priest, if she profanes herself by playing the harlot, she profanes her father; she shall be burned with fire*: it is established that this sentence does not necessarily apply unless she was married. Similarly, concerning what God decreed about her in whom the signs of virginity were not found—namely, that she is to be stoned—we have not found it questioned from the time of **Moses** until now that this is only to be understood regarding one who was a man's wife, and where it was clearly proven that she committed adultery after the betrothal contract, and after she had been warned in the presence of witnesses.

It is the speech of one who does not correctly perceive the facts, nor grasp the foundations, and who detracts from the reputation of the persons through whom the tradition of the Law was received. All of this, therefore, is false. Nothing else leads men to foster this false opinion except that they do not correctly weigh the words of the Sages found in the *Talmud*. <note>The Talmud is the primary source of Jewish religious law and theology, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note> For when they find that an explanation is attributed to *Moses* (which is true, as we have stated before), they fail to distinguish between the foundations received by tradition and the consequences that are drawn out [by reasoning]. And the same [is true] in all such disagreements, which are branches [proceeding] from the branches of branches. As for their saying: *From the time that the disciples of Shammai and Hillel multiplied, who did not devote themselves to the study of the law as much as was necessary, disagreement multiplied in Israel*, its meaning is very clear. For when two are equal in intelligence, insight, and knowledge of the foundations from which consequences are drawn, no discrepancy happens between them in those things they elicit by reasoning—or if it occasionally happens, it is certainly minimal. Thus, we never find a difference between *Shammai* and *Hillel* except in certain specific rituals. This resulted from the fact that the method of reasoning used by each of them in their conclusions was very similar, as were the foundations which were granted as such by both. But when the diligence of the disciples languished, and their reasoning was weakened compared to that of *Hillel* and *Shammai*, their teachers, disagreement arose among them during their disputes in many matters. This was because the reasoning of each one was according to the measure of his own intellect and the foundations he held. Meanwhile, they are not at all to be blamed in these things, since we do not require that when two people dispute, they must dispute according to the intellect of *Joshua* and *Phineas*. <note>Joshua was Moses' successor, and Phineas was a High Priest; here they represent an ideal, superior level of wisdom.</note> Nor are we left in doubt because they differ from one another or because they are not like *Shammai* and *Hillel* or others who excelled them. God, the Best and Greatest, does not demand such obedience from us; rather, this [is required] from us...

<meta>This page continues the author's explanation of how the Oral Law is structured. Having discussed the first three categories of tradition—those directly from Sinai, those derived through logic, and those subject to debate—the author now moves to the final two categories: precautionary decrees and social ordinances. This provides a complete framework for why Jewish law contains both immutable truths and evolving human interpretations.</meta>

<page-num>(19)</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>

it is required that we listen to the learned, of whatever age they may be, just as the Scripture says: [*Either to the judge who shall be in those days, and you shall inquire, etc.* <note>original: "Aut ad judicem qui fuerit diebus illis, & inquires, &c." (Deuteronomy 17:9). The author uses this to justify the authority of contemporary scholars.</note>] And in this way, disagreement arose, not because they erred in reporting what was handed down—with one reporting the truth and the other a falsehood—but because they were applying human reason to new situations. How clear this is to anyone paying attention! And of how much weight is this rule in the Law?

The fourth class [contains] the decrees which the **Prophets** and **Sages** established in each generation to serve as a fence and a rampart for the Law: and these are what **God** commanded to be established in universal terms when he says, [*And you shall keep my charge* <note>original: "Et custodietis custodiam meam" (Leviticus 18:30).</note>] which, according to the tradition, [means] *Make a guard for my guard.* And these are what the Sages call <term>Gezeroth</term> <note>Hebrew term for "decrees"—preventative laws enacted by rabbis to prevent people from accidentally violating a biblical commandment.</note> or Decrees. And in these also, disagreement occurs; while it seemed right to one to forbid a certain thing for some reason, it did not seem so to another: thus it frequently [occurs] in the *Talmud*: *Rabbi N.* established this, for this or that reason; but *Rabbi N.* did not establish it. And this is also one of the causes of disagreement. Do you not see that the rule that *poultry meat with milk* [is not to be eaten] is a decree from our **Teachers** to keep men far away from transgression? For the Law does not forbid any meat except that of domestic and wild animals [with milk], but the **Sages** forbade the meat of poultry to drive men further away from what is illicit. And there are some among them whom this Decree does not please; for *Rabbi Yose the Galilean* allowed poultry meat with milk, so much so that all the inhabitants of that region ate it, as is manifest in the *Talmud*. However, when it happens that everyone agrees on one of these decrees, then it is in no way permitted to transgress it. And when it is widely known in *Israel* that a thing is forbidden by such a decree, one must not go against it, so much so that not even the prophets themselves are allowed to take away from it. This is according to the express testimony of the *Talmud*: that even the prophet *Elijah* himself could not diminish any of the eighteen things established by the *School of Shammai* and the *School of Hillel* <note>Two influential 1st-century schools of Jewish law whose consensus rulings became binding.</note>, and they gave the reason for it, saying, *Because the prohibition of these things is known throughout all Israel.*

The fifth class consists of those decrees made by way of legal determination and for the sake of convenience in human affairs, to which nothing is added to or taken away from the Law: or concerning things that are useful to men in [observing] the precepts of the law; and these are what the **Sages** call Ordinances and Rites. These also may in no way be transgressed, since the entire [Jewish] sect agrees on them; and *Solomon* forbids transgressing them when he says, *If anyone breaks through a fence, a serpent will bite him.* <note>Ecclesiastes 10:8. Here used metaphorically to mean that violating rabbinic "fences" leads to spiritual danger.</note> There are very many decrees of this kind recorded in the *Talmud* and *Mishnah*.

<sig>C 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: pro-</meta>

<summary>This page defines the final two categories of Jewish tradition: "Gezeroth" (precautionary decrees to protect biblical laws) and "Ordinances" (social or ritual rules for communal order). The author explains that while some decrees were debated by individual Sages like Rabbi Yose the Galilean, once a decree is accepted by all of Israel, it becomes unchangeable, carrying a weight that even a prophet cannot overturn.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the structural logic of the Mishnah. Previously, the author explained the different categories of legal tradition; here, he explains the specific sequence of the six "Orders" (Sederim) and why the compiler, Rabbi Judah the Prince, chose this particular arrangement based on the sequence of the Torah.</meta>

...concerning the commandments which properly relate to those things which the earth produces. Since the fruits of the earth provide nourishment for animals, and it is impossible for a man to be preserved among the living unless nourishment is taken, he should worship God with some kind of devotion; therefore, he <note>Referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the compiler of the Mishnah.</note> placed first the discourse on the commandments properly relating to those things which grow from the earth: to which he then joined the <term>Seder Moed</term> <note>The "Order of Appointed Times" or Festivals.</note>, because that is the order of the Biblical text; just as the Lord says, *six years you shall sow your land, and gather its produce; but in the seventh you shall let it rest and lie fallow, etc.; and afterward, Six days you shall do your work, etc. Three times you shall keep a feast to me in each year.* <note>original Latin: "sex annis seres terram tuam... (Exodus 23:10-14)"</note> Then it seemed right to him to place the judgments concerning women before other lawsuits, following the footsteps of the sacred text, because the Lord did so [saying] *When any man shall sell his daughter, etc. When men have brawled and struck a woman, etc. Next, And if an ox shall gore, etc.* <note>See Exodus 21:7, 21:22, and 21:28. The author is showing that laws regarding women appear in the Torah before general property damages.</note> for which reason he placed <term>Seder Nashim</term> <note>The "Order of Women," dealing with marriage and divorce.</note> before the <term>Seder Nezikin</term> <note>The "Order of Damages," dealing with civil and criminal law.</note>. Indeed, the book of *Exodus* encompasses these four subjects, namely the subject of <term>Seder Zeraim</term> <note>The "Order of Seeds" or Agriculture.</note>, <term>Seder Moed</term>, <term>Seder Nashim</term>, and <term>Seder Nezikin</term>. 

Then from the book of *Exodus* he moved to the book of *Leviticus*, according to the series of the book brought down from heaven. Therefore, after <term>Seder Nezikin</term> he placed <term>Kodashim</term> <note>The "Order of Holy Things," dealing with sacrifices and the Temple.</note>, then <term>Seder Taharot</term> <note>The "Order of Purities," dealing with ritual cleanliness.</note>, because that is how the order of the Sacred text stands. Furthermore, he placed the judgments on offerings before the judgments on pollutions and purifications, because [the commandments] concerning purifications have their beginning from [the reading] *And it came to pass on the eighth day, etc.* <note>original: "Fuit autem die octavo, &c." (Leviticus 9:1). This marks the beginning of the laws regarding the priestly service and subsequent laws of purity.</note> 

And when he had now encompassed those six categories, under which all the commandments of the [Law] are comprised; it seemed right to him to divide each one of them into those Species which were necessary (each of which he called a <term>Masekhet</term> <note>original: "Massicta". This is a "Tractate" or individual volume of the Mishnah.</note>): Then those things which are said concerning each species [he divided] into sections, each of which he called a <term>Perek</term> [that is, a Chapter]. Then those things which are said in each chapter into [smaller] sections, so that what is discussed might be more easily rendered, both for holding in the memory and for teaching others: and each of these smaller sections he named a <term>Halakhah</term> <note>A specific legal ruling or procedure.</note>. 

Those things, however, which are said in the <term>Seder Zeraim</term>, he distributed in the manner which I am about to describe: He began first with <term>Berakhot</term> [that is, Blessings]; the reason for this is that a skilled Physician, when he desires to preserve the health of one who enjoys good health in the same state in which it currently is, first takes care by rightly preparing his nourishment: so it seemed right [to the Lord] or to that <note>original Greek: "philalēthei" (truth-lover). This likely refers to the compiler's devotion to the truth of the Law.</note> lover of truth to take his beginning from blessings, since it is not permitted for anyone to eat unless a blessing has first been said; for which reason it seemed best to him to begin with the discourse on blessings, so that he might prepare nourishment by a rational preparation. Then it seemed right to him [to ensure] that nothing should be lacking from [his] discourse on any matter, [to speak] concerning all blessings in general...

<meta>This page continues the explanation of the logical structure of the Mishnah’s first Order, Zeraim (Seeds). The author is justifying why the compiler, Rabbi Judah the Prince, arranged the individual tractates in this specific sequence, often mirroring the order of verses in the Torah.</meta>

(23)

...speaking of blessings which relate to nourishment and the commandments. Why, since there is no commandment that falls upon every person daily except for the <term>Keriath Shema</term> <note>The "Recitation of the Shema," the central prayer of Jewish liturgy (Deuteronomy 6:4).</note>, that is, the *Recitation of 'Hear'*, and because it would not be fitting to speak of the blessings of the *Shema* before he had spoken of the recitation itself, he began with the chapter **"When do they read the Shema?"** and those things which are joined with it. Then, returning to the goal of the Order—which is to speak of the commandments relating to the land—he began with the <term>Massecheth Peah</term> <note>Tractate Peah, or "The Corner."</note>. This follows the section on blessings because all obligations pertaining to seeds only apply to the crop after it has been harvested—with the exception of **Peah** <note>The "corner" of the field that must be left unharvested for the poor.</note>, which is owed while the grain is still standing in the earth; therefore, he placed the discussion of it in the first position. After *Peah* follows <term>Demai</term> <note>Tractate Demai, concerning "doubtful" produce where it is uncertain if tithes were properly taken.</note>, concerning a doubtful matter, because the poor have a right to it just as they do to the corner of the field. This is according to what they say: *They provide that which is in doubt to be eaten by the poor* <note>Produce from which tithes may not have been taken is given to the poor.</note>. After *Demai* comes <term>Cilaim</term> <note>Tractate Kilayim, or "Mixed Species."</note>, because the text of Holy Scripture proceeds in that order in the section **"You shall be holy"**: *You shall not finish harvesting the corner of your field;* <note>original Latin: "Non finies metere angulum agri tui" (Leviticus 19:9)</note> and after that, *you shall not sow your field with diverse seed.* Next, after *Cilaim*, he added <term>Shebiith</term> <note>Tractate Shevi'it, concerning the "Sabbatical Year."</note>. It would have been reasonable for *Cilaim* to be followed by the Tractate <term>Orlah</term> <note>Tractate Orlah, concerning the "uncircumcision" or forbidden fruit of young trees.</note>, as that is the order observed by Holy Scripture, except that he saw that *Orlah* was not a matter of necessity; as long as one does not plant, one is not bound by the law of *Orlah*. But the seventh year is a necessity <note>It occurs automatically every seven years regardless of the farmer's actions.</note>. Furthermore, since the cessation of work in the seventh year is commanded in a specific chapter of the Law, he prioritized the discourse on that Cessation. After *Shebiith*, he placed the Tractate <term>Terumah</term> <note>Tractate Terumah, or "The Offering."</note>, because that offering—the *Terumah*—is the first obligation to be taken from the seeds. After *Terumah* comes <term>Maasher rishon</term> <note>Tractate Ma'aser Rishon, or "The First Tithe."</note>, because it is taken immediately after the *Terumah*. After the First Tithe follows <term>Maasher Sheni</term> <note>Tractate Ma'aser Sheni, or "The Second Tithe."</note> in its proper order. Then comes the Tractate <term>Challah</term> <note>Tractate Challah, or "The Dough Offering."</note>; for after these obligations have been removed from the seeds as we have described—namely the Offering, the First Tithe, and the Second Tithe—the grain is then ground into flour, which is kneaded, and then the dough offering is required. Once the discussion of seeds and the debts arising from them was finished, he began to arrange the discourse on fruits; therefore, after the tractate on the dough offering, he spoke of *Orlah* (the uncircumcision of trees). Then he spoke of <term>Biccurim</term> (First Fruits) in the order observed by Holy Scripture, in which *Orlah* is mentioned in Leviticus, while <margin>Deut. 26</margin> *Biccurim* is cited in the section *Vehayah* <note>Deuteronomy 26:1, "And it shall be (Vehayah) when you enter the land..."</note>. In this way, the division of the discourse on seeds reaches eleven tractates. Then, proceeding to the <term>Seder Moed</term>...

<meta>This page continues the author’s explanation of the logical arrangement of the Mishnah. Having previously justified the order of the first "Order" (Zeraim, or Seeds), the author now moves to the second Order, Moed (Appointed Times), which deals with the Sabbath and festivals.</meta>

(24)

<margin>Exodus 30:12. Leviticus 16.</margin>
When dividing <term>Moed</term> <note>Hebrew for "Appointed Times" or Festivals.</note> into its various parts, just as he had done with the Order of <term>Zeraim</term> <note>Hebrew for "Seeds," the first Order of the Mishnah.</note>, the compiler gave the first place to the tractate on the **Sabbath**. He did this because the Sabbath holds the highest rank in degree of excellence, and also because it is celebrated every seventh day, thus returning more frequently in the sequence of time. Furthermore, the Law <note>The Torah or Pentateuch.</note> begins with the Sabbath wherever it first makes mention of the festivals. After the **Sabbath**, he placed **Erubim** <note>Tractate Eruvin, or "Commixtions." This deals with the symbolic boundaries that allow one to carry items or travel further on the Sabbath.</note>, since it pertains directly to the intention of the Sabbath. After that comes **Pesachim** <note>Tractate Pesachim, or "Passover."</note>, because it concerns the first of the commandments that God commanded through Moses, and the Sabbath is followed by it in the scriptural section on festivals. After that, he placed the tractate **Shekalim** <note>Tractate Shekalim, or "Shekels," concerning the annual tax for the Temple maintenance.</note> according to the order of the Scriptures. Then follows **Cippurim** <note>Tractate Yoma, concerning the "Atonements" or the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur).</note> after **Shekalim**, following that same scriptural order; for the commandment regarding the **Shekels** is found in the section <term>Ki Tissa</term> <note>Exodus 30:11-34:35.</note>, and the commandment regarding the Day of Atonement is in the section <term>Acharei Mot</term> <note>Leviticus 16:1-18:30.</note>.

Then he proceeded to conclude the discussion of the three pilgrimage festivals. Since he had already spoken of **Passover**, there remained the festivals of **Succoth** <note>Tabernacles.</note> and **Shebuoth** <note>The Festival of Weeks, or Pentecost.</note>. Because there was very little to say regarding the Festival of Weeks other than a few things that apply to any festival day—which are the subjects that make up <term>Tractate Betzah</term> <note>Literally "Egg," but referring to the laws of "Yom Tov" or festival days in general.</note>—he placed the tractate **Succoth** before the tractate **Betzah** because of the great number of commandments that relate to the festival of Tabernacles. 

Since nothing then remained for him regarding the times mentioned in the Law <note>The Torah.</note> except for the **New Year**, he spoke after **Betzah** concerning the **New Year** <note>Rosh Hashanah.</note>, and thus his discussion of the distinctions of times mentioned in the Law was finished. Proceeding then to the times mentioned in the books of the Prophets (peace be upon them), such as the days of Fasting instituted by the Prophets, he subjoined the discussion of **Taanioth** <note>Tractate Taanit, or "Fasts."</note> to the discussion of the **New Year**. After **Taanioth**, he placed **Megillah** <note>Tractate Megillah, regarding the "Scroll" of Esther and the festival of Purim.</note>, because that festival is an institution of the Prophets who came after those who ordained the Fasts. Then after **Megillah**, he placed **Moed Katan** <note>Literally "Small Festival," dealing with the intermediate days of Passover and Tabernacles.</note>, because it shares something in common with the days of **Purim**: namely, that in neither of them is it permitted to fast or to give oneself over to mourning. 

Having finished the discussion of the festivities, the things relating to them, and the things joined with them, he concluded this order with the tractate **Chagiga** <note>Tractate Chagigah, concerning the "Festival Offering" or the duty to appear at the Temple.</note>. This tractate concerns those matters pertaining to the three pilgrimage festivals; however, he placed it in the final position because it is not a general commandment, as it applies only to males, just as the Lord said: *All your males [shall appear before me].* And so, the distribution of the things said regarding the festivals reaches twelve tractates. Then, proceeding to divide the discussion concerning women, he began...

<meta>This page continues the author’s explanation of the organization of the Mishnah. Having previously discussed the first two Orders, Zeraim (Seeds) and Moed (Appointed Times), the author now turns to the Third Order, Seder Nashim (Women), which deals with marriage, divorce, and family law.</meta>

(25)

The sequence begins with the tractate <term>Yevamot</term> <note>Hebrew for "Levirate Marriages," concerning the law where a man must marry his deceased brother's childless widow. Original: *Yebamoth*.</note>, which concerns the obligations of brothers. The reason that compelled the compiler to begin with *Yevamot*, rather than starting with the tractate <term>Ketubot</term> <note>Hebrew for "Marriage Contracts," original: *Cetuboth*.</note>—which deals with the legal instruments of marriage contracts and which logic suggests should come first—is as follows: marriage is generally a voluntary matter, and it is not within the power of the Judges to compel anyone to take a wife. However, in the case of Levirate laws, a man is compelled to act, and it can be said to him, <note>original: "Aut calceum exuas, aut Leviri officio fungere"</note> "Either remove the shoe <note>A reference to the ceremony of *Halizah*, where the widow removes her brother-in-law's shoe to release him from the obligation to marry her.</note> or perform the duty of a brother-in-law." It is better to begin with a matter of necessity. Therefore, starting with *Yevamot*, he then added *Ketubot*, and after *Ketubot*, <term>Nedarim</term> <note>Hebrew for "Vows," original: *Nedarim*.</note>. This is because the entire investigation belonging to the section on *Nedarim* concerns the oaths of women; as it says in Scripture, *Between a man and his wife, between a father and his daughter, etc.* <note>Numbers 30:16.</note> Since the marriage is now completed and the bride has been admitted into the bridal chamber, it is within the husband's power to annul her vows; for this reason, he placed *Nedarim* after the tractate *Ketubot*.

After the tractate *Nedarim* comes <term>Nazirut</term> <note>Hebrew for "The Nazirite Vow," original: *Neziruth*.</note>, because a Nazirite vow is also among the types of vows, and if a woman binds herself by a Nazirite vow, it is within her husband's power to make it void. Therefore, he placed *Nazirut* immediately after *Nedarim*. Having finished what was to be said regarding marriage and the dependent matters of annulling vows, he proceeded to speak of divorce; because divorce takes place after marriage, he placed <term>Gittin</term> <note>Hebrew for "Bills of Divorce," original: *Gittin*.</note> after *Nazirut*. After *Gittin* comes <term>Sotah</term> <note>Hebrew for "The Wayward Woman," original: *Sotah*.</note>, or the tractate concerning the woman suspected of adultery; indeed, this is also included under the subject of divorce, since when a woman has committed adultery, the spouses are compelled to divorce, as will be explained in its proper place.

Then, after *Sotah*, comes <term>Kiddushin</term> <note>Hebrew for "Betrothals" or "Sanctifications," original: *Kiddušim*.</note>, which completes the Order of <term>Seder Nashim</term> <note>Hebrew for "The Order of Women," the third of the six main divisions of the Mishnah.</note>. However, a question remains: Why did he place the tractate *Kiddushin* in the last position, when it ought rather to have been placed first, specifically before *Ketubot*? If you were to answer that he did not place it before *Ketubot* so as not to separate the tractates *Yevamot* and *Ketubot*—which share the same goal, namely marriage, and thus their discussion must be continued together as we have said—even then, it seems it should at least have been placed before *Gittin*. This would give the first place to *Kiddushin* in the natural order of things, followed by the tractate <note>original Greek: *τῷ*</note> *Gittin*. The answer must be that he did this to imitate the order of the Scripture, which speaks of divorce before it speaks of betrothals, as seen in the word spoken by God: *And he shall write her a bill of divorce, and give it into her hand, and send her out of his house, and she shall leave his house, and go and become another man's wife.* <note>Deuteronomy 24:1-2.</note> From the phrase *and she shall become another man's*, we have learned a primary principle regarding betrothals, as explained by the Rabbinic saying: <note>original: "Comparat permansionem ejus cum viro, cum exitu ejus"</note> "He compares her joining with a husband with her departure from one." And so...

<meta>This page continues the author's detailed overview of the structure of the Mishnah. Having concluded the Third Order (Nashim, or Women) on the previous page, the author now begins explaining the Fourth Order, Nezikin (Damages), and the logic behind the arrangement of its tractates.</meta>

The division of that discourse concerning **Women** <note>The Third Order of the Mishnah, known as Seder Nashim.</note> is completed in seven tractates.

Then proceeding to divide the discourse concerning **Damages** <note>The Fourth Order of the Mishnah, known as Seder Nezikin, dealing with civil and criminal law.</note>, he first divided it into three parts, beginning with **The First Gate** <note>original: *Baba Kama*</note> <insert>that is, the first gate</insert>, the purpose of which is to investigate damages and how to prevent them: such as <insert>for example, in the case of</insert> a **goring** ox <note>A standard legal category in Biblical law (Exodus 21) regarding property damage caused by animals.</note>, a pit, fire, wounding, and similar matters; for it certainly befits a Magistrate to attend to nothing before he prohibits harm among men. Next follows **The Middle Gate** <note>original: *Baba Metzia*</note> <insert>or the middle gate</insert>, the purpose of which is to investigate claims and deposits, hirings, lending, and leasing, and what appropriately relates to these; following the pattern established in Scripture, which, after the judgments concerning the **goring** ox, the pit, and fire, and the chapter regarding men fighting, spoke of the four guardians <note>The four types of bailees or caretakers in Jewish law: the unpaid guardian, the borrower, the paid guardian, and the hirer.</note>.

<margin>Exodus 21, 22.</margin>
Then **The Last Gate** <note>original: *Baba Batra*</note> <insert>the last gate</insert>, the purpose of which is to investigate the division of lands, the judgments occurring in shared buildings and among neighbors, the dissolution of trade due to an apparent defect, what must be decided regarding the words used in buying and selling, and concerning suretyship and inheritances. He placed this section in the last position because it <insert>depends</insert> entirely on tradition and concerns matters based on inference, which are not explicitly explained in the [Biblical] text.

And since he had already made known the <insert>system</insert> of judgments, establishing a discourse on the judges who decide them, he appended the tractate **The High Court** <note>original: *Sanhedrin*</note> <insert>concerning judges</insert> after the previous <insert>tractate</insert>. Furthermore, the tractate **Lashes** <note>original: *Maccoth*</note> <insert>concerning lashes</insert> in <insert>certain</insert> copies is continued with the tractate **The High Court** <note>original: *Sanhedrin*</note>, and is considered as one with it; for where it had said, *These are those who are strangled* <note>original: "Isti sunt qui strangulantur"</note>, they immediately added, *These are those who are flogged* <note>original: "Isti sunt qui vapulant"</note>. However, this is not correctly done; rather, it is a separate tractate, which is indeed connected with **The High Court** <note>original: *Sanhedrin*</note> because no one can bare a back or determine the number of <insert>lashes</insert> except the judges, as was said by the Lord:

<margin>Deuteronomy 25:2.</margin>
*And the judge shall cause him to lie down, and he shall be beaten before him according to the measure of his wickedness in number.* <note>original: "Et prosternere faciet ipsum judex, & plagis cadet ei coram ipso secundum mensuram impietatis ejus in numero."</note>

After **Lashes** <note>original: *Maccoth*</note>, however, he placed the <insert>tractate</insert> **Oaths** <note>original: *Shebuoth*</note> <insert>concerning oaths</insert> because a certain similarity in judgments occurs between the end of that tractate and the beginning of this one, as is mentioned in the **Talmud**; and it should be added that what is dealt with here is also the business of judges, since no one can compel someone to take an oath except the judge.

Now that the discourse on judgments and judges is finished, as well as on those things in which the judge's office is properly engaged—namely, the imposing of lashes and oaths—he <insert>proceeds</insert> to the section on **Testimonies** <note>original: *Edaioth*</note> <insert>testimonies</insert>, the primary goal of which tractate is to hand down all those things for which men have offered testimony...
