<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Fourth Order of the Mishnah, Nezikin (Damages). The author is explaining the sequence of the tractates, moving from civil laws to the requirements for those who witness and judge those laws.</meta>

...trustworthy persons, and their opinions, since their testimony becomes the rule of practice and is itself a specific form of judgment; for testimonies are brought forth before judges, and in the same way, each of those sayings was brought forth in the consistory <term>The Rabbinic high court or assembly</term>. 

However, he placed this tractate after the tractate *Shebuoth* <note>original: "Shebuoth", meaning Oaths</note>, because oaths are matters which are needed perpetually; but testimonies are declarations of decisions which were admitted when testimony was offered before the judges at certain specific times. 

He then proceeded to hand down those things which are to be established regarding **Idolatry** <note>The tractate *Abodah Zarah*</note>, because [to know] these is also necessary for a judge, and a judge becomes perfect when he is well-versed in the customs of those Idols and what is required for them, and knows what must be decided concerning them. For indeed, he who worships **Saturn** with the ritual of **Venus**, or invokes **Jupiter** in the manner in which **Mars** ought to be invoked, is not guilty of death, according to what has been handed down to us by true tradition; he placed this tractate in the last position because [it concerns matters which] rarely happen. 

And having now completed everything a judge needs, he subjoined the tractate *Aboth* <note>original: *Pirkei Avot*; Ethics of the Fathers</note> <insert>that is, concerning the sentences of the fathers</insert>, and that for two reasons. The first is to make known to you the certainty of the claims and of the tradition—namely, that it was truly received successively <insert>one from another</insert>. Therefore, honor is due to a man of learning, and he must be placed in an eminent rank because the tradition has reached him; for he in his own age is just as those [great leaders] were in their ages. Thus they said: *Shall we inquire into the assembly of Rabban Gamliel, etc.?* <note>A rhetorical question from the Talmud emphasizing that the court of one's own time has the same authority as the courts of the past.</note> They also said: *Samson in his age is as Samuel in his age.* This is taught to men so that no one should say: "Should we embrace the judgment of **so-and-so** <note>original Greek: τῶ δ̃εινο̃, meaning "a certain person" or "Mr. X"</note>, or should we acquiesce to the constitution of **so-and-so**?" For the matter does not stand thus; the judgment of **so-and-so** is not the Judge's, but God's, who commanded it to us, just as He said: *Because the judgment belongs to the Lord.* <note>Deuteronomy 1:17</note> And the judgment is one thing handed down from one person to another through a continuous series of time. 

The second reason is that in this tractate he might record the moral precepts of all the **Sages** (may they rest in peace), so that we may learn praiseworthy character from them. Of all people, a judge has the greatest need of these; for if common people are not rightly refined, it harms not everyone, but only themselves. But a Judge, if he is not rightly refined and of a disciplined character, perishes himself and drags all of humanity into destruction with him. Therefore, the first thing that occurs in *Aboth* is concerning the instruction of judges, namely: [**Be slow in judgment.**] When a Judge has been rightly instructed in those things which the tractate *Aboth* teaches—with slowness and a gentle hesitation in judging (since if he hurries, perhaps something hidden will occur in that judgment, just as the Sages <note>may their memory be blessed</note> say: *A judgment* [is a deep...]

...is something deep) [he shall take care] also that he does not prolong the judgment once he has perceived that nothing hidden remains in it; for this is what is called the *affliction of judgment* <note>original: *afflictio judicii*; a translation of the Hebrew term *innuy ha-din*, referring to the suffering caused by delaying a legal verdict</note>; furthermore, he shall be diligent in questioning the witnesses, and during the questioning, he shall take care lest they seize from his own words that which might direct them toward achieving what they desire; nor shall he suggest arguments to the litigants, for those who [do this are called "arrangers for the judges"] <note>original: *ordinatores judicum*, translating the Hebrew *orchei ha-dayanim*, a term for those who coach litigants or act as advocates in a way that interferes with the court's search for truth</note>; neither shall he easily join himself to the common crowd, lest he be held in contempt; nor shall he make himself difficult to approach, lest the weak man perish; nor shall he pursue leisure and luxuries, lest those things which ought to be performed by him be neglected, and lest desire lead him away toward levity; nor should he love to go before others, [or] be headlong in passing sentence, lest he become suspected, and in most of his judgments he should incline toward settling disputes between the parties.

But if the Judge is able [to act] so as not to pronounce the law at all throughout the entire day, other than to settle disputes amicably between those who disagree, this is certainly by far the best. But if he is unable to reconcile [the disagreeing parties] among themselves, he may pronounce the law, yet in such a way that he does not act with violence; that is, he should appoint long periods of time and grant [the one who is held as the defendant] the opportunity of clearing himself; indeed, even if he should prolong his speech and act foolishly. But if he cannot achieve this, he should decree according to their allegations and what has seemed right to him, passing sentence before he moves from his place. Just as we see the [elders] (may they rest in peace) <note>original: "q. p.", likely an abbreviation for *quiescant in pace*</note> have done, when [they would order] hands to be bound, whips to be brought, [the person] to be beaten urgently, to be stripped of clothes, and deeds of hand confirmed by witnesses to be torn up, when it appeared to [any] of them that this was necessary, along with many other things of this kind: and concerning this kind of severity they say, *Judgment shall pierce the mountain.* <note>original: *Perforabit judicium montem*, a Latin rendering of the Hebrew idiom *Yikov ha-din et ha-har*, meaning that strict law must be applied without compromise if settlement fails</note>

In short, it is necessary that the Judge be like a skilled physician; since a skilled physician, as long as he can heal by the aid of foods, does not use medicines; but if he sees the disease is stronger than can be cured by foods, he applies medicines which come closest to foods, such as syrups and sweet aromatic electuaries; but if he perceives the disease still grows strong, so that it cannot be conquered and attacked by these things, he uses stronger things for healing, offering the sick man scammony, the pith of colocynth, aloes, and other such bitter and unpleasant medicines: so also the Judge shall pursue concord [between the disagreeing parties], which if he cannot [achieve], he shall judge with leniency and receive the litigants with kind words. But if this is not possible because of the violence of one of the litigants, and because he attempts to unjustly overcome the other, [then] he shall drive and compel him by force, as we have described. Furthermore, among those things which befit a judge is that he should not long for the world, or for the love of riches and prominence, just as [it] expressly says.

After **Meilah**, however, follows the tractate **Tamid** [concerning the daily sacrifice], which he placed after the others because it contains no legal inquiry nor any [determination] of what is permitted or forbidden; rather, it only describes the manner in which the daily sacrifice was accustomed to be offered, so that it might always be performed in the same way. 

After **Tamid**, moreover, follows the tractate **Middoth** [concerning measures], whose purpose is none other than to describe the measurements of the Sanctuary, its form, and the method of its construction. The utility of this is that when it is rebuilt in the future, the same form and the same proportion may be observed, since that proportion was received from God himself, as it is said in <margin>1 Chronicles 28:19</margin> *All this the Lord made me understand in writing by His hand upon me*, etc. <note>original: *Omnia in Scriptura de manu Domini super me intelligere fecit*; this verse refers to the architectural plans for the Temple given to King David</note>. 

When he had finished the laws concerning animal offerings and everything annexed to them, as well as the description of the house in which those offerings were made, he joined to these the tractate **Kinnim** [concerning Bird-nests]. Its entire intention is none other than to hand down the rites regarding the mixing of birds, for instances when different bird offerings become confused with one another. He placed this in the last position because it concerns a matter that is not entirely necessary—since birds may or may not be mixed—and because the laws regarding these things are very few, as will be explained in its proper place. With this, he closed the Order of **Kodashim** <term>Kodashim: "Holy Things," the fifth order of the Mishnah, dealing with the Temple service and dietary laws</term>. The division of his discourse on the Order of **Kodashim** contains eleven tractates.

Proceeding then to divide the discourse on **Purifications**, he began with **Celim** [the tractate on Vessels], whose purpose is to encompass the foundations of impurities and to describe those things which can become defiled and those which cannot. Thus, when he later speaks of that which causes pollution, we may distinguish which things are capable of being polluted and which are not. 

After **Celim**, he placed **Oholoth** [the tractate on Tents], which deals with the laws of pollution resulting from [contact with] the dead. He placed this before the others because it is the most severe of all impurities. To this he joined the tractate **Negaim** [concerning plagues], which is a legal inquiry into the impurity of leprosy; this is because the leper defiles the Tabernacle, and there is in that condition a slight similarity to the impurity derived from [contact with] the dead, as will be explained in its place. 

Then, having finished the discourse on impurity from [contact with] the dead and similar categories, he began to treat the cleansing from them, which is performed by means of the Red Heifer <note>The ashes of a red heifer were used in a ritual water of purification for those who touched a corpse</note>. Therefore, after **Negaim**, he subjoined the tractate **Parah** [concerning the Heifer]. Then, having completed the inquiry into the more severe pollutions and the cleansing that follows them, he progressed to the lighter pollutions, which [last] no longer than the setting of the sun. To the tractate **Parah**, he joined the tractate **Taharoth**, which he named **Taharoth** [Purities], a name taken from the act of purification, because in it impurities are discussed; and because

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the organization of the Mishnah, specifically the final Order, Taharoth (Purities). It transitions from the conclusion of the previous Order, Kodashim (Holy Things), to explain why certain tractates follow others based on biblical logic and the nature of ritual purity.</meta>

The knowledge of impurities incites one toward purity. It might seem to some that because the name of the entire **Seder** <term>Seder: one of the six primary "Orders" or divisions of the Mishnah</term> is **Taharoth** <term>Taharoth: "Purities," the name of both the sixth Order and a specific tractate within it</term>, it should be considered a fault of the author that a specific tractate also bears the name **Taharoth**. However, this is not considered a fault among logicians, for a species to be called by the name of its genus.

Then, after finishing the discussion of the more severe impurities and the purification from them, he added the method of purification from them, and joined the tractate **Mikvaoth** <term>Mikvaoth: "Ritual Baths," concerning the requirements for pools of water used for purification</term> to the tractate **Taharoth**. He placed **Niddah** <term>Niddah: the tractate concerning the laws of the menstruant woman</term> after these pollutions because it is not a pollution common to all mankind; therefore, he joined the tractate **Niddah** to **Mikvaoth**. To this, it was fitting to join **Zabim** <term>Zabim: concerning those suffering from a bodily discharge</term>. However, he first placed the tractate **Macshirim** <term>Macshirim: "Preparations," concerning how certain liquids make food susceptible to ritual impurity</term> before it, because Scripture also placed it earlier; for the foundation of the tractate **Macshirim** is in that reading <margin>Leviticus 9:1</margin> *And it shall be on the eighth day, etc.* <note>original: *Eritque die octavo, &c.*</note>, whereas the tractate concerning those suffering from a discharge is found in <margin>Chapter 14:2</margin> *This shall be the law of the leper* <note>original: *Hæc erit lex leprosi.* In the Latin text, the author links the laws of discharge to the section on leprosy, which begins in Leviticus 14.</note>. 

After **Zabim**, he placed **Tebul Yom** <term>Tebul Yom: "One who has immersed that day," referring to a person who has used the ritual bath but must wait until sunset for full purity</term>, just as the Lord said, <margin>Leviticus 15:32</margin> *This is the law of him who has a discharge, and from whom semen flows, etc.* <note>original: *Hæc est lex fluxum patientis, & ex quo profluet semen, &c.*</note>. All these aforementioned impurities pertain to the whole body—that is, if someone comes into contact with them, the whole person is polluted. 

Then, proceeding to hand down what should be determined regarding the pollution of only one limb, he joined **Yadaim** <term>Yadaim: "Hands," concerning the ritual impurity of the hands specifically</term> to the tractate **Tebul Yom**. To that, he added the tractate **Oketzin** <term>Oketzin: "Stalks," concerning the stalks or stems of fruit and how they transmit impurity</term>, which he placed in the final position because it is derived entirely through reasoning, as it has no manifest foundation in the biblical text. And with this, he concluded his book, since the entire division of the discourse on Purifications comprises twelve tractates. 

The tractates of the whole **Mishnah** <term>Mishnah: the first major written collection of the Jewish oral traditions</term> are sixty-one, and the chapters are five hundred and twenty-five. It seemed right to him to list only the names of those authors who were closer in time to **Simeon the Just** <note>Simeon the Just was a High Priest during the Second Temple period, often identified as one of the last members of the Great Assembly.</note>. He used in the **Mishnah** a concise style of speech that encompasses many meanings within itself; it was clear to himself, indeed, by virtue of his innate sharpness and the excellence of his intellect, but obscure to those who were inferior to him. For so the learned men who flourished in ancient times composed books for themselves. 

Therefore, it seemed right to one of his disciples, namely **Rabbi Chiya**, to compose a book in which, following in the footsteps of his teacher, he would explain those things that were difficult in his teacher's words. This book is the **Tosefta** <term>Tosefta: a supplement to the Mishnah, providing additional rulings and explanations</term> <note>The Latin text uses the spelling *Tosiphla*.</note>, in which his purpose was to explain the **Mishnah** and to add questions that could not be drawn out from the **Mishnah** except with great effort; he extracted these, however, so that he might show us how we may elicit conclusions from the **Mishnah**. **Rabbi Oshaya** did the same. **Rav** also composed the **Baraitas** <term>Baraitas: traditions in the Jewish oral law not incorporated in the Mishnah</term>...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Maimonides' preface to his commentary on the Mishnah, specifically focusing on his fourth objective: explaining the mystical and esoteric passages of the sages.</meta>

(33)

...tion, which agree with the senses, he would bring forth. And here was his fourth goal: [to bring forth, I say] mystical explanations, <note>original: "explicationes mysticas"</note> which we ought not to consider as either being placed at an inferior level or of little use. Rather, they belong to a high degree of excellence because of the rare enigmas they contain and their wonderful elegance. For in those explanations, when you have looked into them more deeply, many things will be perceived simply as good—so much so that nothing could be added—and the meaning of the more divine senses and truths will become manifest, including everything held dear by the assembly of scholars as well as whatever the philosophers of all ages have established. 

When, however, you contemplate these things according to their outward appearance, you will find that nothing could be more alien to the intellect. They did this for remarkable reasons: one of which was to sharpen the minds of students; another, to cast darkness over the fools whose hearts are never enlightened and who, because of their own natural defects, turn away from the truth set before them. Concerning such people they say, *They do not reveal the secret to them, because their intellects are not at that level of perfection to receive the truth as it is.* Again, this was done because some of the wise (may they rest in peace) <note>original: "c. p." for *cuius pax*</note> withheld the mysteries of knowledge from one another. 

For they tell of a certain scholar who, when he met some who were well-versed in 
<margin>
a. The science of natural things.
b. The science of sublime things.
</margin>
a. <term>The Work of Creation</term> <note>original: "Maaseh Bereshith"</note> while he himself was well-versed in b. <term>The Work of the Chariot</term> <note>original: "Maaseh Mercabah"</note>, said to them: "Teach me the Work of Creation, and I will teach you the Work of the Chariot." They agreed, but when they had taught him the Work of Creation, he refused to teach them the Work of the Chariot, nor would he do it. 

Far be it from us to think he did this because he envied them their knowledge or desired to be superior to them; such behaviors are worthy of blame even in a fool, so how much more so in illustrious men? Rather, he did this because he considered himself suitable to receive what they knew, but did not consider them suitable to receive what he possessed. And he proved this by citing the saying of <note>King</note> Solomon, <margin>Song of Solomon 4:11</margin> *Honey and milk are under your tongue.* 

The Teachers (of blessed memory) <note>original: "p. m." for *piae memoriae*</note> interpreted this so that the meaning of the words is: pleasant things from which the soul perceives sweetness—just like that which the sense of taste perceives from honey and milk—should not be recounted, nor brought forth from the tongue in any way. This is what is meant by *Under your tongue.* For these are not the kind of things to be taught and explained in schools, but rather things hinted at in books only by obscure clues. And when God removes the veil from someone's heart, as it seems good to Him, that person—after devoting labor to the sciences—will perceive some of those things according to the measure of his own intellect. Nothing remains for anyone, despite his knowledge and diligence, but to turn to God, praying and entreating Him that He [might grant him understanding]...

<meta>This page continues Maimonides' argument regarding the necessity of using parables and riddles to protect deep philosophical and theological truths from those unprepared to understand them. He emphasizes that the "Sages" used these methods not to confuse, but to preserve the sanctity of the "Work of the Chariot" (metaphysics) and the "Work of Creation" (physics).</meta>

(34)

...granting him understanding and guiding him, may He reveal to him those mysteries hidden within the texts of the Scriptures, just as we find David (may peace be upon him) <note>original: "cui pax"</note> did; where he says, <margin>Ps. 119:18</margin> *Open my eyes so that I may behold the wonders of your law.* However, when the Lord has uncovered to someone from [the Law] that which [seemed good to Him] to uncover, [it is necessary that] he should, as we have said, keep it hidden. For if he makes anything known about it through [somewhat obscure] signs, [he shall reveal it only] to one whose intellect is perfect and whose excellence is well-known, as they have explained and made known with many examples in the Talmud. A learned man, therefore, ought not to make public the mysteries he holds except to one who either surpasses or equals him in degree. For if he exposes them to a fool, even if the fool does not revile him for it, he certainly will not think he has done anything worthy of praise; and therefore <margin>Prov. 23:9</margin> the Wise Man said: *Speak not in the ears of a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words.* Furthermore, since the common people cannot be taught except through riddles and parables—so that [this method of teaching] might be common to women, children, and little ones alike—so that when their intellects have become perfected, they may recognize the sense of those parables. And <margin>Prov. 1:6</margin> Solomon implies this where he says: *To make one understand a proverb and the interpretation, the words of the Wise and their dark sayings.* <margin><unclear>Maimonides in The Guide for the Perplexed?</unclear></margin> For these reasons, the Sages (may peace be upon them) <note>original: "quibus pax"</note> spoke enigmatically regarding <term>theological matters</term> <note>These "theological matters" refer to the highest levels of metaphysics and divine science, often called *Ma'aseh Merkavah* or the Work of the Chariot.</note>. Therefore, it is proper for anyone, when he encounters something in their words that seems to shrink away from his own understanding, not to attribute the defect to those words but to his own intellect. And whenever he sees any of their parables whose literal sense is very foreign to his understanding, let him be greatly moved on account of his own intellect, which does not hit the target—so much so that true things seem to him very far removed [from the truth].

Indeed, some intellects surpass others according to the mutual excellence of their <term>temperaments</term> <note>In medieval science, "temperament" referred to the balance of bodily fluids or "humors," which was believed to dictate one's mental capacity and personality.</note>; and just as one person's temperament is better and approaches closer to a balanced state than another's, so too one person's intellect is more perfect and more excellent than the intellect of another. Nor is there any doubt that the intellect of one who knows a certain excellent thing is different from the intellect of one who is ignorant of it—since one is an intellect in action, and the other an intellect in potential. From this it happens that certain things which are very certain and clear to some people may seem impossible to others, according to the measure of [their own] degree in knowledge. I will propose a clear example of this matter to you: let us imagine that we speak to a man skilled in the medical art, arithmetic, and music, as well as one who understands the science of natural things, being moreover of a sharp wit and good disposition, but entirely ignorant of geometry and astronomy. "What do you say (hey, [Name]!) about a man who asserts that the body of the sun, that [body there...]"

<summary>Maimonides explains that the Sages used riddles and parables to hide complex truths from the unlearned, and suggests that if a reader finds these teachings absurd, the fault lies with the reader's own intellectual limitations rather than the Sages' wisdom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Maimonides' argument that complex truths require preparation. Having established that the Sages used riddles to protect deep wisdom, he now uses a mathematical analogy—the size of the sun—to show how a truth can seem impossible to the uneducated but be certain to the scholar.</meta>

<page-num>35</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<sig>e 2</sig>

...that what appears to us as a small circle is actually a spherical body whose volume is as large as the Sphere of the Earth taken one hundred and sixty-six times <note>original: "centies sexagies sexies". The author is citing a standard medieval astronomical measurement, likely from Al-Farghani, regarding the Sun's volume relative to Earth.</note> plus three-eighths; and that the globe of the earth by which we measure that sphere has a circumference of 24,000 miles. By this means, one may perceive how many miles are contained within the measurement of the solar sphere’s magnitude. 

Undoubtedly, that man of sharp intellect we mentioned—even one who is skilled in the other sciences we named—will in no way bring his mind to admit that this opinion is true. Indeed, to him, this whole matter will be something that can in no way be grasped. At first glance, this argument will suggest itself to him: that it is consistent with reason that this opinion is false. For how can it be that someone standing upon the earth, which is but the size of a single span of the hand <note>original: "spithamae unius", a 'span' or the distance between the thumb and little finger.</note>, can determine the quantity of its globe, its circumference, and the measurement of its surface, unless he had surrounded the earth in the same way that he embraces some small part of it that he wishes to measure? How then, regarding the solar body, which is located in the heavens as far as possible from him—and which he cannot truly look upon, seeing only its brilliance—could he reach it so as to measure it, and describe its proper measurement even down to three-eighths? He will consider this as utterly impossible, so much so that he will not doubt in the least that this opinion is false. 

But if he is instructed in books of Geometry and the science of proportions found in spherical and other figures, and then transfers his study to the book composed on this matter and the things relating to it—namely that Astronomical work which is commonly called the *<term>Almagest</term>* <note>The *Almagest* is a 2nd-century mathematical and astronomical treatise by Claudius Ptolemy. It served as the basic guide for astronomers for over a thousand years.</note>—then at last this opinion will appear clear to him. He will decide that the opinion is more true than anything that ought to be called into doubt. Since it is proven by demonstration, he will consider it just as if someone were to doubt whether the Sun of this magnitude exists, or whether the Sun exists at all. His opinion will be changed so that he now affirms as most true the very thing he had thought was furthest from the truth. 

This [is how it is] even though we do not suppose the one to whom we proposed this question to be anything other than a man skilled in other sciences, endowed with excellent wit and a good nature. And if this question we proposed is from the Mathematical sciences—which are the steps by which one ascends to Theology—how much more will this be the case for one who is entirely unrefined in all science, and unaccustomed to any kind of mathematical discipline? Suppose such a man has only made the transition from his mother’s care to the company of his wife <note>A metaphorical way of describing someone who has never ventured into formal education or public intellectual life.</note>; if some question from Theology which is hidden in mystical explanations were proposed to him, would he not find it so? Without a doubt, to him [it will be as far from the truth] as the heaven is distant from the earth. Because of the dullness of his mind, he will not understand any part of it at all; it is necessary...

<summary>Maimonides uses the scientific fact of the Sun's massive size relative to the Earth to illustrate that profound truths often seem impossible to the untrained mind. He argues that just as one must study the Almagest to understand astronomy, one must undergo rigorous intellectual preparation to grasp theological and mystical truths.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the author transitions from the physical impossibility of measuring the sun to the intellectual humility required when reading the works of the Sages. He argues that if we cannot grasp physical truths easily, we should not be quick to dismiss ancient spiritual wisdom.</meta>

<page-num>(36)</page-num>

Therefore, so that we may conceive good opinions of them and weigh their words carefully—rejecting nothing from them rashly—whenever something in them appears incredible, let us apply ourselves to the sciences so that we might understand what they intended by such a saying. This is assuming their meanings are even within the grasp of our intellects. For our <term>Sages</term><note>original: "Doctores nostri". In this context, Maimonides refers to the Rabbis of the Talmud.</note> (may they rest in peace), considering the diligence they possessed in investigating truth, the goodness of their talent, their zeal, their commerce with great men, and their flight from the world and the things belonging to it, nevertheless still proved themselves deficient in comparison to those who preceded them. This is the point of their saying: *The heart of the ancients was like the gate of a porch, but that of the later ones is not even as large as the eye of a sewing needle.*

What then shall be said of us? For besides the fact that knowledge and wisdom have failed us (just as the <margin>Isaiah 29:14</margin> Lord threatened: *Therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvelous work among this people; the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hidden*), each of us is characterized by four specific failings: weakness of intellect, the prevalence of desire, laziness in acquiring knowledge, and a cleverness in acquiring worldly things. Given these four evil judgments, how can we not attribute a deficiency to ourselves when compared to them? 

Since our Sages (of pious memory) knew this—and knew that their words were entirely marrow, containing no dregs—they wished us to be warned of it, forbidding anyone to hold their words in contempt. As they said: *Whoever mocks the words of the Sages shall be condemned to boiling dung.* <note>original: "stercori ferventi". This is a reference to the Talmud (Gittin 57a), a harsh metaphor used to describe the spiritual punishment of those who ridicule the wisdom of the elders.</note> Meanwhile, there is no "boiling dung" more serious than the foolishness that led him to mock them in the first place. Therefore, you will never find anyone who shrinks from their words except one who indulges in desire, follows the pleasures of the senses, and whose heart has not been illuminated by some clearer light. 

Because our Sages knew their own words to be true, they spent their entire lives upon them and commanded that the hours of the night and the final parts of the day be devoted to them. Indeed, they established this as the ultimate end of life, as it truly is. Thus they said: *The Blessed Holy God has nothing in His world except the four cubits of the <term>Halakhah</term>.* <note>original: "Shel Halacah". Halakhah refers to the collective body of Jewish religious laws derived from the Written and Oral Torah.</note> 

Pay close attention to this saying. If you consider it only according to the literal sound of the words, you will think it is as far from the truth as possible—as if four cubits of legal Constitutions were the only goal, and the remaining arts and sciences were to be rejected. Furthermore, in the times of **Shem** and **Eber** <note>Biblical ancestors mentioned in Genesis; traditionally viewed as keepers of ancient wisdom before the giving of the Law at Sinai.</note> and those who came after them, when the Talmudic Constitution did not yet exist, it would mean that God had no portion at all in the world. But if you look deeper into this saying, you will see that it contains an admirable wisdom and encompasses things most beautiful to the intellect. I, therefore, [will explain] it to you...

<page-num>(37)</page-num>
<sig>e 3</sig>

I will explain this, so that it may serve as an example of the other things found among the <term>Talmudic Doctors</term><note>The Rabbinic scholars of the first centuries CE who compiled the Talmud, the central text of Jewish law and tradition.</note>, and so that you may judge it as is fitting. You should know, therefore, that our <term>Ancestors</term><note>original: "Majores". Referring to the ancient Jewish sages and thinkers.</note>—on account of the knowledge they possessed and the excellence of their talent—searched into matters with wondrous diligence and held it as a certainty that for every thing that exists, there is necessarily a <term>purpose</term><note>original: "finis", literally "end" or "goal." In medieval philosophy (Teleology), every object was thought to have a specific reason for being.</note> toward which its existence is directed. For nothing exists in vain. Once this general conclusion was firmly established for them, they began to inquire distinctly into every existing thing, so that they might have the purpose of each species known to them.

They saw, moreover, that the purpose of any man-made thing is too well-known to need deeper searching, since the craftsman only makes it after first conceiving its purpose in his mind. For example: I say that a blacksmith would by no means have made a saw, except after reflecting on how he might divide the joined parts of this wood; once the form of the saw was conceived in his mind, he finally set about making it so that he might saw with it. Therefore, the purpose of a saw is to saw; likewise, the purpose of an ax is to split, a needle to sew clothes, and in the same way for all things produced by the labor of art. 

But regarding those things produced by divine craftsmanship and natural wisdom—such as the various species of fruits, herbs, metals, stones, and animals—there are some whose purpose is found through easy inquiry; others which require greater investigation; and still others whose purpose is so obscure and hidden that it remains entirely unknown, unless it becomes known through revelation or <term>divination</term><note>In this context, a form of inspired or prophetic insight rather than magical practice.</note>, since it cannot be found through scientific research. For it is not within the power of man to investigate for what cause nature produced some ants equipped with wings and others without wings; or why it produced some worms with more feet and others with fewer; or what the purpose of this worm or that ant might be. 

But from these greater things, and those whose operations are more conspicuous, those eager for knowledge claim the glory of science; and the more learned a person is—and the greater his diligence and sharper his talent—the more purposes of things he perceives. Therefore, when the Lord had given <term>Solomon</term><note>The Biblical King Solomon, traditionally regarded as the wisest of all men, who was said to understand the "language" of nature.</note> that wisdom which He promised, he knew about the purposes of these species as much as it is given to a man *as a man* to know, so much so that he spoke concerning the purposes of trees, herbs, and [various] species of animals, as the Scripture says:

<margin>1 Kings 4:33.</note>
> *And he spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even unto the hyssop that springs out of the wall: he spoke also of beasts, and of fowl, and of creeping things, and of fishes.*

Which was a testimony of the divine power within him. It says, therefore, afterward:

<margin>v. 34.</margin>
> *And there came of all people to hear the wisdom of Solomon, etc.*

Truly, to speak briefly, it must be known that all things found under the <term>sphere of the moon</term><note>In ancient and medieval cosmology, this refers to the terrestrial world (Earth and its atmosphere), which was thought to be the region of change and decay located below the orbit of the moon.</note> were made for the sake of man alone, and from the species of animals some

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding teleology—the study of purpose in nature. Having established that man-made objects have specific purposes, the author now extends this logic to the natural world, arguing that all animals and plants exist for the benefit of humanity, and that humanity itself has one singular, higher purpose.</meta>

<page-num>38</page-num>

...given to him as food, such as sheep and oxen, etc.; others for uses other than food, such as donkeys, so that he might place upon them those things he could not move with his own hands to be carried; and horses, so that he might complete long journeys in a short time. Moreover, there are other species whose utility we do not know, yet they possess qualities that are useful to man, even if he himself does not know it. Of fruits, some are for food, others for the healing of diseases; similarly with herbs, and in the same way with other kinds of things.

If you ever find any animal or plant that seems to be useful for nothing and does not serve as food, this happens because of the narrowness of our knowledge. For it cannot be that every herb and fruit, and every species of animal from the elephant down to the worm, does not have something in it that benefits mankind. The proof of this is that in every century, species of herbs and fruits become known that were unknown to those who came before, from which they derive many benefits. Nor is it possible for anyone to comprehend the virtues of all plants, as is proven by the experience of generations succeeding one another.

But perhaps you will say: why were lethal poisons created, such as the herb *Bish* <note>original: "Bish". This refers to Aconite or Monkshood, a highly toxic plant known in medieval pharmacology.</note> and the <insert>blood-herb *Hashishatol dam*</insert> <note>original: "Hashishat al-dam". An Arabic term meaning "herb of blood," used for plants believed to affect blood flow or possessing toxic properties.</note>, which bring destruction rather than utility to men? You must know, therefore, that they have their uses; for although they kill if eaten, when they are applied to the exterior part of the body, they do not kill.

If it is clear to you that there is great utility to man from the viper <note>Viper venom and flesh were frequently used in medieval "theriacs" or universal antidotes.</note>, how much more from those things that are less harmful? When, therefore, [the Sages] discovered that the purpose of all these things is that man should exist, it is necessary that we also ask: why does man exist? And what is his specific purpose?

After they had searched deeply into this matter, they found that man has many different functions. For in all species of animals and trees, there is either only one action or at most two, and their goal is one. Just as we see that the palm tree has no other function than to produce dates, which is also the case with other fruit-bearing trees. And so we find some animals that only weave, like the spider; others that build, like the swallow; others that store away what is necessary for their food, like the ant. 

Man, however, performs many and diverse actions. By examining all of these one by one to see what their purpose might be, they found that his ultimate purpose is only one single action—with all other actions <insert>directed</insert> toward his preservation so that this one action might be better perfected in him—and that is the **apprehension of intellectual concepts** <note>original: "intelligibilium apprehensio". The ability of the human mind to grasp abstract truths and universal laws.</note> and the **knowledge of truths** as they truly are. Since it is impossible that the purpose of man should be to eat, to drink, to engage in sexual acts, or to [build] a wall...

<summary>This page argues that every element of the natural world, including poisonous plants and dangerous animals, has a hidden utility for mankind. It concludes that while animals have simple, singular functions, man's diverse activities all serve the ultimate goal of intellectual and spiritual understanding.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding the ultimate purpose of human existence. <page-num>(39)</page-num>
<meta>catchword: susten-</meta>

...to build or to be a King, since all these are accidents <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are properties that can change—like being a king or a builder—without changing what a thing fundamentally is.</note> coming to him from the outside, which add nothing to his substance; and since all these actions are common to him and other species of animals; but knowledge <note>original: *scientia*</note> is that which increases his substance and transfers him from a lowly state to a sublime one. When he who was a human in potentiality has now emerged as a human in actuality. For a man, before he is endowed with knowledge, is like the beasts. Nor is he distinguished from other species of animals by anything other than reason, namely that he himself is a "rational animal."

By "reason," however, I mean the grasping of intelligible things <note>Concepts that can be understood by the mind rather than just felt by the senses.</note>; and the chief of intelligible things is the grasping of the unity of God, <term>the Best and Greatest</term> <note>original: *Opt. M.*, an abbreviation for *Optimi Maximi*, a title used to denote supreme divinity.</note>, along with other things joined to it, namely Theological matters. For the other sciences [aim toward this end], that [a man] may be exercised by them until he arrives at Theology. To weave a full discourse on these matters would be very long indeed. 

But together with the grasping of intelligibles, it is necessary that he avoid excess in bodily pleasures, since the first intelligible thing that is grasped is this: that the destruction of the soul is [joined] with care for the body, while care for the soul is with the destruction of the body. For as long as a man follows desires, choosing those things obvious to the senses, and subjecting his intellect to his desire, and behaves like beasts and cattle (which conceive of nothing other than what is fit for eating and drinking, and what pertains to lust <note>original: *Venerem* (Venus), referring here to sexual or physical desire.</note>), the divine power—namely the Intellect—does not yet appear in him, but he is mere matter swimming in the "sea of matter" <note>original: *τῆς ὑλης* (tēs hylēs). This is a Neoplatonic metaphor for being trapped in the physical world and sensory distractions.</note>. 

From these premises it is clear that the goal of our world, and of those things in it, is a Man endowed with knowledge, and a good one. Since, therefore, knowledge and works are truly present in some individual of the human race (by "knowledge" I mean the grasping of truths as they truly are, and the disposition of all things that it is possible for a man to achieve; by "works," however, the moderate use of natural things and the flight from excess, so that he takes nothing from them except that by which the body is sustained, and the habits of the universe [itself] are more rightly ordered), he who conducts himself thus is the proposed goal. 

This opinion was not only made known by the Prophets, but also by the learned from ancient sects—even those who never saw the prophets nor heard their wisdom taught the same thing: namely, that no man is perfect unless he has joined knowledge and works together. And how excellent is the saying of that distinguished Philosopher: "The aim of God in us is that we may be understanding and good." For if anyone endowed with knowledge and intelligence follows desires, he is not truly a knower, since the beginning of knowledge [consists in this]: that one does not take from bodily pleasures, except by which...

It defines the "perfect human" as one who transcends animalistic desires to achieve intellectual and moral excellence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the perfection of the human soul. The previous page established that humanity's unique purpose is "reason"—the grasping of spiritual and intellectual truths—rather than physical power or social status. Here, the author addresses why, if knowledge is the goal, so few people actually achieve it.</meta>

...the body might be sustained. However, those things which relate to this point, we shall treat more extensively in our explanation of the tractate *Aboth* <note>original: *Aboth*; refers to *Pirkei Avot* or "Ethics of the Fathers," a collection of ethical teachings from the Talmud.</note>; we will clarify those matters there as is fitting and necessary. And in this way, we find that the Prophet rebuked the man who, while attributing knowledge to himself, meanwhile transgressed the law and indulged the desires of his soul, by this saying of his: *How do you say, "We are wise, and the Law of the Lord is with us," etc.* <note>original: *Quomodo dicitis, Sapientes sumus, & Lex Dei nobiscum est, &c.*; a reference to Jeremiah 8:8.</note> 

By the same reasoning, if someone should be devout and abstemious, fleeing from pleasures except for what is required to sustain the body, and should hold a middle course in all the ways of nature, and also embrace all things looking toward the integrity of morals, yet lack knowledge—neither has this man (although more perfect than the former) attained perfection, since those works of his are not yet true and firm. Therefore the Sages <note>original: *Sapientes*; referring to the Rabbis of the Talmud.</note> say: *The boor is not a fearer of sin* <note>original: *Brutus non est peccatum metuens*; a Latin translation of the Hebrew maxim *Lo bur yere chet*.</note>, just as we have explained. And whoever claims that an unlearned person can be pious, he accuses the Sages (who precisely affirmed this) and even reason itself of a lie. For this reason, throughout the whole law you will find the commandment: *And you shall learn them, and then, you shall do them* <note>original: *Et discetis ea, & deinde, & facietis ea*; a reference to Deuteronomy 5:1.</note>, placing knowledge before works, because knowledge leads to action, but action does not lead to knowledge. And this is what the <term>Doctors</term> <note>original: *Doctores*; the learned teachers of the law.</note> said: *That study leads to action.*

One question remains here, since someone might say: "You have affirmed that divine wisdom made nothing in vain, and that man is the most noble of all <term>sublunary</term> <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to the Earth and everything below the moon, which in ancient science was the region of change and decay.</note> creatures, and the end of the human race is to grasp <term>intelligible things</term> <note>Concepts understood by the mind/intellect rather than the senses.</note>; why then did God make all those men who do not grasp intelligible things? For we see the greatest part of men lack knowledge and follow their desires, and a man endowed with knowledge and contempt for worldly things is something rare and foreign—the kind of person who is scarcely found once in a century." 

The answer is that all these others exist for two reasons. The first is that they may serve that One [the wise man]. For if all were devoted to science and students of philosophy, the world would perish and come to nothing, and the human race would be utterly wiped out in the shortest space of time. For man is very needy and has need of many things, so much so that it would be necessary for him to learn the art of plowing, reaping, threshing, grinding, baking, and manufacturing the tools serving all these, so that food might be prepared for him. In the same way, it would be necessary for him to learn the art of spinning and weaving, that he might weave what he would wear; and also architecture, to build for himself what might cover him, and the way of making tools suitable for all these. Nor would the age of <term>Methuselah</term> <note>A biblical figure said to have lived 969 years; used here as a symbol of extreme longevity.</note> suffice for learning all these arts which a man necessarily needs within the term of his life, and when at last...

<summary>The author argues that while moral virtue is important, it is incomplete without intellectual knowledge. He justifies the existence of the "unlearned" masses by explaining that they provide the essential labor and infrastructure required for the rare philosopher to pursue ultimate truths.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the social structure of humanity. The author explains that while intellectual perfection is the ultimate goal, the majority of people are created to fulfill the physical needs of society, thereby allowing the "wise man" the leisure to pursue knowledge.</meta>

...how would that person acquire wisdom or devote himself to study? Therefore, all these others were created to perform those tasks which are necessary in a state, whereas the **Man endowed with knowledge** was created for his own sake. Thus, the earth is cultivated and wisdom is found at the same time. How skillfully, then, did that person say (whoever it was): *If there were no fools, the earth would be desolate*? 

For what folly is equal to this: that a man, weak in spirit and frail in the structure of his body <note>original: *corporis*</note>, should travel from the beginning of the "second climate" to the beginning of the "sixth" <note>In ancient and medieval geography, the world was divided into seven "climates" or latitudinal zones; the author is describing a journey across most of the known world.</note>, crossing the seas in winter and the deserts through the burning winds of summer, exposing himself to the danger of wild beasts and serpents, perhaps so that he may gain money? Then, when he has collected a sum of those coins—for which he has spent his three souls <note>A reference to the three parts of the soul (vegetative, sensitive, and rational) or perhaps simply the entirety of his life force.</note>—he begins to distribute it to architects so they may build him a firm foundation of gypsum and stone on solid ground. Upon this he raises a wall intended to last a hundred years, though he knows for certain he does not have enough life left to outlast even a wall made of reeds. What folly, I ask, is greater than this? 

In this way, worldly pleasures and desires are sheer folly, yet they look toward the preservation of the earth. For this reason the **Sages** <note>original: *Sapientes*; referring to the Rabbis of the Talmud</note> (on whom be peace) called those devoid of knowledge the *People of the Land* <note>original: *Populum terræ*; a translation of the Hebrew term *Am Ha'aretz*</note>, as if to say: those who were created for the purpose of cultivating the land. Therefore, the Sages considered them related to the earth. 

And if someone should say: "But we see some light-minded and fatuous man enjoying peace in the world, not troubled by anything, with others serving him and carrying out his business—while sometimes even a man endowed with knowledge is occupied with that fool's affairs!" The matter is not as it seems to him. Rather, that fool enjoys tranquility because he himself is a servant to that man whom the Creator proposed as the goal. For by means of his tranquil state and his great abundance of resources or possessions, he commands his servants to build a high fortress or plant a great vineyard, as Kings and those like Kings are accustomed to do. Meanwhile, that fortress is being prepared for some excellent man who, in ages to come, might one day seek shade under its walls and thus be delivered from destruction. Or perhaps a measure of wine will one day be taken from that vineyard to make a theriac <note>original: *theriaca*; a famous ancient medical concoction used as a universal antidote against poison and disease.</note>, by which some perfect man, bitten by a viper, might be healed. For such is the economy and wisdom of Almighty and Glorious God, by which He made nature subservient: 

->*Counsels from of old are faithfulness and truth.*<-

In these, he also revealed the errors in the decisions of all who came before him, while he himself is not criticized in them at all, except in a few rulings that do not even reach ten in number. Moreover, the extant expositions of all the *Geonim* excel each other according to the degree of their excellence of intellect, so that any student of the *Talmud* endowed with understanding can recognize from their words and expositions what sort of man each *Gaon* was. 

When it came to our time, persisting in what we found in those who preceded us, we [girded] ourselves with inquiry, diligence, and study—according to the measure of our strength—to seek out all those things through which we hope to profit before God. so that through this work the method of examining and explaining the words might be opened to the student, just as if he were an expert in the entire *Talmud* <note>The massive collection of Jewish law and tradition that comments on the Mishnah.</note>; and this will be a great help to him in [perceiving] the whole *Talmud*. I also intend to give the reasons why those words were spoken, and the reasons why differences of opinion arose among those who disagree in certain controversies, and according to whose opinion the legal practice <note>original: *praxis*; the final decision on how to act.</note> is directed, just as it is explained in the *Talmud*. It seemed good to me to arrange my book in the same order as all the previous interpreters, namely, that after setting down the words of the *Mishnah* to the end of a sentence, I shall then speak of those things which serve the explanation of that sentence according to our plan; then I shall proceed to the second sentence, and so on until the end of the *Mishnah*. Meanwhile, we describe every clear sentence as it is, but we engage in no discussion regarding it. You should know, however, that wherever the followers of *Shammai* and the followers of *Hillel* <note>Two famous rival schools of Jewish legal thought from the 1st century; Hillel's school is generally more lenient and Shammai's more strict.</note> disagree, the legal ruling follows the followers of *Hillel*, except in certain well-known matters where the opinion of the House of *Shammai* prevails. Therefore, in those sentences only, I tell you during the explanation that the opinion follows the House of *Shammai*. Similarly, in every *Mishnah* stated plainly without controversy, the practice follows what is expressed in the text, except for a few rare cases. Therefore, in those rare cases, I tell you that what is plainly stated here is rejected and is not the custom. As for the remaining disagreements, I do not trouble you with them, showing only whose opinion the custom follows; even if there is a disagreement between one individual and many, I say nonetheless, "The Law <note>original: *Halacah* (Halakha); the collective body of Jewish religious laws derived from the Written and Oral Torah.</note> is according to the sages." ### Section one: Concerning the number of Sages whose mention is made in the *Mishnah*, and to whom traditions are attributed by name.

We said at the beginning of our discourse that the Author of the *Mishnah* only recorded the names of those authors of traditions who flourished from the time of *Simeon the Just* <note>A High Priest during the Second Temple period, famously described as one of the last members of the Great Assembly.</note> down to his own age, and that all traditions are considered received from Simeon the Just. Moreover, the number of men in whose name the judgments, legal decisions, constitutions, and all decrees throughout the entire *Mishnah* were composed, is ninety-one. They are:

## Section Four. Concerning the Contemporaries of some of them.

*Simeon* the Just and *Rabbi Dosa son of Hyrcanus* were <term>contemporaries</term> <note>original Greek: *σύγχρονοι* (synchronoi)</note>; indeed, *Rabbi Dosa son of Hyrcanus* lived so long that he reached the time of *Rabbi Akiva* and his <term>contemporaries</term> <note>original Greek: *συγχρόνους* (synchronous)</note>. And this is the first class. The second class consists of *Antigonus, the man of Socho*, and *Rabbi Eleazar son of Harsom*. The third class: *Jose son of Joazer*, a man of *Zeredah*, and *Jose son of Johanan*, a man of *Jerusalem*. The fourth: *Johanan son of Mattathias*, and *Joshua son of Perachiah*, and *Nittai the Arbelite*. The fifth class: *Honi the Circle-maker*, and *Elioenai son of Hakaph*, and *Judah son of Tabbai*, and *Simeon son of Shetach*. The sixth class: *Akavia son of Mahalalel*, and *Shemaiah*, and *Abtalion*, and *Rabbi Measha*, and *Hanan*, and *Admon*. The seventh class: *Shammai*, and *Hillel*, and *Menahem*, and *Judah son of Bathyra*, and *Rabbi Papias*, and *Rabbi Johanan son of Bag-Bag*, and *Hananiah son of Hezekiah son of Garon*, and *Hananiah son of Hakkanah*, and *Baba son of Buta*, and *Rabbi Johanan of Ha-Choran*, and *Rabban Gamaliel the Elder*, and *Nahum the Scribe* <note>original: *Libellarius*</note>. These seven classes existed under the **Second Temple** from its beginning until its end, and they did not see its destruction; but the class which followed, which did see the **destruction** <note>original: *excidium*, referring to the Roman destruction of the Temple in 70 CE</note>, consists of: *Rabbi Eliezer son of Jacob*, *Rabbi Zadok*, *Rabbi Eleazar* his son, *Rabban Johanan son of Zakkai* and his disciples, and *Rabbi Ishmael son of Elisha* the High Priest, and *Abba Saul*, and *Rabbi Eleazar of Modi'in* <note>original: *Hammodai*</note>, *Rabbi Hananiah* the deputy of the priests, and *Rabban Gamaliel*, and *Rabbi Simeon* his son, and *Rabbi Haninah son of Antigonus*, and *Rabbi Haninah son of Dosa*, and *Rabbi Haninah son of Tation*, and *Samuel the Small*, and *Rabbi Eleazar son of Perata*, and *Rabbi Eleazar son of Dama*, *Hananiah son of Hachinai*, and *Rabbi Judah son of Abi*.

### The second class of those who lived after the destruction.

*Rabbi Tarfon*, *Rabbi Akiva*, *Rabbi Eleazar son of Azariah*, *Rabbi Ishmael*, *Rabbi Joshua son of Korcha*, *Hananiah* the man from *Ono*, *Simeon son of Nanos*, *Johanan son of Baroka*, *Rabbi Ishmael* his son, *Rabbi Johanan son of Gudguda*, *Rabbi Eleazar Chasma*, and *Rabbi Judah son of Tema*.

### The third class.

*Rabbi Meir*, *Rabbi Judah*, *Rabbi Jose*, *Rabbi Nathan*, *Rabbi Joha-* <note>The name is cut off and continues on the next page</note>

**Fourth Class.** *Rabbi Judah the Prince <note>the compiler of the Mishnah</note>, Rabban Gamaliel, and Rabbi Simeon his sons, Rabbi Simeon son of Yochai, Rabbi Eleazar his son, Rabbi Simeon son of Eleazar, Rabbi Ishmael son of Jose, Rabbi Jonathan*; and this is the final **Class of the Mishnaic Sages.**

### Section Five. *Concerning those among them known to have shared a relationship of Student and Teacher.*

At the beginning of our discourse, we already stated that *Rabbenu Hakkadosh* <note>meaning "Our Holy Teacher," a title for Rabbi Judah the Prince</note>, the compiler of the **Mishnah** <term>Mishnah</term> <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions, organized by topic</note>, was the student of his father. In the same manner, from his ancestors, the sons were the students of their fathers all the way back to **Hillel**, and from him back to **Simeon the Just**, as we have recorded. Similarly, **Rabban Johanan son of Zakkai** was a student of **Hillel**; and the students of **Rabban Johanan son of Zakkai** were five in number, namely: **Rabbi Eliezer son of Hyrcanus**, a man of great renown; **Rabbi Joshua son of Hananiah**; **Rabbi Jose the Priest**; **Rabbi Simeon son of Nathaniel**; and **Rabbi Eleazar son of Arach**. And this is the group to whom the "world to come" <note>the afterlife or Messianic age</note> was promised (as is known from the **Talmud** <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, containing the Mishnah and the Gemara (commentary)</note>), specifically to them, along with their students and their students’ students.

**Rabbi Akiva** was likewise a student of **Rabbi Eliezer son of Hyrcanus**, who was his primary teacher. This **Rabbi Akiva** also read some lessons with **Rabbi Tarfon**, though Tarfon was not his teacher, but rather his colleague. Nevertheless, **Rabbi Akiva** showed great honor to **Rabbi Tarfon** and used to call him "*Rabbi*" <note>my master</note>, whereas **Rabbi Tarfon** would call him [simply] "*Akiva*." Furthermore, **Rabbi Akiva** used to say, "*Rabbi, allow me to bring forth before you something from that which you have taught me*," [just as] it is declared in the **Sifra** <term>Sifra</term> <note>An ancient legal commentary on the biblical book of Leviticus</note>.

Both **Rabbi Meir** and **Rabbi Simeon son of Yochai** were students of **Rabbi Akiva**, for he was their primary teacher. **Rabbi Meir** had also learned from **Rabbi Ishmael** and others. **Rabbi Judah** studied under **Rabbi Eleazar son of Azariah**, who was his primary teacher. Wherever you read in the **Mishnah** "Rabbi so-and-so" <note>original Greek: *ὁ δεῖνα* (ho deina)</note> in the name of "Rabbi such-and-such" <note>original Greek: *τῷ δεῖνι* (to deini)</note>, know that the former was the student of the latter, and therefore credited that [opinion] to him. **Rabbi Judah the Holy**, however, devoted himself to his lessons under **Rabbi Eleazar son of Shammua**. And **Sameus** <note>likely Shammai, or a later sage of a similar name</note> was a student of **Rabbi Meir**, though he did not manage to achieve his desire of studying under **Rabbi Judah** after the death of **Rabbi Meir**.

...for the sake of further explanation. Rabbi **Eliezer**, when referred to simply by that name in the **Mishnah** <term>Mishnah</term> <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions, organized by topic</note>, is Rabbi **Eliezer** son of **Hyrcanus**, who was a student of **Rabban Johanan son of Zakkai**. Similarly, Rabbi **Joshua** mentioned alone is Rabbi **Joshua** son of **Hananiah**, a student of **Rabban Johanan son of Zakkai**. Rabbi **Judah**, when mentioned simply, refers to Rabbi **Judah** son of **Ilai**, of whom it is said indefinitely in the **Talmud** <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara, or commentary</note>, "**The deed of a certain pious man**" <note>original: *Factum pii cujusdam*</note>; that title is well-known as his among the scholars.

Furthermore, Rabbi **Eleazar** mentioned simply is Rabbi **Eleazar** son of **Shammua** the Priest, who was a **companion** <note>original Greek: *σύντροφος* (*syntrophos*), meaning one raised or educated alongside another</note> of **Rabban Gamaliel**. When **Our Holy Teacher** <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the compiler of the Mishnah</note> desired to study under him, his students allowed him to read only a very small amount. Rabbi **Simeon**, when mentioned simply in the **Mishnah**, is Rabbi **Simeon** son of **Yochai**, a student of **Rabbi Akiba**, famous for the events that transpired between him and **the Emperor** <note>This refers to the Roman Emperor; the story tells of Rabbi Simeon hiding in a cave for thirteen years to escape Roman execution for his criticisms of their rule</note>. Rabbi **Eleazar** son of **Rabbi Simeon** is his son. **Ben Azzai**, **Ben Zoma**, and **Ben Nanasi** are **Simeon** son of **Azzai**, **Simeon** son of **Zoma**, and **Simeon** son of **Nanasi**. **Ben Bathyra** is Rabbi **Joshua** son of **Bathyra**, and **Ben Bag-Bag** is Rabbi **Johanan** son of **Bag-Bag**. **Johanan the High Priest** is the famous **Johanan** son of **Mattathias**, who is mentioned in the prayers regarding the **history of the victory over the Kings of Greece** <note>This refers to the Maccabean Revolt and the origin of the holiday of Hanukkah</note>.

Now, when Rabbi **Meir** and Rabbi **Nathan** wished to embarrass **Rabban Gamaliel** (the father of **Our Holy Teacher**) regarding a matter that would be too long to narrate here, he removed them from his assembly. Because of this, when an opinion is recorded from either of them, if it is attributed to Rabbi **Meir**, it is stated as "**Others say**" <note>original: *Alii dicunt*</note>, but if it is attributed to Rabbi **Nathan**, it is stated as "**There are those who say**" <note>original: *Sunt qui dicunt*</note>. Indeed, what is said in the **Mishnah**, in the name of Rabbi **Ishmael**, that "**a certain student [spoke] before Rabbi Akiba**," is to be understood as referring to Rabbi **Meir**.

As for those called "**Those who judge before the Sages**" <note>original: *Judicantes coram Sapientibus*</note>, they are these five men: Rabbi **Simeon** son of **Azzai**, Rabbi **Simeon** son of **Zoma**, Rabbi **Simeon** son of **Nanasi**, **Chanan**, and **Hananiah** the man of **Ono**. Rabbi **Meir** is otherwise called Rabbi **Nahurai** (both names have the same meaning <note>both relate to "giving light" or "enlightenment"</note>), though his primary name was Rabbi **Nehemiah**.

When the **Mishnah** says "**The Sages**" <note>original: *Sapientes*</note>, sometimes this title designates only one of those whose names preceded it, while at other times it refers to the entire assembly. Thus, in the **Talmud**, it frequently asks for the sake of explanation, "**Who are these Sages?**" and answers, "Rabbi So-and-so" <note>original Greek: *R. ὁ δεῖνα* (*ho deina*), a placeholder meaning "the such-and-such person"</note>. This occurs when it is found that many scholars have embraced what was said by that specific Sage; therefore, because many follow that opinion, the text uses the term "Sages," even though the one to whom the opinion is credited is but one person. Where it says the "**House of Shammai**" and the "**House of Hillel**," it indicates the assembly of those who embrace the opinions of **Shammai** and **Hillel**, since...

### Section Seven: Concerning their Ranks, just as the Author of the Mishnah arranged them.

Those whose mention is made in the **Mishnah** (who are, as we stated before, one hundred and twenty-eight individuals) are distributed into three ranks. When someone was held in great honor by the author and was the most supreme of all, he calls him by his name alone—for example: **Hillel**, **Shammai**, **Shemaiah**, **Abtalion**. This is a sign of their greatness, since no **title** <term>Epithet</term> could be found by which their fame could be made more illustrious, just as the **Prophets** are not celebrated with any specific title.

But those who were of a rank lower than these, he calls **Rabban** <note>A title meaning "our master," higher than "Rabbi" but used specifically for the Patriarchs/Heads of the Sanhedrin</note>, as when he says: **Rabban Gamaliel** and **Rabban Johanan son of Zakkai**. Those who are finally lower in rank than these are called **Rabbi** <note>A title meaning "my master," used for ordained scholars</note> by him, as when he says: **Rabbi Meir** or **Rabbi Judah**. He also calls those of this rank **Abba** <note>A term of endearment or respect, literally "Father"</note>, as when he says: **Abba Saul**. 

Sometimes, however, their title is omitted voluntarily, such as when he says: **Simeon the brother of Azariah**, and **Eleazar of Bartuta**. Now, all those whom he called by their own names as a mark of honor are these: **Simeon the Just**, **Antigonus the Man of Soco**, **Jose son of Joezer**, **Jose son of Johanan**, **Johanan the High Priest**, **Joshua son of Perachiah**, **Nittai of Arbela**, **Honi the Circle-maker**, **Elihoeinai son of Ha-Koph**, **Hananeel the Egyptian**, **Judah son of Tabbai**, **Simeon son of Shetach**, **Akaviah son of Mahaleel**, **Shemaiah**, **Abtalion**, **Hanan**, **Admon**, **Hillel**, **Shammai**, **Nahum the Scribe** <note>original Latin: *Hallablar*, from the Hebrew/Aramaic *Ha-Lavlār*</note>, **Hananiah son of Hezekiah son of Garon**, **Baba son of Buta**; and if there are any others besides these mentioned by their names...

### Section eight. On the Description of these Sages with respect to their homeland, crafts, persons, and tribes.

Among the number of Authors whom he <note>Referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the compiler of the Mishnah</note> has described in other ways for the sake of greater clarity, there are some whom he described by their crafts, to make them better known. For instance, when he says, **Nahum the Scribe** <note>original: *Nabum Hallablar*; the text notes *Librarius* as the Latin equivalent for the Aramaic *Hallablar*</note> and **Rabbi Simeon of Shezur** <note>original: *Hashazuri*</note>. There are others described by their homeland, as when he says, **a man of Hadid**, **a man of Ono**, or **a man of Bartuta** <note>These refer to specific towns in ancient Judea</note>. However, when he says, **a man of Zeredah**, or **a man of Jerusalem**, or of other prominent places, he implies that the person was the most learned and celebrated among the [inhabitants] of those locations; it is as if he were saying that this person, out of all the inhabitants of that place, most deserves to be called a "**Man**." Others are described by the name of their father or brother, such as **Rabbi [Name] son of Rabbi [Name]** or **Rabbi [Name] brother of Rabbi [Name]**, which occurs often. Finally, there are those described by their tribe, such as **Rabbi Zadok the Priest**.

### Section nine. On those between whom disagreement most frequently occurs.

Those whom you will find in the **Mishnah** disagreeing with one another most often are **Rabbi Meir**, **Rabbi Judah**, **Rabbi Simeon**, and **Rabbi Jose**. You will find a discrepancy between any pair of these, and indeed among all four individually. You will also find **Rabbi Eleazar** disagreeing with each of them, though less frequently than they disagree among themselves. Similarly, you will find **Rabbi Akiva**, **Rabbi Eliezer**, and **Rabbi Joshua** each dissenting from the others, and the three of them disagreeing with each other, though less often than the four previously mentioned. You will also find differences between **Rabbi Akiva**, **Rabbi Ishmael**, **Rabbi Tarfon**, and **Rabbi Eleazar son of Azariah**, but the discrepancy is smaller than those mentioned before. Closest to these in their frequency of disagreement are the **House of Shammai** and the **House of Hillel** <note>These represent the two primary schools of legal thought in the 1st century</note>. After these come **Rabban Gamaliel**, or **Rabban Simeon son of Gamaliel**, or **Rabbi** <note>Judah the Prince</note> with each of the aforementioned; among these persons, there is disagreement in the greatest part of the **Mishnah**, with only a few exceptions.

### Section seven. On their ranks, as the author [of the *Mishnah*] arranged them.

Those mentioned in the **Mishnah** (who are, as we noted before, one hundred and twenty-eight) are divided into three ranks. When someone was held in great honor by him and was supreme above all others, he calls him by his own name alone—for example, **Hillel**, **Shammai**, **Shemaiah**, **Abtalion**—which is a sign of their greatness, since no title <note>original: *Epitheton*</note> could be found to make their fame more illustrious, just as the **Prophets** are not celebrated by any title. Finally, those who are lower in rank than these are called **Rabbi**, as when he says **Rabbi Meir** and **Rabbi Judah**. He also calls those of this rank **Abba**, as when he says, **Abba Saul**. Sometimes, however, their title is omitted by choice, as when he says **Simeon the brother of Azariah** and **Eleazar the man of Bartuta**. ## Section eight. On the description of the Sages with respect to their homeland, professions, persons, and tribes.

From the number of authors whom the Editor described in other ways for the sake of greater explanation, there are some whom he described by their professions to make them better known, as when he says: **Nahum Hallablar** <gloss>that is, the Scribe</gloss> and **Rabbi Simeon Hashazuri** <note>original: *Hashazuri*, likely referring to a weaver of multi-stranded rope</note>. ## Section nine. On those between whom disagreement most frequently occurs.

Those whom you will find in the **Mishnah** to disagree most often among themselves are **Rabbi Meir**, **Rabbi Judah**, **Rabbi Simeon**, and **Rabbi Jose**. You will find a disagreement between any pair of these; indeed, you will find it among each of the four. You will also find **Rabbi Eleazar** disagreeing with each of them, though more rarely than they disagree among themselves. Similarly, you will find **Rabbi Akiva**, **Rabbi Eliezer**, and **Rabbi Joshua** each differing from the others, as well as each of the three from one another, yet more rarely than the aforementioned four. You will also find differences between **Rabbi Akiva**, **Rabbi Ishmael**, **Rabbi Tarfon**, and **Rabbi Eleazar son of Azariah**, but less so than the disagreements mentioned above. Closest to these in frequency of disagreement are the **House of Shammai** and the **House of Hillel**; after these, however, come **Rabban Gamaliel**, or **Rabban Simeon son of Gamaliel**, or **Rabbi** <note>referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince</note> with each of the aforementioned. Among these individuals, disagreement exists in the greatest part of the **Mishnah**, with only a few exceptions.

...are presented as handed down, such as *Rabbi Eliezer son of Jacob*, as the sages have said: *The teaching of Rabbi Eliezer son of Jacob is a small measure but pure* <note>original: *cabus & purus*; Hebrew: *kav ve-naki*. ## CONCERNING THE FORMULAS OF PRAYERS.
### CHAPTER I.

From what time do they recite <gloss>1</gloss> the *Shema* in the evening? From the time that the <gloss>2</gloss> Priests are admitted to eat their heave-offerings <note>original Latin: *primitias*, referring to the *Terumah*, the portion of the harvest given to the priests</note>, until the end of the <gloss>3</gloss> first watch. These are the words of Rabbi Eliezer: but the Sages say until midnight. Rabban Gamaliel says, until the <gloss>4</gloss> column of dawn has ascended. **Case.** When his sons returned from a house of feasting, they said, "We have not yet recited the *Shema*"; to whom he replied: "If the column of dawn has not yet ascended, <gloss>5</gloss> you are obligated to recite it." And not—

---

<gloss>1 The Shema.</gloss> They call the three sections <note>pericopes</note> by this name from the first word שמע (*Shema*), "Hear," which they are accustomed to recite in order twice daily, in the evening and the morning. These are taken from Deuteronomy 6:4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9; 11:13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21; and from Numbers 15:37, 38, 39, 40, 41. These sections are clearly indicated immediately below in chapter II. 2, and in *Tamid* V. 1, and they exist under this name in the Liturgies of the Jews. Therefore, it is a serious oversight of men very well-versed in Jewish letters who confuse this formula with the *Tephillin*, or the formula of the **Phylacteries** <note>Small leather boxes containing Torah verses worn during prayer</note>; and thus they frequently translate "the recitation of the *Shema*" as the *Recitation of the Phylacteries.* So does Lightfoot in his book written in the vernacular <note>English</note> concerning the *Ministry of the Temple*, section IX. 4; and in his *Hebrew and Talmudical Exercitations* on Matthew 10:34, 14:23, and elsewhere frequently. The sections accustomed to be written on the parchments of the Phylacteries are four. *Menachoth* III. 7, concerning which see below, III. 1. Let the reader consult the ritual books of the Jews—Maimonides’ *Yad*, the *Shulchan Aruch*, the *Arba’ah Turim*, etc.—and he will find what I have said to be true.

<column-break/>

<gloss>2 Priests.</gloss> Namely, those who had been ritually impure, and are not admitted to the feast of the heave-offerings until after sunset, when the stars now appear.

<gloss>3 Watch.</gloss> The Jews divide the night into three watches. See Maimonides and Bertinoro; compare also the Rabbis Solomon <note>Rashi</note> and Kimchi on Judges 7:19. Therefore, Joseph Scaliger <note>A famous 16th-century French scholar</note> was mistaken when he recorded in his work *On the Improvement of Chronology* that the Hebrews divided the entire day and night <note>original Greek: *nychthemeron*</note> into four parts, which they called watches. No Hebrew would have said that. Nevertheless, the Gospels place a fourth watch of the night in Matthew 14:25, etc. But that is according to the Roman discipline.

<gloss>4 The column of dawn has ascended.</gloss> That is, until daybreak. The Arabs also like to speak this way: <term>سطع الصبح</term> <note>original Arabic: *sata'a al-subh*, "the dawn shone"</note> and <term>انصدع</term> <note>original Arabic: *insada'a*, "it split"</note>; that is, the column of dawn was raised up, or split itself open. See Al-Jauhari in the entry <term>صدع</term> <note>original Arabic: *sada'a*, "to split"</note>.

<gloss>5 You are obligated.</gloss> Another reading: "It is permitted to recite."
