# OF THE FIRST ORDER: SEEDS <note>Latin: *Zeraim*</note>

...and not only this; but wherever the Sages said "until midnight," the commandment remains valid until the column of dawn has ascended. Regarding the burning of the fats and limbs <note>on the altar of the Temple</note>, the commandment is valid until the column of dawn has ascended. And for all things that are to be eaten on the same day, the commandment regarding them is valid until the column of dawn has ascended. If so, why did the Sages say "until midnight"? In order to keep people far from transgression <note>to create a "fence" around the law so a person does not accidentally wait too long and miss the deadline</note>.

2. From what time do they recite the *Shema* in the morning? From the time when one can distinguish between blue and white. Rabbi Eliezer says: between blue and leek-green. They must finish before the sun shines forth. Rabbi Joshua says: <gloss>1</gloss> before three hours have passed; because it is the custom of the sons of Kings to rise only at the third hour. He who recites from then on does not lose his reward, for he is like one who reads from the Law <note>the Torah</note>.

3. The School of Shammai <note>Latin: *Sammæani*</note> say: in the evening, everyone should recline and recite, but in the morning they should stand, because it is said (Deuteronomy 6:7, 11:19): *when you lie down and when you rise up.* But the School of Hillel <note>Latin: *Hillelæi*</note> say: everyone recites <gloss>2</gloss> just as he happens to be, because it is said (ibid.): *when you walk by the way.* If so, why is it said, *when you lie down and when you rise up*? Surely to indicate the time when people usually lie down and when they usually rise. [Said <gloss>3</gloss> Rabbi Tarphon: when I was on a journey, I reclined to recite according to the opinion of the School of Shammai, and I was put in danger by robbers. They said to me: you deserved to have been responsible for your own harm, because you transgressed the words of the School of Hillel.]

4. In the morning they recite <gloss>4</gloss> two prayers before, and a single one after; in the evening, two before, and likewise two after: <gloss>5</gloss> one long, and the other short. In a place where they ordered a long one to be used, it is not permitted for him to use a short one;

<columns>2</columns>

1 *Before three hours have passed.*] That is, before the first quarter of the day has passed. For in the Mishnah, hours are always understood as <term>temporal</term> <note>Arabic original: *al-zamāniyya*</note>, as Maimonides says; that is, "seasonal" hours, which increase and decrease variously according to the inequality of the days. Our Savior expresses such hours in John 11:9: <note>original Greek: *hai dōdeka hōrai tēs hēmeras*</note> *Are there not twelve hours in the day?*
2 *Just as he happens to be.*] In Hebrew <term>according to his way</term> <note>original Hebrew: *ke-darko*</note>, literally "according to his road."
3 *Rabbi Tarphon.*] So the Jews read it. The ancients pronounced it <term>Tryphon</term> <note>original Greek: *Tryphōn*</note>. A name well enough known from the Books of Maccabees, Josephus, and Justin Martyr. The words included in brackets are absent from the Jerusalem Talmud.
4 *Two prayers.*] The first is called by the Jews <term>Former of Light</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Yotzer Or*</note>, and thus it begins: <note>Hebrew: *Baruch atah Adonai...*</note> *Blessed are You, O Lord our God, King of the world, who forms light.* The second is called <term>Great Love</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Ahava Rabba*</note>, and thus it begins: *With great love You have loved us.* Then follow the three aforementioned sections <note>of the Shema</note>, and after them the prayer called <term>True and Firm</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Emet ve-Yatziv*</note>, because it begins with those words. And this entire formula is called the morning *Shema*. The evening *Shema*

<column-break/>

has two prayers before it, of which the first is called <term>Who Brings on the Evenings</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Ma’ariv Aravim*</note>, because it begins thus: *Blessed are You, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who by His word brings on the evenings.* The second is called <term>Eternal Love</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Ahavat Olam*</note>, because it begins thus: *With eternal love You have loved the house of Israel, Your people.* Then follow the same three sections; after them two prayers, the first of which is called <term>Truth and Faithfulness</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Emet ve-Emunah*</note>, because it begins with these words. The second is <term>Cause Us to Lie Down</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Hashkivenu*</note>, because it begins thus: *Cause us to lie down in peace.* Whoever desires the full versions may seek them from the Liturgies.
5 *One long, etc.*] <term>This refers to the two preceding prayers</term> <note>original Hebrew citation from Obadiah of Bertinoro</note>, says Bertinoro; these things pertain to the two prayers before the *Shema*. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> wishes them to pertain to the two after the evening *Shema*. Moreover, both Rabbi Obadiah and Maimonides hold that it is called "long" when it both begins and ends with *Blessed are You, O Lord*, etc.; and "short" on the contrary, when it does not both begin and end that way. But these are the interpretive plays of the Gemarists. I approve the opinion of Rabbi Solomon, so that the words refer to the two prayers after the evening *Shema*, of which one is long and the other truly short.

5. They mention the departure from <note>2</note> Egypt in the nights. Indeed, said Rabbi Eleazar son of Azariah, I was like a man of seventy years, and I did not achieve the understanding that the departure from Egypt should be recited at night, until Ben Zoma derived it from what is said (Deuteronomy 16:2): *that you may remember the day of your departure from the land of Egypt all the days of your life.* *The days of your life* indicates the days; *all the days of your life* includes the nights. But the Sages say: *The days of your life* refers to this world; *all the days of your life* is to include the days of the Messiah <note>the future era of peace and redemption</note>.

## CHAPTER II.

1. If someone who is reading in the Law <note>original: *Lege*, referring to the Torah</note> reaches the time for recitation, provided he did so with an intent heart, he is discharged <note>he has fulfilled his religious obligation</note>; if not, he is not discharged. In the breaks between sections, they may greet others out of honor and return greetings; in the middle of a section, they may greet out of fear <note>e.g., greeting a superior or someone who might cause harm</note> and return greetings. These are the words of Rabbi Meir. But Rabbi Judah says: in the middle they greet out of fear and return greetings out of honor; in the breaks they greet out of honor and return greetings to any man.

2. The breaks between the sections are these: between the first blessing and the second; between the second and "Hear" <note>The *Shema*, Deuteronomy 6:4</note>; between "Hear" and "And it shall come to pass if you obey"; between "And it shall come to pass if you obey" and "And [the Lord] spoke"; between "And [the Lord] spoke" and "True and stable" <note>The prayer *Emet ve-yatziv*</note>. Rabbi Judah says: between "And [the Lord] spoke" and "True and stable," one must not stop. Rabbi Joshua son of Korcha said: why is "Hear" <term>תשׁ</term> <note>Shema</note> placed before "And it shall come to pass if you obey"? Surely so that they first take upon themselves the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, and then afterward take upon themselves the yoke of the commandments. "And it shall come to pass if you obey" <term>את</term> comes before "And [the Lord] spoke" <term>תשׁ</term> because "And it shall come to pass if you obey" applies by day and by night, while "And [the Lord] spoke" <note>3</note> applies by day only.

3. He who recites the *Shema* so that the sound does not reach his own ear has fulfilled his obligation. Rabbi Jose says he has not fulfilled it. If while reciting he did not enunciate the letters accurately, according to Rabbi Jose he has fulfilled it; according to Rabbi Judah he has not. He who recites out of order has not fulfilled his obligation; if he made an error while reciting, he returns to the place where he erred.

4. Ar-

<columns>2</columns>

<note>1 To add a closing formula.]</note> Maimonides <note>a famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note> says this simply means to stop. But the Hebrew term *chatam* <term>חתם</term> means not only to conclude, but also to place something like a "crown" at the end. This "crown" <note>original: *coronis*</note> is a formula expressed from the beginning of the prayer. For example, in the prayer "Creator of Light" <term>יוצר אור</term>, a crown is added: "Blessed are you, Lord, who forms the luminaries" <term>בא״י יוצר המאורות</term>. Almost all other Jews do this, and Maimonides himself follows this late-

<column-break/>

-r in his work *Yad Hachazakah, Laws of Reciting the Shema*, book 7.

<note>2 They mention the departure.]</note> That is, they recite the third section of the *Shema*, in which mention is made of the Exodus from Egypt. Numbers 15:41.

<note>3 By day only.]</note> Not that this section is not to be recited in the Evening *Shema*, which would be false. But rather that the commandment contained within it regarding the wearing of fringes <note>original: *peniculamento*, referring to the Tzitzit</note> is obligatory during the day only.

4. Workers may recite [the Shema] atop a tree, or on the summit of a wall: which is not permitted to do during the [main] prayer <note>referring to the *Amidah* or Standing Prayer, which requires a more formal posture and environment than the *Shema*</note>.

5. A bridegroom is exempt from the recitation of the *Shema* on the first night, and until the end of the Sabbath [following the wedding], unless he has performed the deed <note>consummated the marriage</note>. There is the case of Rabban Gamaliel, who recited it on the first night when he had married. His disciples said to him: "Did you not teach us, Master, that a bridegroom is exempt from the recitation of the *Shema* on the first night?" He said to them: "I will not listen to you, so as to cast off from myself the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven <note>original: *jugum regni caelorum*</note> even for a single hour."

6. He washed himself on the first night after the death of his wife. His disciples asked him: "Did you not teach us, Master, that it is forbidden for a mourner to wash himself?" He replied to them: "I am not like other men; for I am weak <note>original: *infirmus*; the Greek *asthenes*</note>."

7. And when his servant Tabi died, he accepted condolences for him. His disciples asked him: "Did you not teach us, Master, that condolences for servants are not to be accepted?" He replied: "My servant Tabi was not like any other servants; he was upright."

8. If a bridegroom wishes to recite the *Shema* on the first night, let him recite it. Rabban Simeon son of Gamaliel thinks that not everyone who wishes to take a name [for piety] upon himself is permitted to take it <note>meaning one should not perform extra-legal religious acts just to appear more pious than others unless they are truly at that spiritual level</note>.

## CHAPTER III.

1. IF anyone has a deceased person among his own [family] lying before him, he is considered exempt from the recitation of the *Shema*, from the [Standing] prayer, and from <term>Phylacteries</term> <note>Hebrew: *Tefillin*; small leather cases containing scriptural verses worn on the head and arm</note>. <meta>Those carrying</meta>

---

<columns>2</columns>

...obligates. However, the commandment concerning the **Study of the Torah** <note>original Hebrew: *Talmud Torah*</note> or regarding the instruction of sons in the Law, which is contained in the previous section, always holds.

¹ **Of a wall.**] Maimonides <note>a famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note> notes here and at *Chel.* XX. 3. that many have stumbled over explaining the word *Nidbach*. He explains it as one of two planks six cubits long and about two high, which are held at a distance by interposed wood according to the thickness of the wall you wish to build, until the earth poured in hardens into a wall. But he adds that the wall itself of this type is called a *Nidbach*; especially in this place. Commonly called *Tapir* or *Tabia*: as Rabbi Tanchum of Jerusalem cites from Maimonides. And certainly Pliny teaches that in Africa and Spain, walls are made of earth which they call "molded" <note>original: *formaceos*</note>, because they are stuffed between two boards on either side rather than being built. (Natural History XXXV. 14). Johannes de Laet notes that such molded walls are called *Tapias* by the Spaniards, clearly the same word used by Maimonides. But certainly, whatever Maimonides says, it is clear enough that a *Nidbach* is something else, and in fact signifies a row or "course" of stones (as Vitruvius <note>a Roman architect</note> would say) in ordinary construction.

<column-break/>

This is clear from Ezra 6:4 and will be even clearer below from *Middot* III. 7 and *Oholot* XIV. 1. Therefore, Rabbi Tanchum, following the authority of others, more correctly explains it through the words *Domos* and *Damotos*, which are Greek words <note>original: *δόμος*</note> adopted for the use of Arabian architects. It is well known what a *domos* [a layer of masonry] is in Herodotus, the Septuagint translators, and Josephus; from which comes the "Isodomos" and "Pseudisodomos" structures in Vitruvius, according as the *domoi* (that is, the rows of stones) were equal or unequal. This kind of *domos* or course is called a *Nidbach* by the Hebrews, and here it is used as a part for the whole to represent the wall itself. But more on this matter at *Middot* III. 7, where I will also bring light to two passages of Josephus not yet sufficiently understood. I will not take up here what I intend to say there.

² **Weak.**] <note>original: *istinis*</note>. It is the Greek *asthenes*. "Therefore I use the bath."

³ **Tabi.**] A masculine name, the feminine of which is *Tabitha* in the Acts of the Apostles.

⁴ **Phylacteries.**] Concerning Phylacteries, I have already advised above that they contain four sections of the Law taken from Exodus and Deuteronomy: Exodus 13:2-10; and 11-16 [and two sections from Deuteronomy].

1. **M**orning prayers may be said until noon. Rabbi Judah says, until the fourth hour. Afternoon prayers may be said until the evening. Rabbi Judah says, until the middle of the <margin>$^3$ afternoon time.</margin> afternoon time <note>The Hebrew term *Minchah* refers to the afternoon offering and the corresponding prayer service</note>. ---

If one considers the usage of the Arabs for this word, he will understand that it is correctly adapted to every discharge according to its origin. The Jews use it for the sake of decency for the matter I have mentioned; namely, to veil a shameful thing with a respectable word. I have written this at length so that I might finally tear away the error that has occupied almost everyone's minds. Therefore, what is read as *nocturnal discharge* <note>original Hebrew: *miqreh laylah*</note> in Deuteronomy 23:10 should not properly be translated as "from a chance" or "from an accident of the night," but as "from a nocturnal flow" <note>original Greek: *ek physeōs nyktos*</note>, as the Seventy [the Septuagint] have it.

<margin>$^1$ Until he has.]</margin> The Gemara <note>The portion of the Talmud containing rabbinic commentary and debate on the Mishnah</note> notes that this passage is deficient. Maimonides <note>A preeminent 12th-century Jewish scholar</note>, following the Gemara, supplies the deficiency thus: "And he shall not recite in the presence of urine until he has poured [water over it]," etc. The Gemara very often detects or imagines such deficiencies elsewhere as well.

<margin>$^2$ Rabbi Judah exempts.]</margin> Because he thinks it is pointless to remove a minor impurity through washing while a major one remains.

<margin>$^3$ Afternoon time.]</margin> *Minchah* <note>The afternoon prayer</note>, as defined by Maimonides, encompasses that period of the day when two and a half "seasonal" hours <note>A "seasonal hour" is 1/12th of the time between sunrise and sunset, meaning its length changes throughout the year</note> still remain. Thus, according to him, the middle of that time falls at the end of the three-quarters of the eleventh seasonal hour. Bertinoro also says this. But a certain Arabic commentator on the Liturgy of the Alexandrian Jews in a manuscript sent from the East by the illustrious Robert Huntington says something quite different. That author calls himself Salih ben Joshua. He explains the afternoon prayer in Arabic as *Salat*

<column-break/>

3. *al-Isha* <note>Arabic: "the evening/night prayer"</note>: the Prayers of the time of *ha-Isha*. What this *ha-Isha* might be, he further declares: "And the time of *al-Isha* in which this prayer is performed is from the time when the decline of the sun is clear, namely from the last half of the seventh hour until the setting of the sun." And indeed, Maimonides himself later in the *Yad* <note>His legal code, the *Mishneh Torah*</note>, *Laws of Prayer* 3:2, 3, 4, comes to the same opinion. He notes that the entire afternoon time is divided into two *Minchahs* or "afternoons" <note>original Greek: *deilas*</note>: the first, from half an hour after noon until half an hour after the ninth hour, is called the *Great Minchah* <note>original: *deilē meizōn* or *deilē prōia*</note>; that which follows it until three-quarters of an hour after the tenth, or rather until sunset, is the *Small Minchah* <note>original: *deilē elattōn* or *deilē opsia*</note>. He establishes that this entire afternoon period is suitable for these prayers.

<margin>$^4$ Additional prayers.]</margin> Those of Sabbaths and festival days <note>Known as *Musaf*</note>.

<margin>$^5$ Rabbi Judah.]</margin> The bracketed words are absent from the manuscript and the Jerusalem Talmud.

<margin>$^6$ They asked him.]</margin> The disciples. So the Jerusalem Talmud adds. The formulas, however, are found in both Talmuds, but not without significant discrepancy. Let the reader seek them there, or from the commentaries of Maimonides.

# Title I. BLESSINGS <note>original: *Beracoth*</note>.

3. Rabban Gamaliel says: every day, each person should recite the Eighteen <note>original: *Octodenas*, referring to the *Shemoneh Esrei* or Eighteen Benedictions, the central standing prayer of Jewish liturgy</note> prayers. Rabbi Joshua says: one may say an abbreviated form <note>original: *scopum*, literally the "target" or "essence"</note> of the Eighteen. Rabbi Akiba says: if a person's prayer is fluent in their mouth, they should pray the full Eighteen; if not, they should say an abbreviated form of the Eighteen.

4. Rabbi Eliezer says: he who makes his prayer a fixed task <note>original: *pensum*, translating the Hebrew *keva*, implying a burdensome or mechanical duty</note>, his prayer is not a true supplication. Rabbi Joshua says: he who travels through a dangerous place should say a short prayer, [an abbreviated version of the Eighteen,] as follows: *“Save, O Lord, Your people, the remnant of Israel; at every crossroads <note>original: *transitus diverticulo*</note> may their needs be before You. Blessed are You, O Lord, who hears prayer.”*

5. One who is riding a donkey should dismount; if he cannot dismount, he should turn his face [toward Jerusalem]; if he cannot turn his face, he should direct his heart toward the Holy of Holies <note>The innermost chamber of the Temple in Jerusalem</note>.

6. One who is sitting in a ship, or a wagon, or a <term>carriage<gloss>original: *esseda*</gloss></term>, should direct his heart toward the Holy of Holies.

7. Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah holds that additional prayers <note>original: *addititias*, referring to the *Musaf* service said on Sabbaths and festivals</note> should not be per-

---

formed... [The text here refers to] the Amsterdam edition of the Mishnah, where they are printed at the end of this Order. One should remember to compare the second part with the prayer of the Pharisee in Luke 18:11-12. One egg is not more like another than these two.

$^1$ *The Eighteen.*] These appear in the Liturgies immediately after the *Shema*, and the Jews attribute them to Ezra as the author. Maimonides, *Laws of Prayer*, I. 5. To these, Rabban Gamaliel added a nineteenth, as Maimonides notes (ibid. II. 1), or it was added at his command by Rabbi Samuel the Younger, according to Rabbi David Ganz (year 4785); specifically, after the Sanhedrin was moved to Jamnia <note>Yavne</note>, which is to say, immediately after the crucifixion of Christ. That prayer was composed against the **Heretics** <note>original: *Ha-Minim*</note> who at that time were enticing Jews away from their religion. By "Heretics," they understood the Christians who had then first appeared. Regarding the name *Ha-Minim*, we shall discuss it below in IX. 5. This prayer, introduced by the authority of Rabban Gamaliel, is now found as the twelfth in the order of the Liturgy.

$^2$ *An abbreviated form of the Eighteen.*] Let no one be led into error by the authority of Lightfoot, who teaches that the Hebrew word *ma'ein* denotes a "summary" or epitome, so that *ma'ein 18* would be a "Summary of the Eighteen Prayers," just as the Lord's Prayer is a summary of all things to be asked for by Christians. He says this in his *Hebrew and Talmudic Exercitations* on Matthew 6:9 and Luke 11:1, but without evidence. According to Maimonides, *ma'ein* is the Arabic *gharad*, meaning "scope" or "intent," with the "m" being a prefix. Therefore, the words mean "that which achieves the scope of the Eighteen," or "that which expresses the sense of the Eighteen." The same turn of phrase appears below in VI. 8 and in Maimonides, *Laws of Prayer* XII. 3, where he teaches that the portion from the Prophets to be read every Sabbath must be *ma'ein* of the section read from the Law—that is, having the same theme.

$^3$ *A fixed task.*] In the *Ethics of the Fathers* <note>original: *Pirke Aboth*</note> II. 13, 

<column-break/>

this saying is attributed to Rabbi Simeon: *“When you pray, do not make your prayer* <note>original Hebrew: *keva*</note> *a fixed task, but* <note>original Greek/Hebrew: *oiktimōn deēseis* / *rachamim u-tachanunim*</note> *mercy and supplications before God.”* I will explain what "mercy" means there. "Supplications" are for obtaining grace; such are not the prayers of one who treats them as a *pensum* <note>a set task</note>, that is, as a troublesome and annoying burden which he would gladly be rid of.

$^4$ *Which [achieves] the scope.*] I have restored the bracketed text from a manuscript and the Jerusalem Talmud. They are absent from other editions.

$^5$ *At every crossroads.*] The phrase is not quite clear, and the scholars of the Gemara offer mere wordplays as an explanation. Thus, according to Mar Ukba: *"Even at the time when You are full of* <note>original: *evrah*</note> *wrath against them like a* <note>original: *ubarah*</note> *pregnant woman, let all their needs be &c."* Or as others report his words: *"Even when they are* <note>original: *overei aveirah*</note> *transgressors of the precepts of the Law, let all their needs be &c."* And yet, later Jews like Rabbi Nathan, Maimonides, and Bertinoro seize upon these wordplays as explanations. Buxtorf explains the phrase *bi-parashat ha-ibbur* with vowels, citing the example "at the time of the intercalation," but he does not say where this comes from. I hardly doubt that, following Rabbi Nathan, he wanted to express this passage. I do not know how it happened that he wrote "at the time" instead of "the section." Elsewhere he has "the section of intercalation" and explains "the meaning of intercalation." Whether I have translated it correctly myself, let others judge.

$^6$ *Carriage.*] The Hebrews explain this as a "raft" both here and in *Zavim* III. 1, and their lexicographers Rabbi Nathan and Rabbi Tanchum clearly describe a raft. If we are to trust the Jews on a foreign word, I would compare it with the Greek *schedia* <note>a raft or float</note>, but for *schedia* we will read *askadia* below in *Negaim* XII. 1, although Rabbi Nathan reads *asda* there as well. Truly, *asda* seems to be what I have set down.

Order I. SEEDS <note>original: *Zeraim*</note>

...[one should] offer them only with the $^1$ congregation of the city. The Sages say: both with the congregation of the city and without the congregation of the city. Rabbi Judah $^2$ reports in his name: wherever there is a congregation of the city, an individual is exempt from the additional prayers.

# CHAPTER V.

1. **O**ne does $^3$ not stand up to pray except with a composed mind <note>literally "a heavy head," a Hebrew idiom for seriousness and reverence</note>. The ancient saints used to pray after waiting for an hour, so that they might fix their hearts upon God. Even if a king were to greet one of them, he would not return the greeting; and even if a serpent were coiled around his heel, he would not interrupt [his prayer].

2. They $^4$ mention the mighty power of the rains in the prayer for the *Resurrection of the Dead*; and they ask for rains in the $^5$ *Blessing of the Years*. $^6$ The *Separation* <note>original: *Separatio*, referring to the Havdalah prayer marking the end of the Sabbath</note> is recited in the *Bestower of Knowledge* prayer. Rabbi Akiba says: they make it a fourth little prayer by itself. Rabbi Eliezer says it should be recited in the *Thanksgiving* prayer.

3. If someone says at a bird's nest, $^7$ *“May Your mercy reach [the bird's nest]”*...

<column-break/>

<margin>1 **Congregation.**</margin> Maimonides translates this as "with the scholar of the city," <term>al-madinah<gloss>the city</gloss></term>; I preferred to follow the Rabbis Solomon [Rashi] and Obadiah [Bertinoro], especially since Maimonides himself embraces the same sense, and the meaning emerges more clearly this way.

<margin>2 **In his.**</margin> That is, in the name of Rabbi Eleazar [ben Azariah], as Maimonides and Bertinoro correctly note. The formerly most learned translator of this title, Samuel Clerk, suggests it refers to [Judah] himself. This is not correct.

<margin>3 **They do not stand.**</margin> The illustrious Samuel Clerk seems to have hardly understood this passage. Certainly, no one would understand it correctly from his translation. He translates it thus: *They do not stand to pray except with a lowered head*, as if the words referred to the physical posture of the body; nothing is further from the truth. I will say what the matter is: *To stand for prayer* is *to apply oneself to prayer while standing*. And <term>koved rosh<gloss>heaviness of the head</gloss></term> is a disposition of the mind arising from occupation with serious and sober matters. It is contrasted with <term>kalut rosh<gloss>lightness of the head</gloss></term>. The latter includes <term>laughter, jesting, and idle talk<gloss>original Hebrew: שחוק וחוכא ושיחה בטלה</gloss></term> (Maimonides, *Laws of Prayer* XI. 6). The meaning, therefore, is: No one should stand to pray except with a calmed and composed mind. The reader will understand this better if I include Maimonides' words, which describe the opposite mental state unfit for prayer: "They do not stand up to pray immediately after play, after lightheadedness, after conversation, a quarrel, or anger; but only after matters of the Law." Yet, not even after a dispute about a custom, however much it concerns the Law, lest the mind be distracted by that matter. "But rather immediately after matters of the law that do not require intense mental focus, such as decided customs." And the Practice of the Ancient Saints, which follows immediately, supports this sense of the passage.

<column-break/>

<margin>4 **They mention.**</margin> They bring a grateful mention of the rains sent by God into the prayer called <term>Techiyat HaMetim<gloss>Resurrection of the Dead</gloss></term>, which is the second of the Eighteen Benedictions. They include this during the winter season, from the last festival of Tabernacles <note>original: *Scenopegia*, the Greek name for Sukkot</note> until Passover; as Maimonides (*Laws of Prayer* II. 15) and Sameh ben Joshua in the previously praised Alexandrian Liturgy define the time with minor discrepancy.

<margin>5 **Blessing of the years.**</margin> This is the ninth of the Eighteen Benedictions. From the seventh day of the month of Marcheshvan in Palestine—and in Babylonia, Syria, and neighboring regions from the sixtieth day after the autumnal equinox—until Passover, they inserted a petition for rain into this prayer. (Maimonides, *Laws of Prayer* II. 16, and Sameh ben Joshua).

<margin>6 **Separation.**</margin> This is the name for the prayer formula <note>Havdalah</note> used when reciting the Eighteen Benedictions at the conclusion of the Sabbath, to distinguish between the Holy and the Profane—that is, between the <term>rest day<gloss>original Greek: ἄεργον (aergon)</gloss></term> and <term>working days<gloss>original Greek: ἐργασíμους (ergasimous)</gloss></term>. It is inserted into the fourth of the Eighteen, which is called <term>Chonen Da'at<gloss>Bestower of Knowledge</gloss></term>, because it begins with: *“You bestow knowledge upon man.”* Rabbi Akiba wants it recited separately before the fourth blessing. Rabbi Eliezer wants it included in the seventeenth, which is called <term>Hoda'ah<gloss>Thanksgiving</gloss></term>, because it begins: *“We give thanks to You.”* Let the reader note: when I call it the seventeenth, I am omitting the prayer of Rabban Gamaliel, which fills the twelfth place <note>The author refers to the fact that the "Eighteen" Benedictions actually contains nineteen blessings; the twelfth was a later addition regarding heretics</note>.

<margin>7 **May Your mercy reach.**</margin> "Have mercy on us, just as You had mercy on the birds, forbidding the mother to be taken along with the young" (Deuteronomy 22:6). If someone prays this way upon finding a nest, they are silenced...

# Title I. BLESSINGS <note>original: *Beracoth*</note>

¹ **"M**ay your name be remembered for the good." ² **"W**e give thanks, we give thanks": [if someone says these things in public prayer], they silence him. ³ **I**f the one who goes before the ark <note>the chest containing the Torah scrolls, where the prayer leader stood</note> should make a mistake, another shall go in his place; and one should not be stubborn at that hour. Where does the successor begin? From the beginning of the specific prayer <note>original: *preculæ*</note> in which the first man erred.

⁴ **T**he one going before the ark shall not answer "Amen" after the priests, lest he be distracted. If no other priest is present besides himself, he shall not lift his hands <note>to perform the Priestly Blessing</note>; however, if he is confident that he can lift his hands and then return to his prayers, he is permitted to do so.

⁵ **H**e who makes a mistake while praying, it portends an evil sign for him. If he is the Representative of the Congregation <note>original: *Legatus Congregationis*; the person chosen to lead the prayers</note>, it portends an evil sign for those who delegated him, since a person's representative is like the person himself. They relate of Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa that when he prayed for the sick, he used to say, "This one shall live, that one shall die." When asked, "How do you know this?" he replied, "If my prayer is fluent in my mouth, I know it is accepted; but if not, I know the person is snatched away."

### CHAPTER VI.

1. **H**ow do they bless for fruits? For the fruits of a tree they say, *“Who creates the fruit of the tree”*; except for wine, for over wine they say, *“Who creates the fruit of the vine.”* For the fruits of the earth they say, *“Who [creates the fruit of the ground]”*...

---

...they silence [those who say such things], if any be present, because it suggests that God consulted for the birds in that commandment; whereas the Jews believe the commandment to be purely arbitrary, <term>an auditory law<gloss>a law received by hearing/tradition without a rational basis</gloss></term> <note>original Greek: *thesmō akroamatikō*</note>, for which no reason can be given, as Maimonides speaks of it. However, Maimonides himself later disputes this in his *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *More*</note> against those who feel this way about the whole Law, and specifically about this commandment in Book III, Chapter 48. After he himself had given a reason for this commandment, he anticipates an objection thus: <note>original Hebrew/Arabic text follows, which the author translates into Latin; here rendered in English</note> "Do not object to us their saying: 'If someone says "To a bird's nest your mercy reaches," etc.' for this is one of two opinions we mentioned above; namely, the opinion of those who believe no other reason for the Law can be assigned except for the naked will of God. We, however, follow the second opinion." See the same author in Chapter 31.

1 *Propter bonum.*] "For the good." In the same way they impose silence on him who prays with these words, because it seems to imply that God is only to be praised for the good, and not also for the bad.

2 *Gratias agimus.*] "We give thanks." Or with these words [repeated], because by this repetition in the seventeenth of the Eighteen [Benedictions] he seems...

<column-break/>

3 *Prodiens ante arcam.*] "Going before the ark." The <term>Representative<gloss>Shaliach Tzibur</gloss></term>, or "Angel of the Church," was delegated by the whole assembly to recite the prayers; and he was usually a layman, as Maimonides teaches in *The Laws of Prayer* XIV.14. He stood a little apart from the assembly toward the ark. Hence he is called "the one passing before" or "descending before the ark." And "to go before the ark" is to undertake this duty at the assembly's command. He recited the prayers distinctly and in a loud voice, while the people responded "Amen," or other responses as custom dictated.

4 *Sacerdotes.*] "The Priests." While they recite from the platform the <term>Priestly Blessing<gloss>Birkat Kohanim</gloss></term>. Concerning this, the commandment is found in Numbers 6:23, etc., where it is expressed in these words: "May the Lord bless you and keep you. May the Lord make His face shine upon you and be gracious to you. May the Lord lift up His countenance upon you and give you peace." This blessing the Priests (if any were present) were bound to pronounce to the people, having mounted the platform with hands uplifted. Hence the pronunciation of the blessing itself is sometimes called <term>The Lifting of the Hands<gloss>Nesi'at Kapayim</gloss></term>. In this paragraph, "to lift the hands" means to pronounce this blessing. This was how they performed it: while the Representative of the Congregation recited the sixteenth prayer of the Eighteen...

# Order I. SEEDS <note>original: *Zeraim*</note>

*“Who creates the fruit of the earth”*: except for bread; for over bread they say, *“Who brings forth bread from the earth.”* Over vegetables they say, *“Who creates the fruit of the earth.”* Rabbi Judah prefers, *“Who creates species of herbs.”*

2. He who says the blessing for the fruits of a tree as *“Who creates the fruit of the earth,”* has fulfilled his obligation; but for the fruits of the earth, if he says *“Who creates the fruit of the tree,”* he has not fulfilled it. For all things, if he says, *“Through whose word all things exist,”* he has fulfilled his obligation.

3. For a thing which does not grow from the earth, they say, *“Through whose word all things exist.”* For vinegar, for fallen fruit <note>fruit that dropped prematurely or is of poor quality</note>, and for locusts, they say, *“Through whose word all things exist.”* For milk, cheese, and eggs, they say, *“Through whose word all things exist.”* Rabbi Judah holds that for anything which is a species of calamity <note>referring to blighted crops or perhaps the locusts mentioned above</note>, a blessing is not to be said.

4. If various species are served to someone, Rabbi Judah says: if one of the <gloss>1</gloss> seven species is among them, he says the blessing over it; but the Sages say, he says the blessing over whichever of them he prefers.

5. He who said the blessing over the wine before the meal has exempted the wine that comes after the meal. He who said the blessing over <gloss>2</gloss> condiments <note>original: *opsonia*</note> before the meal has exempted the condiments after the meal. He who said the blessing over the bread has exempted the condiments; but the blessing over the condiments does not exempt the bread. The School of Shammai <note>original: *Sammæani*</note> say: it does not even exempt that which is cooked in a pot.

6. If they sit down to eat, each person says the blessing for himself; if they recline <note>the formal Roman and Near Eastern style for a communal banquet</note>, one says the blessing for all. If wine is brought to them during the meal, each individual says the blessing for himself; but after the meal, one says the blessing for all. That person also makes mention of the incense burner <note>original: *thuribulum*</note>, even though they do not bring in the incense until after the refreshment.

7. To whom—

<column-break/>

—he was reciting, the priests who were present would ascend the platform. Then, as soon as the Representative <note>the leader of the congregation</note> had finished the seventeenth prayer, they would turn toward the people and recite the blessing, with the Representative leading them and dictating each word separately; meanwhile, the people responded “Amen” after each verse. Once the blessing was thus completed, the Representative would return to the eighteenth or final prayer; and after that was finished, the priests would descend and go to their places. Whoever desires the remaining small details may seek them from Maimonides, *Laws of Prayer* XIV. 3, 4, 5, 6.

<gloss>1</gloss> *Seven species.*] On account of which the Holy Land is celebrated. These are: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, and dates.

<gloss>2</gloss> *Condiments.*] The word is *parperet* <note>original: פרפרת</note>. Rabbi Tanchum explains it as <note>original Judeo-Arabic: "the condiment used as a relish with bread, whatever it may be," etc.</note> whatever is eaten as a side dish with bread, such as broth, roasted or boiled meat, eggs, cheese, berries, dates, etc. Thus in the tractate *Shabbat* XXIII. 2: "Someone may count his guests and his <note>Hebrew: ופרפרותיו</note> side dishes from memory, but not from a written list." Here it seems to be understood as something usually passed around before and after a meal—sometimes before, sometimes after—to excite the appetite

<column-break/>

or to settle the stomach; for the former, you might correctly use Petronius’s *gustatio* <note>tasting</note>, Martial’s *first course*, or Apuleius’s *pre-dinner*; for the latter, the *Epidipnis* <note>dessert/after-dinner treat</note> of Petronius and Martial. Certainly, it is taken plainly for a less important matter in the *Chapters of the Fathers* <note>original: *Aboth*</note> III. 18: *“Rabbi Eleazar ben Hasma says: The laws of bird-offerings and the beginnings of menstrual impurity are the essential Body of the Law;”* but <note>Hebrew: תקופות וגמטריאות</note> *astronomical calculations and geometric computations are the* <note>Hebrew: פרפראות</note> *condiments of Wisdom.* The allusion is clearly to the "Body" of the dinner, to which the *parperet* is opposed as a less essential part. Cohen de Lara, the most learned of the Jews in Greek, wishes the word to be the Greek <term>periphora</term> <note>a "carrying around," signifying a course of dishes</note>; namely, the serving of dishes which are set before the guests, either for each individual or for groups of four, as is now the custom. Those are the Latin words of Budé: but they hardly fit the matter we are discussing. Indeed, Cohen de Lara himself saw that it did not fit in this last passage, so he found it necessary to flee to another Greek word, <term>periphereia</term> <note>periphery or circumference</note>. But in both cases, he labors in vain. It does not seem to be a Greek word at all; rather, it is regularly formed from the Hebrew root <term>porer</term> <note>Hebrew: פורר</note> meaning *to break* or *to crumble*.

<meta>This page continues the translation of the first tractate, Blessings (Berakhot), from the Mishnah. The previous page discussed blessings over bread, wine, and various food species. # Title I. BLESSINGS

7. For one to whom a salted relish is served first, and with it a morsel of bread, by saying the blessing over the relish he exempts the bread; for indeed the bread is an accessory to it. This is the general rule: Wherever there is a primary dish and an accessory with it, by blessing the primary dish, the accessory is exempted.

8. He who eats figs, grapes, or pomegranates, recites three blessings after them. Thus says Rabban Gamaliel. But the Sages say: a single blessing which summarizes the purpose of the three. Rabbi Akiba says: if he eats even **Beets** <note>original: *Betam*</note> as his main meal, he recites three blessings after it. He who drinks water to quench his thirst says, *“Through whose word all things exist.”* Rabbi Tarphon would prefer, *“Who creates many souls, [² and their lack.]”*

---

### C H A P T E R VII.

<margin>1</margin>
1. Three who have eaten together are obligated ³ to summon one another <note>This refers to the *Zimman*, a formal call to prayer after a meal.</note>. This applies even to one who has eaten ⁴ doubtful produce <note>produce where it is uncertain if tithes were paid</note>, or ⁵ first tithes from which the heave-offering

---

<margin>1</margin> **Beets.]** I have placed this here based on the authority of related languages. Indeed, in Chaldean it is *silka* <note>original: <term>סילקא</term></note>, in Syriac *habizo* <note>original: <term>ܚܒܺܝܨܳܐ</term></note>, and in Arabic *silq* <note>original: <term>سلق</term></note>, meaning *beet*. However, the Chaldean-Samaritan Interpreter puts *dacha* for any kind of vegetable. Genesis 1:30. To Maimonides it is *from whatever thing was boiled* <note>original: <term>מסלוק מן אי שי כאן שלק וגו׳</term></note>. To Rabbis Solomon and Obadiah, it is a decoction or broth made from vegetables. Likewise, the Arabic *silqiyya* to Zamakhshari is a *decoction of mixed millet*. The Syriac *habizo* is *boiled or cooked* <note>original: <term>المسلوق المطبوخ</term></note>, according to Isa bar Ali and other anonymous Syriac lexicographers. If anyone wishes to substitute "decoction" for "beet," I will not argue. Yet I think the former is better; although I am aware that elsewhere in the Mishnah, *teradin* is used for beets.

<margin>2</margin> **And their lack.]** That is, whatever they need for nourishment. I have restored this phrase from a manuscript. It is supported by the Jerusalem Talmud and Rabbi Obadiah.

<margin>3</margin> **To summon.]** The term is *Zimman* <note>original: <term>זמן</term></note>. The illustrious Lightfoot, in his notes on Matthew 15:36, explains this as giving thanks in the plural number for the whole assembly by saying, "Let us bless." But he is mistaken. *Zimman* signifies nothing other than ordering the guests, by a previous warning (the various formulas of which follow in this paragraph), to be ready for the giving of thanks; that is, to summon them to grace. For the *Zimman* summons to grace is one thing, and the actual act of giving thanks is another. To help you understand the matter, I will provide at least one formula from the Liturgies. If only three are present, one of them summons grace thus: **Blessed**

<column-break/>

**be He of whose bounty we have eaten.** <note>original Hebrew: *Baruch she-achalnu mi-shelo*</note>. The remaining two respond: **Blessed be He of whose bounty we have eaten, and by whose goodness we live.** <note>original Hebrew: *Baruch she-achalnu mi-shelo u-ve-tuvo chayinu*</note>. By this, they testify that they are ready. Then he who summoned repeats these very words and continues the thanksgiving: **Blessed be He, and blessed be His name, etc.** <note>original Hebrew: *Baruch hu u-varuch shemo*</note>. Now you know what *Zimman*, or "summoning to grace," is.

<margin>4</margin> **Doubtful produce.]** <note>original: *Demai*</note>. That is, a thing about which it is not established whether the tithes have yet been taken. From this, first, a hundredth part—the tithe of the tithe—had to be taken and given to the Priest; this is called here the "heave-offering" <note>original: *primitiae*</note>. Then the second tithes were to be eaten in Jerusalem. However, one was not bound to give either the first tithes or the tithes for the poor, as I will show more fully below at Demai 1:1. If someone ate of this produce, provided those first heave-offerings were taken, but not the second tithes—even if he should not have done so—the summons to grace must be made for him.

<margin>5</margin> **First tithes.]** To fully grasp this passage, understand the heave-offerings and tithes as follows. From the entire harvest of crops, after the **completion of their processing** <note>original: <term>גמר מלאכתן</term></note>—that is, after they have been fully prepared and adapted for human use—before they could pass into common use, various offerings and tithes had to be taken in this order. First, the **Great Heave-Offering** <note>original: <term>תרומה גדולה</term>, Greek: <term>ἀπαρχὴ μέγα</term></note>, a small portion or "greater first-fruits" to be given to the Priest. Since the Law left the amount of these to one’s discretion, the Teachers determined they should consist of between a fortieth and a sixtieth part of the whole harvest. From the remainder, they took the **first tithes** <note>original: <term>מעשר ראשון</term></note> to be given to the Levites. And from those, the Levites paid the Priest a **tithe from the tithe** <note>original: <term>מעשר מן המעשר</term></note>, also called the **tithe of the tithe**.

# First Order: SEEDS

the heave-offering of the tithe <note>original: *terumat ma'aser*</note> was taken, or the second tithes or consecrated items <gloss>1</gloss> which have been redeemed; also for a servant who has eaten an olive-sized portion, and a <gloss>2</gloss> Cuthite <note>a Samaritan</note>; for these, one issues the summon <note>the formal invitation to Grace after meals</note>. But for one who has eaten untithed produce <note>original: *tevel*</note>, or first tithes from which the heave-offering has not yet been taken, or second tithes or consecrated items which have not been redeemed; or for a servant who has eaten less than an olive-sized portion, and for a foreigner; for these, one does not issue the summon.

2. For women, slaves, and minors, one does not issue the summon. For what minimum quantity do they issue the summon? Up to the size of an olive. Rabbi Judah says: up to the size of an egg.

3. How is the summon issued if three are present? He says: *“Let us bless”*; if there are three besides the leader himself, he says: *“Bless ye.”* If ten are present, he says: *“Let us bless our God”*; if ten besides himself, *“Bless ye.”* It is the same for ten as it is for one hundred thousand. <gloss>3</gloss> If one hundred are present, he says: *“Let us bless the Lord our God”*; if one hundred besides himself, *“Bless ye.”* If one thousand are present, he says: *“Let us bless the Lord our God, the God of Israel”*; if one thousand besides himself, *“Bless ye.”* If ten thousand are present, he says: *“Let us bless the Lord our God, the God of Israel, the God of hosts, who dwells between the Cherubim”*; if ten thousand besides himself, *“Bless ye.”* Just as he blesses, so—

---

<term>primitias decimarum</term> <note>original: תרומת מעשר, the "heave-offering of the tithe," a portion given by Levites to Priests</note>. Furthermore, from the remainder they would set aside the <term>second tithes</term> <note>original: מעשר שני</note> to be consumed in Jerusalem; however, in the third and sixth years of the seven-year cycle <note>original: *Heptateridis*</note>, these were changed into <term>tithes for the poor</term> <note>original: מעשר עני</note>, to be given to the poor and the Levites at the gates of every town. Produce prepared in this way, before the heave-offerings and tithes were removed, was called <term>Untithed</term> <note>original: טבל, *Tevel*</note>, which I interpret as "unconsecrated"; sometimes also called <term>Certain</term> <note>original: ודאי, *Vada’i*</note>, regarding which it is certain that the tithes were not taken; this is the opposite of <term>Doubtful produce</term> <note>original: דמאי, *Demai*</note>. Bertinoro identifies this as "Manifestly Untithed" in his commentary on *Demai* V.9. A Levite was regularly required to receive tithes only after the great heave-offerings were paid. But if he ate the first tithes, which he had received as ears of grain from the owner, and thus cheated the Priest of the greater heave-offerings (since they were not yet due to him), provided he paid the "tithe of the tithe," the summon may be issued for him.

1. *Which have been redeemed.*] Simply; without the additional fifth part penalty required by the Law.

2. *Cuthite.*] <note>original: Οἱ κατὰ μὲ τὴν ἑβραίων γλῶτταν Χαθαῖοι, κατὰ δὲ τὴν ἑλλήνων σαμαρεῖται</note> "Those who in the Hebrew tongue are called Cuthites, but in the Greek, Samaritans." Josephus, *Antiquities* IX.14. The Jews called this mixed crowd by that name because Salmanassar brought them from the regions of Cuthah (variously spelled in Josephus) into Samaria to replace the ten tribes deported to Media. II Kings XVII.24. Josephus locates this region, as well as a river of the same name, in Persia.

<column-break/>

However, the great scholar Isaac Vossius, in a letter to Andreas Colvius, records that the Cuthites were formerly summoned from the Carmanian desert. Indeed, the *Kethoi* are located there by Ptolemy. You may read the passage in Ptolemy from two manuscript codices in the Seldenian Archives, one of which is ancient and of high quality, the other more recent: <note>original: κατανέμονται δὲ τὴν ἐρήμον τὰ μὲ μεσημβρινὰ ἰσατίχου, καὶ κῆθοι, τὰ δὲ μέσα γαδαιώπυδρες</note> "The southern parts of the desert are inhabited by the Isatichae and the Kethoi [Cuthites], and the middle parts by the Gadaiopy dres." All printed editions say *Zethoi*, though Mercator has *Cuthi* in his maps. The Carmanian desert borders Persia to the east, or rather is "deeper within Persia and Media," as Josephus speaks elsewhere of the seat of the Cuthites (X.11), so that you may know Josephus and Ptolemy agree well on this matter. Regarding this and other passages in the Mishnah where Cuthites are mentioned, Maimonides notes (on Title VIII.8 of this work) that the Jews once believed they had converted to their religion, until an investigation by the Sages found them offering honor to Mount Gerizim and to an idol placed there in the form of a dove. Therefore, wherever a prerogative is granted to them over other nations in the Mishnah, as here and elsewhere quite frequently, it is to be understood as referring to the time before that investigation; for after their idolatry was detected, they fell below the status of other nations. See Rabbi Azariah, chapter XXI, and Rabbi David Ganz for the year 4881 [1121 CE], in addition to our own more common sources.

3. *If one hundred are present.*] These details follow the private opinion of Rabbi Jose the Galilean.

# Title I. BLESSINGS

...they respond in turn after him, *“Blessed be the Lord our God, the God of Israel, the God of hosts, who dwells between the Cherubim, for the food we have eaten.”* Rabbi Joses the Galilean says: they bless according to the size of the gathering, for it is said (*Psalm 68:27*): *“In the congregations bless ye God, even the Lord, from the fountain of Israel.”* Rabbi Akiba said: what do we find in the Synagogue? It is the same whether there be many or few; he says, *“Bless ye the Lord.”* Rabbi Ishmael says, *“Bless ye the Lord, who is to be blessed.”*

**4.** Three who have eaten together are not to divide <note>that is, they must perform the invitation to grace as one unit</note>, nor are four, nor five; six may divide up into two groups of three until they reach ten; but ten must not divide until they reach twenty <note>because ten is the minimum number for including the name of God in the invitation</note>.

**5.** Two groups of diners who have taken their meal in the same house may be joined together for the invitation <note>original: *indictionem*</note> provided that some members of each group can see one another; otherwise, these ones invite separately and those ones invite separately. They do not say the blessing over wine until it has been mixed with water <note>Ancient wine was often too strong to drink undiluted</note>. So says Rabbi Eliezer; but the Sages say the blessing should be said regardless.

### CHAPTER VIII.

**1.** **T**hese are the matters of controversy between the followers of Shammai <note>original: *Sammæani*</note> and the followers of Hillel <note>original: *Hillelæi*</note> regarding a meal. <gloss>1</gloss> The Shammaites hold that the blessing should be said for the day <note>the Sanctification or *Kiddush*</note>, and afterward for the wine. The Hillelites hold the blessing should be said for the wine, and afterward for the day.

**2.** <gloss>2</gloss> The Shammaites say: they pour water over the hands first, and afterward mix the cup. The Hillelites, however, say: they mix the cup first, and afterward pour water over the hands.

**3.** The Shammaites say: after wiping their hands, they lay the towel <note>original: *mappa*</note> on the table. The Hillelites prefer it to be placed on the <gloss>3</gloss> cushion.

**4.** The Shammaites say: they sweep the house first, and afterward pour water over the hands. The Hillelites want the water poured over the hands first, and afterward the house swept.

**5.** The Shammaites say: <gloss>4</gloss> Lamp, and Food, Spices, and Separation. The Hillelites...

---

<gloss>1 The Shammaites hold.</gloss>] See also Pesachim 10:2.
<gloss>2 The Shammaites say: they pour.</gloss>] The reasoning of the Shammaites is this: lest perhaps the liquid clinging to the cup be defiled by unwashed hands, and by its contact defile the cup itself. The Hillelites' reason is: lest the exterior of the cup, being unclean, defile the hands themselves by the contact of liquid which was not fully wiped away after washing. A further explanation of this and the following paragraph depends on many minutiae regarding ritual defilements, which I provide explained only in the Sixth Order <note>The "Sixth Order" refers to *Tohorot* (Purities), the final section of the Mishna</note>.
<gloss>3 Cushion.</gloss>] Upon which one reclines during the meal. However, this paragraph and the following one are transposed in the manuscript.

<column-break/>

<gloss>4 Lamp.</gloss>] They are noting the order in which the blessings are to be recited at the conclusion of the Sabbath. The Shammaites want the blessing recited first for the lamp, then for the food, then for the spices, and finally the blessing called *Havdalah* <note>original: *הבדלה*</note> (Separation), of which we spoke above. The Hillelites hold the opposite. Furthermore, it is noted in both versions of the Talmud <note>the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmuds</note> that the dispute is not correctly represented in this Mishna. We do not have the leisure to linger over the trifles of the Gemarists <note>The "Gemarists" are the later commentators in the Talmud; the author here shows a typical Renaissance/Early Modern scholarly impatience with their complex arguments</note>. The lamp spoken of here is the great wax candle, which they call the *Havdalah Lamp* <note>original: *נר הבדלה*</note>, or the Lamp of Separation, which they light at the end of the Sabbath to distinguish between the holy day that has passed and the ordinary days that follow.

# TITLE I. BLESSINGS (BERAKHOT)

...of evil. If anyone prays for something that has already happened, this is a vain prayer. In what way? For example, if his wife is pregnant and he says, *“May it please God that my wife bears a male child,”* this is a vain prayer. If someone who is traveling hears a cry of distress in the city and says, *“May it please God that these are not members of my household,”* this is also a vain prayer. <note>A prayer is "vain" if it asks for a miracle to change a reality that has already occurred, as God is not tested by asking Him to change the past.</note>

**4.** He who enters a fortified city says two prayers: one upon entering, and one upon exiting. Ben Azzai says: four; two upon entering, and two upon exiting. <gloss>1</gloss> He gives thanks for what is past, and he petitions for what is to come.

**5.** Every person is bound to bless God for the bad just as much as for the good; for it is said (Deut. 6:4-5): *And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might. “With all your heart,”* means with both of your inclinations, the good and the bad; *“with all your soul,”* means even if He takes your life away; *“with all your might,”* means with all your wealth. Another interpretation: *“With all your might,”* <gloss>2</gloss> means for every single measure that He measures out to you, you should give Him the greatest thanks you are able. No one should behave <gloss>3</gloss> irreverently before the Eastern Gate, which faces directly toward the Holy of Holies. Nor should one enter the Temple Mount with a staff, or wearing shoes, or with a <gloss>4</gloss> money-belt, or...

---

...so long as it shows the appearance of evil at first glance, the formula *“Blessed is the true Judge”* must be used. This is how I interpret the passage, which has been a cross to many scholars. The Babylonian Gemara <note>The Gemara is the rabbinic commentary on the Mishnah; together they form the Talmud.</note> understood these things in a sense that is plainly the opposite.

> <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: "One blesses for the bad... How so? For instance, if a flood has inundated his land, even though it is ultimately good for him because it brings silt <term>syrtos<span>Greek: συρτὸν; silt or a sand-bank washed up by the water</span></term> and improves the land, for now, at least, it is a misfortune. And for the good... How so? For instance, if one finds a treasure, even though it could be bad for him because if the King hears of it, he will extort it... for now, at least, it is a good thing."</note>

I confess that I in no way grasp how these things can agree with the text of the Mishnah; unless perhaps the Mishnah should be translated thus: *One must bless for the bad, even if it results in good; and for the good, even if it results in bad.* But this can in no way be supported. However, if the examples brought by the Gemara were inverted to fit the sense of the passage as we have given it, they would illustrate the matter significantly. It is useless to consult the Rabbis Rashi <note>original: Jarchium</note>, Maimonides, Bertinoro, etc., on this point. They all alike follow the Gemara; and they all alike talk nonsense. The same error is common to them all: that in the first case they took "evil" to mean only *apparent* evil; and in the second case, "good" to mean only *apparent* good; when the contrary is true. The "evil" in the first case, and the "good" in the se-

<column-break/>

-cond, is that evil which has the look or appearance of good, and that good which has the appearance of evil. If the reader pays attention to the matter, he will admit that I have clearly explained a passage in which all the Jewish interpreters have most miserably stumbled.

**1** *Give thanks.*] In both places, upon entering and upon exiting: thus, four times.

**2** *For every single measure.*] There is a wordplay <note>original: paronomasia</note> in the Hebrew words *midah* (measure), *moded* (measurer), *modeh* (thanking), and *me’od* (might/exceedingly), which is lost in the translation.

**3** *Behave irreverently.*] What is meant by <term>kalut rosh<span>Hebrew: "lightness of head"; a term for frivolity or lack of proper respect</span></term> or "vileness of the head," we have discussed above. From this, "to make one's head light" is to behave irreverently.

**4** *Money-belt.*] This Mishnaic word is written in various ways and interpreted even more variously. It is written as *pundah* or *apundah*. Regarding its interpretation, Maimonides here (and in other commentaries) maintains it is a garment worn closest to the skin to keep sweat away from expensive clothing. In Arabic he calls it *ma'adaqa*. You might not incorrectly call it a *sweat-undershirt*. Might this be the Greek word *ependytes* <note>original: ἐπενδύτης</note> read in John 21:7? Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> says: *“ependytes: the innermost garment, which is also called a tunic.”* Similarly, the one who translated the New Testament into modern Greek used "tunic" for *ependytes*. Yet Theophylact <note>An 11th-century commentator</note> says: *“The ependytes is a certain linen cloth which Phoenician and Syrian fishermen wrap around themselves, either when they are naked or over other garments that have been put on—simply put, like the wraps that painters give to...*

# TITLE I. BERAKHOT (BLESSINGS)

...of evil. If anyone prays for that which has already come to pass, such a petition is indeed in vain. In what way? For example, if his wife is pregnant and he says, *“May it please God that my wife bears a male child,”* this is a vain prayer. Or, if a man is traveling and hears a cry of distress coming from the city and says, *“May it please God that these are not the people of my own household,”* this too is a vain prayer.

**4.** He who enters a fortified city must pray twice; once upon his entry, and once upon his departure. Ben Azzai says he must pray four times: twice upon entry and twice upon departure. <gloss>1 He gives thanks for what has passed and petitions for what is to come.</gloss>

**5.** Every person is bound to say a blessing for the evil that befalls them just as they do for the good; for it is said (Deuteronomy 6:5), *“And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength.”* "With all your heart" means with both of your inclinations—the good inclination and the evil inclination. "With all your soul" means even if He takes your soul away. "With all your strength" means with all your wealth. Alternatively, "With all your strength" <gloss>2 means for every single measure that He measures out for you, you should give Him the greatest thanks possible.</gloss> <gloss>3 No one should behave with levity while facing the Eastern Gate, which looks directly toward the House of the Holy of Holies. Nor should anyone enter the Temple Mount with a staff, or wearing sandals, or with a 4 money-belt,</gloss> or—

<columns>2</columns>

—provided that at first glance it presents the appearance of evil, one must use the formula, *“Blessed is the True Judge.”* This is how I interpret the passage, which has caused many to struggle. The Babylonian Gemara <note>The "Gemara" is the Rabbinic commentary on the Mishna; together they form the Talmud.</note> understood these matters in a sense that is plainly the opposite. 
<note>original Hebrew: "One blesses for the evil... How so? For example, if a flood washes over his land; even though it is good for him in the long run because it deposits silt and improves the soil, for now it is an evil. And for the good... How so? For example, if he finds a lost object; even though it may be an evil for him because if the King hears of it he will seize it from him, for now it is a good."</note> One must bless for evil, etc. In what way? For instance, if a torrent inundates the land; although this may be good in itself because the water leaves behind <term>silt</term> <note>original Greek: syrton</note> and thus the land is improved, for the moment it is nonetheless an evil. And for the good, etc. In what way? For instance, if someone finds a treasure; although it might be an evil in itself because if the King hears anything of it, he will extort it, for the moment it is nonetheless a good. I confess I do not at all grasp how these examples can agree with the text of the Mishna, unless perhaps the Mishna is to be translated thus: "One must bless for the evil, even if it results in good; and for the good, even if it results in evil." But this interpretation cannot be sustained. However, if the examples brought by the Gemara were reversed to fit the sense of the passage as we have given it, they would illustrate the matter quite well. It is useless to consult the Rabbis Jarchi <note>Rashi</note>, Maimonides, Bertinoro, etc., on this point. They all follow the Gemara, and they all equally lose their way. The same error belongs to them all: they take the word <term>evil</term> <note>original Hebrew: ra'ah</note> in the first case to mean only that which *appears* to be evil, and in the second case they take <term>good</term> <note>original Hebrew: tovah</note> to mean only that which *appears* to be good; whereas the truth is the contrary. 

<column-break/>

"Evil" in the first case and "good" in the second refers to that which is truly evil but has the appearance of good, or that which is truly good but has the appearance of evil. If the reader pays attention to the matter, he will admit that I have clearly explained a passage in which all the Jewish interpreters have most miserably stumbled.

**1** *He gives thanks.*] In both places, upon entering and upon exiting: thus, four times.

**2** *For every measure.*] There is a wordplay (paronomasia) in the Hebrew words <term>me'od</term> (strength/exceedingly), <term>middah</term> (measure), and <term>moded</term> (he who measures), which is lost in translation.

**3** *Behave with levity.*] We have already discussed what "lightness of the head" <note>original Hebrew: kallut rosh; a term for irreverence or frivolous behavior</note> entails. From this comes "making one's head light," which is to behave irreverently.

**4** *Money-belt.*] This Mishnaic word is written in various ways and interpreted even more variously. It is written as <term>punda</term> or <term>apunda</term>. Regarding the interpretation, Maimonides here (and in other places) claims it is a garment worn closest to the flesh to keep sweat away from one's expensive clothing. In Arabic, he calls it a <term>ma'arka</term>. You might not be wrong to call it a *sweat-shirting*. Might it be the Greek word *ependytes* mentioned in John 21:7? Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> defines the *ependytes* as the innermost garment, also called a "hypokamison" (undershirt). Likewise, the one who translated the New Testament into modern Greek uses "undershirt" for this term. Yet Theophylactus <note>A Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note> says the *ependytes* is a linen cloth that Phoenician and Syrian fishermen wrap around themselves, either when they are naked or placed over their clothes; to put it simply, like the aprons that painters wear.

# Order I. ZERAIM (Seeds)

Column 1:
<margin>He wore it at length over his garments. <note>Original Greek: ἐπάνω τῶν ἱματίων εἶχεν μῆκες.</note></margin>
...or with dust clinging to his feet; nor should he make it a **shortcut** <note>Original Latin: *viam compendiariam*.</note>; much less should he spit there. In all the closing formulas of blessings in the Sanctuary, they used to say, "From eternity." <note>The Hebrew *olam* can mean "world" or "eternity."</note> From the time that **Heretics** introduced corruptions, asserting that there is only a single world, they decreed that it should be said, "From eternity to eternity."

<margin>Julius Pollux brings this [term] from Sophocles, Thespis, and Nicochares; however, it is not easy to determine what kind of garment it was. Maimonides adds to Shabbat 10:3, and Rabbi Tanchum from him, that this inner garment was equipped with pockets, and that the *chaluk*, or tunic, was worn over it.</margin>
<margin>Pomarius calls it a military outer garment; *a soldier's overcoat, with many seams, to hold money or other things.* Others hold it to be a belt in which they used to hide coins, of the kind mentioned in Matthew 10:9. So say Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] and Obadiah [Bartenura], and also Tanchum and Pomarius. To say what I think: the *punda* is one thing, and the *chaluk* is another, and Rabbi Nathan correctly distinguished them; although scribes almost always confuse them. The word *apunda* is the Greek *ependytes* [an outer garment]. Certainly, it is taken as an outer garment in Kelim 29:1, listed among cloaks, robes, tunics, mantles, and embroidered garments. The *punda*, however, is the Latin *funda*, that is, a net-like purse or pouch. Both meanings appear together in Shabbat 10:3, which place I would read as follows: "If anyone carries something out in his *funda* [purse] with its mouth downward, or if he carries it between his *apunda* [outer garment] and his tunic." In the first instance, you have the *funda* as a purse, as in Macrobius’s *Saturnalia* 2.4: "lowering his hand into a poor man's purse, he brought out a few coins." In the second, it is a joined garment, exactly as in Nicochares’s *Hercules Choragus*: "he now quickly put on the tunic and the outer garment." In this passage, I prefer "purse"; indeed, the Gemara cites an ancient tradition from which this Mishnah was taken:</margin>

> No man shall enter the Temple Mount with his staff in his hand, nor with his shoes on his feet, nor with money bound in his wrap, and his **punda** [purse] slung behind him.

That is: A *punda* slung behind him is exactly what I said; namely, a net-bag that used to be hung from the back. Horace says in *Sermones* 1.1:
---
->so that if<-
> You should happen to carry a heavy bag of bread for sale on your shoulder.

**1. A shortcut.]** Constantinus L’Empereur struggled needlessly to hammer the word *pampandaria* <note>The Hebrew *kapandaria*</note> out of some Greek words like *nepoia* and *andra*. The word is purely Latin, *Compendiaria* [a short way]; and the Jewish description agrees with this meaning. As for the dropping of the 'b' or 'm' before the 'k', that is done according to the custom of the Hebrew language. Thus,

<column-break/>

they call a hedgehog *kippod*, which to the Arabs is *qunfudh* and *qunfud* <note>Original Arabic: <unclear>قنفذ</unclear> and <unclear>قنفط</unclear></note>; and a beetle *chafushin*, which to the Arabs is *chafas* and *chanafas* <note>Original Arabic: <unclear>خفس</unclear> and <unclear>خنف</unclear></note>; and what is *lappid* in Hebrew, the Greeks and Latins call *lampada* or *lampadem* [a lamp].

**Heretics]** Those foolish Jews who so greatly boast of the antiquity of their Mishnah nevertheless write that the **Heretics** <term>Minim: a Hebrew term for sectarians or heretics, often used for early Christians or Sadducees</term> are named after Mani the Heresiarch. So says Rabbi Elias Levita in his *Tishbi*; Abarbanel in *Mihaloth Elohim* 2.5; the glossator to the Jerusalem Talmud in this place; and many others. They are ignorant, of course, that Mani lived only a few years past the age of the Emperor Diocletian. Others, more prudent, trace their origin to the disciples of Antigonus, namely Sadoc and Boethus, whom they believe laid the foundations of Sadduceeism even before the time of Christ. So say Rabbi Abraham bar Dior and his follower, Rabbi Abraham of Salamanca, the Jewish historians. For both write thus concerning "the beginning of the heresy" of Boethus: "And this was the origin of *Minaism* [Heresy]." They seem to follow Maimonides as their authority, who, in his commentary on *Aboth* 1.3, after narrating the history of these schismatics, adds: "And from then on arose those cursed sects called *Minim*." But Maimonides uses *Minim* there as a general term. And certainly, heresies existed among the Jews long before that legendary schism of Antigonus’s disciples, as the Jews themselves are aware. However, that schism is purely legendary; and the name of Boethus himself was taken from the "monstrous tales" <note>Original: *teratologia*</note> of the Valentinians, a fact which has escaped even the most learned until now, as I shall show below. But more on this in its proper place. Rabbi Obadiah seeks their origin even deeper. For he asserts that Ezra and his colleagues instituted this [liturgical change] because of the corruptions of the Heretics (*Minim*). But nothing is more uncertain than the history provided by the Rabbis. Among so many disagreeing opinions, let us hear our Jerome in his letter to Saint Augustine (number 89 in Victor's edition). He writes: "To this day, throughout all the synagogues of the East, there is a heresy among the Jews called that of the Minaeans, which is still condemned by the Pharisees; they commonly call them Nazarenes, who believe in Christ the Son of God, born of the Virgin Mary, and they say he is the one who suffered under Pontius Pilate and rose again, in whom we also believe. But while they want to be both Jews and Christians, they are neither Jews nor Christians." Therefore, the Minaeans were the same as the Nazarenes to Jerome, who accepted Christ in such a way that they did not abandon the observations of the old law, as he notes elsewhere. But were the Nazarenes the only ones called *Minim*? Certainly Epiphanius supports Jerome in a wonderful way, offering this example of the Jews' most bitter hatred toward the Nazarenes: that "rising in the morning, at midday, and toward evening..."

# Title I. BLESSINGS (BERAKHOT)

...they established [it], from eternity to eternity. They also decreed that people should greet one another using the Name of God, because it is said (Ruth 2:4): *“And behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem and said to the reapers: The Lord be with you; and they answered: May the Lord bless you.”* Elsewhere it is said (Judges 6:12): *“The Lord is with you, O mighty man of valor.”* Elsewhere (Proverbs 23:22): $^1$ *“Do not despise your mother when she is old.”* Elsewhere (Psalm 119:126): $^2$ *“It is time for the Lord to act, for they have made void your law.”* Rabbi Nathan says: *“They have made void your law, because it is time for the Lord to act.”*

---

<columns>2</columns>

“...in the evening, three times a day, when they perform prayers in their synagogues, they curse them and anathematize them, saying that God should curse the Nazarenes.” <note>Original Greek: ἑσπέραν, τρὶς τῆς ἡμέρας, ὅτε εὐχὰς ἐπιτελῶσιν... The author is quoting the Church Father Epiphanius (4th century) describing Jewish liturgical practices.</note> No one can doubt that he understood the **Blessing against the Heretics** <note>Original Hebrew: *Birkat ha-Minim*</note> to be that which was accepted into the Eighteen Benedictions <note>The *Amidah*, the central prayer of the Jewish liturgy.</note> by the authority of Gamaliel. To Epiphanius, the “Nazarenes” <note>A term for early Christians.</note> were the same as those the Jews call *Minim* <note>Heretics</note>. It is likely, however, that the name had a broader meaning for the ancient Jews, and included even true Christians—but specifically those who had defected from Judaism. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator.</note> at Rosh Hashanah 17a: “The **Minai** <note>Heretics</note> are the disciples of Jesus the Nazarene, who turned the words of the living God to evil.” <note>Original Hebrew: המינין תלמידי ישו הנוצרי אשר הפכו דברי אלהים חיים לרעה</note> This is the restored text from the *Corrections to Maimonides* (Laws of Repentance, Chapter 3), which is usually corrupted in the printed editions that underwent censorship. Other manuscripts here have **Epicureans** <note>A term used by Jews to describe those who deny divine providence or the afterlife.</note>. This is perhaps a better reading, unless *Minim* here refers to the Sadducees. Yet one manuscript does have *the Minim*. It is common for the Jews to confuse these names to deceive the Censors. For the more subtle distinctions used by the Jews between **Heretics**, **Epicureans**, **Deniers**, **Apostates**, **Schismatics**, **Informers**,

<column-break/>

and **Traitors**, etc., let whoever wishes look at Maimonides, Laws of Repentance, Chapter 3. Nicolaus Fuller <note>An English philologist and orientalist (1557–1623).</note> argues that *Min* <note>the word for Heretic</note> is derived from *me-ayin* <note>meaning "from nothing"</note>, so that it literally means “One who denies the faith.” This does not displease me.

$^1$ *Do not despise.*] This custom has already prevailed since ancient times; therefore, do not despise the customs of the ancients. This would be the sense of that proverb of Solomon.

$^2$ *It is time to act.*] If you despise the customs, it will be time to act. Rabbi Nathan explained this text differently. You will understand if I provide the words of the **Gemara** <note>The portion of the Talmud that contains rabbinic commentary and analysis of the Mishnah.</note>: “Rabba said: This verse is interpreted from its beginning to its end, and from its end to its beginning.” <note>Original Hebrew: אמר רבא האי קרא מרישיה לסיפיה מדרש ומסיפיה לרישיה מדרש</note> Rabba says: This text is explained either as **former-before-latter** or **latter-before-former**. <note>Original Greek: *proteron hysteron* or *hysteron proteron*.</note> It is explained as **former-before-latter** as: “It is time for the Lord to act; for what reason? Because they have made void your law.” It is explained as **latter-before-former** as: “They have made void your law; for what reason? Because it is time for the Lord to act.” By this latter interpretation, Rabbis Jarchi <note>Rashi</note> and Kimchi understand the violation of the law formerly practiced or permitted by the Prophets due to some special cause at that time only. Thus, Elijah violated the law and offered a sacrifice outside of Jerusalem on Mount Carmel. But there was a special reason at that time: it was “time for the Lord to act,” for the prophets of Baal had to be slaughtered.

# ORDER I. SEEDS (ZERAIM)

# TITLE II. PE’AH
### OR
## CONCERNING THE CORNER OF THE FIELD TO BE LEFT FOR THE POOR.

->Wherein is also treated the matter of Gleanings, and the Forgotten Sheaf;<-
->likewise concerning the clusters of the vineyard, concerning the grapes falling away<-
->during the vintage, and concerning the beaten olives, by virtue of the<-
->precepts in Leviticus 19:9, 10; 23:22; and Deuteronomy 24:<-
