# CHAPTER I.

1. These are the things for which there is no fixed measure: The Corner of the field <note>Hebrew: *Pe'ah*</note>, and <gloss>1</gloss> the Firstfruits, and <gloss>2</gloss> the Appearance [at the Temple], and Acts of Kindness, and the Study of the Law. These are the things whose fruit a man enjoys in this world, while the principal remains for him in the world to come: Honoring one's father and mother, Acts of Kindness, and the Making of Peace between men. But the Study of the Law is equal to them all.

2. They leave no less for the corner of the field than a sixtieth part. Although it has been said that the Corner has no fixed measure, nevertheless the whole matter is determined by the size of the field, the number of the poor, and the abundance of the yield.

3. They may designate the corner either at the beginning of the field or in the middle. Rabbi Simeon says: provided that at the end [of the harvest] there is also given the required amount. Rabbi Judah thinks: if even a single stalk is left, one may rely upon it as the "corner"; otherwise, if nothing is left at the end, the harvest is considered to have been gathered into the common store <note>meaning the owner would then be liable for tithes on the portion that should have been left for the poor</note>.

---

<columns>2</columns>
<gloss>1</gloss> *Firstfruits.*] Thus I translate <term>Bikkurim</term> <note>original Hebrew: בכורים</note>, which for the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> are "first-born products" <note>original Greek: πρωτογεννήματα</note>, and for Josephus "preliminary offerings" <note>original Greek: προτέλεια</note>. I have followed the Vulgate in Exodus 23:16. I could also call them "early-ripening fruits," for such they were in reality, as is evident below from Tractate Bikkurim 3:1. In my judgment, those who translate this as "First-offerings" are in error. That term is better suited to <term>Terumah</term> <note>original Hebrew: תרומה; the portion of the harvest given to the Priests</note>. But most of our writers think nothing of confusing these terms. Others, while they 
<column-break/>
translate <term>Bikkurim</term> as "Firstfruits," use the word "Truma" for <term>Terumah</term>, not even daring to express it in Latin.
<gloss>2</gloss> *Appearance.*] The solemn appearance before God during the three "Great Assemblies" <note>original Greek: πανηγύρεσιν; the three pilgrimage festivals of Passover, Shavuot, and Sukkot</note>. Here, however, it stands for the Sacrifices which they were bound to bring during that appearance or assembly, according to the precept of the Law in Deuteronomy 16:16: *“They shall not appear before the Lord empty-handed.”*

## Title II. PEAH.

4. They have handed down a general rule concerning the **Corner**: Whatever serves as food, is guarded <note>meaning it is private property rather than wild</note>, has its growth from the earth, is harvested all at once, and is gathered in to be stored—is subject to the law of the Corner. And by this rule, grain and legumes are included.

5. Among the trees: sumac, carobs, nuts, almonds, vines, pomegranates, olives, and palms are subject to the law of the Corner.

6. $^1$ It is given in the name of the Corner at any time, and it is also free from tithes until it is **polished** <note>original: *perpoliatur*; refers to the final smoothing of the grain pile</note>. And it may be brought into the common store, which is also free from tithes until it is polished. And fodder may be provided for cattle, wild animals, and birds, which is also free from tithes until it is polished. And seed taken from the threshing floor may be sown, which is also free from tithes until it is polished. $^2$ These are the words of Rabbi Akiba. If a Priest or a Levite buys a threshing floor, the tithes belong to them $^3$ **before the polishing**. One who consecrates his crop, if he redeems it, is bound by tithes, $^4$ unless the $^5$ **Prefect of the Treasury** has polished it.

->CHAPTER.<-

<columns>2</columns>

1 **At any time**.] Even after the harvest; so that if someone has harvested the entire field and has not left a corner in the standing corn, he is obliged to pay from the fallen ears, or even from the threshed and ground grain, which is also held to be free from tithes, provided it is before the <term>miruach</term> <note>original: מירוח; the finishing or smoothing of the grain pile</note>. However, after the <term>miruach</term>, the tithes must first be tasted <note>meaning set aside</note>. But what exactly <term>miruach</term> is, is not sufficiently agreed upon among the Jews. To Rabbis Solomon, Nathan, and Obadiah, it is said to be when <gloss>the heap of grain is leveled with a shovel</gloss>. To Maimonides, it sounds in Arabic like <term>tsadlaf</term> <note>original: צדלף</note>, that is, <gloss>polishing</gloss>; and he wishes it to be a metaphor from the polishing of vessels, which is the final work done upon them. I approve of this. I do not approve, however, that he distinguishes it from <gloss>cleansing</gloss>. Nor is he quite consistent with himself. In my judgment, Rabbi Tanchum is correct: <note>original: "Metaphorâ à politura deductâ vocant quamlibet expiacionem, vel lavigationem, vel purgationem; מירוח ubique autem dignoscitur ex sensu loci."</note> "Deducing the metaphor from **polishing**, they call any purification, or smoothing, or cleansing <term>miruach</term>; however, <term>miruach</term> is recognized everywhere according to the sense of the passage." Here, therefore, it is the final cleansing of the grain. In the same sense, you may read "to polish" <note>original: *expolire*</note> and "to re-polish" in that excellent author of Latinity, Columella <note>a Roman writer on agriculture from the 1st century AD</note>. Moreover, these things are free from tithes because the obligation for tithes does not yet apply until the crops are finally polished. But the Corner, and a field which is under common law, are always held immune from tithes, unless the obligation existed before one separated it for the Corner, or the other became common property. The same reasoning applies to grain given as fodder.

2 **The words of Rabbi Akiba**.] Namely, those things concerning the sowing of grain taken from the threshing floor, according to his private opinion; for this is to be referred to the fourth member of the rule.

3 **Before the polishing**.] Why not also after, when they have already taken possession? Because the Sages imposed this fine upon them to extort the tithes after they themselves had polished the crops bought in bad faith, lest any of them should rush into the threshing floors and

<column-break/>

vats at an unseasonable time, and thus defraud the others of their tithes.

4 **Unless he has polished it**.] Because what is consecrated to God is held immune from tithes; and so, if it was polished by the Prefect of the Treasury before redemption, the time for paying tithes is judged to have passed without any obligation.

5 **Prefect of the Treasury**.] <term>Ganzabar</term> <note>original: גנזבר</note>, a word of Persian origin, only known to the Jews after the captivity. For <gloss>Gaza</gloss> among the Persians is <gloss>treasure</gloss>, as is known from Curtius, Mela, and Servius; that is, <term>Ganz</term> <note>original: גנז</note>, a word which occurs only in Ezra and Ezekiel, and even today exists in the Persian language, as well as in Armenian, in the same way with an epenthetic 'N'. For in Persian it is <term>ganj</term> <note>original: گنج</note>, and to the Armenians <term>gandz</term> <note>original: գանձ</note> is <gloss>treasure</gloss>. From this also comes the Arabic <term>kanz</term> <note>original: كنز</note>, with the same meaning. Furthermore, **bar**, or **war**, is a termination by which even today the Persians form possessives in their language. They write it as **war** <note>original: ور</note> or **wâr** <note>original: وار</note> using letters borrowed from the Saracens. The Armenians use the broader <term>uôr</term> <note>original: ւոր</note>. From this comes <term>Ganzavar</term>, which even today the Persians would call <term>Ganjwar</term> <note>original: گنجوار</note>, and the Armenians <term>Gandzavor</term>; the Armenian translator uses this very word in the same sense in 1 Esdras 2:11, meaning <gloss>over the treasure</gloss>. However, with the element 'N' elided or softened, it becomes <term>Gazavâr</term>. To the Chaldeans <note>Aramaic speakers</note> it is the same, <term>Ganzabarin</term>, with the ending changed to 'N' according to the custom of that language. Hence <term>Ganzabarin</term> in Daniel 3:2, 3. Such elisions of that letter are quite familiar. Thus the Hebrews call an <gloss>ear of grain</gloss> <term>shibboleth</term> <note>original: שבולת</note>, while the Arabs call it <term>sunbulat</term> <note>original: سنبلة</note>; a <gloss>spider</gloss> the Hebrews call <term>akabish</term> <note>original: עכביש</note>, the Chaldeans <term>akabit</term>, and the Arabs <term>ankabut</term> <note>original: عنکبوت</note>; a <gloss>goat</gloss> the Hebrews call <term>ez</term> <note>original: עז</note>, and the Arabs <term>anz</term> <note>original: عنز</note>; and lest...

# C H A P T E R II.

1. **T**hese¹ things divide a field into two parts regarding the Corner: a trench, a ² stream, a ³ private road, a public road, a public path, and a private path that is used in both summer and winter, fallow land, newly plowed land, and a crop of a different kind. One who cuts a crop for fodder <note>intended as animal feed rather than grain harvest</note> divides the field. Thus says *Rabbi Meir*. But the Sages say, it does not divide the field unless he also plows that area.

2. A water channel ⁴ that is so wide it cannot be harvested from both sides at once <note>meaning a reaper cannot reach across it to cut grain on the other side</note> divides the field, according to the opinion of *Rabbi Judah*. And concerning ⁵ any mountains that are dug with a hoe—even though oxen with their plowing instruments cannot pass through them—they give only one corner for the entire area.

3. All these things divide the field for sown crops. However, for trees, nothing divides them except a stone wall. And if the branches of the trees interlace, even a wall does not divide them; rather, one corner is given for the whole.

4. For carob trees, ⁶ the rule applies as far as one tree can see another. *Rabban Gamaliel* said, "The house of my father used to give one corner for all the olives they had in any direction; but for carobs, they gave one corner as far as one tree could see another." *Rabbi Eleazar*, son of *Rabbi Zadok*, reports in his name: they even gave one corner for all the carobs they had in the entire city.

5. One who sows a field with a single species, even if he gathers it into two separate threshing floors, gives a single corner. If he sows it with two species, then—

---

To provide more examples, the very word of the Chaldeans, or Persians, is <note>original: "גוזא" - *Givza*</note>; the Syrians pronounce it *Gaza*.
<gloss>When it branches off from it</gloss>
There were three such <note>original: "גזברין" - *Gizbarin*</note>, Prefects, or Treasurers of the sacred Treasury.
1 *Divide.*] They divide the field in such a way that it is no longer considered a single unit, and therefore multiple corners must be left for the poor.
2 *Stream.*] What exactly a <note>original: "שלולית" - *shlulit*</note> is, is debated in the *Gemara* <note>the commentary on the Mishnah</note>, *Baba Kama* 61a. One authority argues it is "a place where rainwater flows," *that is, a torrent*. Another says it is "a water stream that distributes 'plunder' <note>original: "שלל" - *shalal*; a pun on the Hebrew name for the stream</note> to its banks." The author here is correct, even if *Maimonides* <note>a famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legalist</note> misunderstood it, perhaps deceived by a faulty reading; for instead of "to its banks," he read "to its companions," describing it as a stream that yields its "plunder" to others. Following this, *Buxtorf* <note>a prominent 17th-century Christian Hebraist</note> translated it. He explains the word as a "water canal from which smaller streams are drawn to irrigate other places." But the *shlulit* is actually the stream itself diverted from a river to irrigate a field, as that scholar of the Gemara correctly noted, even if he was somewhat foolish in his etymology by trying to derive it from the word for "plunder." You would do better to seek the meaning in the Arabic language, where a metaphor

<column-break/>

taken from a sword is used: "the stream unsheathed a rivulet."
<gloss>When it branches off from it</gloss>
"The stream unsheathed the rivulet when it was diverted from it," says *Zamakhshari* <note>a medieval Persian scholar of the Arabic language</note>. Hence the ancient poet *Dhu 'r-Rumma* says, "A rivulet unsheathed the river, drawn out like a sword." From this comes the word for rivulet, <note>original: "سلالة" - *sulalah*</note>, which is exactly our word <note>original: "שלולית" - *shlulit*</note>.
3 *Private road.*] This is four cubits wide; a public road is sixteen.
4 *That cannot.*] Meaning its sides cannot be reached simultaneously.
5 *Any mountains.*] These words are found in *Isaiah* 7:25. They refer to steep mountains which, although they cannot be plowed and thus interrupt the plowing of the field on either side, are nonetheless not considered to "divide" the field because they can still be turned over by a hoe or mattock.
6 *As far as one.*] For that entire space where visibility ends, even if a wall intervenes, only one corner is given.

6. This case occurred when *Rabbi Simeon of Mispah* <note>A scholar from the town of Mizpah</note> brought it before *Rabban Gamaliel*; they entered the Chamber of Hewn Stone <note>original: "Conclave cæsi lapidis"; the hall in the Temple where the Sanhedrin, the high court, met</note> and investigated the matter. *Nahum the Scribe* said: "I have received a tradition from *Rabbi Measha*, who received it from his father, who received it from the Pairs <note>original: "Conjugatis" or Greek "Syzugois"; these are the pairs of scholars who headed the Sanhedrin in successive generations</note>, who received it from the Prophets; it is a Decree of Moses from Sinai: that if one sows a field with two species of wheat, and gathers them into a single area, he gives one corner; if into two areas, he gives two."
7. A field harvested by Gentiles, or by thieves, or devastated by ants, or crushed by the wind or by cattle, is considered exempt <note>from the requirement of leaving a corner for the poor</note>. If half of it was harvested and thieves harvested the other half, it is exempt; because the obligation for the corner only applied to the standing crop.
8. If half was harvested by thieves and the owner harvests the remaining half, he gives the corner for the portion he harvested himself. If he harvests half and sells the other half, the buyer gives the corner for the whole. If he harvests half and dedicates the other half to the Temple, the person who redeems it from the Treasury Official gives the corner for the whole.

## CHAPTER III.

1. Regarding small plots of grain among olive trees, the followers of *Shammai* <note>original: "Sammæani"; a school of legal thought known for stricter interpretations</note> judge that a corner must be given for each individual plot. However, the followers of *Hillel* <note>original: "Hillelæi"; a school of legal thought known for more lenient or communal interpretations</note> say one corner suffices for all. They agree that if the tops of the plots are mixed together, one corner is given for all.
2. If one harvests a field in patches like a leopard’s spots <note>leaving patches of standing stalks while harvesting others</note>, *Rabbi Akiba* says he must give a corner for each individual patch. But the Sages say: one for all. However, the Sages agree with *Rabbi Akiba* concerning someone who sows dill or mustard in three places: he must give a corner for each.
3. One who thins out <note>original: "deglabrat"; to pluck or strip portions of a crop</note> green onions for the market, while keeping the dried ones for the storage area, gives a corner for each separately. It is the same for chickpeas. And so too in a vineyard: one who thins it out gives for the remainder based on what he left; but one who thins from one side only gives for the remainder based on the whole.

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion of Tractate Pe'ah within the First Order, Zeraim (Seeds). # First Order: ZERAIM <note>Seeds</note>

4. <margin>1</margin> Seed onions are liable for the corner. Rabbi Jose exempts them. Regarding beds of onions placed among other vegetables, Rabbi Jose thinks a corner must be left from each individual bed; the Sages say one corner suffices for all of them.

5. Brothers who have divided an inheritance of land must give two corners <note>one for each new plot</note>. If they become partners again, they give a single corner. Two people who bought a tree together give a single corner. If one bought the northern part of the tree and the other bought the southern part, each gives a corner for his own portion.

6. If a person sells the trunks <note>or stems</note> of trees in his field, a corner is given for each. "When is this the case?" asks Rabbi Judah. "Only when the owner of the field has left nothing for himself; but if the owner has retained any part of the field for himself, he is the one who gives the corner for the whole."

7. Rabbi Eliezer says: A plot of land that holds a <margin>2</margin> *quarter-measure* <note>original: "quadrantem"; 1/4 of a Kab</note> of seed is liable for the corner. Rabbi Joshua says: one that yields two *seahs* <note>original: "sata"</note>. Rabbi Tarphon says: a plot that is six handbreadths square. Rabbi Judah ben Bathyra says: one that is large enough—

---

<margin>1 Mothers.]</margin> That is, seed onions <note>onions kept in the ground to produce seeds rather than for eating</note>.

<margin>2 Quarter-measure.]</margin> The smallest measure for dry goods, which is equal to the *Log* in liquid measures. It is named in relation to the *Kab*, of which it is one quarter. A plot of land capable of bearing a quarter-measure of grain is defined as a square of approximately 10.5 cubits. Moreover, since there is frequent mention of measures in these books, and their use is almost constant, I will explain the Jewish teaching on this matter once here, so that the reader may return to this spot whenever necessary. The Jews usually relate all these measures to average eggs, which they define as the largest of chicken eggs. Maimonides <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>, a most diligent evaluator of these things, was not content to explain them only by eggs; he also estimated the weight in Egyptian *drachmas* (each of which equals approximately 61 grains of barley) and the dimensions in cubic inches. According to his calculations, here are the most noteworthy measures. The rest can be easily deduced from these. "L" designates a liquid measure, and "A" a dry measure.

| | Weight in | Capacity in | Volume in |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | *drachmas* | *eggs* | *cubic inches* |
| L. *Quarter-log* <note>original: "Quartarius"</note> | 26 | 1 ½ | 10 5/12 |
| L. *Log* | 104 | 6 | 43 1/3 |
| A. *Quarter-measure* <note>original: "Quadrans"</note> | 416 | 24 | 172 2/3 |
| A. *Kab* | 416 | 24 | 172 2/3 |
| A. *Omer* | 748 4/5 | 43 1/5 | 311 1/25 |
| L. *Hin* | 1248 | 72 | 518 2/5 |
| A. *Seah* <note>original: "Satum"</note> | 2496 | 144 | 1036 4/5 |
| L. *Bath* <note>original: "Batus"</note> | 7488 | 432 | 3110 2/5 |
| A. *Ephah* <note>original: "Epha"</note> | 7488 | 432 | 3110 2/5 |
| A. *Kor* <note>original: "Corus"</note> | 74880 | 4320 | 31104 |

<note>Rows bracketed together in the original (Quarter-measure/Kab and Bath/Ephah) share the same values.</note>

Thus, in dry measures, a Kor holds ten Ephahs; an Ephah holds three Seahs, or ten Omers, which are therefore

<column-break/>

called *Asharonim* <note>original Hebrew: עשרונים</note>, or *Assarons* <note>original Greek: Aσσαρῶνες</note> in Josephus <note>A 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note>; that is, "tenths." A Seah holds six Kabs; a Kab holds four quarter-measures; for the term *revia* <note>original Hebrew: רביע</note> always signifies a quarter of a Kab. In liquid measures, the Bath is equal to the Ephah and holds six Hins; a Hin holds twelve Logs, which are equal to the same number of dry quarter-measures; a Log holds four quarter-logs; for the term *revi'it* <note>original Hebrew: רביעית</note> is always understood as the fourth part of a Log, which I call a "quarter-log" <note>original: "quartarium"</note> to distinguish it from the dry "quarter-measure" <note>original: "quadrante"</note> which is equal to a full Log. There are also liquid measures for a half, a third, a quarter, and a sixth of a Hin, and an eighth of a Log, which are clear enough from what has been said. The *Letek* <note>original Hebrew: לתך</note> in dry measures is a half-Kor. I add one thing: the weights defined here in drachmas should be understood as referring to wine or oil, according to how much those measures hold. For Maimonides correctly observed that the weights not only of different items but even of different liquids differ specifically. Therefore, he notes in his commentary on *Eduyot* 1, 2, that a quarter-log of wine weighs 26 drachmas, water 27, grain 21, and flour 18, approximately. The other numbers should be increased or decreased according to that proportion. Rabbi Joseph ben Aqnin, who wrote a short treatise on measures in Arabic, followed our numbers. Another, Rabbi David, said to be the sixth descendant of Maimonides, covered the same material in a brief commentary and assigned only 25 drachmas to the quarter-log; he keeps the same proportion in the rest, which is enough to mention here. Meanwhile, I know all these things are very different from what Georgius Agricola <note>A 16th-century German scholar known as the "father of mineralogy"</note> diligently and eruditely discusses regarding Hebrew measures based on Josephus; this serves as a warning to me not to try to substitute Attic or Roman measures for Hebrew ones. However, if I were to assign a Roman measure equivalent to the Hebrew, I think the *modius* comes very close to the *Seah* [satum]. For since the *modius*, if estimated by Agricola’s calculations, weighs 2968 drachmas when full of wine and about 2133 when full of oil, Maimonides' calculation (estimated neutrally between oil and wine) sits almost in the middle of these numbers. For this reason, the Syriac translator of the Gospels always uses *satum* for the Greek *modios* <note>referring to the "bushel" in Matthew 5:15</note>.

## Title II. PEAH

<meta>catchword: 8 Aufe-</meta>

—is such that it is only harvested at the second stroke. And according to his opinion, the Law prevails. Rabbi Akiba thinks that a plot of land of any size whatsoever is liable for the Corner and for the first fruits; it is also sufficient for a <term>judicial caution</term> <note>original: "judicialis cautio"; referring to the Prozbul</note> ^1 to be written upon it, and for <term>non-pledgable goods</term> ^2 <note>movable property</note> to be acquired along with it, whether by cash, by a legal document, or by long-term possession.

8. If a person, while lying ill, gives away his goods in writing, and he has left behind even the smallest plot of land, his gift is valid; but if he has not left behind even that much, the gift is ^3 void. If a person gives his goods in writing to his sons, and also gives his wife even the smallest plot of land, she ^4 loses her dowry. Rabbi Joses says: if she accepted it for herself, even if he did not technically "give" it, she has lost her dowry.

9. If anyone gives his goods to his slave in writing, that slave goes out into freedom. If the owner left behind even the smallest plot of land, the slave does not go out free. [^5 Rabbi Joses thinks he should go out free.] Rabbi Simeon says: he always goes out free, unless the owner specifically said: *All my goods are given to N. my slave, except for a ^6 ten-thousandth part of them.*

### CHAPTER IV.

1. The Corner is given from that which is attached to the ground. Regarding a hanging vine or a palm tree, the master of the house brings the produce down and distributes it to the poor. Rabbi Simeon thinks the same applies to ^7 smooth nuts. If there are ninety-nine who say the produce should be divided—

---

1 *Judicial caution.*] <term>Prozbul</term>. A caution <term>before the councils</term> <note>original Greek: "πρὸς βουλὰς"</note>, or an agreement entered before judges, concerning a debt to be claimed even after the year of remission <note>the Sabbatical year</note>. This caution was entered into when land was pledged. See Shebiit X. 3, 4, 6.

2 *Non-pledgable goods.*] Goods are divided into <term>assets that have no guarantee</term> and <term>assets that have a guarantee</term> <note>original Hebrew: "she-ein lahem" and "nechasim she-yesh lahem achrayut"</note>. <term>Guarantee</term> <note>original Hebrew: "achrayut"</note> refers to goods which are subject to pledging. The first type consists of lands or estates (called *praedia* by the Latins, from *praes* meaning a surety; both derived from *praestando* [to provide/stand for], as Varro prefers), which are always considered to be placed as a pledge; so much so that if someone sells them to another to elude a creditor, a "place for eviction" <note>legal reclamation</note> exists to help the creditor. The other type consists of movable goods, which are not assumed to be bound as a pledge to a creditor, and in which the buyer undergoes no danger of eviction. The Greeks would call these <term>guaranteed substance</term> or <term>guaranteed possessions</term>, and <term>non-guaranteed</term> <note>original Greek: "engua ousia," "engua ktemata," "engua anengua"</note>. However, <term>non-guaranteed</term> goods are not acquired otherwise than by <term>drawing</term> <note>original Hebrew: "meshikhah"</note>, unless they come along with <term>guaranteed</term> goods so that they follow their legal condition. The latter are acquired in the three ways mentioned here. See Kiddushin I. 5 and Bava Batra IX. 7.

3 *Void.*] Because he thus reveals that he only

<column-break/>

gave the gift because he thought he was about to die immediately.

4 *Loses her dowry.*] If she, being prudent and knowing the situation, acquiesced to the gift.

5 *Rabbi Joses.*] Restored from the manuscript and from Maimonides. These words are absent from the printed editions.

6 *Ten-thousandth part.*] By expressly reserving to himself any portion whatever; for in this way the exception extends to the slave himself <note>implying the slave remains part of the reserved property</note>.

7 *Smooth nuts.*] He seems to mean hazelnuts. For they are the offspring of a very smooth trunk. To Maimonides, "smooth nuts" are <note>original Hebrew: "chalikei egozim"</note> which are <note>original Arabic: "afrak"</note>, i.e., a species of nut from a tall tree, as he himself explains. Rabbi Tanchum says: <note>original Arabic: "Nux mollis, levis, fractu facilis..."</note> "A soft nut, light, easy to break, which is therefore called the *Fark* nut, because it is broken even by rubbing <note>frictu</note>." If you put these together, they seem to have understood it as a "mollusk" nut <note>soft-shelled walnut</note>. Whether there is a nut which is called by the Arabs <term>the easy-to-peel nut</term> <note>original Greek: "káryon euphlyés"</note>, is not clear to me. Certainly, I find no such thing among the Arab physicians or herbalists, such as Ibn Jazla, Avicenna, Ibn al-Khatib, or the author of the book *Malayesa*, and Ibn al-Baitar. However, at the end of the Title *Orlah* III. 7, mention is made of *Fark* nuts, where Maimonides clearly takes *Fark* as a proper name.

# THE FIRST ORDER: SEEDS

<meta>catchword: do not</meta>

...demand to snatch the produce, and one individual demands to distribute it, they listen to the former, since he demands it according to the Constitution.

2. In the case of a hanging vine or a palm tree, the situation is different. If ninety-nine demand to snatch it, and one individual demands to distribute it, they listen to the latter, because he demands it according to the Constitution. <note>In high or dangerous places like palms, orderly distribution is required for safety, whereas in open fields, the poor are generally allowed to scramble for the produce.</note>

3. If someone grabs a part of the corner and throws it over the rest, he has no right to any of it. If he throws himself upon it or spreads his cloak over it, ¹ they take it away from him. The same applies to the <term>gleanings</term> <note>original: "spicilegio"; the fallen ears of grain</note> and to the <term>forgotten sheaf</term> <note>original: "prætermisso"; grain left behind by mistake</note>.

4. They do not harvest the Corner with sickles, nor do they uproot it with axes, so that one person does not strike another.

5. Three ² <term>searches</term> <note>stata tempora; designated times for gathering</note> are held during the day: morning, noon, and in the afternoon. Rabban Gamaliel says: This was said for no other purpose than that they should not have fewer. Rabbi Akiba says: For no other purpose than that they should not have more. The people of Bethnamar used to harvest by the cord and would give the Corner from every single row.

6. A foreigner who becomes a <term>proselyte</term> <note>a convert to Judaism</note> only after the field has been harvested is held exempt from the laws of gleanings, the forgotten sheaf, and the Corner. Rabbi Judah considers him bound by the law of the forgotten sheaf, because the forgotten sheaf does not technically exist until the time when the bundles are made.

7. If someone consecrates his standing grain to the Temple and then redeems it while it is still standing grain, he is liable for the poor-taxes. If he consecrates it as bundles and redeems it as bundles, he is liable. But if he consecrates it as standing grain and redeems it only after it has been made into bundles, he is exempt; because at the time the obligation would have fallen upon him, he was exempt <note>as the property then belonged to the Temple sanctuary</note>.

8. In the same way, if someone consecrates his fruits before they have reached the season for tithing and then redeems them, they are liable for tithes. If he redeems them after they have reached the season for tithing, they are liable. If he consecrates them before they have been fully processed, and then redeems them from the <term>Treasury Official</term> <note>original: "Præfecto Ærario"; the Temple bursar</note> only after they have been processed, they are considered exempt; because at the time the obligation would have fallen, they were exempt.

9. If someone picks the Corner and says: "Let this be for the use of N. the poor man," Rabbi Eliezer says he is considered to have acquired the right for him. But the Sages say: he must give it to the poor person who happens to come first. ³ Gleanings, the forgotten sheaf, and the Corner

---

1 **They take it away from him.**] Alternatively: they pull him away from there. So also says Maimonides (Gifts to the Poor, II. 18) and Moses of Coucy (Negative Precept 284).

2 **Searches.**] That is, the fixed times at which the opportunity for searching for gleanings, etc., is granted to the poor. The Jewish interpreters diverge in various directions regarding this word. I defend my translation from the Aramaic Paraphrast, who at Isaiah 1:8 translates the <term>observations</term> <note>original Greek: παραφυλάξες</note> thus: "As a hut in a vineyard after the grape-gathering; as a lodging-bed in a cucumber field after they have <term>searched</term> <note>original Aramaic: אבעיוהי (ab'ayuhi)</note> it." Where "to gather grapes" in a vineyard and "to seek out and search for the remains of the cucumbers" in a cucumber field are clearly opposed

<column-break/>

to one another. Regarding these words of the Paraphrast, Rabbi Solomon says: <term>And that is the phrasing of the Mishnah: 'three searches are held in a day.'</term> <note>original Hebrew: והוא לשון המשנה שלש אבעיות ביום</note> Perhaps I might more correctly translate it as "missions," so that the action refers to the owner, who sends the poor into the field three times a day. Thus, "one who sends" <note>original Aramaic: בעו (be'u)</note> in the Babylonian Talmud (Bava Kamma 1:1) is he who sends his beast to graze in another's field, as we shall discuss there.

3 **Gleanings, etc.**] These are commonly exempt from tithes. But if they are gathered from the field of a foreigner, tithes must be paid from them; because the law concerning the Corner, gleanings, and the forgotten sheaf does not apply to him.

->Title II. PE’AH (THE CORNER)<-

...the resident alien is held liable for <term>tithes</term> <note>religious taxes paid on produce</note>, unless he has acted according to common law.

10. What is a <term>gleaning</term>? <note>original: "spicilegium"; grain that falls during the harvest</note> That which <insert>falls</insert> during the *harvesting*. <insert>If</insert> the harvester cuts a full handful, or pulls up a full fistful, and a thorn strikes him so that it falls from his hand, this belongs to the owner. Whatever falls from the middle of the hand or the middle of the sickle belongs to the poor; whatever falls from the back part of the hand or sickle belongs to the owner. Regarding what falls from the very edge of the hand or sickle, Rabbi Ishmael judges it to belong to the poor; Rabbi Akiba judges it for the owner.

11. ¹ Ants’ burrows found in the middle of a standing crop are considered the owner’s; those found behind the harvesters—the upper part belongs to the poor, and the lower part to the owner. Rabbi Meir judges the whole to belong to the poor, because whatever is a matter of doubt regarding gleanings is treated as gleanings.

## CHAPTER V.

1. Whatever touches the ground beneath a **s**tack <note>original: "Meta"; a heap of harvested grain</note> where the ground has not yet been cleared belongs to the poor. If the wind scatters the sheaves, one must estimate by conjecture how many gleanings would likely have been made, and that amount must be given to the poor. Rabban Simeon, son of Gamaliel, judges that they should be given ² according to the measure of what usually falls.

2. An ear of grain found in the harvested area, whose head reaches into the standing crop: if it can be harvested along with the crop, it belongs to the owner; if not, it belongs to the poor. If an ear belonging to the gleanings becomes mixed into a stack, ³ he <note>the owner</note> tithes one ear and gives it to him <note>the poor person</note>. Rabbi Eliezer said: But how can this poor man ⁴ exchange a thing ⁵ which has not yet come into his possession? Rather, the owner ⁶ grants him a legal right to the entire stack; ⁷ then he tithes one ear and gives it to him.

---

<columns>2</columns>

...nor is he bound to give: however, his field in the land of Israel is not considered exempt from tithes. This entire section follows the private opinion of Rabbi Meir, whose rule is this: *A Gentile has no legal possession in the land of Israel such that it can rescind the obligation of tithes.* <note>original Hebrew: "Ein kinyan l'goi b'Eretz Yisrael l'haphkia min ha-ma'asrot"</note> See below, *Demai* V. 9.

1 **Ants’ burrows.**] Meaning the grain found within them.

2 **According to the measure of what fell.**] This is the sense of the Hebrew *bikhdey nephilah*. Rabbis Samson and Obadiah understand this as what falls during the harvest; but in this way, they struggle in vain to distinguish between the opinion of Rabban Simeon and the earlier teaching. Maimonides <note>a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> understands it as what falls during sowing, or what is scattered—that is, the quantity of seed the ground takes where the sheaves were scattered. Thus, I might translate it: "according to the measure of the seed sown." This phrase is used openly in this way in *Bava Metzia* IX. 5: "if there is in the yield as much as was in the sowing" <note>original Hebrew: "im yesh bah kikhdey nephilah"</note>. So also in other places.

<column-break/>

### 3. Non

<gloss>As what falls in a "Seah's" house of land</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: "kenophel l'beit se'ah"</note>. A twenty-fourth part of what falls in the sowing of a field: that is, what is planted. *Kilayim* II. 2.

3 **Tithes the ear, etc.**] That is, the owner takes any one ear chosen from the heap, frees it from tithes, and gives it to the poor man in exchange for that specific "gleaning" ear that was mixed into the heap. He frees it from tithes because gleanings are naturally exempt from tithes. This is done as follows: taking two ears, he says: "If this ear be the gleaning ear, it is well; if not, let the tithes owed for it be established upon this other ear." Then he hands it to the poor man.

4 **Exchanges a thing.**] That is, swapping the specific gleaning ear for any other.

5 **Which not yet, etc.**] According to your own opinion explained in the previous chapter, paragraph 9. For Rabbi Eliezer's objection is a pure *argumentum ad hominem* <note>an argument based on the opponent's own logic</note>: it is not necessarily his own view.

6 **Grants a legal right.**] On the condition that the poor man returns the rest.

7 **Then.**] After the restoration of the stack's legal status.

# Order I. SEEDS
<columns>2</columns>

...[if they] demand [the division of the corner], and one person asks to plunder it <note>original: "diripiendum"; to grab the produce freely rather than have it measured out</note>, they listen to him, since he asks according to the Ordinance.

2. Regarding the hanging vine and the palm tree, it is otherwise. If ninety-nine demand to plunder and one person asks to divide, they listen to him, because he asks according to the Ordinance <note>In high or dangerous places like palms, formal division is preferred for safety, whereas in open fields, free plundering is often the rule</note>.

3. If someone grabs a portion of the corner and throws it over the rest of the crop, he has no right to any of it. If he throws himself upon it or spreads his cloak over it, <gloss>1</gloss> they take it away from him. The same applies to gleanings <note>original: "spicilegio"; grain fallen during harvest</note> and the forgotten sheaf <note>original: "prætermisso"</note>.

4. They do not harvest the corner with sickles, nor do they uproot it with axes, so that one person does not strike another.

5. Three <gloss>2</gloss> searches <note>original: "perquisitiones"; scheduled times for the poor to gather</note> are held during the day: morning, noon, and afternoon. Rabban Gamaliel says: This was said for no other purpose than that the searches should not be fewer. Rabbi Akiba says: For no other purpose than that they should not be more. The people of Beth-Namary used to harvest by the cord and give a corner from every row.

6. A foreigner who becomes a proselyte <note>a convert to Judaism</note> only after the field has been harvested is held exempt from the laws of gleanings, the forgotten sheaf, and the corner. Rabbi Judah thinks him bound by the law of the forgotten sheaf, because the law of the forgotten sheaf does not take effect until the sheaves are actually bundled.

7. If someone consecrates his standing crop [to the Sanctuary] and then redeems it while it is still a standing crop, he is liable [for the poor-tithes]. If he bundles the sheaves and then redeems them while they are bundled, he is liable. But if he consecrates the standing crop and redeems it only after it has been bundled, he is exempt; because at the time the obligation would have fallen upon it, it was exempt <note>Property owned by the Sanctuary is exempt from agricultural tithes</note>.

8. In the same way, if one consecrates his fruits before they have reached the time for tithing and then redeems them, they are liable. If he redeems them after they have reached the time for tithing, they are liable. But if he consecrates them before they are processed, and then redeems them from the Treasurer <note>original: "Præfecto Ærario"</note> only after they have been processed, they are considered exempt; because at the time the obligation would have fallen upon it, they were exempt.

9. If someone collects the corner and says, "*Let this be for the use of N. the poor man*," Rabbi Eliezer says he is considered to have acquired the right for him. But the Sages say he must give it to the poor man who happens by first. <gloss>3</gloss> Gleanings, the forgotten sheaf, and the corner...

<gloss>2 Searches.]</gloss> That is, the fixed times in which the opportunity to search for gleanings etc. is granted to the poor. Jewish interpreters go in various directions regarding this word. I defend my version from the Chaldean Paraphrast <note>the Targum, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note>, who paraphrases Isaiah 1:8 thus: "As a hut in a vineyard after the grape-gathering; as a lodging-bed in a cucumber field after they have <note>original Aramaic: אבעיוהי</note> searched it." Where "to gather" in a vineyard and "to seek and search" for the remains of cucumbers in a cucumber field are clearly opposed.

<column-break/>

Regarding those words of the Paraphrast, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator</note> says: "And that is the phrase of the Mishnah: Three searches are held during the day." Perhaps I might more correctly translate it as "sendings," so that the action refers to the owner, who sends the poor into the field three times a day. Thus in the Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kama 1:1, it refers to one who "sends" his beast to graze in another's field, as we shall discuss there.

<gloss>3 Gleanings, etc.]</gloss> These are commonly exempt from tithes. But if they are collected from the field of a foreigner, tithes must be paid from them; because the law of the corner, gleanings, and the forgotten sheaf does not apply to him.

10. What are gleanings <note>original: "spicilegium"; Hebrew: "leket"</note>? That which falls during reaping. If a reaper cuts a full handful, or pulls up a full fistful, and a thorn pricks him so that it falls from his hand, this belongs to the owner. Grain from the middle of the hand or the middle of the sickle belongs to the poor; from the back part of the hand or the sickle, it belongs to the owner; from the tip of the hand or the sickle, Rabbi Ishmael judges it belongs to the poor; Rabbi Akiba says it belongs to the owner.

# First Order: SEEDS (Zeraim)

3. **They shall not bring in moisture.** <note>original: "Non inducent uliginem"</note> So says Rabbi Meir. But the Sages permit it, because it is possible ******** <note>The text here is likely referencing the practice of flooding or irrigating a field, which might make the ground too muddy for the poor to gather the gleanings.</note>
4. **The head of a household** who is pressed by poverty while on a journey may take the gleanings, the forgotten sheaves, the corner of the field, and the poor man's tithe; then, upon returning home, he shall repay it. So says Rabbi Eliezer. But the Sages say: He was a poor man at that specific time <note>and therefore has no obligation to repay what was legally his to take at the moment of need</note>.
5. **If anyone** makes an exchange with the poor, what is his own remains ² exempt; what belongs to the poor remains liable. Of two people who have taken a field for ³ sharecropping, this one gives to that one the poor man’s tithes from his portion, and that one gives to this one the poor man’s tithes from his portion. ->He who<-
->reaps<-

---

1 **They bring in moisture.]** That is, they do not water the fields with moisture brought in by water-wheels, lest the gleanings <note>original: "spicilegium"; the grain left for the poor</note> be destroyed or made inaccessible. I have followed here Rabbi Daniel, an ancient interpreter and brother of the lexicographer Nathan; the Jerusalem Talmud also favors his exposition. The words of both are cited by Rabbi Nathan, but not without a serious error in the common editions. I restore the passage thus: <note>original Hebrew: "The explanation of Rabbi Daniel: 'that he shall not soak his field so much that it becomes sodden... because it harms the poor.' Jerusalem Talmud: 'A man may water his field before the poor come down into it; if his potential loss exceeds their loss, it is permitted; but if the loss to the poor exceeds his own, it is forbidden.'"</note> Rabbi Daniel explains it to mean *that a person shall not irrigate his field to the point that it is so wet that it makes other things wet, because this harms the poor.* The Jerusalem Talmud says: *A man may irrigate his field before the poor descend into it; if his loss exceeds their loss, it is permitted; but if the loss to the poor exceeds his loss, it is forbidden.* Rabbi Judah says, whether this happens or not, he places [the grain] upon a stone wall, and the poor man comes and takes what is his. Maimonides understands this passage of the Mishnah far differently; to him, the word *galgal* <note>wheel</note> here denotes "negligence" or "extra labor," regarding the rolling and additional work in performing tasks, so that one thing is done within the context of another. Furthermore, *tophah* is *traphman*, which is a type of grain, if I am not mistaken, a species of millet <note>original: "melica"</note>, which is discussed below in VI. 7. Thus the words would mean: "They do not reap millet together," namely with other grain. He believes this is forbidden lest the gleanings of the millet—that is, the inferior species—fall, and thus the poor suffer a loss. It can scarcely be said how feeble this commentary is. This paragraph is clearly mutilated at the end, though the Jews are too dull to perceive it.

2 **Exempt]** From tithes, because it belonged to the poor, and therefore was free from the obligation of tithes <note>The "poor man's share" was already considered "taxed" by the fact that it was designated for charity</note>.

3 **sharecropping.]** <note>original: "culturam partiariam"</note> Among the Jews, just as among the Romans, there are two kinds of tenants: those who rent a field to be cultivated for a fixed payment, and those who rent it for a specific share of the produce. The former, who return a determined payment to the owner, are called *chocherim* or *chakirim* if the payment is in crops, and the payment is called *chikor*; if the payment is in counted money, the tenant is a *shocher* and the payment *sechirut*. Hence that saying cited by Rabbi Nathan from the Title *Demai*: <note>original Hebrew: "What is the difference between a *shocher* and a *chocher*? The *shocher* pays in coins and the *chocher* in fruit."</note> These words do not appear in the Mishnah, but in the Baraita of that Title, as they are cited from there by the *Maggid Mishnah* to Maimonides' *Laws of Hiring*, VIII. 1. Both are rightly included by Roman legal experts under the name of "colonists" who cultivate for money. See the Law "If bees" in the Digests, *On Thefts*, where one may consult Dionysius Gothofredus. For the sake of distinction, we always use *rent-paying tenants* for *chocherim*, and *money-paying tenants* for *shocherim*. Those who cultivate for shares are called *arissin*, *Colonists*, or *sharecropping redeemers*, as Cato speaks in *On Agriculture*, 137, who pay a certain portion of the produce to the master of the estate. Such were those "farmers" <note>original Greek: "geōrgoi"</note> of the Gospel parable in Matthew 21:33, and in the parallel passages of Mark and Luke. The Chaldean-Samaritan interpreter puts this word for *Issachar* in Genesis 49:15.
<image-desc>Decorative Samaritan script characters for the name Issachar (יששכר)</image-desc>
The Latin interpreter clumsily translated this as: *And he was a shepherd to the guests.* I translate: *And he became a tax-paying tenant.* For *pelacha* here is a "Tenant," just as elsewhere in the same Interpreter the verb <image-desc>Samaritan characters for the verb root "plh" (to serve/till)</image-desc> is "to cultivate" (Deuteronomy 28:39) and <image-desc>Samaritan characters for a derivative noun</image-desc> is "agriculture" (Genesis 9:20). However, <image-desc>Samaritan characters</image-desc> determines the species, so that he is a *Sharecropping* or *tax-paying tenant*. See also Deuteronomy 20:11. Similarly, among the Arabs, *Aris* and *Arisi* seem to be this kind of tenant, although Phiruzabadius explains *Aris* simply as a "farmer." The verb in the second conjugation, *arriza*, means to take on such a tenant, that is, "he employed him as an *Aris*," as the same author of the *Camus* dictionary states, which the famous Golius seems not to have understood sufficiently; at least he does not express it adequately when he explains it thus: *He sought the work and service of someone, and made use of it.* For *Aris*...

...contracted for the reaping, he is forbidden from the gleanings, the forgotten sheaves, the corner of the field, and the poor man’s tithes. But when is this the case? asks Rabbi Judah. If he contracted for a half, a third, or a fourth part of the yield. If they agreed thus: "A third part <gloss>1</gloss> of what you reap shall be yours," then the gleanings, the forgotten sheaves, and the corner are considered permitted to him; however, he is forbidden from the poor man’s tithes.

6. If anyone sells a field <gloss>2</gloss>, the gleanings are permitted to the seller <note>because he has now become poor by losing his land</note>, but forbidden to the buyer. No one shall hire a laborer on the condition that his son may glean after him. Whoever does not allow the poor to glean, or allows one but not another, or helps one of them to the exclusion of others, robs the poor. Concerning this, it is said (Proverbs 22:28 & 23:10): "Do not move back the boundary <gloss>3</gloss> of those who ascend."

A sheaf which the laborers forgot, but not the owner; or which the owner forgot, but not the laborers; or a sheaf before which the poor stood, or which they covered with straw, is not considered a "forgotten sheaf" <note>Hebrew: *Shikh’chah*; these laws require the sheaf to be truly overlooked by everyone to qualify as poor-relief</note>.

From this comes our term *Arisut* <gloss>sharecropping: which elsewhere is called</gloss> *Kablanut*; just as *Kablanuta* and *Kablanut* <gloss>sharecropping, and contracting for a fixed payment</gloss> are contrasted in the Babylonian Gemara, *Baba Metzia* 104a. <gloss>From which also come</gloss> *Kablan* and *Mekabbel* <gloss>a tenant or sharecropping contractor.</gloss> Although the term sometimes has a broader meaning and is correctly applied to all kinds of hiring. It does not escape me that Rabbi Tanchum defined the *Mekabbel* type of tenant as different from the *Aris*, with this distinction: the *Aris* is a tenant to whom the landowner promises a certain portion of the produce as wages, while the owner provides the costs of cultivation and improvement; so that perhaps you might not incorrectly understand him as a <term>Bailiff</term> <note>A manager who oversees the land for a share of the crop</note>. The *Mekabbel* is one who contracted to cultivate the field on the condition that he pays a certain portion of the crops to the owner, but he himself bears all the costs of cultivation and improvement. But I do not know on what authority of the ancients these distinctions rest. Certainly, I have learned through experience that it is not always safe to trust Rabbi Tanchum. Read, if you please, *Demai* VI and the Jerusalem Gemara there; *Baba Metzia* IX; Maimonides' *Laws of Hiring* VIII and on *Bikkurim* I.2; also Rabbi Nathan in the entry *Chakar*, besides more recent authors. As for the origin of the word *Aris*, I by no means approve of the opinion of Musaphia, who wants it to be Greek, and to denote <term>guardian</term> in that language. He means, if I am not mistaken, Homer’s *ouros* <note>guardian or watcher</note>. But this is too far-fetched. Rabbi Nathan brings *Aris* instead of *Arisi* from *Baba Batra* 46b (not 42, as incorrectly noted in the manuscripts); and it is from here that Cohen de Lara compares it with the Arabic *gharīs* and explains it as <term>steward</term>. But *gharīs* never means <term>steward</term> to the Arabs: although...

1 <gloss>Of what you reap.</gloss>] So that the right falls to him only after the harvest: while the crops are still attached to the earth, he has no claim.

2 <gloss>Sells.</gloss>] And thus becomes poor <note>thereby qualifying to take the gleanings from the land he once owned</note>.

From here Columella <note>a Roman writer on agriculture, c. 4–70 AD</note> says: 
> Grain can also be kept buried, as in certain provinces across the sea, where the earth, dug out in the manner of wells which they call **siroi**, receives the fruits it has produced.

# Order I. SEEDS (Zeraim)

...regarding that, it is not considered forgotten: from there into the threshing floor, it is granted as forgotten. If one gathers it into a heap, it is granted as forgotten: from there into the threshing floor, it is not granted. This is the general rule: If one gathers into a place where the work is finished, it is granted as forgotten; from there into the threshing floor, it is not granted. Into a place where the work is not finished, it is not granted as forgotten; from there into the threshing floor, it is granted.

## C H A P T E R  VI.

1. The School of Shammai say: Property gathered for the poor in common ¹ is communal. Against them, the School of Hillel do not judge it to be communal unless it is also communal for the rich, like the Sabbatical year <note>A year when all land is left fallow and its produce is free for everyone</note>. If individual sheaves in a field are of one *cab* [a measure of volume] each, except for one which contains four *cabs*, and that one is forgotten, the Shammaites say it is not considered "forgotten." The Hillelites judge it to be "forgotten."

2. A sheaf left by oversight near ² a gate, a heap, oxen, or tools: the Shammaites say, ³ it is not considered forgotten. The Hillelites judge it to be forgotten.

3. The beginnings of rows are identified by the sheaf which is opposite ⁴ them. A sheaf that had been picked up to be carried into the city, if it is subsequently left by oversight, they agree that it is not considered forgotten.

4. This is how the starts of rows are determined. When two people begin from the middle of a row, one facing north and the other facing south, if they leave something behind by oversight both in front and behind: what is in front is considered forgotten; what is behind, ⁵ is not considered forgotten.

From this comes <term>kumrah</term> <note>Arabic: *kmrh*</note>, a rounded mass of dates. A rounder heap of sand or earth: as Golius elegantly and faithfully expresses "Camulum." Next follows <term>hurar</term> <note>Hebrew: *ḥurar*</note>, i.e., a cake. Here, however, a "cake-like" <note>Greek: *plakentōdēs*</note> heap is understood.

2 *Gate.*] <term>geder</term> <note>Hebrew: *geder*</note> according to Maimonides is "the entrance of the path" <note>Arabic: *mulaj al-dariqa*</note>, a gate of a garden, specifically wider and lower, suited for carriages. Rabbi Judah Harizius, who expressed Maimonides' preface to this Order and the commentary on the first five Titles in Hebrew, ineptly translated this as "the gate of the circle" <note>Hebrew: *sha'ar ha-agulah*</note>. <meta>This page continues the legal analysis of Tractate Peah from the Mishnah, specifically the laws of Shikh’chah (the "forgotten sheaf"). It builds on the previous definitions of when a sheaf is legally considered "forgotten" and thus belongs to the poor, versus when it remains the property of the owner.</meta>

# Title II. PEAH (The Corner)

If a single worker starts from the beginning of a row and forgets something—whether it be ahead of him or behind him—what is ahead is not considered "forgotten," but what is behind is considered "forgotten" because it falls under the prohibition in Deuteronomy 24:19, *you shall not return* <note>original Latin: "non reverteris"</note>. This is the general rule: Whatever is covered by the prohibition "you shall not return" is considered forgotten; whatever is not covered by it is not considered forgotten.

<margin>1 Bundles</margin>
<margin>2 Grape-gleanings</margin>
5. Two sheaves are considered "forgotten," but three are not. Two heaps of olives or carobs are considered "forgotten," but three are not. Two bundles <margin>1 Bundles</margin> of flax are considered "forgotten," but three are not. Two individual grapes are considered "grape-gleanings" <margin>2 Grape-gleanings</margin> <note>Hebrew: *peret*</note>, but three are not. Two ears of grain are considered "grain-gleanings" <note>Hebrew: *leket*</note>, but three are not. This is according to the School of Hillel. However, regarding all of these, the School of Shammai says: Three items belong to the poor, and four belong to the owner.

6. A sheaf containing two *se'ah* <note>original Latin: "sata," referring to the Hebrew unit of volume, the *se'ah*</note> left by oversight is not considered "forgotten." Regarding two sheaves that together contain two *se'ah*, Rabban Gamaliel says they are considered to belong to the owner. But the Sages maintain they belong to the poor. Rabban Gamaliel asked: "Does a larger number of sheaves make the owner's condition better or worse?" They admitted it makes it better <note>meaning the more grain there is, the less likely it is to be legally abandoned</note>. He replied: "Therefore, if a single sheaf containing two *se'ah* is not considered forgotten when left behind, is it not right that two sheaves which together contain two *se'ah* should also not be considered forgotten?" They answered: "Not at all. If you say that of a single sheaf, which is like a large stack, would you say the same of two sheaves, which are merely like small bundles?"

7. A crop that contains two *se'ah* left by oversight is not considered "forgotten." If it does not contain two *se'ah*, but is of such a size that it would...

---

<columns>2</columns>

1 **Bundles** <note>original: "Fasces"</note>.] The printed codes should be corrected, as they contain [Hebrew: הזוצי]; which the more recent commentators also read. This is a nonsense word. Rabbi Nathan formerly read [Hebrew: חצני]; and so do the Maimonides manuscript and Rabbi Tanchum. Now [Hebrew: *chezen*] is a word well known from the Bible, although I do not know if it has been sufficiently explained. Setting aside the interpretations of others, the true meaning of the word is clear from the Arabic language, where [Arabic: *hizn*] is defined by their critics as *the part of the body below the armpit, that is, the flank*. From this comes the Arabic [Arabic: *ihtazana*], meaning to carry a thing held against that part of the body—that is, under the armpit, between the arm and the side. Hence also the Arabic [Arabic: *hizn*] and in

<column-break/>

Hebrew [Hebrew: חצן, *chezen*] is the place between the arm and the side where it is so carried. Psalm 129:7: *nor he who binds sheaves his "chezen."* The Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> has "armpit" there, and Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] uses the vernacular [Old French: "aissela"], which is very close to the meaning. Finally, for us here, [Hebrew: *chezen*] means a bundle—specifically, as much as someone can carry under their arm. And the Arabs also use their [Arabic: *hizn*] in this way. Zamakhshari <note>A medieval scholar of Arabic</note> says: *He gave him a "hizn" of grain, that is, the amount he could carry between his arm and his side.*

2 **Grape-gleanings** <note>original: "Acinilegio"</note>.] [Hebrew: *Peret*] properly refers to individual grapes, or at most a pair, which are shaken off during the vintage. Hence the Seventy [the Septuagint translators] for *peret* in Leviticus 19:10 simply put the Greek [Greek: ῥῶγας, *rhogas*] <note>meaning fallen grapes</note>.

It also includes a detailed linguistic study of the Hebrew word for a "bundle" of grain, drawing on Arabic and biblical precedents.</summary>

# Order I. ZERAIM (Seeds)

...ought to make two measures <note>original Latin: "fata," likely referring to the legal quantity of two se'ahs</note>, even if it is <gloss>1</gloss> of *typha* <note>original: "typhæ." A poorly identified grain, possibly wild oats or a type of poor-quality barley.</note>; they hold it in the same category as if it were a barley harvest.

8. A standing crop <gloss>2</gloss> exempts the sheaf and the harvest. A sheaf does not exempt either a sheaf or the standing crop. What kind of standing crop exempts a sheaf? Any that is not considered overlooked, or even a single stalk.

9. A measure <note>original Latin: "Satum," referring to the Hebrew unit, the se'ah</note> of uprooted grain and a measure of grain not yet uprooted (and similarly with trees, garlic, and onions) are not combined [<gloss>3</gloss> to make up two measures, but instead they yield to the poor.] Rabbi Joses says: If the ownership of the poor intervenes <note>i.e., if the poor have already acquired a right to part of it</note>, they are not combined; otherwise, they are combined.

10. Regarding grain cut for fodder, or into <gloss>4</gloss> bundles; and likewise concerning <gloss>5</gloss> bundles of garlic, and also bundles of garlic and onions; these are not subject to the law of the "forgotten" sheaf. Regarding all things hidden in the soil, such as <gloss>6</gloss> arum <note>a tuberous plant, *Arum palaestinum*</note>, garlic,

---

<margin>1 Typha.]</margin> Wherever the term <term>Tofah</term> <note>original Hebrew: טופה</note> occurs, Maimonides <note>A preeminent 12th-century Jewish scholar and philosopher</note> understands it as the <term>Kartaman</term> <note>original Arabic: קרטמאן; safflower</note> of the Physicians. Above at Chapter 5, Section 3, and at *Tebul Yom* 1.2, he wishes it to be a grain whose properties closely approach barley. Here, it is so unfruitful that a very large area produces few seeds, with almost everything turning into straw and wood. Regarding *Kilayim* 1.1, he describes it as a white, round grain, difficult to break, naturally approaching barley. Regarding *Shebiit* 9.4, he says it grows spontaneously without cultivation. He seems to mean a species of millet or sorghum, which Pierre Belon <note>A 16th-century French naturalist</note> notes is called *hareoman* by the Arabs. He should have said *hartoman*. Indeed, <term>hartoman</term> <note>original Arabic: هرطمان</note> and <term>kartaman</term> <note>original Arabic: قرطمان</note> are the same, as the Beitharides and the author of the *Malayesæ* teach in express words. In Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and famous physician</note>, it is incorrectly read as *hazaratman*, for which Gerard of Cremona <note>A 12th-century translator of Arabic scientific works</note> has *hareoman*, even more corruptly. Perhaps Belon's *hareoman* came from there. Without doubt, Avicenna wrote *hartoman*. And so it is in Ebn Jazla. Thus also Bellunensis and Plempius. However, what exactly *hartoman* or *kartaman* is, is not well agreed upon among the Arabs. Beitharides applies the description of *bromos* <note>oats</note> from Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> Book II. Ebn Al-Cabatius in the *Malayesæ* more accurately says, as it seems: <note>original Arabic: هو حب يشبه الجلبان وبعضهم يجعله جلبانا وليس كذلك لان الهرطمان فيه حمرة وسواد وذلك يشوبه غيره ونباته كالحنطة وثمرته في غلف مقسومة نصفين</note> "It is a grain resembling the chickpea, and some treat it as a chickpea, but it is not so because the *hartoman* has redness and blackness in it, and other colors are lightly mixed with it; the stalk is like that of wheat, and the fruit is in pods divided in two."

It is a grain similar to a pea, which some indeed take for a pea. But the matter is otherwise. For *Hartoman* is distinguished by redness and blackness, with other colors lightly mixed in; the stalk is like that of wheat; the fruit is in 

<column-break/>

divided pods. And indeed <term>Chiltit</term> <note>Hebrew: חלתית, asafetida</note> is in some places in the Mishnah attributed to the grain genus, as here; elsewhere to the legume genus, as in *Kilayim* 1.1. This seems to be the reason why Maimonides wanted it to be *kartaman*; because it reflects both genera in some way. But he would hardly persuade me of this. Certainly, if its stalk is like grain, it seems hardly possible that in *Kilayim* 1.1 it would not be held as a different genus from legumes. For this reason, I think that opinion of Maimonides, which he brings up so often, should be rejected. Here it seems to be taken for a degenerate barley. I have put "Typhani"; whether rightly or wrongly I do not quite know. But the sound matches: and so Musaphias and Cohen de Lara explain it. In the Jerusalem Talmud, <term>miltah</term> <note>Hebrew: מילתה</note> is put for <term>tofah</term>, but I do not know what that is. I shall assert that the passage in modern codices is not quite sound regarding *Kilayim* 1.1.

<margin>2 Exempts.]</margin> Frees from the danger of being considered "forgotten."

<margin>3 To make up two.]</margin> So that they are not liable to the law of the "forgotten"; for whatever equals two measures is not held by that law. Truly, the words included in brackets are absent from the Jerusalem Talmud and from the manuscript. They seem to have crept in from a gloss.

<margin>4 Bundles.]</margin> Maimonides says "small bundles." Less correctly.

<margin>5 Bundles.]</margin> <term>Agidi</term> <note>Hebrew: אגידי</note>. Maimonides interprets this as many garlic stalks rising from the same root and naturally joined. And this is without precedent. <term>Agidim</term>, or as it is better read in the Jerusalem Talmud, <term>Iggudim</term>, are bundles. Rabbi Nathan from Tractate *Sukkah* says, "the bundle was loosened" <note>original: איגודו הותר</note> referring to the <term>eiresione</term> <note>original Greek: εἰρεσιώνη, a laurel or olive branch wound with wool</note>, which they are accustomed to carry in the Festival of Tabernacles.

<margin>6 Arum.]</margin> The word <term>Luf</term> <note>Hebrew: לוף</note> recurs a hundred times in the Mishnah; and yet the Jews do not know what it is. Maimonides does not doubt it is a species of onion. Hence Rabbi Tanchum says: "It is a species of the varieties of wild onion"; not knowing that elsewhere one also reads <term>Luf Shoteh</term>, the "foolish" or "wild" arum, to distinguish it from the garden variety. He adds: "Although there are those who take it for colocasia [taro], because it is eaten as that is eaten... and it is said to be the bulb of the squill." But *Luf* is arum; Dioscorides calls it <note>original Greek: Ἄρον τὸ</note> "The Arum..."

# Title II. PEAH (The Corner of the Field)

...with garlic and onions. Rabbi Judah says: it is not considered overlooked. The Sages, however, maintain that it is considered overlooked.

II. If anyone reaps by night, or binds sheaves [at night], or if a blind man reaps, the law of the forgotten sheaf <note>original: "prætermissum," referring to the Hebrew *Shikh'chah*</note> applies. But if he intended to pick only the larger specimens <note>original Latin: "crassiuscule delibare," to select the thickest</note>, the law of the forgotten sheaf does not apply to it. If he said, $^1$ *“I am reaping on this condition: that if I overlook anything and pass it by, I shall later come back to take it,”* the law of the forgotten sheaf still applies to it <note>Because one cannot make a private agreement to bypass the laws of the Torah regarding the poor</note>.

->CHAPTER VII.<-

I. Any olive tree that has achieved fame in the field, $^2$ such as a Netophathite olive <note>A famous variety from Netophah, near Bethlehem</note> in its season, if it is left behind through forgetfulness, it is nevertheless not regarded as "overlooked" <note>This is because its distinctiveness makes it unlikely to be truly forgotten; it remains the owner's property</note>. In what sense are these distinctions made? Namely, by its name, its yield, or its location. By name: such as a Saphconite or $^3$ Besanite tree. By yield: such as being exceptionally fruitful. By location: such as being placed...

<columns>2</columns>

...called by the Syrians *lephia* <note>original Greek: "καλεύμον παρὰ Σύροις λέφια"</note>. *Luph* <note>original Arabic: لوف</note>, which is what the Arabs also call *arum* <note>a tuberous plant, *Arum palaestinum*</note>. Their ancient physicians describe two species, the smooth and the curled, the latter being the *dracontium* of the Greeks, the former the *arum*. This is the view of Ibn Jazla and Avicenna <note>Famous medieval Persian/Arabic physicians</note>. So too say the Arabic encyclopedist Serapio and many others cited by him. More recent writers, like Ibn al-Khabaz in *Malayefa* and Beitharides, add a third species: the *arisarum* of Dioscorides. However, Abi-Hanifa and others in the *Pandects* simply define *Luph* as *Arum*. The *dracontium* is called *Luph al-hayya* <note>Arabic: لوف الحية, literally "serpent’s arum"</note>. From this, some in the circle of Rabbi Tanchum explain *Luph* as *Colocasia* <note>The Taro root</note>. So too does Rabbi Daniel, the brother of the lexicographer Nathan, whom he perhaps follows. Understand "colocasia" here not as the one described by Dioscorides (which is the true Egyptian bean growing in the Nile and not a bulbous plant), but the bulbous type mentioned by Palladius, Aetius, and other ancients, which common herbalists describe as being very similar to arum, or perhaps the arum itself. A spurious note in Dioscorides regarding arum says: *“the Cypriots also call it kolokasion”* <note>original Greek: "οἱ δὲ Κύπριοι καὶ κολονάσιον λέγουσι"</note>. Beitharides writes: *“It is said that 'Elephant’s Ear' is colocasia, and it is also said to be the large luph, that is, the dracontium; the latter is more correct.”* Beitharides wants "Elephant's Ear" to be the *dracontium*, and says it is called *Fil-gush* in Greek <note>Note: This is an error in the original text; it is actually Persian</note>. But according to Ibn Jazla, *Fil-gush* encompasses both types of *Luph*: arum and dracontium. The word is not Greek, but Persian. Zein al-Attar, a Persian, says: *Fil-gush in Persian is Bil-lush,*

<column-break/>

*...they call it; but it is Luph* <note>original Persian: خوانند وان لوفست i.e. Persice فيلجوش i.e. aurem elephantis vocant; est autem لوف</note>. Indeed, the leaves of the arum look quite a bit like elephant ears. This, then, was why some called it colocasia—a name Beitharides does not approve of. He was unaware of the bulbous colocasia, which is a species of arum; he only describes the aquatic kind, which differs from arum as much as the whole sky. Now, as for the fact that in the Mishnah *Luph* almost always appears joined with garlic and onions, this also fits arum well. Aetius says of his colocasia (the arum species): *“the power of its roots is very similar to leeks and onions”* <note>original Greek: "παραπλησία ταύτης ἡ ῥίζας ἡ δυνάμίς ἐστι ταῖς γηθυλίσι, καὶ κρομμύοις"</note>. Abu-Hanifa al-Dinawari, cited in Serapio regarding arum, says: *“it has a bulb like the bulb of a squill”* <note>original Arabic: "وله بصل شبيه ببصل العنصل"</note>. In the Medical Glosses, *colocasia* is defined as *a bulb, or a squill-onion*. Hence, the authority praised by Rabbi Tanchum correctly identified it as a type of squill.

1 *On this condition.*] Since a condition of this sort is deemed void as being contrary to the Law. The rule of law is: *“If anyone makes a condition against what is written in the Torah, the condition is void.”* <note>original Hebrew: "כל המתנה על מה שכתוב בתורה תנאו בטל"</note>.
2 *Such as.*] In some editions, the word *Afilu* <note>“even”</note> is read, but it should be deleted, as neither the manuscript nor Maimonides recognizes it. It likely crept in from the following paragraph.
3 *Besanæa.*] The Jews interpret these words as descriptive names, somewhat ridiculously. I am uncertain about the "Saphconite." However, "Besanite" is a local designation from Beth-Shean, which the famous Arabic geographers al-Idrisi and Abulfeda call *Beisan* (dropping the 'b' sound). So too in the Jerusalem Talmud (Megillah 73d), the *Bishnai* are the people of Beth-Shean, or Scythopolis <note>A major city of the Decapolis in the Roman period</note>. The other Talmud (Megillah 24b) says: *“A man from Haifa or Beth-Shean should not lift up his hands”* <note>in the priestly blessing, due to their distinct dialect</note>.
