# Order I. SEEDS (Zeraim)

<columns>

...located near a winepress, or near a broken fence. Regarding all other olive trees: two [left behind] are considered "overlooked" <note>Hebrew: *Shikh'chah*</note>; but three are not considered overlooked <note>Jewish law generally rules that a single item or a pair might be forgotten by accident, but three items constitute a distinct group that the owner likely intended to return for</note>. Rabbi Jose says: The law of the forgotten sheaf does not apply to olives.

2. An olive tree that is found standing between $^1$ three rows of two garden plots, if it is left behind through forgetfulness, is nonetheless not considered "overlooked." An olive tree that yields two *seahs* <note>a dry measure of volume</note>, if it is left behind through forgetfulness, is not considered "overlooked." In what sense are these things said? As long as the harvest has not yet begun. But if the harvest has begun, whatever happens is like the Netophathite olive in its season: if left behind through forgetfulness, it is considered "overlooked." As long as any of the harvest $^2$ remains for him [the owner] beneath the olive tree, it remains also at the top. Rabbi Meir says: $^3$ from the moment the beating rod has departed.

3. What is the $^4$ gleaning of berries? <note>original Latin: *acinilegium*, referring to the Hebrew *Peret*</note> It is whatever falls off during the time of the vintage. If a harvester picks a cluster of grapes, and it becomes entangled in the leaves and falls from his hand to the ground and is broken, it still belongs to the owner. He who places a basket under the vine at the time he performs the vintage is robbing the poor. Regarding this matter it is said (Proverbs 22:28 and 23:10): *Do not move back the boundary of $^5$ those who come up.* <note>The Hebrew text of Proverbs refers to the "ancient boundary," but the commentator here interprets "Olam" (ancient/eternal) as "Olim" (those who come up), meaning the poor who come up to the fields to collect their dues</note>

4. What is a $^6$ stunted cluster? <note>original Latin: *racemus*, referring to the Hebrew *Ollelot*</note> A cluster of grapes that lacks a $^7$ "shoulder" and a $^8$ "pendant." If it has a shoulder or a pendant, it belongs to the owner; if there is a doubt, it belongs to the poor. A stunted cluster that is cut down along with a full cluster on the same branch belongs to the owner; otherwise, it belongs to the poor. Rabbi Judah considers a single berry to be a cluster; the Sages consider it a stunted cluster.

5. He who thins out his vines: just as he thins his own portion, so he may thin the portion of the poor. Such is the opinion of Rabbi Judah. Rabbi Meir says: He is permitted in his own portion, but in the portion of the poor, it is not allowed.

6. $^1$ Vi-

<column-break/>

**Notes and Commentary:**

*A man from Hifa or Bethshean shall not lift his hands:* <note>original: "Hifaneus, vel Besanaus non elevabit manus"</note> that is, he shall not pronounce the priestly blessing from the platform. Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] explains there: A priest from the inhabitants of *Hifa*, or from the inhabitants of *Bethshean* <note>These residents were barred from leading the blessing because their Galilean accent failed to distinguish between certain guttural Hebrew letters, which could change the meaning of the prayer</note>. Indeed, in the Gemara itself it follows immediately: *They do not allow the men of Bethshean or the men of Beth-Hifa to pass before the Ark.* That town is in the region of the Decapolis. But the olives of the Decapolis were also commended by Pliny. The Decapolis of Syria is very small, and though its capers are no larger than a piece of meat, they are nevertheless commended for their oil. This is how Dalechamp reads the passage.

1 *Three rows of two garden plots.*] That is, in the middle of three rows, between which are two plots, in this manner:

<image-desc>A text-based diagram illustrating tree placement in an olive grove. It consists of three rows of characters. Top row: eight circles (o). Middle row: four circles, an asterisk (*), then three circles. Bottom row: eight circles. The asterisk represents an untouched olive tree amidst the rows.</image-desc>

where the letters o o etc. arranged in lines designate the rows of olive trees; the spaces between the lines represent the garden plots; the asterisk represents an olive tree left untouched by the harvester. This is not considered "overlooked" because it is so covered on all sides by the remaining trees that it easily escapes the harvester’s diligence. See above, V. 7.

2 *For him.*] The owner.

3 *From the moment.*] From then on, nothing remains for the owner; but everything that is left over passes to the poor.

4 *Whatever falls off.*] Understand this as individual berries, according to what was said above, VI. 5. Hence for the Hebrew word *Nesher* [falling], the Chaldeans and the Syrian use *Netar*, meaning "a falling away."

5 *Those who come up.*] See above, V. 6.

6 *Stunted cluster.*] The "stunted cluster" <note>Ollelot</note> and the "cluster" <note>Eshkol</note> differ in the same way as the Greek terms *epiphyllis* [small secondary cluster] and *botrys* [main cluster], as is evident from the Glosses of Cyril. The main clusters are larger and have thicker berries; the stunted clusters are smaller and thinner. This is why Pliny refers to the "most cluster-filled" Columbine vine (following Turnebus's correction), because that kind of vine mostly produces "racemes," that is, sparse clusters. Columella, Book III, chapter 18: *From which the shoots sprout, either sterile or certainly less fruitful, which the peasants call "racemiarios" [cluster-bearers].* Correctly, therefore, I use "stunted cluster" <note>racemum</note> for the Hebrew *Ollelot*, following the Latin Vulgate, and "cluster" <note>uvam</note> for the Hebrew *Eshkol*. Since for the Jews these differ in like manner. Hence *Ollel* is the verb for "to glean stunted clusters," that is, to gather the *epiphyllides*.

7 *Shoulder.*] This is what they call the small clusters <note>Greek: botrydia</note> projecting crowded together on the upper stalk of the grape cluster.

8 *Pendant.*] <note>original Latin: "stiria," meaning icicle or drop</note> So that the berries joined together on the lower part of the stalk present the appearance of a pendant or icicle.

</columns>

# Title II. PEAH

6. <note>original: *Vineæ quadrimæ*</note> Four-year-old vines: The Shammaites <note>a school of Jewish law known for stricter interpretations</note> think there is no need for a "fifth" <note>an additional 20% payment when redeeming the fruit's value</note> or for a *polluctura* <note>a sacred meal or sacrificial offering</note>. The Hillelites <note>a more lenient school of law</note> think it is necessary. The Shammaites think that the fallen berries and the defective clusters belong to the owner, but the poor may <margin>2. **Redeem.** For common use, after setting aside a price to be spent on food and drink in Jerusalem.</margin> redeem them for themselves. The Hillelites want the <margin>3. **Whole harvest to go.** To the owner, with no portion going to the poor. They consider it "God's property" <note>Hebrew: *Mammon Gavoah*</note>, and therefore the poor have no legal right to claim it.</margin> whole harvest to go to the winepress.

7. In a vineyard that consists entirely of defective clusters <note>Hebrew: *Ollelot*; clusters that lack the usual structure of a grape bunch</note>, Rabbi Eliezer says it belongs to the owner. Rabbi Akiba says it belongs to the poor. Rabbi Eliezer said: *When you harvest your vineyard, you shall not go back for the clusters* (Deuteronomy 24:21). If there is no harvest <note>meaning no normal clusters</note>, how can there be gleanings? To him, Rabbi Akiba replied: *You shall not glean your vineyard* (Leviticus 19:10), even if the whole thing is made of gleanings. If so, why does the scripture say, *When you harvest your vineyard, you shall not go back for the clusters*? It is to ensure the poor do not claim the gleanings before the main harvest begins.

8. If someone consecrates a vineyard to the Temple before the defective clusters can be identified, the clusters do not belong to the poor; but if he consecrates it after they are identified, the clusters are <margin>4. **Considered the poor’s.** Because of the legal rule: *No man can consecrate a thing which is not his own* <note>Hebrew: *Ein adam makdish davar she-eino shelo*</note>.</margin> considered to belong to the poor. Rabbi Jose says: The poor must still pay the price of the growth <note>the value added as the grapes ripened while consecrated</note> to the Sanctuary. What is considered "overlooked" on a vine-trellis <note>vines grown on a raised frame or pergola</note>? <margin>5. **Whatever cannot.** Whatever is passed over in such a way</margin> whatever cannot be picked with an outstretched hand. In <margin>6. **Ground vines.** Those that spread across the earth; called "prostrate" by the Roman writer Columella.</margin> ground vines, however, it is considered overlooked <margin>7. **As soon as the harvester.** That is, whatever remains is taken as being "overlooked."</margin> as soon as the harvester has moved away from the vine.

### CHAPTER VIII.

1. At what time does the right to collect gleanings <note>Hebrew: *Leket*</note> belong <margin>8. **To everyone.** To both the rich and the poor alike, becoming the property of whoever finds it first.</margin> to everyone? From the time the <margin>9. **Late gleaners.** This is how the Jews explain the word *Nemoshot*. Maimonides says: "They are the remnants... who gather after the first gatherers; they are compared to the elderly because they are slow and find very little." The Gemara <note>the part of the Talmud that comments on the Mishnah</note> asks: *Who are the late gleaners?* Rabbi Jochanan says: *Old men who walk leaning on a staff.* Resh Lakish says: *Those who glean after the first group of gleaners.*</margin> late gleaners have departed. As for the fallen berries and defective clusters, it is as soon as the poor who entered the vineyard have returned.

<columns>2</columns>

1. **Four-year-old vines.** Trees are considered "uncircumcised" <note>Hebrew: *Orlah*; Greek: *aperitmētos*</note> for three years after planting, according to the law in Leviticus 19:24. During that time, the fruit they produce is forbidden. Only in the fourth year are they considered sacred to God, so that they may be eaten in holiness in Jerusalem. For this reason, the Hillelites want the fruit of a four-year-old vine to follow the rules of the "Second Tithe," meaning a fifth of the value is added when it is redeemed; they also want them to be entirely removed from the house during the "Removal of Tithes" at the end of the third and sixth years of the seven-year cycle (the day before Passover). See Tractate *Maaser Sheni* Chapter 5, where this paragraph appears again.

<column-break/>

fit, that it cannot &c.

# Order I. ZERAIM <note>Seeds</note>

...they remain. $^1$ Regarding olives: when the $^2$ second rain has already fallen. Judah says: Are there not some people who do not beat their olives until after the second rain? Truly, it is only then, when a poor person goes out, that he does not bring back $^3$ four *assarion* <note>original: *quaterna affaria*; small Roman coins of low value</note> worth.

2. $^4$ They are held to be trustworthy concerning gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner of the field during their proper season; and concerning the tithes of the poor throughout $^5$ their designated year. A Levite has

---

other gleaners. You have the same in *Baba Metzia* 21b. Benjamin Musaphia <note>A 17th-century Jewish scholar and physician</note> thinks the word <term>הנמשת</term> <note>original: *ha-nimset*</note> is Greek, by which is signified <term>one who eats and then returns the food into his mouth to eat it time after time</term> <note>original: *ha-okhel ve-chozer ha-okhel le-tokh piv ve-okhel pa'am acher pa'am*</note>, *that is, one who chews and brings it back into the mouth and eats a second time, i.e.,* <note>original: ἀναμασώμενος</note> *ruminating*. Thus, it is used metaphorically to denote old people, who only perform their gleaning after others have finished. You see into what trifles more recent Jews have fallen through ignorance of the Mishnaic dialect. Quite simply, Pomarius <note>A lexicographer</note> says <term>נמש</term> <note>original: *namash*</note> becomes <term>searching for a thing as they do in gleaning</term> <note>original: *namash bikesh kemo she-osin be-leket*</note>, *which means to seek out, as they do in gleaning.* Hence he explains <term>נמשא</term> <note>original: *namsha*</note> as *Collector, he who goes searching.* However, <term>נמשות</term> <note>original: *nemashot*</note> is the plural of a masculine form like *reshuyot* <note>authorities</note>, *lakuchot* <note>purchases</note>, *derorot* <note>liberties</note>, etc., which were omitted by the Grammarians. Furthermore, the Jerusalem Talmud notes that others read <term>ממשות</term> <note>original: *mamashot*; tangible things</note> in this place.

1 *Regarding olives.*] Regarding the gleanings of olives.

2 *Second rain.*] See what we discuss on this matter below at *Nedarim* VIII. 5.

3 *four assarion.*] Gleanings that are worth that much.

4 *They are held to be trustworthy.*] The poor: so that if at harvest time they bring the crops they have as gleanings, forgotten sheaves, or the corner portion, they are considered exempt from tithes.

5 *In his year.*] The third or sixth year of the <term>Heptaeteris</term> <note>the seven-year Sabbatical cycle</note>, when the tithes of the poor take the place of the "second tithes." For in these years, according to the constant and perpetual opinion of the Jewish legal experts, the second tithes are converted into the tithes of the poor. Thus Maimonides teaches in the clearest words in *Laws of the Gifts to the Poor* VI. 4, and in his commentary on *Demai* IV. 3, *Maaser* II. 11, and frequently elsewhere; as does Moses of Coucy in *Positive Precept* 136—to pass over a dense line of other more recent authors. Moreover, this same opinion was preceded by legal books of the highest authority among them, such as the *Sifre* and *Pesikta Zotarta* on the passage in Deuteronomy 14:28, and the Babylonian Gemara in *Rosh Hashanah* 12b. And this same doctrine is clearly enough suggested in the Mishnah itself, *Yadayim* IV. 3. Therefore, Joseph Scaliger <note>A famous French Renaissance scholar</note> is most gravely mistaken—hallucinating, as it were—who, in his short work on the tithes of the Jews, wrote that in these years the tithes of the poor took the place of the *first* tithes <note>the portion given to the Levites</note>. Sextinus Amama, an author crawling on the ground and hanging on Scaliger's every word, poorly supports the wavering Scaliger with his own very cold arguments in his commentary on Mosaic tithes. They failed to see that if it were done this way, nearly the entire annual grain supply of the Levites would be intercepted in those years by admitting the poor into partnership. And this, indeed, by the force of that law by which, as they would have it, God wished to provide 

<column-break/>

for the increase of the Levitical estate. But our own Selden <note>John Selden, a prominent English jurist and polymath</note> long ago uncovered Scaliger's error. Meanwhile, I would not wish to settle the dispute of whether the Jewish jurists teach correctly that the second tithes are converted into poor tithes in these years; or whether those feel more correctly who establish the poor tithes as something else *in addition* to the second tithes. So says Josephus in *Antiquities* IV. 8, in words that seem clear to some. So also the Greek version of Tobit 1:7; and if the criticism of some is to be followed, the Seventy Interpreters <note>the Septuagint</note> in Deuteronomy 26:12. Finally, Aben Ezra on Deuteronomy 14:28 says: <term>These (of which the text speaks there) are the third tithes; in this year, however, he shall take no second tithes; though there are some who say that all three ought to be taken from it.</term> <note>original: *Ha-ma'aser shelishi ve-lo yotsi ba-shanah ha-zot ma'aser sheni ve-yesh omerim ki yotsi sheloshtan*</note> Nevertheless, to defend the accepted opinion of those Jews for a little while, I say: First, the text of Deuteronomy 26:12 seems to work in their favor (*When you have finished paying all the tithe of your produce in the third year, the year of tithing, you shall give it to the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, so that they may eat within your towns and be filled.*). Here, the entire tithing of the third year seems to be distributed between the Levite tithes (or first tithes) and others to be given to the sojourner, the orphan, and the widow (or poor tithes). Second, the version of the Seventy Interpreters, according to the accepted construction of the words, does not so much tear down that opinion in this place as perhaps bolster it: <note>original: ἐὰν δὲ συντελέσῃς ἀποδεκατῶσαι πᾶν τὸ ἐπιδέκατον τῶν γεννημάτων τῆς γῆς σου ἐν τῷ ἔτει τῷ τρίτῳ, τὸ δεύτερον ἐπιδέκατον δώσεις τῷ Λευίτῃ καὶ τῷ προσηλύτῳ &c.</note> *But if you have finished tithing all the tithe of the fruits of your land in the third year, you shall give the second tithe to the Levite and the sojourner, etc.* Where "the second tithe" is given to the sojourner, the orphan, and the widow: that is, the second tithes in this year were spent on the poor. I fear that the invention of Montagu <note>Richard Montagu, an English bishop</note>, which is also followed by that most learned man who has served the Church so well, Thomas Comber, by which they might evade the force of this passage, is more clever than it is solid. They want <note>original: ἐπιδέκατον</note> *epidekaton* by the force of the word to signify not simply "tithes," but "super-added" or "additional tithes," so that it is contrasted against <note>original: δεκάטῃ</note> *dekate* <note>tenth</note>; and thus, since *epidekaton* signifies tithes added to tithes, "the second *epidekaton*" would signify the second additional tithes. But besides the fact that they produce no example to support this use of the word; and besides the fact that in Xenophon and Aristotle it occurs simply for "tithes"; and that Suidas notes that *epidekaton* is put for *dekaton* <note>a tenth</note>, just as <note>original: ἐπίπεממτον</note> *epipempton*...

# Title II. PEAH <note>The Corner of the Field</note>

...the fifth <note>original: "πλον for πέμπτον"</note>. Beyond these things, I say, they seem not to have paid enough attention to the use of this word among the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> themselves. Certainly, this subtlety was so unknown to them that they use the word indiscriminately for any tithes whatsoever. I will cite one passage out of many, Numbers 18:26: *If you take from the sons of Israel the tithe, which I have given to you from them as an inheritance, you shall also set apart from it a heave-offering to the Lord, a tithe of the tithe* <note>original: "ἐὰν λάβητε παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ τὸ ἐπιδέκατον, ὃ δέδωκα ὑμῖν παρ’ αὐτῶν ἐν κλήρῳ, καὶ ἀφελεῖτε ὑμεῖς ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ἀφαίρεμα κυρίῳ ἐπιδέκατον ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐπιδεκάτου"</note>. You see that "tithe" <note>original: "ἐπιδέκατον"</note> is used here by them clearly for the "first tithes," and then also for the "tithe of tithes" without any distinction at all. 

Thirdly, finally, perhaps the passage from Tobit itself does not oppose the Jewish legal scholars—and Selden, who followed them—as much as it has seemed to some. That passage reads as follows: *I used to give the first tithe to the sons of Levi who ministered in Jerusalem; and the second tithe I would sell and go and spend it in Jerusalem every year; and the third I gave to those to whom it was due* <note>original: "τὴν πρώτην δεκάτην ἐδίδουν τοῖς υἱοῖς Λευὶ τοῖς θεραπεύουσιν εἰς Ἰερουσαλὴμ, καὶ τὴν δευτέραν δεκάτην ἀπεπρατιζόμην, καὶ ἐπορευόμην καὶ ἐδαπάνων αὐτὴν ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις καθ’ ἕκαστον ἐνιαυτόν, καὶ τὴν τρίτην ἐδίδουν οἷς καθήκει"</note>. I confess this passage is read this way in all manuscripts; and that the Syrian and Armenian translators read it thus, as well as the authors of the paraphrases which Fagius and Munster published in Hebrew under the name of Tobit. 

But Jerome, working from a Chaldean source <note>Aramaic</note>—from which a translator skilled in both languages dictated in Hebrew while Jerome expressed it in his Latin Tobit, as he himself notes in the preface to Heliodorus and Chromatius—represents the latter part of the verse to us with a change of person (as is his custom throughout the book) like this: *so that in the third year he might provide the entire decimation to the proselytes and strangers*. I can hardly doubt that one of two things happened: either that through the carelessness of scribes the manuscripts wrongly have "and I gave the third" instead of "and in the third year I gave"; or that the Greek translator himself did not sufficiently understand the Chaldean text. This could easily have happened if it were written in Chaldean: *in this very year and the third I gave* <note>original Aramaic: "בהדא הוא שתא ותליתאה יהבית"</note> etc., which a less skillful translator would readily turn into the other meaning shown in modern manuscripts. 

Whether you restore it this way in the Greek manuscripts, or whether an equivalent reading was once held in the Chaldean source, the words of Tobit thus restored will most clearly explain the doctrine of the Jews. *The second tithes*, he says, *I collected, and having set out for Jerusalem I spent them annually; but in every third year I gave them to those for whom they were intended.* 

There remains only the authority of Josephus, which is indeed of some importance. He, however, seems to leave no room for escape, while he expressly calls it *the third in addition to the other two in every third year* <note>original: "τρίτην πρὸς αὐταῖς κατὰ τὸ ἔτος τρίτον"</note>. And yet it perhaps deserves to be weighed whether he calls it "third" only because these tithes are entirely different in nature and condition from the "second" tithes, even though they take their place. Certainly, we heard Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a medieval Spanish rabbi and scholar</note> speaking in the same way above, 

<column-break/>

while he nevertheless acknowledges that in the third year, according to the more common opinion, there is no place for the "second tithes." 

And so much for these matters for now; I propose what occurs to me regarding this noble question in Jewish Law to learned men and those skilled in these affairs. Far be it from me to wish to renew disputes already agitated by too much contention in the past. For I am certain that these things, whatever they may be, can in no way touch the question of the *Divine Right of Evangelical Tithes* <note>The debate over whether modern church tithes are mandated by God or human law</note>. For the second tithes among the Jews pertained to the <term>clergy</term> <note>original: "τὸν κλῆρον"</note> by right in no other way than that the owners themselves could be the possessors, as is abundantly clear from infinite passages in the Mishnah. This one fact, if correctly understood, clearly removes the foundation of the dispute so fiercely contested between Selden and Montagu <note>referring to Richard Montagu, a 17th-century bishop and critic of Selden</note>. 

Furthermore, as I have already said that I wrote these things not for the purpose of rashly interjecting myself as an arbiter in the disputes of the greatest men, but only to teach what can probably be said for the other opinion, I must also confess—so as not to deceive the reader—that I do not entirely trust the reasons brought forward above, and indeed I feel quite the opposite about some of them. Specifically, I feel very differently about that passage of the Seventy Interpreters than I myself set forth above, or than anyone else, as far as I know, has felt until now. For in that phrase "the second tithe" <note>original: "τὸ δευτερον ἐπιδέκατον"</note>, in my opinion, "second" is not used as an adjective, but as an adverb; so that the passage should be translated thus: *But when you have finished tithed all the tithes of your land's increase in the third year, for a second time (or repeatedly) you shall give a tenth part, or you shall give other tithes to the Levite, the proselyte, etc.* 

For they seem to have understood the word <term>tithe</term> <note>original Hebrew: "מעשר"</note> in the Hebrew text not as a noun, but as the second person of the past tense of the verb <term>to tithe</term> <note>original: "עשר"</note>, meaning *to do a second time, or repeatedly*, so that the Hebrew words would sound like: *you shall tithe again, and give* <note>original: "שנה תמעשר ותתנה"</note>. Although (to tell the truth) the verb "to tithe" <note>original: "עשר"</note> in this sense usually comes constructed with the letter *Bet* elsewhere. And thus the Seventy Interpreters seem to recognize tithes in the third year above the tithes of a common year, or to speak with Josephus, *in addition to those two* <note>original: "πρὸς αὐταῖς ταῖς δυσίν"</note>. 

I note one thing further: the Chaldean Paraphrast Pseudo-Jonathan also recognizes three tithes even in every third year; but he makes the "tithes of the poor" the *second* ones in this year—entirely by his own invention—inserting them between the first tithes and the "poor" tithes <note>original: "πτωχάς"</note>, commonly called the second. For he paraphrases Deuteronomy 26:12 thus: *When you have made an end of tithing all the tithes of the produce in the third year from the release,* <gloss>you shall give the first tithes to the Levite, the second tithes—which are the same as the tithes of the poor—to the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow, so that eating in your towns they may be satisfied; and the third tithes you shall carry up and eat before the Lord your God.</gloss> <note>original Aramaic: "ותיתנון מעשרא קמאה לליואי מעשרא תניינא הוא מעשר מסכניא לגיורא ליתמא ולארמלתא וייכלון בקרוויכון וישבעון ומעשר תליתאי תיכל ותיכול קדם יי אלהך"</note>. This passage is poorly divided and not well translated in the London Bible <note>The London Polyglot Bible (1657)</note>. But enough of these things; I fear I may seem to have said too much.

# Order I. ZERAIM <note>Seeds</note>

...is considered trustworthy at all times. No one is considered trustworthy except regarding a matter in which people are usually accustomed to being careful.

3. People are considered trustworthy regarding wheat, but they are not considered trustworthy regarding flour or bread <note>Because people are often negligent in tithing processed goods</note>. They are considered trustworthy regarding rice-meal <note>original: "farre oryzaceo"</note>; however, they are not considered trustworthy regarding the rice itself, whether raw or cooked. They are considered trustworthy regarding beans, but they are not considered trustworthy regarding crushed beans, whether raw or cooked. They are considered trustworthy regarding oil if they say it belongs to the tithes for the poor; however, they are not considered trustworthy if they say it comes from "shaken olives" <note>term for olives knocked from the tree rather than hand-picked</note>.

4. They are considered trustworthy regarding raw vegetables, but they are not considered trustworthy regarding cooked vegetables, unless someone perhaps has a very small amount; for a master of the house <note>original: "paterfamilias"</note> is often accustomed to taking a small portion from the cooking pot.

5. They must give to the poor at the threshing floor no less than a half-cab <term>cab: an ancient measure of volume, about 2 liters</term> of wheat; a cab of barley (Rabbi Meir says a half-cab); a cab and a half of spelt-meal; a cab of dried figs; a mina <note>a unit of weight</note> of pressed fig-cake (Rabbi Akiba says a half-pound); a half-log <term>log: a liquid measure, roughly the size of six eggs</term> of wine (Rabbi Akiba says a quarter-log); a quarter-log of oil (Rabbi Akiba says an eighth-log). Regarding all other types of produce, Abba Saul says: as much as can be sold to buy food for two meals.

6. This measure is prescribed for Priests, Levites, and Laypeople <note>original: "Laicis," referring to Israelites who are not of the priestly tribes</note>. He who wishes to set aside a portion for himself <note>to give to his own poor relatives</note> may take half for himself and distribute the other half to the poor. If less than the required measure remains, he should place it before them so they may divide it among themselves.

7. They must give to a traveling poor person no less than a loaf of bread worth a dupondius <note>a small Roman coin</note>, when four seahs <term>seah: a dry measure equal to six cabs</term> of grain sell for one tetradrachm <note>a silver coin worth four drachmas</note>. If he stays there for the night, they provide him with the necessities for an overnight stay. If he stays for the Sabbath, they provide him with food...

---

<columns>2</columns>

1 **Regarding flour.**] Because people are not usually accustomed to setting aside the "forgotten corner," the "dropped ears," or the "gleanings" when it comes to flour or bread. The same applies to the other items.

2 **Rice-meal.**] "Rice barley" <note>original: שעורה של אורז</note> is, according to Maimonides, "rice-chaff" <note>original: מכבלה של אורז</note>, meaning the whiskers or husks of the rice; but I do not approve of this. In my judgment, Rabbi Samson is better, and Bertinoro followed him, in understanding it as rice that has not yet been husked, so that the phrase "rice itself" which follows is understood as husked rice.

3 **Shaken olives.**] "Shaken olives" <note>original: זיתי ניקוף</note> are contrasted with "plucked olives" <note>original: זיתי מסיק</note>, as seen in Tractate Challa III. 9. The latter are plucked for the use of the Master of the House; the former are left to be shaken down by the poor. However, so few are usually left that no one would bother to press oil from them <note>thus, if someone claims his oil is from these leftovers, he is not believed</note>.

4 **From the pot.**] A master of the house, having forgotten to separate the tithes of vegetables, sometimes takes them out of the pot while they are cooking. In the text, the word for "pot" is *kedirah* <note>original: קדרה</note>, which elsewhere appears as *alpas* <note>original: אלפס</note> or *lekas* <note>original: לכס</note>. I cannot easily say whether they intended to express the Greek *lebes* <note>original: λεβης, a cauldron</note> or *lepas* <note>original: λεπας, a bowl</note> with this word. Perhaps *lekas* is *lebes*, and the other two are *lepas*.

5 **The poor at the threshing floor.**] This refers to individuals when they come to seek charity at the threshing floor. If someone gives at home, no specific measure is prescribed for him.

<column-break/>

6 **Laypeople.**] This is the meaning of "Israel" <note>original: ישראל</note> in the Mishna when it is contrasted with Priests and Levites.

7 **To set aside.**] To reserve some to distribute to poor relatives. He who wishes to do this takes half for that purpose and distributes the rest to the poor who come seeking it.

8 **Less.**] Than the amount required to distribute the standard measure.

9 **Themselves.**] The poor people.

10 **Of a dupondius.**] I must give the reason why I translated *pundion* <note>original: פונדיון</note> this way. The word *pundion* is without a doubt borrowed from the Latin or Greeks; however, they have no *pondium* or *pyndion* <note>original: πυνδιον</note>, but rather *dupondius* <note>original: δυπηνδιον</note>. Furthermore, the ratio of a *dupondius* to an *as* among the Romans, and a *dypendis* to an *assarion* among the Greeks, is double. Varro says: "Since the *as* is a single unit, it is called a *dupondius* because it weighed two *as*es." Cleopatra says: "A *dypendion* likewise weighs 2 drachmas." Similarly, for the Jews, the ratio of a *pundion* to an *issar* <note>original: איסר</note> is double. The first syllable was lost in the foreign word, as happens in several others. Regarding this coin, as well as the tetradrachm and others, I will discuss them more conveniently and at greater length below at Maaser Sheni II.

## Title II. PEA <note>The Corner of the Field</note>

...food for three meals. He who has enough food for two meals should take nothing from the <gloss>1</gloss> Plate; he who has enough for fourteen meals should take nothing from the <gloss>2</gloss> Basket. The Basket is collected by <gloss>3</gloss> two men; it is distributed by <gloss>4</gloss> three men.

8. He who possesses two hundred drachmae <note>original: "drachmæ," referring to the Hebrew "zuz"</note> should not take the gleanings, the forgotten sheaves, the corner of the field, or the tithes for the poor. If he has two hundred <gloss>5</gloss> minus one denarius <note>original: "denario"</note>, even if a thousand people contribute to him at once, he may accept. If his funds have been given as a pledge to a creditor, or for a wife’s dowry, he may accept. He is not obliged to sell his house or his furniture <note>to qualify for aid</note>.

9. He who possesses fifty drachmae with which he does business should not take. Whoever takes without being in need will not <gloss>6</gloss> depart from this world until he truly depends on the help of men. And whoever is in need, yet does not take, will not <gloss>7</gloss> die of old age until he supports others from his own means. Of such a person the scripture speaks (Jeremiah 17:7): *Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and whose confidence is the Lord.* [<gloss>8</gloss> And so it is for a Judge who speaks the law according to the truth. Whoever is not <gloss>9</gloss> crippled, nor blind, nor lame, and yet feigns one of these, will not die of old age until he becomes like one of them. For it is said (Proverbs 11:27), *He who seeks evil, it shall come upon him.* It is also said (Deuteronomy 16:20), *Justice, justice you shall pursue.* Any Judge who accepts a bribe to pervert the law will not die of old age until his eyes grow dim. For it is said (Deuteronomy 16:19), <gloss>10</gloss> *You shall not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise.*]

---

1 *Plate.*] <gloss>Tamchui</gloss> <note>original: "תמחוי"</note> *an eating-plate. Here, however, they understand this plate to be that which the* <gloss>Collectors of the Plate</gloss> <note>original: "גבאי תמחוי"</note> *carried around daily to private homes so that they might collect scraps of food in it to be divided among the poor in the evening.*

2 *Basket.*] <gloss>Kuppah</gloss> <note>original: "קופה"</note> *a basket, which the* <gloss>Collectors of the Basket</gloss> <note>original: "גבאי קופה"</note> *carried around every week on the eve of the Sabbath to collect a donation of money, which they would then distribute among the poor fellow-citizens.*

3 *Two men.*] *The donation to be contributed to the basket was certain and defined; if anyone was unwilling to contribute, the Collectors of the basket could enter the house and take furniture as a pledge. This is why there must be two men, according to the rule of law:* <gloss>Public authority is not to be established over the community with fewer than two men.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: "אין עושין שררה על הצבור פחות משנים"</note>

4 *Three men.*] *Because it is a financial matter. But* <gloss>Financial cases are determined by three men.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: "דיני ממונות בשלשה"</note> *See Sanhedrin 1:1.*

5 *Minus a denarius.*] *That is, one hundred and ninety-nine; for the* <gloss>zuz</gloss> <note>original: "זוז"</note> *drachma and the* <gloss>denarius</gloss> *are the same, as we teach below.*

6 *Depart from the world*] *Another reading is "die of old age." So it is in the manuscript.*

7 *Die of old age.*] *The manuscript says "depart from the world."*

<column-break/>

8 *And so it is for a Judge etc.*] *These words and those following to the end are absent from the manuscript. There are also discrepancies in those codices, which it matters little for us to note scrupulously.*

9 *Crippled.*] *The word* <gloss>chager</gloss> <note>original: "חגר"</note>, *which I translate here as* crippled, *in the Chaldean Paraphrasts <note>the Targums</note> almost always corresponds to the Hebrew* <gloss>pesach</gloss> <note>original: "פסח"</note> *lame, which appears here in the third place. And this synonymy seems to have offended someone, who noted in a certain codex of mine that the reading should be* <gloss>ivver</gloss> <note>original: "עור"</note> *blind. But that is the same as the second word,* <gloss>suma</gloss> <note>original: "סומא"</note>. *It seems that* "chager" *has a broader meaning than* "pesach". *It perhaps denotes an excess of some limb which hinders its use. Hence for* <gloss>heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue</gloss> <note>original: "כבד פה וכבד לשון"</note>, *Exodus 4:10, the Chaldean Pseudo-Uzielides (or as Rabbi Nathan often calls him, the Jerusalemite) has* <gloss>chagir pum ve-chagir mamlel</gloss> <note>original: "חגיר פום וחגיר ממלל"</note> <term>crooked of mouth and crooked of speech</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀγκύλος τὸ στόμα, ἀγκύλος τὴν λαλιάν"</note>. *Likewise Rabbi Nathan, from a certain Chaldean Paraphrase, for* <gloss>uncircumcised of lips</gloss> <note>original: "ערל שפתים"</note> *in Exodus 6:12, brings again* <gloss>chagir mamlel</gloss> <term>crooked of speech</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀγκύλος τὴν λαλιάν"</note>, *which is not read this way in modern codices.*

10 *A bribe etc.*] *Other codices here cite Exodus 23:8, where the words vary slightly.*

# Order I. SEEDS (Zeraim)
### I

...he is considered trustworthy at all times. No one is considered trustworthy except regarding those things with which people are usually familiar.

3. They are considered trustworthy regarding wheat, but they are not considered trustworthy $^1$ regarding flour or bread. They are considered trustworthy regarding $^2$ rice-chaff <note>original: "farre oryzaceo"</note>, but they are not considered trustworthy regarding the rice itself, whether raw or cooked. They are considered trustworthy regarding beans, but they are not considered trustworthy regarding crushed beans, whether raw or cooked. They are considered trustworthy regarding oil, if they say it belongs to the tithes of the poor; but they are not considered trustworthy if they say it is $^3$ "shaken-down" oil.

4. They are considered trustworthy regarding raw vegetables, but they are not considered trustworthy regarding cooked ones—unless perhaps someone has a very small amount, because a householder often $^4$ takes that much from the cooking pot.

5. They must distribute to $^5$ the poor at the threshing floor no less than half a *kab* <note>a *kab* is a measure of volume, roughly 1.4 liters</note> of wheat; a *kab* of barley; (Rabbi Meir says, half a *kab*); a *kab* and a half of spelt; a *kab* of dried figs; a *mina* of fig-cake; (Rabbi Akiba says, half a pound); half a *log* <note>about 0.3 liters</note> of wine; (Rabbi Akiba says, a quarter); a quarter-measure of oil; (Rabbi Akiba says, an eighth). For every other kind of produce, Abba Saul says: as much as can be sold to buy food for two meals.

6. This measure is prescribed for Priests, Levites, and $^6$ Laymen. One who wishes to $^7$ set aside a portion may take half for himself <note>to distribute to poor relatives</note> and distribute the other half. If $^8$ less than this remains, he places it before $^9$ them so they may divide it among themselves.

7. They must distribute to a traveling poor person no less than a loaf of bread worth $^10$ a *dupondius* <note>a small Roman coin</note>, when four *sata* <note>about 30 liters</note> of wheat sell for a *tetradrachm* <note>a silver coin</note>. If he stays overnight, they supply him with what is necessary for the night. If he stays for the Sabbath, they provide him with food...

---

1 *Regarding flour.*] Because people are not accustomed to separating the "corner of the field," the forgotten sheaves, or the gleanings from flour or bread. The same applies to the other items.

2 *Rice-chaff.*] In Hebrew: *shura shel orez* <note>original: שורה של אורז</note>. Maimonides considers this to be *seca* <note>original: סוכלתא</note>, or the crest of the rice; but I do not approve of this. In my judgment, Rabbi Samson—and Bertinoro who follows him—understand it better as rice that has not yet been husked, so that the "rice itself" which follows refers to husked rice.

3 *Shaken-down.*] *Decussiva* <note>shaken down</note> oil <note>original: ייתי ניקוף</note> is contrasted with *strictiva* <note>original: ייתי מסיס</note> or "stripped" oil (Challah 3:9). The latter is stripped by hand for the householder's use; the former is left for the poor to beat down from the trees. However, so little is usually left that no one would bother to press oil from it.

4 *From the pot.*] A householder who forgot to separate the tithes of vegetables never takes them from the pot once they are cooked. For "pot," the text uses *kedirah* <note>original: קדרה</note>, for which elsewhere we find *alpas* or *sir*; I cannot easily say whether they intended to express the Greek *lebes* <note>a kettle</note> or *lapas* <note>a bowl</note> by this word. Perhaps *kedirah* is *lebes*, and the other two are *lapas*.

5 *Poor at the threshing floor.*] Referring to individuals when they come to seek produce at the floor. But if one distributes from home, no specific measure is prescribed for him.

<column-break/>

6 *Laymen.*] This is the meaning of *Israel* <note>original: ישראל</note> in the Mishnah when it is contrasted with Priests and Levites.

7 *Set aside.*] To reserve it so that he may distribute it to his poor relatives. He who wishes to do so takes half for that purpose and distributes the rest to the poor who come to ask.

8 *Less.*] Less than the prescribed amount for distribution.

9 *Them.*] The poor.

10 *Dupondius.*] I must give the reason why I translated *pundion* <note>original: פונדיון</note> this way. The word is undoubtedly borrowed from Latin or Greek; however, they have no word *pondium* or *pondion*, but rather *dupondius* <note>original: $\delta\iota\pi o\nu\delta\iota o\nu$</note>. Furthermore, the ratio of a *dupondius* to an *as* for the Romans, and a *dipondios* to an *assarion* for the Greeks, is double. Varro says: "Since the *as* is a single unit, it is called a *dupondius* because it weighed two *asses*." Cleopatra <note>the physician</note> says: "The *dipondion* likewise weighs two *drachmae*." Similarly, for the Jews, the ratio of a *pundion* to an *isar* is double. The first syllable was lost in this foreign word, as happens in several others. Concerning this coin, as well as the *tetradrachm* and others, I will speak more conveniently and at length below at Maaser Sheni 2.

It also defines the minimum support required for a traveling poor person based on current market prices.</summary>

# Title II. PEAH
### E 3

...food for three meals. He who has enough food for two meals should take nothing from the $^1$ Dish; he who has enough for fourteen meals should take nothing from the $^2$ Basket. The Basket is collected by $^3$ two men and distributed by $^4$ three men.

8. He who possesses two hundred drachmae <note>A drachma or "zuz" was a standard silver coin; 200 was considered the minimum annual living expense for a single person</note> should not take the gleanings, the forgotten sheaves, the corner of the field, or the tithes of the poor. If he has two hundred $^5$ minus one denarius <note>meaning he has 199 coins</note>, even if a thousand people contribute to him at once, he may take them. If his funds are given as a pledge to a creditor, or intended for a wife’s dowry, he may take them. He is not forced to sell his house or his household furniture <note>to reach the poverty threshold</note>.

9. He who possesses fifty drachmae which he uses for trade should not take [charity]. Whoever takes charity without being in need does not $^6$ depart this world until he truly depends on the help of men. And whoever is in need yet does not take, does not $^7$ die of old age until he can support others from his own means. Of such a person the Scripture says (Jeremiah 17:7): *Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and whose trust is the Lord.* [$^8$ And likewise for a Judge who renders judgment according to the truth. Whoever is not $^9$ crippled <note>original Latin: "membro captus"</note>, nor blind, nor lame, and yet pretends to be one of these, does not die of old age until he actually becomes like one of them. For it is said (Proverbs 11:27): *He who seeks evil, it shall come to him.* It is also said (Deuteronomy 16:20): *Justice, justice shall you pursue.* Whatever Judge accepts a bribe to pervert justice does not die of old age until his eyes grow dim. For it is said (Deuteronomy 16:19): $^{10}$ *You shall not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise.*]

---

1 *Dish.* <note>original Hebrew: "Tamchui"</note> A communal food-tray. Here they understand this dish as the one which the $^1$ Collectors of the Dish charity carried daily to private homes to collect leftover food to be divided among the poor in the evening.

2 *Basket.* <note>original Hebrew: "Kuppah"</note> A charity-box which the Collectors of the Basket carried around every week on the eve of the Sabbath to collect a money tax, which they would then distribute among their poor fellow citizens.

3 *Two men.* The contribution to the basket was a fixed and defined tax. If someone refused to pay, the Collectors of the Basket could enter the house and take furniture as a pledge. For this reason, there must be two men in charge, according to the legal rule: <note>original Hebrew: "No public authority is to be appointed with fewer than two men"</note>.

4 *Three men.* Because this is a financial matter. <note>original Hebrew: "Financial cases are determined by three men"</note>. See Sanhedrin 1:1.

5 *Minus one denarius.* That is, one hundred ninety-nine; for a <note>Hebrew: "zuz"</note> drachma and a <note>Hebrew: "dinar"</note> denarius are the same, as we show below.

6 *Depart this world.* Another version says: "dies of old age." Thus the Manuscript.

7 *Dies of old age.* The Manuscript says: "departs this world."

<column-break/>

8 *And likewise for a Judge etc.* This and what follows to the end are absent from the Manuscript. There are also discrepancies in those codices, which it is of little importance for us to note scrupulously.

9 *Crippled.* The word <note>Hebrew: "chagar"</note>, which I translate here as "crippled" <note>original Latin: "membro captus"</note>, in the Aramaic Paraphrases almost always corresponds to the Hebrew <note>Hebrew: "piseah"</note> "lame," which comes third in this list. This ambiguity seems to have troubled some readers, as someone noted in one of my codices that it should read "blind." But that is the same as the second word <note>Hebrew: "ivver"</note>. It seems *chagar* has a broader meaning than "lame." It perhaps denotes an excess in a limb that prevents its use. Hence, for the phrase "heavy or slow of mouth and tongue" in Exodus 4:10, the Aramaic of Pseudo-Uzziel (or as Rabbi Nathan often calls him, the Jerusalemite) has "crippled of mouth and crippled of speech" <note>original Greek: "the mouth, unsparing in speech"</note>. Likewise, Rabbi Nathan, citing an Aramaic Paraphrase for "uncircumcised lips" in Exodus 6:12, again brings forward "crippled of speech" <note>original Greek: "unsparing in speech"</note>, though it is not read this way in modern codices.

10 *You shall not accept a bribe etc.* Other codices here cite Exodus 23:8, where the words vary slightly.

---

Order I. SEEDS

# TITLE III. DEMAI.

### OR

## CONCERNING DOUBTFUL MATTERS.

They call produce bought from the *Am ha-aretz* <note>original Hebrew: "עם הארץ"; literally "people of the land," referring to the common unlearned folk who were often suspected of negligence in religious law</note> or plebeians a "doubtful matter" [*Demai*]. For the plebeians were subject to suspicion regarding the failure to tithe their produce. For this reason, since men's consciences were in a wretched state of uncertainty, it eventually happened in the time of John the High Priest <note>John Hyrcanus, who reigned c. 134–104 BCE</note> that no one needed to personally inquire about a "doubtful matter," as the Mishnah expressly teaches at the end of the Title *Maaser Sheni* <note>The Second Tithe</note>, and repeats again in *Sotah* 9:10.

The understanding of "doubtful produce," and the law concerning it introduced by the authority of this High Priest John, depends upon the history of this matter, which is explained in this Title. Since before this time, most men had become rather negligent about paying tithes, it caused the more religious—whom Maimonides calls "those who follow the strict" <note>original Hebrew: "אחר החרדי"</note> or "those who are exact concerning the law" <note>original Greek: "τοὺς περὶ τ. νόμον ἀκριβοῦντας"</note>—to find it difficult to buy anything from the market unless they were first made certain whether it had been tithed or not.

If there was any doubt, they would abstain from the purchase entirely so that they would not have to pay the tithes at their own loss; for it was a matter of religious duty not to use produce unless the first-fruits and all kinds of tithes had first been properly set aside, to their certain knowledge. However, many who were less strict frequently used to buy and eat "doubtful produce" without any hesitation. From this, a great scandal arose.

In order to remedy both inconveniences, that John decreed that all produce bought from plebeians should be considered a "doubtful matter" [*Demai*]; but that the buyer would only be bound to set aside the "tithe of the tithe" <note>The *Terumat Maaser*, the ten percent of the tithe given by the Levite to the Priest</note> and the "second tithe" <note>The tithe eaten by the owner in Jerusalem</note>. One was not, however, bound to set aside the "great first-fruits" <note>The *Terumah Gedolah*, the first portion given to the Priest</note>, the "first tithes" <note>for the Levites</note>, or the "tithes for the poor." He wished the produce to be exempt from the great first-fruits because he had sent examiners throughout all Israel and found that everyone, led by religious devotion, was careful to pay them, as the omission of that specific duty would draw down sin.

<summary>This page introduces the tractate Demai, explaining the historical context of "doubtful produce" and the reforms of John Hyrcanus regarding tithes. It describes the compromise made to ensure that both the scrupulous and the common people could participate in the marketplace without violating religious law.</summary>

<keywords>Demai, John Hyrcanus, Am ha-aretz, Tithes, Maimonides, Jewish Law, Second Tithe, Terumah, Marketplace Ethics</keywords>

--- Page 121 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of John the High Priest’s (John Hyrcanus) reforms regarding "doubtful produce" (Demai). The previous page explained that religious Jews avoided buying from the common people to avoid the risk of eating untithed food.</meta>

...lest it should draw upon them a punishment to be atoned for by death inflicted from heaven. From the first tithes and the tithes of the poor, because there was no "holiness" <note>The "first tithe" went to the Levites and the "poor tithe" to the needy; unlike the "heave-offering" given to priests, these did not carry the same ritual penalty if eaten by a non-priest</note> inherent in them, the well-known rule of law held place here: **"The burden of proof lies with the claimant"** <note>original Hebrew: המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה; original Latin: Actori incumbit probatio</note>. Thus, the Levites and the poor were unable to claim these tithes unless they could first prove that the tithes had not yet been paid; in which case, the doubt would cease.

He [John the High Priest] ordered that the "tithe of the tithes"—which is one-hundredth of the whole—must be paid. This was not because the Priests had a better legal claim to them than the Levites or the poor had to theirs (for the same rule of proof would stand in the way here), but because these portions possessed the same ritual holiness as the "great heave-offerings." There was the same danger of sin and **death** <note>original Greek: θανάτου</note> if they were treated profanely, even though the common people at that time thought otherwise. Finally, he also required the "second tithes" <note>A tithe to be eaten by the owner in Jerusalem</note> to be set aside, because this caused no financial loss to the owner; the owner's only obligation was to spend either the tithes themselves or their monetary value in Jerusalem.

See the Jerusalem Gemara <note>The commentary on the Mishnah</note> at the end of the Title *Maaser Sheni*; and both commentaries at *Sotah* 9:10; Maimonides' *Laws of Tithes* 9, and his commentary on the Mishnah in the places cited. Concerning John the High Priest, see our observations below at *Maaser Sheni* 5:15.

## CHAPTER I.

1. **I**n a case of doubt, the following are considered exempt: ² **early figs** <note>original: *olynthi*; refers to figs that drop before ripening</note>, ³ **lotus fruit** <note>original: *connari*</note>, ⁴ **service berries** <note>original: *sorba*</note>, ⁵ **white figs**, **sycamore figs**, **fallen dates**, ⁶ **late-ripening grapes**, **capers**, and in Judea, **sumac**, **vinegar**, and **coriander**. Rabbi Judah says: all early figs are considered exempt except for those from trees that bear fruit twice a year.

---

1 [*As exempt.*] The fruits listed here are rarely guarded or stored because of their low value; therefore, it is doubtful whether they even fall under the general rules of tithing to be explained later in *Maaseroth* 1:1. Furthermore, if there is a doubt as to whether they have already been tithed or not, two doubts coincide. The legal rule is: **"Wherever two doubts coincide, the law leans toward exemption"** <note>original Hebrew: הרי ספיקי להקל</note>.

2 [*Early figs.*] A certain Rabbi Johanan in the Babylonian Gemara, *Berakhot* 40b (where this Mishnah is cited), considers the term *shitin* <note>Hebrew: שיתין</note> to be a species of fig, but does not explain further. Benjamin Musaphia says that, were it not for Johanan's authority, he would prefer to identify this with a fruit of the same name used by the Greeks and Latins, which has three or four seeds and is unfit for eating when first picked until it softens for several days under straw. 

<column-break/>

With this crude description, he understands them to be **Setanian medlars** <note>A small, apple-like fruit that requires bletting (softening) to be edible</note>. However, there is nothing to support this view except for a slight similarity in the name. I have used "early figs" <note>original: *olynthos*</note>, which Pliny (interpreting Theophrastus) calls "abortive figs," and others call "grossi" <note>unripe green figs</note>. Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel, cited by Rabbi Nathan in the entry *Benot Shuach*, says: *"From the emergence of the leaves until the budding of the unripe figs is thirty days; from the unripe figs to the fallen early figs is fifty days; from the early figs to the fully ripe figs is fifty days."* To Rabbi Simeon Abba (or the son of Ammi) in the Jerusalem Talmud, the *shitin* are those **figs** which grow out from under the leaves...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the classification of fruits and the specific rules for "doubtful produce" (Demai), which were products purchased from common people whose tithing status was uncertain.</meta>

# Order I. SEEDS

...twice-bearing; all are considered jujubes <note>original: *connari*; likely the fruit of the *Ziziphus* tree</note> except those from Sycamine; all sycamore figs except those that are **split** <note>original: *fissa*</note>.

2. For **doubtful produce** <note>original: *Rei dubiæ*; referring to *Demai*, food bought from a person who might not have tithed it</note> there is neither an added **fifth** <note>Normally, a 20% penalty was added when redeeming tithes for money</note>, nor is there a **removal ceremony** <note>original: *pollustura*; referring to *Biur Maaser*, the clearing out of all tithes every three years</note>. It may be eaten by a mourner <note>A person in the period between a relative's death and burial, who is usually restricted from holy food</note>. Having entered Jerusalem, it may be **carried out again** <note>Unlike certain tithes that must stay within the city walls once entered</note>. A tiny portion of it may be consumed on the journey. It may be **given to a common person** <note>original: *Plebeio*; an *Am Haaretz* who is not scrupulous about tithing laws</note>, so long as an equal amount is **eaten in its place** <note>The owner must eat a corresponding amount of their own produce in Jerusalem with the appropriate level of holiness</note>. It may be **deconsecrated** <note>original: *Profanatur*; the "holiness" of the tithe is transferred to money to make the food "common" and edible</note> by exchanging silver for silver, copper for copper, silver for copper, or copper for produce. Indeed, the produce may be turned back into money according to the opinion...

<margin>which come out under the leaves. These are the early figs. Athenaeus, citing Theophrastus, says: "There is also another kind of fig tree in Greece, and around Cilicia and Cyprus, which bears early figs; it carries the true fig in front of the leaf, but the early fig behind it." (Book III, chapter 4).</margin>

<margin>^3 **Jujubes.** <note>original: *Connari*</note> The Gemara <note>The rabbinical commentary</note> there explains the Hebrew *rimin* as *konnari*. So it appears in the printed books; but Rabbi Nathan cites it as *konnari*, that is, the Greek *konnaros*. This authority is supported by Agathocles of Cyzicus in Athenaeus (Book XIV, chapter 17), who describes jujubes in a way that closely resembles the *zizyphus* fruit. Now, it is said in the tractate *Kilaim* (I, 4) that *ziziphin* (jujubes) and *rimin* (lotus-jujubes), although very similar, are of different species. To this we add that Maimonides <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish scholar</note> considers the *rimin* to be the Arabic *unnab*. These are the *nabq* <note>original: النبق</note>, the fruit of the *sidr* tree <note>original: سدر</note>, which is a species of lotus. Not the lotus of Homer and the Lotus-eaters, but the Cyrenaic type mentioned by Theophrastus. Polybius describes this fruit as being reddish in color and similar in size to round olives. If it is not the very same as Agathocles' jujube, it is at least very close. Regarding the jujube, he says: "the fruit is very sweet, and the size of a Phaulian olive." Finally, Rabbi Nathan explains it in the vernacular as *pulsaraco*, which in common Italian is *Pulsaraca*; this is derived from the Syriac *Puls* (a somewhat barbaric name for the Syrian bean). The Syrian bean is the same as this species of Lotus.</margin>

<margin>^4 **Sorb apples.** <note>original: *Sorba*</note> The Gemara uses the word *tolshi*, for which Rabbi Samson reads *toshlayi*, but likely in error. One of the Gaons <note>Leaders of the Babylonian academies</note> explains this in Arabic as *jannar* or *jazar*, and considers it a certain red fruit. The Arabic *jannar* <note>original: جنار</note>, it seems to me, comes from the Greek *konnaros*. To the Persians, it is the plane tree, which bears no fruit. But to Abu-Hanifa it is the same as the Arabic *dulb* <note>original: دلب</note>, which is not only the plane tree as commonly understood, but also a berry-bearing tree. Beitharides and Ebn-Al-Cabatius describe it (citing Isaac son of Amran) in a way that makes me think it is the wild service tree <note>original: *sorbo torminali*</note> of Pliny, which has plane-tree leaves. However, Maimonides considers *arud* to be the medlar <note>original: *mespilo*</note>. Indeed, for the Arabs, *al-za'rur* <note>original: الزعرور</note> is the medlar tree described by Dioscorides. Whatever it may be, it is almost always mentioned alongside pears, crab-apples, and quinces, as seen in *Kilaim* I, 4.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Mishnah Maaserot I. 3; Oketzin I. 6.</margin>
<margin>5 **White figs.** See below, *Shebiit* V. 1.</margin>
<margin>6 **Late vines.** So says the Gemara in the place cited above, *shilei gufni*. To Maimonides, *gufni* is a vegetable similar to dill; or according to others, it is the *sebesten* plum or *myxa*. Anyone can see how different these things are. In considering it a vegetable, Maimonides seems to have followed the authority of the Jerusalem Talmud, where it is explained as *shamerar*, that is, the Greek *smyrnion* <note>Alexander's parsley or horse-parsley</note>.</margin>

---

1 **Sycaminenses.** <note>original: שקמונית</note> The name of a place, Sycamine <note>A town near Mount Carmel</note>.
2 **Split.** <note>original: *Fissa*; Hebrew: חסופין</note> Rabbi Nathan, and after him Rabbi Samson and Obadiah, say: These are figs that are allowed to ripen on the tree until they gap open of their own accord. However, we should consider if there is a deeper meaning here. It is a well-known fact from Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Athenaeus, and Pliny that sycamore figs ripen with difficulty unless they are "scratched" or scored with an iron tool to let out the milky sap, which otherwise prevents maturity. In this sense, I take the word *chasufin* to mean "scratched" or "split by scratching." The point of the passage is that fruits that are not usually guarded are exempt from tithes. But anyone who takes the trouble to scratch them shows he cares for the fruit. The Mishnah in *Shebiit* II. 5 speaks openly about the "scratching" of unripe figs.
3 **Doubtful produce.** The second tithes of doubtful produce differ from the "true" second tithes in these specific ways.
4 **Fifth.** An additional payment made by the owner when converting the produce into money.
5 **Removal ceremony.** <note>original: *Pollustura*</note> Occurring at the end of every third year. See *Maaser Sheni* V. 6.
6 **Carried out again.** After being converted into money. But true second tithes, once they have entered Jerusalem, cannot be redeemed for money to be carried out; they must be consumed there in their original form. See *Maaser Sheni* III. 5, 6.
7 **Given to a common person.** This would be unlawful with true second tithes, lest the person eat it while ritually impure.
8 **Eaten.** By the owner, with the same level of sanctity and under the same conditions as required for eating second tithes.
9 **Exchanged.** <note>original: *Profanatur*</note> So that silver exchanged for these tithes may be exchanged again for other silver, and so on for the rest.
10 **Indeed, the produce.** The codes contain the phrase "provided that he returns," and so it is in the Manuscript; thus it should be translated: "In such a way, however, that they are valued in money again." Bertinoro dislikes this reading, and in my judgment, he is right. Rabbi Meir permits...

# Title XIII. DEMAI <note>original: "Demai"; refers to agricultural produce purchased from a common person who may not have properly tithed it.</note>

...the opinion of Rabbi Meiri. The Sages <note>The "Sapientes" or rabbinic authorities</note> judge that the crops must be transported to Jerusalem and consumed there.

3. If anyone buys produce to carry it elsewhere, or for animal fodder, or flour for treating hides, or oil for a lamp, or oil for greasing a vessel, it is considered outside the status of "doubtful produce" <note>Demai</note>. Anything beyond Ecdippa <note>A coastal town, modern Achziv, marking a historical border</note> is held to be exempt from the status of "doubtful produce." <gloss>2</gloss> The dough-portion of a common person <note>original: "Secium plebeii"; referring to Challah</note>, <gloss>3</gloss> a thing mixed with first-fruits, a thing bought with second-tithe money, <gloss>4</gloss> and the remains of meal-offerings are all exempt from the status of "doubtful produce."

<columns>2</columns>

...a further valuation in money; he does not command it. The Sages do not even permit it. He reads, therefore, "and he shall return" <note>original: ויחזור (*ve-yachzor*)</note>.

<margin>1 Beyond Ecdippa, exempt.] The manuscript states that within Ecdippa, one is liable.</margin>
The Jews frequently distinguish between the Land of Israel "occupied by those who came up from Egypt" <note>original: עולי מצרים (*Olei Mitzrayim*)</note>, which the Jews seized after leaving Egypt; and the land "occupied by those who came up from Babylon" <note>original: עולי בבל (*Olei Bavel*)</note>, which those returning from the Babylonian captivity took into their possession. Ecdippa is the furthest northern boundary of the territory held by the people who returned from Babylon.

2 The dough-portion <note>original: "Secium"</note>.] I interpret the word "Challah" <note>original: חלה</note> according to Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a Roman grammarian</note>. It is a small portion taken from the kneaded dough to be given to the Priest according to the Law in Numbers 15:19-21.

<margin>Mixed with first-fruits <note>original: מדומע (*Medumah*)</note></margin>
3 A thing mixed with first-fruits.] From the word *Demua* <note>דמוע</note> comes *Medumah* <note>מדומע</note>. *Demua* means "mixed" or "infected." Now, the word *Dema* <note>דמע</note> occurs in Exodus 22:29 in a sense very different from the most common meaning used by the Rabbis, which denotes a "tear." Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous medieval commentator</note> explains it in that passage as "first-fruits" <note>original: תרומה (*Terumah*)</note>, while adding that the true etymology of the word was unknown to him. Certainly, the word *Dema* itself is used for "first-fruits" in the Mishnah (Oholot 16:4), besides infinite places where a verb derived from it means "to mix with first-fruits." In that Rabbi Solomon confesses his own ignorance regarding the true origin of the word, he is far wiser than others of his nation who foolishly measure the breadth of the Hebrew language only by the meager remnants that remain to them today. Thus, Saadia, Kimchi, and whoever followed them are being foolish when they restrict the word to oil and wine, which flow from the press "drop by drop like tears," if you please. Nowhere in Scripture does *Dema* signify a "tear," but rather *Dim'ah* <note>דמעה</note>. Since the Jews are ignorant of what *Dema* is, I myself shall teach them. It signifies the marrow, the best and most excellent part of any thing—the "choice portion." Let the Aramaic-Samaritan Translator provide the evidence, as he often uses this word in this sense. Thus in Genesis 45:18, "And you shall eat the fat <note>original: חלב (*chelev*)</note> of the land," the Aramaic-Samaritan translates "the marrow of the land." He uses the same word in Numbers 18:12, where for the Hebrew "fat of the new wine" <note>original: חלב תירוש (*chelev tirosh*)</note> he has "the marrow." The Latin translator very foolishly rendered this as "the liquid of the dry," following Jewish lexicons to the detriment of the meaning. I translate it as "marrow" or "the most excellent part," i.e., the first-fruits of the must. Likewise, the same word corresponds to the Hebrew "fat" <note>חלב</note> in verses 29 and 32 of the same chapter, where the text

<column-break/>

discusses the first-fruits of the tithes; here again, the Latin translator makes the same mistake. Finally, where the Jewish text reads: "For the Lord's portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance" (Deuteronomy 32:9), the Samaritan text adds at the end the word for "marrow" <note>original: *al-dam*</note>; so that it may be read and punctuated as the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX) translators</note> read and punctuated: "And the Lord's portion was his people Jacob, the lot of his inheritance Israel." The Aramaic-Samaritan translator here also seems to have read not *al-dam* but *al-dam-an-u*, for he translates it as "the marrow or the most excellent part of his lot, Israel." Finally, there is the same use of the word in the Samaritan Liturgy: "The marrow of marrows," which the Arabic translator renders as "the best or most excellent part of created things." Add to these the Arabic word *dimagh* which, besides the "brain," denotes "marrow" (Hebrews 4:12 in Erpenius's translation). What *Dema* is, therefore, I have sufficiently revealed—and I am the first to do so. Now, *Medumah* is that which is mixed and "infected" by *Dema* (first-fruits), so that the whole becomes unlawful for anyone but Priests to eat. However, for a thing to be considered "infected" in this way, the infecting particle must be at least one part in a hundred. For if one part of first-fruits is mixed with one hundred parts of properly prepared common produce, the whole is not "infected" (as Buxtorf incorrectly teaches); rather, only the 1/101 part emerges as needing to be restored to the Priest, as will be established below in Terumot 4:7. They used to sell a thing thus "infected" to a Priest at a price valued according to the first-fruits, minus the price of the "infecting" part, as will be handed down in Terumot 5:1. For this reason, if "doubtful produce" is so infected, the law regarding the first-fruits of tithes and second tithes to be taken from it ceases, because the whole now belongs to the Priest.

<margin>4 Remains of the meal-offerings.] I call "meal-offerings" *Minchot* <note>מנחות</note>, that is, grain offerings of every kind. Their "remains" are the portions that stay with the Priest after the handful has been taken for the altar.</margin>

# Order I. SEEDS <note>original: "Zeraim"; the first of the six orders of the Mishnah, dealing primarily with agricultural laws.</note>

...are doubtful. Scented oil from the school of Shammai <note>A stricter school of Jewish legal thought in the 1st century</note> is considered subject to the laws of doubtful produce, but the school of Hillel <note>A more lenient school</note> considers it exempt.

4. In cases of doubt, communal mixtures and joint-ownership arrangements are entered into. $^1$ For such produce, a blessing is said and a command is given. It may be separated by a person who is naked, $^2$ and during the evening twilight. $^3$ Indeed, if someone takes the second tithe before the first tithe, it is of no effect. Oil which a weaver smears on his fingers is subject to the law of doubtful produce; that which a wool-comber uses to dye wool is considered outside the category of doubtful produce.

## CHAPTER II.

1. These items are tithed as doubtful produce in every place: $^4$ Pressed fig-cakes, $^5$ dates, carobs, rice, and cumin. However, whoever uses rice from abroad is exempt.

2. He who takes it upon himself to be considered trustworthy $^6$ <note>original: "fide dignus"; in Hebrew, a *Ne'eman*</note> tithes whatever he eats, whatever he sells, and whatever he buys; nor does he stay as a guest with common people <note>original: "plebeios"; in Hebrew, *Am Ha-Aretz*, referring to those not scrupulous in tithing laws</note>—

---

1 *Communal mixtures and joint-ownership arrangements.*] These refer to the "mixture of boundaries" <note>original: *Eruvei techumin*</note>, by which the limit of a Sabbath journey is extended beyond two thousand cubits toward some direction; and the "mixture of courtyards" <note>original: *Eruvei chatzerot*</note>, by which all dwellings opening into the same courtyard, and the courtyard itself, are considered as one house, so that residents may carry whatever they wish from the dwellings into the courtyard, from the courtyard into the dwellings, or from one dwelling to another on the Sabbath. "Joint-ownership of streets" <note>original: *Shitufei mevo'ot*</note> refers to the same license extended to streets and alleys. These are discussed below throughout the second Title of Order II.

2 *Naked.*] This is because the tithe of tithes and the second tithes for doubtful produce are separated without a blessing. Therefore, a naked person is permitted to perform it. But a naked person is not permitted to recite a blessing.

3 *Evening twilight.*] Literally "between the suns" <note>original: *Bein Ha-Shemashot*</note>. Wherever "between the evenings" <note>original: *Bein Ha-Arbayim*</note> is read in the sacred text, the Aramaic translator Onkelos puts "between the suns," as does the Pseudo-Jonathan. This is our Mishnaic phrase "between the suns." And yet, if one compares this passage with Pesachim V. 3, he will see that "between the evenings" designates a different time than our "between the suns," and is rightly extended to the entire afternoon. But more on this there. In the meantime, an old *Baraita* <note>An "Extraordinary Tradition" or a teaching from the Mishnaic era not included in the standard Mishnah</note>, or "the repetition placed outside" <note>original Greek: η εξω κειμενη δευτερωσις</note>, cited at the very beginning of the Jerusalem Talmud, reveals to us what "between the suns" is: *It is taught: As long as the eastern horizon is red, it is still day; when it turns pale, that is the time called "between the suns"; as soon as it turns black, and is equally dark in both the upper and lower parts of the hemisphere, then it is night.* The same tradition <meta>catchword: tradition</meta>

<column-break/>

is also cited in the Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 34b, but in a less pure form; this provides the scholars of the Gemara with ample opportunity for debate. Let the reader who wishes seek it there; it is enough for us to indicate the place. Furthermore, in both Talmuds, this same time is defined differently by different people: Rabbi Nehemiah measures it by the journey of half a mile, Rabbi Joses by the blink of an eye; others in other ways. Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic philosopher and legal scholar</note> asserts in the Laws of the Sabbath V. 4 that the entire time from sunset until three middle-sized stars appear is called "between the suns."

4 *In every place.*] Even beyond Ecdippa <note>The northern border of the Land of Israel for certain legal purposes</note>.

5 *Pressed fig-cakes etc.*] Not just any, but only those which are recognized as owing their origin to the Land of Israel due to their remarkable quality.

6 *He who takes it upon himself to be considered trustworthy.*] Let the words of Maimonides in the Laws of Ma'aser X serve as commentary: *He who takes it upon himself to be considered trustworthy regarding tithes, so that his crops are not held as doubtful produce, must tithe whatever he eats, whatever he sells, and whatever he trades, and must not stay as a guest with a common person. And it is necessary that he takes these things upon himself to be observed publicly. And if he can bring two faithful men to bear witness that he took these conditions upon himself publicly and has continually accustomed himself to them, then he is considered trustworthy if he asserts that his crops have been tithed.* Opposed to the trustworthy are the "suspected persons" <note>original: *Chashudim*</note>, of whom frequent mention is made hereafter. Therefore, Selden <note>John Selden, a 17th-century English jurist and scholar</note> is mistaken in thinking that the "trustworthy" <note>original: *Ne'emanim*</note> were officials appointed by the Sanhedrin to oversee and look out for the payment of tithes with public authority. That opinion is plainly contrary to Mishnaic law throughout this Title. Nor can it be proven in any way from Nehemiah XIII. 13, although he seems to have held that opinion based on the authority of that passage.
