# Title III. DEMAI
### F 2
<meta>catchword: Tar-</meta>

...to a common person. <note>original: "plebeium"; in Hebrew, *Am Ha-aretz*, referring to people not scrupulous in following the agricultural and purity laws of the Torah.</note> **Rabbi Judah says: Indeed, even he who stays as a guest with a common person can be considered trustworthy. They replied to him: If he is not trustworthy regarding his own property, how can he be trustworthy regarding the property of others?**

3. **He who takes upon himself the status of an** $^1$ **Associate** <note>original: "Socii"; in Hebrew, a *Chaver*</note> **should not sell to a common person either moist or dry produce; nor should he buy moist produce from him; nor should he stay as a guest with a common person, nor receive him as a guest in his own garments.** <insert>Rabbi Judah adds</insert> **Rabbi Judah adds: Also, he should not raise small livestock; nor be prone to vows or laughter; nor defile himself for the sake of the dead; but he should serve in the school. They replied: These things do not fall under the rule** <note>These additional pieties are not part of the formal requirements for Associate status.</note>.

4. **The Sages did not require bakers to separate more than what is necessary for the first-fruits of the tithes and the dough-offering.** $^2$ **Shopkeepers are not permitted to sell doubtful produce.** **Whosoever accumulates a large measure, it is permitted for them to sell doubtful produce. Those who accumulate a large measure are** $^3$ **wholesalers and grain sellers.**

5. **R.**

---

1 *Associate.]* To Maimonides <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note>, "Associate" is the same as "Disciple of the Sages." But he is gravely mistaken, or I am much deceived. One can be a disciple of the Sages without taking upon himself the "laws of association" <note>original: *divrei chaverut*</note>, as is clearly established from the *Baraita* (an external tradition), which can be read in the Babylonian Talmud, *Bekhorot 30b*: *The Teachers taught: If anyone wishes to take upon himself the laws of the Association, he must do so before a tribunal of three Associates; even a Disciple of the Sages must do so.* The Associates were, it seems to me, a class of men far more scrupulous than the common people regarding the minutiae of ritual impurities; they formed a society and bound themselves by certain laws so that they might interact more safely among themselves and avoid the impurities resulting from trade with the common people. The laws or conditions they imposed on themselves are listed in this Mishnah, all of which concern purity. First, *that they should not sell moist or dry crops to common people,* lest they be the cause of those items becoming impure. Second, *that they should not accept moist crops from them;* lest they perhaps be already defiled, because it is well known that by being moistened, produce becomes susceptible to receiving impurity. Third, *that they should not stay as guests with common people;* lest they themselves become impure and thus defile clean things. Fourth, *that they should not receive common people as guests in their own garments;* because the garments of common people were considered more impure than the people themselves, as being contaminated by *midras* <note>impurity caused by sitting, lying, or leaning on an object</note>, or "pressure." There are also many rules about admitting Associates to this society, about instructing them, and about rejecting them for violating the laws, and other such matters which the reader may seek in the Talmud at the aforementioned place and in the *Tosefta* <note>a supplement to the Mishnah</note> of this chapter. Whether these Associates are the same as the Pharisees—such that all Pharisees took the laws of this society upon themselves—I cannot easily say. Certainly, anyone who considers all that is read in the Gospels (Matthew 15, Mark 7, etc.) regarding the anxious concern of the Pharisees in avoiding impurities

<column-break/>

might believe this to be at least likely. Bertinoro <note>a 15th-century commentator on the Mishnah</note> openly asserts that "Associate" and "Pharisee" are the same thing. And in *Chagigah II, 7*, it is said: *The garments of common people are considered "midras" [contaminated by pressure] to Pharisees;* just as the Pharisees there regard the garments of common people in the same way the Associates do here. Therefore, citing this passage, Nathan the Lexicographer speaks thus of the Pharisees: *They are the Associates who eat common or profane things in a state of ritual purity.* The same men, therefore, were called "Associates" and "Pharisees," but from different perspectives. They were "Pharisees" <note>original: *perushim*, meaning "separated ones"</note> because they separated themselves *from all uncleanness, and from unclean food, and from the common people who are less concerned about food,* as the same Rabbi Nathan says. They were called "Associates" <note>original: *chaverim*</note> in respect to the Society they entered into among themselves to avoid impurity. Men of any condition, even the lowest, could be admitted into this society; hence in the very next paragraph, Bertinoro understands "bakers," and in III, 1 "the poor," to also be Associates. See below, VI. 9, 12.

2 *Whosoever accumulates etc.]* That is, the wholesalers or large-scale dealers, as opposed to shopkeepers and retailers. For the former are accustomed to give the retailers an "over-measure" <note>original: *epimetron*</note>, a heap or a bonus. They sell by *a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over,* as Saint Luke says [Luke 6:38], using a phrase not at all foreign to our own.

3 *Wholesalers.]* The Greek word is *sitōnēs*, that is, one who buys grain to resell it, as the terms *sitōnēs* and *sitokapēlos* [grain-dealer] appear together in Gregory Nazianzen. Maimonides is therefore wrong when he says below (V. 6) that a wholesaler is one who sells liquids and types of fruit. This is nearly the same definition given by the same Rabbi.

The commentary explores the historical identity of these Associates, linking them to the Pharisees mentioned in the New Testament.</summary>

# Order I. SEEDS (ZERAIM)

are doubtful. The scented oil of the $^1$ Shammaites they consider liable to the laws of doubtful produce, while the Hillelites consider it exempt.

4. In a case of doubt, $^1$ mixtures and partnerships are entered into. A blessing is recited for it, and it is proclaimed. One may separate tithes while $^2$ naked, and at the $^3$ evening twilight. Indeed, if someone separates the second tithes before the first, it is of no consequence. The oil that a weaver smears on his fingers is subject to the law of doubtful produce; however, that which a wool-comber uses to treat wool is considered outside the category of doubtful produce.

---

## CHAPTER II.

1. These items are tithed as doubtful in $^4$ every place: $^5$ Fig-cakes, dates, carobs, rice, and cumin. However, whoever uses foreign rice is free from this obligation.
2. $^6$ He who takes it upon himself to be considered trustworthy must tithe whatever he eats, whatever he sells, and whatever he buys; and he must not stay as a guest with a $^6$ common person—

---

1 **Mixtures and partnerships.]** These refer to the "mixtures" of boundaries, by which the final limit of a Sabbath journey is extended beyond two thousand cubits in a certain direction; and the mixtures of courtyards, by which all dwellings opening into the same courtyard—and the courtyard itself—are treated as a single house, so that residents may carry items from the dwellings to the courtyard, or between dwellings, on the Sabbath. "Partnerships" refers to streets and alleys, extending the same permission. These are discussed below in the second Title of the Second Order. <note>These are the laws of *Eruv*, which allow for movement and carrying on the Sabbath by creating a legal "shared" space.</note>
2 **Naked.]** This is because the "tithe of the tithe" and the "second tithe" of doubtful produce are separated without reciting a blessing. Therefore, a naked person is permitted to perform this. However, it is not permitted for a naked person to recite a blessing.
3 **Evening twilight.]** Literally, "between the suns." Wherever the sacred text reads "between the evenings" <note>Hebrew: *Bein Ha-arbayim*</note>, the Chaldean translator Onkelos writes "between the suns" <note>Aramaic: *Bein Shimshaya*</note>, as does the Pseudo-Jonathan. This is our Mishnic phrase "between the suns" <note>Hebrew: *Bein Ha-shemashot*</note>. Nevertheless, if one compares this passage with Pesachim V. 3, they will see that "between the evenings" designates a different time than our "between the suns," and is rightly extended to the entire afternoon. But more on that there. Meanwhile, an old *Baraita* <note>original: "Traditio Extravagans"; an external tradition or teaching not included in the main Mishnah</note>, cited at the very beginning of the Jerusalem Talmud, explains "between the suns" to us thus: *It is taught: As long as the face of the east is red, it is still day; when it grows dim, that time is called "between the suns"; as soon as it blackens, and is equal in both the upper and lower parts of the hemisphere, then it is night.* This same 

<column-break/>

*Baraita* is also brought in the Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 34b) but in a less pure form, which provides the scholars of the Gemara with ample occasion for dispute. Let the reader seek it there if they wish; it is enough for us to indicate the location. Furthermore, in both Talmuds, this same time is defined differently by different people: Rabbi Nehemiah measures it by a journey of half a mile, Rabbi Jose by the blink of an eye, and others in other ways. Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> asserts (Laws of Shabbat V. 4) that the entire time from sunset until three medium-sized stars appear is called "between the suns."
4 **Every place.]** Even beyond Ecdippa <note>The northern boundary of the land of Israel, modern-day Achziv.</note>.
5 **Fig-cakes etc.]** Not just any, but only those which, because of their notable quality, are recognized as originating from the land of Israel.
6 **He who takes it upon himself to be considered trustworthy.]** Let the words of Maimonides (Laws of Ma'aser X) serve as a commentary: *He who takes it upon himself to be considered trustworthy regarding tithes, so that his produce is not considered doubtful, must tithe whatever he eats, sells, or buys, and must not stay as a guest with a common person* <note>original: "plebeium"; referring to an *Am Ha-aretz*, one not scrupulous in tithing laws</note>. *And it is necessary that he accepts these observances publicly. If he can bring two faithful men to testify that he took these conditions upon himself publicly and has consistently followed them, then he is considered trustworthy if he claims his produce has been tithed. Opposed to the trustworthy are the* **Suspected** <note>Hebrew: *Ha-chashudim*</note>, *who are frequently mentioned hereafter.* Therefore, Selden <note>John Selden, a 17th-century English jurist and scholar</note> is mistaken in thinking that the "Trustworthy" <note>Hebrew: *Ne'emanim*</note> were public officials appointed by the Sanhedrin to oversee tithing. That opinion is plainly contrary to the laws of the Mishnah throughout this entire Title, nor can it be proven from Nehemiah 13:13, even though he seems to have held that view based on that passage.

# Title III. DEMAI.

They answered him: If he is not considered trustworthy regarding his own property, how can he be considered trustworthy regarding the property of others?

3. He who takes upon himself the status of an <note>1</note> **Associate** must not sell to a common person either moist or dry produce; nor may he buy moist produce from him; nor should he stay as a guest with a common person, nor receive him as a guest in his own clothes. <note>A common person’s clothes were considered ritually impure by "pressure" (*midras*).</note> **Rabbi Judah** adds: He also should not raise small cattle; he should not be prone to taking vows or to levity; and he should not defile himself for the sake of the dead; but let him serve in the school. The response given was: These specific additions do not fall under the general rule.

4. The **Sages** did not require bakers to separate more than what is necessary for the "first-fruits of the tithes" <note>The portion the Levite gives to the Priest.</note> and the dough-offering. **Shopkeepers** are not permitted to sell "doubtful produce." <note>2</note> However, whoever heaps up a large measure is permitted to sell doubtful produce. Those who "heap up a large measure" are <note>3</note> **corn-merchants** and grain sellers.

---

1 *Associate* [Hebrew: *Chaber*].] **To Maimonides**, the "Associate" is the same as a "Disciple of the Wise" <note>Hebrew: *Talmid Chakhamim*</note>. But he is greatly mistaken, or I am very much in error. A disciple of the wise can be someone who has not taken upon himself the "laws of the Association" <note>original: *divrei chaberut*; Greek: *ta tēs hetaireias*</note>, as is clearly evident from the *Baraita*, or "Extravagant Sanction," which can be read in the Babylonian Gemara, *Bekhorot 30b*: *The Masters teach: If anyone wishes to take upon himself the laws of Association, he must do so before a tribunal of three associates; even a disciple of a sage must do so before a tribunal of three associates.* The Associates were, it seems to me, a class of men far more scrupulous than the common people regarding the minutiae of ritual impurities; they entered into a society and bound themselves by certain laws so that they might act more securely among themselves and avoid the impurities arising from commerce with the common folk. The laws or conditions they imposed on themselves are enumerated in this Mishnah, all of which relate to purity. First, *That they do not sell moist or dry crops to commoners*; so they are not the cause of them being defiled. Second, *That they do not receive moist items from them*; lest they perhaps be defiled, because it is established that moistening makes food susceptible to receiving impurity. Third, *That they do not stay as guests with commoners*; lest they themselves, being thus defiled, defile clean things. Fourth, *That they do not receive commoners as guests in their own clothes*; because the clothes of commoners were to them *midras* [Hebrew], or contaminated by pressure. There are also many rules about admitting Associates into this Society, about instructing them, and about rejecting them for violating the laws, along with other such matters which anyone who wishes may seek from the Gemara in the aforementioned place, and from the *Tosefta* of this chapter. Whether these Associates are the same as the Pharisees, such that all Pharisees took the laws of this Society upon themselves, I cannot easily say. Certainly, anyone who considers all those things that are read in the Gospels (*Matthew 15, Mark 7*, etc.) regarding the anxious concern of the Pharisees in avoiding

<column-break/>

impurities might believe this to be at least likely. **Bertinoro**, however, openly asserts that "Associate" and "Pharisee" <note>Hebrew: *Chaber* and *Parush*</note> are the same. And in *Chagigah 2:7* it is said: *The clothes of the common people are considered "midras" [contaminated by pressure] for the Pharisees*; so that the Pharisees there hold the clothes of commoners in the same regard as the Associates do here. For this reason, citing this passage, **Nathan the Lexicographer** speaks thus of the Pharisees: *They are the Associates who eat their profane or common food in a state of purity.* Therefore, they are the same men called "Pharisees" and "Associates," but in different respects. They were called *Pharisees* because they had separated themselves <note>original: *perushim*</note> "from all uncleanness, and from unclean food, and from the common people who are less concerned about food," as the same **Rabbi Nathan** says. They were called *Associates* <note>original: *chaberim*</note> in respect to the Society entered into among themselves to avoid impurity. Moreover, men of any condition, even the lowest, could be admitted into this Society, which is why in the very next paragraph bakers, and in 3:1 even the poor, are understood as "Associates" by **Bertinoro**. See below, 6:9, 12.

2 *Whoever heaps up, etc.*] That is, wholesalers or large-scale merchants, who are contrasted with shopkeepers and retailers. For the former are accustomed to give the retailers a "surplus" <note>Greek: *epimetron*</note>, a heap, or a corollary. They sell with a *good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over*, as **Saint Luke** says [Luke 6:38], in a phrase not at all foreign to our own.

3 *Corn-merchant*.] The Greek word is *sitōnēs*, that is, one who buys grain to resell it, just as they appear joined together in **Gregory Nazianzen** as *corn-merchants and grain-retailers*. **Maimonides** is therefore wrong below in 5:6 when he says: *A "Sitona" is one who sells types of liquids and fruits.* Which is almost the same as that same **Rabbi**—

And that which is usually measured with a **small measure**, if it is measured with a large one, the large follows the status of the small. What constitutes a large measure? For dry goods, three *cabi* <note>A *cab* or *kav* is a measure of volume; three cabi is approximately 4-6 liters.</note>; for liquids, a measure worth a **denarius**. **Rabbi Joses** says: If someone sells baskets of figs or grapes, or crates of vegetables by estimation <note>original: *conjectura*; meaning sold as a bulk lot rather than by precise weight or volume</note>, he is exempt from the strictures of the large-measure rule.

### CHAP. III.

1. **Doubtful produce** <note>Hebrew: *Demai*—produce purchased from a common person where it is uncertain if the tithes were separated.</note> may be given to the poor and to guests to eat. **Rabban Gamaliel** used to give doubtful produce to his laborers to eat. # Title III. DEMAI [Doubtful Produce]

...if he wishes to return it, let him not return it unless he tithes it; <sup>1</sup> because nothing is lacking except for the counting. If while buying, someone sees another, better bundle, he can return it, because he has not yet <sup>2</sup> **drawn** <note>Latin: *traxit*; Hebrew: *meshikah*. In Jewish law, a transaction for movable goods is often finalized by physically pulling or lifting the item.</note> it.

3. He who finds crops and picks them up to eat, then changes his mind and wishes to put them back, let him not put them back unless he tithes them. But if he first picked them up so that they would not perish, he is exempt. It is not permitted to sell any "doubtful" thing <note>Produce where it is uncertain if tithes were taken.</note>, nor is it permitted to send a "doubtful" thing to another. **Rabbi Joses** permits sending a certain thing <note>Produce known to be properly tithed.</note>, provided that he informs the recipient.

4. If someone sends wheat to a **Cuthean** <note>A Samaritan. The Sages often viewed Samaritans as observant of some laws but suspect in others.</note> miller or to a **common person** <note>Latin: *plebeio*; Hebrew: *Am ha-aretz*. A person not strictly observant of tithing laws.</note> to be ground, it remains in its own status regarding tithes and the crops of the **Sabbatical Year** <note>The seventh year of the agricultural cycle when the land must lie fallow and crops are communal.</note>; but if sent to a foreign miller, <sup>3</sup> the matter becomes "doubtful." If someone deposits crops in the care of a Cuthean or a common person, they remain in their own status regarding tithes and the crops of the Sabbatical Year; but if in the care of a foreigner, they are considered to be that person's own crops. **Rabbi Simeon** argues that the matter becomes "doubtful."

5. He who hands anything over <sup>4</sup> to an **innkeeper** tithes what he hands over, and also that which he receives back from her, because she is subject to the suspicion that she might swap it. **Rabbi Joses** says to the contrary: We are not made the guarantors of fraudsters; he tithes only what he receives back from her.

6. He who hands anything over to his **mother-in-law** tithes what he hands over, and that which he receives back from her, because she is held under suspicion of having swapped a spoiled item <note>Likely meaning untithed or inferior produce.</note>. For **Rabbi Judah** thinks that a woman wishes to win favor for her daughter and be held in respect by her son-in-law. **Rabbi Judah** acknowledges that if someone hands something to his mother-in-law during the Sabbatical Year, she would not be subject to suspicion of swapping it, so that she would not <sup>5</sup> **feed her daughter** with the crops of the Sabbatical Year <note>Which are subject to strict rules of consumption and cannot be hoarded or traded.</note>.

->CHAPTER NOTES<-

<columns>2</columns>

1 *Because nothing is lacking except for the counting.*] The commentators suppose these are bundles of vegetables already bought and "drawn" on the condition that the buyer pays a certain price for each bundle soon to be counted. Because nothing is lacking except the counting of the bundles, they become the buyer's property, and he cannot return them unless they are first tithed. However, I suspect a textual error in this passage, especially since in the **Jerusalem Talmud** <note>One of the two great collections of Jewish law and tradition.</note> the word for "tithe" is read instead of "lacking"; this is also how **Rabbi Samson** and **Bartenura** <note>Prominent medieval commentators on the Mishnah.</note> clearly read it.

2 *Drawn.*] For "drawing" <note>original: *Tractio*</note>, or the lifting up of a purchased thing, is necessarily required in movable property to transfer the legal right of ownership. See Kiddushin 1:5.

3 *The matter becomes "doubtful."*] Because when many bundles of grain are brought to a miller at once, a foreigner, who is not guided by religious concern, might mix tithed grain with untithed grain out of mere carelessness. But there is no room for this doubt (though **Rabbi Simeon** thinks otherwise) in the case of a foreign depositary, who might perhaps swap it with his own crops; however, those are free from tithes. It would not be mixed with the crops of another Israelite depositor, as there might not be one, and thus it would not be held as a "doubtful" matter.

<column-break/>

4 *Innkeeper.*] From the Greek *pandokidi* or *pandokeutria*, as she prepares food for him to eat. He tithes what he gives her so that he does not provide her a "stumbling block" <note>A biblical concept (Leviticus 19:14) of causing another person to sin.</note>, lest he himself be the cause of her eating untithed food that she swapped for her own. However, **Rabbi Joses** thinks it is sufficient if he simply looks out for himself.

5 *Feed her daughter.*] This is the common reading. The sense would be that she does not wish to swap crops that are not from the Sabbatical Year—which were brought to her by her son-in-law—for crops of the Sabbatical Year, so as not to impose the burdens on her daughter that accompany the eating of Sabbatical Year produce. However, **Maimonides** <note>The 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legalist.</note> plainly reads "family" <note>Latin: *familiam*; Hebrew: *mishpacha*</note> instead of "daughter." In his Arabic commentary, it is *li-nas ahlahum*, that is, "for the people of their family." Therefore, according to Maimonides, the passage should be translated: ***Rabbi Judah acknowledges that if someone hands Sabbatical Year crops to his mother-in-law, she will not be subject to suspicion of swapping them, as she would not want to feed her family with Sabbatical Year crops.***

Order I. SEEDS (Zeraim)

# CHAPTER IV.

1. If someone bought produce from a person who is not considered trustworthy <note>Latin: *fide dignus*; Hebrew: *Ne'eman*. This refers to someone scrupulous in separating tithes.</note> regarding tithes, and he forgot to tithe it, he may ask the seller on the Sabbath day and eat based on his word.<gloss>1</gloss> However, once darkness falls at the end of the Sabbath, he may not eat until he tithes. If the seller cannot be found, and someone else who is also not considered trustworthy tells him that the produce was tithed,<gloss>1</gloss> he may eat based on that person's word. But once darkness falls at the end of the Sabbath, he may not eat until he tithes. If the "tithe of the tithes" <gloss>2</gloss> <note>Latin: *primitiae decimarum*; Hebrew: *Terumat Ma'aser*. This is the ten percent of the tithe that a Levite must give to a Priest.</note> fell back into its original place <note>Meaning it became mixed with the rest of the grain again, making the whole pile forbidden until separated.</note>, Rabbi Simeon of Sezor says: Even on a weekday, if he asks the seller, <gloss>3</gloss> he may eat based on his word.

2. If someone binds another by a vow to eat with him, but the guest does not trust the host regarding tithes, he may nevertheless eat with him on the first Sabbath, even if he does not normally trust him; this is permitted as long as the host tells him the tithes have been removed. On the second Sabbath, however, even if the host has forbidden him from receiving any benefit through a vow, the guest may not eat unless he first tithes the food himself.

3. Rabbi Eliezer says: No one is required <gloss>4</gloss> to designate by name the "tithe for the poor" in a case of "doubtful" produce <note>Latin: *rei dubiae*; Hebrew: *Demai*. Produce purchased from a common person where it is uncertain if it was tithed.</note>. But the Sages hold that one must designate it by name, though one is not required to physically separate it.

4. If someone has designated by name the "tithe of the tithes" for doubtful produce, or the "tithe for the poor" for "certain" produce <note>Latin: *rei certae*; Hebrew: *Vadai*. Produce known to have not been tithed at all.</note>, he may not physically remove them on the Sabbath. However, if a Priest or a poor person is accustomed to eating with him, they may come and eat; <gloss>5</gloss> provided that he makes the situation known to them.

5. If someone tells a person who is not trustworthy regarding tithes: "Buy for me from someone who is trustworthy," or "from someone who tithes," and the person responds, "Person N is not trustworthy, but Person M is trustworthy." If the messenger then went to buy it and later said, "I did not find the person you specified, but I bought for you from another trustworthy person," he is not considered trustworthy.

6. If someone enters a city where he knows no one and asks, "Who here is trustworthy?" or "Who here tithes?" and someone responds, <gloss>6</gloss> "I am," that person is not considered trustworthy. But if he says, "Person N is trustworthy," he is believed.

---

1 *Based on his word.*] For the rule is, <note>Hebrew: *Ein adam chote v'lo lo*</note> "No one is wicked for no reason," or without personal gain. <note>The idea is that a person would not lie about a religious obligation if it does not benefit them financially, especially on the Sabbath.</note>
2 *Into its place.*] That is, if they are mixed again into the crops from which they were taken.
3 *Based on his word.*] The common person <note>Latin: *plebeius*; Hebrew: *Am ha-aretz*.</note>, whom he previously knew to have separated the tithe, if he claims to have separated it again.
4 *To designate by name.*] To "designate by name" or "mark out" the first-fruits or tithes is to define and destine a certain part or portion of the crops for the tithes or first-fruits by naming it; as if someone were to say, "The first-fruits or tithes which I must pay from this heap shall be from this or that part,"

<column-break/>

designating the place from which he wishes them to be taken, even if he has not yet physically removed them.
5 *Provided that he makes the situation known to them.*] For otherwise, it is unlawful to feed guests with first-fruits or tithes <note>Unless they are qualified to eat them, such as Priests or the poor.</note>.
6 *I am: he is not considered trustworthy. But if he says, Person N is trustworthy, etc.*] So that it reads, "I am not trustworthy, but Person N is." And so the manuscript has it, except that "trustworthy" is omitted there. Other codices read: "I am not trustworthy; Person N is trustworthy."

### CHAPTER V.

1. How does one tithe who buys from a baker? He takes enough for the tithe of the tithes <note>Latin: *primitiis decimarum*; Hebrew: *Terumat Ma'aser*—the portion a Levite gives to a Priest</note> and the dough offering,² saying: *“A hundredth part of what is here, on this side, is considered tithes, and the rest of the tithes are adjacent to it. That which I have designated as tithes shall become the tithe of the tithes for them, and what remains is the dough offering. Let the Second Tithe be to the north or to the south; and let them be redeemed with money.”*

If one wishes to set aside the Great Offering <note>The first portion given to the Priest</note> and the tithe of the tithes together, he takes a thirty-third part and a third,³ saying: *“A hundredth part of what is here, on this side,⁴ shall be common, and what remains is the Great Offering for the whole. <meta>catchword: be</meta>

---

1 *Old grain.*] Grain of the past year. For one fears to buy new grain <note>Latin: *hornas*</note> because perhaps the first-fruits offering <note>the Omer</note> has not yet been brought.
2 *On this side.*] Designating a specific portion, which contains one hundredth, and additionally one forty-eighth of the whole mass or loaf; the former for the tithe of the tithes, the latter for the dough offering.
3 *Thirty-third part and a third.*] That is, a fiftieth for the Great Offering, and a hundredth for the tithe of the tithes, which together make up a thirty-third and a third. However, this portion is slightly larger than is strictly necessary; for if the Great Offering must contain a fiftieth part, or two-hundredths of the whole, the tithe of the tithes would be a hundredth not of that same whole, but only of the remainder. Thus, the Great Offering and the tithe of the tithes would not make up three hundred parts out of ten thousand (which is a thirty-third of the whole plus a third), but only two hundred and ninety-eight parts.
4 *Shall be common.*] That is, as Bertinorius <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro, a 15th-century commentator</note> explains: <term>ישאר חולין כמו שהוא עתה בטבלו</term> "It shall remain common <note>non-sacred</note> in the same state it has been until now, while it is still untithed." The reader should note the use of the word <term>חולין</term> <note>Chullin; common or profane things</note>

<column-break/>

which is quite unusual twice in this paragraph. In both places, it is used for *untouched matter* <note>matter from which no offerings have yet been removed</note>.
5 *Of the hundred parts.*] The passage is not entirely sound. I follow the reading: <term>מאה חולין שיש כאן הרי זו</term> <note>One hundred common parts that are here, behold this...</note>. The manuscript omits the first "this." So also Maimonides, who comments on the passage thus: <term>תם יקול מאה חולין שיש כאן הרי בצד זה מעשר וישיר פי דלך אלי טבאקי מן אלתלאתה אלדי קד געלה חולין</term> <note>Original in Judeo-Arabic</note> "Then he says: 'Of the hundred parts of common matter here, let this side be the tithe,' pointing his finger to that part of the three which he had made common." Hence it is that <term>מאה חולין</term> is interpreted as *one hundredth part*. Yet he does not say this explicitly. Nor can the words be so sounded. "One hundredth of the common matter" is said in Hebrew as <term>אחד ממאה מהחולין</term>, not <term>מאה חולין</term>. Rabbis Samson and Obadiah read <term>מהחולין</term> instead of <term>חולין</term>, so the words sound: "From the common matter which is here, let this portion on this side be the tithe." I judge the reading I have followed to be better.
6 *Tithe of the tithes.*] Almost all printed editions add: *“and the rest is the dough offering.”* So too the Talmud.

<meta>This page continues Chapter 5 of the tractate Demai, focusing on the laws of tithing produce purchased from different types of merchants. It explores whether one may set aside tithes from one batch of goods to cover another, depending on the reliability of the source and whether the items are of the same variety.</meta>

# Order I. ZERAIM <note>Zeraim, meaning "Seeds," is the first section of the Mishnah, dealing primarily with agricultural laws.</note>

<columns>2</columns>

...the second shall be to the north, or to the south; and thus they are redeemed <note>The "redemption" refers to the practice of transferring the sanctity of the Second Tithe from the produce itself to a coin, which is then spent in Jerusalem.</note>.

3. One who buys from a baker may set aside tithes from warm bread for cold bread, and from cold bread for warm bread, even if they are of different molds. This is the view of Rabbi Meir. But Rabbi Judah forbids this. For I might say, he says, that yesterday's wheat $^1$ belonged to one person, and today's to another. Rabbi Simeon forbids the setting aside of the "tithe of the tithes" <note>Latin: *decimarum primitias*; Hebrew: *Terumat Ma'aser*</note> in this manner, but he permits it for the dough offering <note>Latin: *speciem*; likely referring to the *Challah* portion</note>.

4. One who buys from a $^2$ reseller <note>Latin: *pratere*; from the Greek *prater*</note> must give tithes from each mold individually. This is the view of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Judah says: he may give from one for all. However, Rabbi Judah acknowledges that one who buys from a monopolist <note>Latin: *monopola*; a merchant who buys up all the bread to resell it</note> must set aside tithes from each mold individually.

5. One who buys from a poor person—and likewise a poor person himself to whom pieces of bread or fragments of fig-cakes <note>Latin: *palathæ fragmina*</note> were given—sets aside tithes from each piece individually. However, with dates and dried figs, he may mix them together and then take the portion. When is this so? Rabbi Judah says: if the gift was a generous one; but if it was a meager gift, he must tithe each one individually.

6. One who buys from a grain merchant <note>Latin: *fitona*, likely a corruption of *sitona*; Greek: *sitones*</note>, if he buys again from the same person a second time, he may not give tithes from this batch for the previous one, even if they are from the same basket or the same species. Trust is given to the grain merchant $^3$ if he says they both belonged to the same man.

7. One who buys from a householder, if he buys again from the same person a second time, may give tithes from one for the other, even if they come from two different baskets or two different towns. A householder who sells vegetables in the market, as long as they were brought from his own gardens, may give tithes from one for all; but if they came from someone else's gardens, he must tithe each individually.

8. One who buys un-tallowed <note>Latin: *rem illibatam*; refers to produce from which no offerings have been taken yet (untithed)</note> produce from two different places may give tithes from one for the other; even though it is said that no one is permitted to sell untithed produce except in a case of urgent necessity.

9. Tithes are taken from the produce of Israelites $^4$ for the produce of Gentiles, and from the produce of Gentiles for the produce of Israelites; from the produce...

---

...both; so it appears in the Venice Mishnah with the commentaries of Maimonides and Bertinoro, the Cracow edition with the commentaries of Bertinoro and Yom Tov, and the first Amsterdam edition. The only one I know, the vocalized Amsterdam edition, which agrees with the Manuscript, omits these words; however, they confuse the sense and clearly crept in from the previous paragraph.

$^1$ *Belonged to one person, and today's to another.*] One of whom perhaps usually pays his tithes, while the other does not. But it is not permitted to pay tithes from a batch already tithed for one that has not been tithed.

$^2$ *Reseller.*] The word *palter* <note>Hebrew: פלטר</note> is a corruption of the Greek *prater*. By "reseller," they mean a retailer who sells bread bought from a baker. Because he buys from many different bakers, Rabbi Meir requires anyone who buys from a reseller to pay tithes for each different mold separately.

<column-break/>

Indeed, he judges that bread of this mold was bought from one baker, and that mold from another. Rabbi Judah does not consider this necessary unless the bread was bought from a monopolist; that is, from someone who buys the entire output of the bakers to resell it.

$^3$ *If he says they both belonged to the same man.*] In which case he can give tithes from one for the other.

$^4$ *For the produce of Gentiles.*] For the produce of Gentiles grown in the land of Israel must be tithed according to the rule: <note>Hebrew: אין לגוי קניין בארץ ישראל להפקיע מן המעשרות</note> "A Gentile does not have a legal possession in the Land of Israel such as would abolish the obligation of tithes." Maimonides accepts this rule. Bertinoro thinks the opposite is true; and therefore he attributes both the rule itself and the Mishnah based on it to the private opinion of Rabbi Meir.

### TITLE III. DEMAI <note>Demai refers to "doubtful" produce purchased from common folk, where it is uncertain if the required priestly portions and tithes were properly removed.</note>

...produce of Israelites for the produce of Cutheans <note>original: "Cuthæorum"; the Samaritans, a group whose adherence to tithing laws was viewed with suspicion by the Rabbis</note>, and from the produce of Cutheans for the produce of Cutheans. ¹ Rabbi Eliezer forbids [setting aside portions] from the produce of Cutheans for the produce of Cutheans.

10. A **perforated jar** is regarded as the soil itself <note>In Jewish law, if a pot has a hole large enough for a root to reach the earth, the plants inside are legally considered "attached" to the ground</note>. If someone sets aside first fruits <note>original: "primitias"; here referring to the *Terumah* or Great Heave-offering for the priest</note> from the soil for a perforated jar, or from a perforated jar for the soil, the offering is valid. From a ² **non-perforated** jar for a perforated one, it is considered ³ **first fruits**; but he must set aside other first fruits again. From a perforated jar for a non-perforated one, it is considered first fruits; ⁴ however, they may not be eaten until the first fruits and tithes are first taken from them.

11. If someone sets aside first fruits from ⁵ **doubtful produce** for doubtful produce, or from doubtful produce for certain produce, it is considered first fruits; but he must set aside other first fruits again. From certain produce for doubtful produce, it is first fruits; however, they may not be eaten until the first fruits and tithes are first taken from them.

## CHAPTER VI.

1. ⁶ He who **leases a field for cultivation** from an Israelite, a foreigner, or a Cuthean, shall ⁷ **divide the crop in their presence**. He who leases a field for a fixed rental from an Israelite pays the rent only after the first fruits have first been taken. But when is this? asks Rabbi Judah. If he pays from that same field and of the same species. But if he pays from another field, or from a different species, he pays only after the tithes have also first been taken.

2. He who leases a field for a fixed rental from a foreigner, after the tithes have first been taken—

---
<columns>2</columns>
¹ *Rabbi Eliezer forbids, etc.*] For he believes that some Cutheans are careful about paying tithes, while others are not touched by any concern for them. Maimonides recognizes various sects of Cutheans <note>original: "Mi-Cuthim perek"; from the tractate on Cutheans</note> no fewer than Epiphanius does <note>Epiphanius was a 4th-century Christian bishop who wrote about various Jewish and Samaritan sects</note>.

² *Non-perforated.*] Whatever grows in non-perforated jars, since it cannot be said to have grown from the earth, is not bound by the Law regarding first fruits and tithes, but only by the decrees of the Teachers <note>The Rabbis</note>. Therefore, first fruits set aside from there cannot suffice for the soil, or for what is of the same condition, such as a perforated jar.

³ *They are first fruits.*] That is, they go to the Priest by the rite of first fruits.

⁴ *They may not be eaten.*] By the Priest; because however much they might go to him by the rite of first fruits, nonetheless those very fruits are considered untithed, insofar as they were set aside for produce that has no obligation for first fruits under the Law.

⁵ *For doubtful produce.*] The reasoning of this paragraph and the previous one is similar, while a comparison is made between a doubtful matter and a non-perforated jar on one side, and a certain matter and a perforated jar on the other; except that they differ in this one case: 
<column-break/>
that, while the setting aside would be valid if one set aside from a non-perforated jar for another non-perforated jar—even though this case was omitted in the previous paragraph—because the reasoning for both is equal, and the same obligation exists in both cases from the decrees of the Sages; on the contrary, if one sets aside from doubtful produce for doubtful produce, he will be obliged to set aside again. This is because it is possible that one of these has indeed long ago paid the first fruits, but the other has not; and it is forbidden to set aside first fruits from that which has already paid for that which has not yet paid.

⁶ *He who leases a field for cultivation.*] We spoke above at Peah 5.5 about the various types of farmers among the Jews. There we held *aris* <note>Hebrew: אריס; a sharecropper</note> and *mekabbel* <note>Hebrew: מקבל; a contractor</note> to be synonyms, so that each is a sharecropping tenant. Bertinorius confirms our observation on this passage: <note>Hebrew: "One who receives a field for a half, a third, or a quarter, in the manner of the arisin [sharecroppers]."</note> *He who leases a field for cultivation, namely for a half, third, or fourth part, in the manner of the* **sharecroppers** <note>Hebrew: "ha-arisin"</note> *the sharecropping tenants.* Moreover, wherever I place "lease for cultivation" in the version, understand it as by sharecropping right.

⁷ *Divide it in their presence.*] Without the setting aside of first fruits and tithes <note>This implies the division of the raw crop happens before any religious taxes are removed, so each party handles their own obligations</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of tithing obligations for sharecroppers and partners (Order Zeraim, Tractate Demai). It specifically addresses cases where Priests, Levites, and laypeople enter into contracts to cultivate land and how the sacred portions—the First Fruits (Terumah) and Tithes (Ma'aser)—are distributed between them. It also covers the "Fellows" (Haverim) who are scrupulous in their religious duties compared to the common folk.</meta>

# Order I. ZERAIM <note>Seeds; the first division of the Mishnah focusing on agricultural laws.</note>

...pays after the tithes have been removed. Rabbi Judah adds: Even he who rents his father's field from a foreigner <note>non-Jew</note> for cultivation pays after the tithes have been removed.

3. If a Priest or a Levite rents a Layman's field for cultivation, just as they divide the common produce as sharecroppers, so too they divide the $^1$ **first fruits** <note>original: "primitias"; here referring to the *Terumah*, the portion given to the Priest</note> as sharecroppers. Rabbi Eliezer says: On the contrary, the $^2$ **tithes** belong to them [the Priest or Levite renters], because they entered into the agreement on that condition.

4. If a Layman rents a Priest’s or Levite’s field for cultivation, the tithes go to the owner of the land. Rabbi Ishmael adds: If a peasant rents the field of a man from Jerusalem for cultivation, the Second Tithes <note>A tithe to be eaten by the owner within the walls of Jerusalem</note> go to the Jerusalemite. But the Sages believe that the peasant himself can eat them in Jerusalem after they have been brought there.

5. $^3$ If anyone rents olive trees to produce oil, just as they divide the common produce as sharecroppers, so too they divide the first fruits as sharecroppers. If a Layman rents olives for oil production $^4$ **for half the profit**, Rabbi Judah asserts that the tithes belong to the owner.

6. The School of Shammai say: Let no one sell his olives except to a **Fellow** <note>original: "Socio"; a *Haver*, one who is strictly observant of tithing and purity laws</note>. The School of Hillel permit selling even to one who [merely] tithes. However, the more scrupulous among the Hillelites followed the ruling of the Shammaites.

7. Of two people who bring their vintages to the same wine-press, if one tithes but the other does not; the one who tithes $^5$ **tithes what is his**, and his portion wherever it may be.

8. Of two people who rent a field for sharecropping, or receive an inheritance, or possess it in partnership, one can say to the other: "You take the wheat from there, and I will take the wheat from here; you take the wine from there, and I will take the wine from here." But he may not say: "You take the wheat, and I will take the barley; you take the wine, and I will take the oil."

9. If a Fellow and a commoner are co-heirs to a commoner father, the Fellow may say: "You take the wheat from there, and I will take the wheat from here; you take the wine from there, and I will take the wine from here." But he may not say: "You take the wheat, and I will take the barley; you take the liquid [produce], and I will take the dry [produce]."

10. If

---

1 *They divide the first fruits as sharecroppers.*] Or the tithes; so that the Layman, as owner of the land, may contribute the portion of the first fruits or tithes that falls to him to any other Priest or Levite at his own discretion.

2 *Tithes.*] And first fruits. Note here and in what follows that <term>terumah</term> <note>heave-offering for the priest</note> or <term>ma'aser</term> <note>tithe</note> are used for both first fruits and tithes by synecdoche <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note>; which also occurs elsewhere.

3 *If anyone.*] A Layman from a Cleric [Priest or Levite], or a Cleric from a Layman.

4 *For half the profit.*] The Jerusalem Talmud says "or for half the profit." And so says Rabbi Obadiah; thus there is a difference here between renting for oil production—namely, for a specific part of the oil eventually made—and taking it to be managed for half the share of the

<column-break/>

increase or gain.

5 *What is his, etc.*] It is unlawful for him who claims <term>trustworthiness</term> <note>original Greek: "axiopistian"</note> in tithing to hand over untithed material to someone else who is not trustworthy. Therefore, if two people are involved, of whom one is trustworthy and the other is not, the one is bound to tithe *what is his*—that is, the portion he receives in the division—and moreover *his portion wherever it may be*; that is, to pay tithes additionally from his own property for the half-share that the other receives, since it consists equally of the produce of both, lest he should seem to have handed over untithed produce to the other. This is how Rabbi Samson explains this passage. The other commentators, if I see anything at all, see nothing.

<meta>This page continues the third chapter of Tractate Demai, which deals with produce where there is a doubt as to whether it has been properly tithed. ### Title III. DEMAI <note>Produce suspected of not being tithed.</note>

10. If a convert and a gentile are co-heirs to their gentile father, the convert may say: "You take the idol, and I will take the money; you take the <gloss>1</gloss> wine, and I will take the grain." But once these items have come into the possession of the convert, such an exchange is no longer permitted. <note>The law forbids a Jew from profiting directly from idols or wine used for pagan libations; however, during the division of an inheritance, the convert can opt for the "clean" assets before they are legally his.</note>

11. If someone selling grain in <gloss>2</gloss> Syria claims that it is from the Land of Israel, it must be tithed. If he adds that it has already been tithed, he is considered trustworthy, because the same authority that bound the obligation also released it. <note>This is a legal principle: if the seller didn't have to admit the grain was from Israel (which "bound" it to tithing laws), his claim that it is already tithed (which "released" it) is believed.</note> If he says the grain is from his own field [in Syria], it must be tithed; but if he adds it has already been tithed, he is believed, for the same authority that bound also released. However, if it is well known that he owns a field in Syria, the grain must be tithed.

12. If a common person <note>An *Am Ha-aretz*, someone not scrupulous with tithing laws.</note> orders a Fellow <note>A *Haver*, a member of a group dedicated to strict tithing.</note> as follows: "Buy me a bundle of vegetables" or "Buy me a <gloss>3</gloss> small roll," and the Fellow buys them without further specification, they are exempt from tithing. But if the commoner says, "This is for me, and that is for my friend," and they are later mixed together, they must be tithed, even if there are a hundred of them.

---

->**CHAPTER VII.**<-

1. **IF** someone is invited to eat with another person [whose tithing status he does not trust], and he does not believe him regarding the tithes, he speaks thus on the eve of the Sabbath: "Whatever I am going to separate tomorrow shall be the tithe, and the remainder of the tithe shall be adjacent to it. That which I have designated as tithes shall be made the first-fruits of the tithe <note>original: *decimarum primitiae*; the *Terumah* of the Tithe given by the Levite to the Priest.</note> for the rest. The Second Tithe shall be to the north, or to the south, and be redeemed with a coin."

2. **When** they mix a cup of wine for him, he speaks thus: "What I intend to leave in the bottom of the cup shall be the tithe, and the remainder of the tithe shall be adjacent to it. That which I have designated as tithe shall be made the first-fruits of the tithe for the rest. The Second Tithe shall be at the top of the cup, and be redeemed with a coin." 3.

<margin>1 *Wine.*</margin> The wine of a gentile is considered <term>Yayin Nesek</term> <note>original: יין נסך; libation wine used for idolatry.</note>.
<margin>2 *Syria.*</margin> By "Syria," the Mishnah understands <term>Aram Soba and Aram Naharaim</term> <note>original: ארם צובה & ארם נהרים; regions in Upper Mesopotamia and around Aleppo.</note>, which were formerly brought under dominion by David. They consider this region to be of an intermediate status between the Land of Israel and <term>foreign land</term> <note>original: חוצה לארץ; literally "outside the land."</note>. This is because David conquered these nations before the Promised Land itself was fully subdued. Otherwise, whatever is a <term>conquest of the public</term> <note>original: כבוש רבים; a communal or national conquest.</note> by the people of Israel is considered part of the Land of Israel. Therefore, an Israelite is not obligated to tithe grain grown in Syria unless the field itself belongs to him.
<margin>3 *Small roll.*</margin> <term>One *gluska*</term> <note>original: גלוסקיו אחת; a fine bread roll or cake.</note>. Thus it appears in the manuscript and the Jerusalem Talmud: other codices write it as <term>gluskan</term> to match a plural ending, but it refers to the same form of the word. Elsewhere it is read as <term>gluska</term> in the singular and <term>gluska'ot</term> in the plural; or even with a 'p' instead of a 'b'. The Syrian lexicographers also have <term>ka'ka</term> <note>original: ܟܥܟܐ; a type of cake.</note>,

<column-break/>

which Isa bar Ali explains as <term>leavened cake</term> or <term>white bread</term>; another anonymous author simply calls it <term>cake</term>. To that word, the term <term>fine flour</term> <note>original: ܚܫܝܐ</note> is added in red ink above, so that you may understand it as a roll made of fine flour. Nearly the same definition is found in Bar Bahlul. Hence, Musaphias believes the word is derived from the Greek <term>kollyra</term> <note>a coarse roll or bun</note>. Cohen de Lara seems to aim for the same, asserting it means in Greek <term>a bun or a ring of bread</term> <note>original Spanish: "bollo, o rosca de pan."</note>. But since it clearly relates to the form of the word, I rather take it for the Greek <term>glykinas</term>. Now, <term>glykinas</term> is "a cake made with sweet wine and oil among the Cretans." So says Seleucus in the glosses found in Athenaeus. From this, the entry in Hesychius under <term>Glykinas</term> should be corrected.

<meta>This page continues Chapter VII of Tractate Demai, which provides the specific verbal formulas used by individuals to tithe produce when its status is uncertain (Demai) or when they are unable to physically separate the tithes immediately. It specifically addresses workers, travelers, and buyers of wine from Samaritans.</meta>

# Order I. SEEDS (ZERAIM)

3. A worker who does not trust the householder <note>The employer or master of the house.</note> regarding tithes, and who is taking a single dried fig to eat, speaks thus: *“Let this one, and the nine that follow it, be the tithe for the ninety I am about to eat. Let this one be the heave-offering of the tithe <term>Terumat Ma'aser: the portion of the tithe given to the Priest</term> for them. Let the second tithe be in the last ones, and let it be redeemed <note>Original: "profanatae" — the process of transferring the sanctity of the fruit onto money so the fruit can be eaten.</note> by money.”* Then he should set aside one dried fig. Rabban Simeon, son of Gamaliel, forbids setting it aside because it would diminish the householder's work <note>Wasting time on the employer's clock.</note>. Rabbi Joses also forbids setting it aside, ¹ on account of the **Pact of the Sanhedrin**.

4. He who buys wine from the Cutheans <note>Samaritans, whose adherence to tithing laws was considered unreliable by the Rabbis.</note> speaks thus: ² *“Two logs <term>Log: a liquid measure, roughly the volume of six eggs</term> which I intend to separate shall be the heave-offering; ten shall be the first tithe, and nine shall be the second tithe. Then he begins to drink.”*

5. If someone has untithed figs at home, but he is currently in the school <note>The House of Study or Yeshiva.</note> or in the ³ field, he speaks thus: *“The two figs which I will eventually separate shall be the heave-offering; ten shall be the first tithe, and nine shall be the second tithe.”* If the produce is of doubtful status <note>Demai.</note>, he speaks thus: *“What I will separate tomorrow shall be the tithe, and the rest shall be the tithe adjacent to it. This which I have designated as tithe shall be the heave-offering of the tithe for them. Let the second tithe be to the north, or to the south, and be redeemed by money.”*

6. If a person, before whom two baskets of untithed produce are placed, says: *“The tithes of this one are in that one,”* the first is considered tithed. If he says: *“The tithes of this in that, and that in this,”* ⁴ the first is tithed. If he says: *“The tithes of both are in each other,”* ⁵ he has already designated them by name.

7. Regarding a hundred parts ⁶ of untithed produce and an equal amount of "profane" <note>Common or already tithed.</note> produce mixed together, he takes—

---

<margin>Jerusalem Talmud: A condition of the Court that it shall be...</margin> 1 *On account of the Pact of the Sanhedrin.*] The pact is recorded as follows: *“It is a pact of the Sanhedrin that the heave-offering of the tithe is the responsibility of the worker, and the second tithe is the responsibility of the householder.”* I saw at first glance that this seemed clearly contrary to the meaning of our Mishnah; I did not doubt that by a mistake of scribes or printers, the words *worker* and *householder*, or at least *heave-offering of the tithe* and *second tithe*, had swapped places. For if the heave-offering of the tithe fell upon the worker, he would be obligated to set it aside for that very reason. Our conjecture is clearly supported by Rabbi Samson, who, citing the Jerusalem Talmud and the Tosefta, records the words of the pact thus: *“It is a pact of the Sanhedrin that the heave-offering of the tithe falls upon the householder, and the second tithe upon the worker.”*

2 *Two logs.*] A fiftieth part of a hundred logs; thus you should understand that the wine purchased is restricted here to a hundred logs; this is also to be understood regarding the figs in the following paragraph. I believe that in an older version of the *Mishnah* <note>Original: "deuterosi"</note> from which this was taken, there was an explicit mention of a hundred logs. For I think it cannot be doubted that from such passages, where the meaning is incomplete without a supplement, an invincible argument is found against

<column-break/>

the Jews who believe that before our current Mishnah, no traditions had ever been committed to writing. But this is discussed elsewhere. The remaining numbers here are not perfectly accurate: for the tithes of a hundred logs, after the heave-offerings are removed, are not ten logs, but a fifth less than ten; and thus the second tithe is not nine logs, but eight with forty-two fiftieth parts.

3 *Field.*] Supplement this: on the eve of the Sabbath, so that he fears the Sabbath may begin before he can separate the tithes.

4 *The first is tithed.*] But not the second, because of the rule: *“One should not separate tithes from the exempt for the obligated.”* <note>Original: "Non separandae sunt primitiae decimarumque de re immuni pro nexa." One cannot use produce that is already free of tithe obligations to fulfill the obligation for "connected" or untithed produce.</note>

5 *He has already designated them by name.*] So that he cannot thereafter fulfill the obligation from elsewhere.

6 *Untithed produce.*] Not simply untithed, but that from which the heave-offering of the tithe has not yet been taken. If such untithed produce and other common produce are mixed in equal quantities, they require that a hundredth part of the common produce be added to the untithed in the separation. In this way, the heave-offering of the tithe—which is one hundredth part of the produce—will fall into the hundred parts of common produce along with the remaining ninety-nine. # Title III. DEMAI.

...one hundred and one parts must be taken. From one hundred parts of untouched produce <note>Produce from which no offerings have been taken; Hebrew: *Tevel*.</note>, and as many of tithes, one hundred and ^1 one must be taken. From one hundred parts of secular produce <note>Produce already tithed and permitted for common use; Hebrew: *Hullin*.</note> properly prepared, and as many of tithes, one hundred and ten must be taken. From one hundred parts of untouched produce and ninety of tithes, or ninety of untouched produce and eighty of tithes, nothing is lost. This is the general rule: If the untouched produce exceeds in quantity, nothing is lost.

8. If someone who has ten rows available to him, each containing ten jars of wine, speaks thus: “Let one from a certain outermost row be the ^2 tithe,” but it is not established from which row; he takes ^3 two jars ^4 diagonally opposite. “Let one from a certain half-outermost row be the tithe,” but it is not established from which row; he takes four from the four corners. “Let one from a certain row be the tithe,” but it is not established from which row; he takes one diagonal row. “Let one from a certain half-row be the tithe,” but it is not established from which row; he takes both diagonal rows. “Let one jar be the tithe,” but it is not established from which row; he takes from every jar.

3. A laborer who does not have the trust of the master of the house <note>The "master of the house" refers to the landowner or employer; original Latin: *patrifamilias*.</note>, when taking a single dried fig, speaks as follows: *"Let this fig and the nine that are to follow it be the tithes for the ninety figs I am about to eat. 1 *Because of the agreement of the Sanhedrin.*] The Jerusalem Talmud records the agreement thus: <note>original Aramaic: תנ"י בו שחא : תרומת מעשר משל פועל ומעשר שני משל בעל הבית</note> "The agreement of the Sanhedrin is that the tithe-heave-offering falls upon the laborer, and the second tithe upon the master of the house." 3. Order I. SEEDS

# TITLE IV. CHILAIM.

## CONCERNING MIXTURES.

->*That is, concerning the unlawful mixing of different kinds in agriculture and the cultivation of vineyards, in the breeding and labor of animals, and in the fashioning of garments; according to the laws of Leviticus 19:19 and Deuteronomy 22:9, 10, 11.*<-

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>I.</margin>
WHEAT and <gloss>1</gloss> darnel <note>original Latin: lolium; a weed often found among wheat, historically known as "tares"</note> are not considered <gloss>2</gloss> of diverse kinds from one another. Barley and <gloss>3</gloss> fox-tail grass; <gloss>4</gloss> emmer wheat <note>original Latin: far adoreum; an ancient hulled grain</note> and <gloss>5</gloss> oats <note>original Latin: siphon; likely referring to wild oats or a similar cereal</note>; broad beans and peas; vetchling and bitter vetch; white beans and hyacinth beans <note>original Latin: smilax hortensis</note> are not considered of diverse kinds from one another.

---

1. **Darnel.** <note>original Hebrew: זונין – Zunin</note> Were it not for the Arabic language, in which the same word occurs <note>original Arabic: زوان – zuwan</note>, I would believe that *Zunin* was written with an old error for *Zuni*. Certainly, I think it is hardly to be doubted that *zizania* <note>original Greek: ζιזάνια</note>—a word you would find nowhere else but in the Gospels, and from there used among Ecclesiastical writers—is this very word of ours.

2. **Of diverse kinds.** <note>original Latin: Diversi generis</note> The true origin of the word *Chilaim* <note>original Hebrew: כלאים</note>, which was completely hidden from the Jews, was first revealed by Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century scholar of biblical animals and geography</note> from the Ethiopic language, which corresponds in a marvelous way with Hebrew. In Ethiopic, *kela'ium* <note>original Ethiopic: כלא</note> means "diverse"; and so it was once for the Hebrews. From this, in the dual number, comes *Chilaim*, referring to two diverse things, or things of a diverse kind; as in that verse: <note>original Hebrew: שדך לא תזרע כלאים</note> *"Your field you shall not sow with two kinds of seed"* [Leviticus 19:19] and similar passages.

3. **Fox-tail.** <note>original Latin: Spica vulpis</note> Maimonides and following him Rabbi Tanchum also provide the Arabic <note>original Arabic: סנבל אלתעלב – sunbul al-tha’lab</note> "fox-tail," which, however, I do not find among the Arabic herbalists. So also in the Babylonian Talmud [tractates] Pesachim 25a and Menachot 70b, it is called in Aramaic <note>original Aramaic: שבולי תעלא – shibbole thala</note>. I myself consider the Hebrew "fox-tail" <note>original Hebrew: שבולת שועל – shibbolet shu’al</note> to be a certain species of millet, as its head resembles the tail of a fox.

4. **Emmer wheat.** <note>original Latin: Far adoreum</note> Many things suggest

<column-break/>

that this is the Hebrew *Cusmet* <note>original Hebrew: כסמת</note>. First, the Seventy-Two Interpreters <note>the translators of the Septuagint</note> always put *zea* <note>original Greek: ζέα</note> or *olyra* <note>original Greek: ὀλύרה</note> for it, both of which Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> considers to be of the same kind. Next, Rabbi Tanchum wants it to be the Arabic *alas* <note>original Arabic: עלס</note>; but Beitardes <note>likely Ibn al-Baitar, the botanist</note> accommodates the description of *zea* by Dioscorides and Galen to *alas*; and Ibn al-Kabatius says much the same. However, it is the *zea* or *zeia* of the Latins, called "ador wheat," as is known from the famous passage of Dionysius of Halicarnassus and from Asclepiades in Galen's writings. In the Babylonian Talmud, in the places just cited, *Cusmet* is explained as *gulba* <note>original Aramaic: גולבא</note>; what that might be, I confess I do not know. Cohen de Lara <note>a 17th-century lexicographer</note> also interprets this as *zea*, asserting that the Arabic *gulab* signifies the same thing. But that Arabic word is not known to me either. Following Rabbi Solomon [Rashi], he interprets it as *zea*; for his own word for this is <note>original Yiddish/Old German: אשפילטא</note> *spelta* [spelt].

5. **Oats/Siphon.** <note>original Latin: Siphon</note> Finally, in the same dual Talmudic passage, *shiphon* <note>original Hebrew: שיפון</note> is explained as *dishra* <note>original Aramaic: דישרא</note>. This, as it is also the Syriac *dishra* <note>original Syriac: ܕܝܫܪא</note>, is clearly the Arabic *dusar* <note>original Arabic: دوسר</note>; which Rabbi Tanchum also provides for *shiphon*. Among the Arabs, *dusar* is said...

<header>Title IV. KIL’AYIM.</header>

...also called <insert>rashan</insert> <note>Arabic: رشن — a type of weed or wild grass</note>, as described for us by the physician Ibn Jazla, famous among the Arabs:
> It is a grass whose leaves resemble wheat leaves, but they are softer. It has a fruit with two or three coverings, and upon it is a likeness of barley.

These words require no other interpretation than for me to provide the description of *Aegilops* <note>Goat-grass</note> from Dioscorides, from which they were clearly taken.
*Dioscorides writes:* "Aegilops is a plant having leaves like wheat, but softer; and at the tip of the head it has two or three fruits in husks, upon which bristles have grown like walls."
Where, however, Ibn Jazla seems to have read "in 2 or 3 husks" <note>original Greek: ἐν β’. ἢ γ’. ἐλύτροις</note> for the original Greek. For so sound the words:
> having a fruit, which has two or three envelopes, or coverings.

So also Beitarides <note>Ibn al-Baitar, a 13th-century botanist</note> (who himself describes the same passage in Dioscorides under the entry for *dusar* <note>Arabic: دوسر — wild oats</note>, even prefixing the word <insert>al-itlas</insert> <note>Arabic: العتلاص</note>—most erroneously transcribed, as often happens in these matters, for *Aegilops*):
> and at its tip is a fruit in two or three coverings.

It is not for nothing, then, that in the spurious works of Dioscorides (if indeed all those are spurious which appeared so to the Saracens), it is read concerning *aegilops*: "some call it *sitaphela*, some *siphon* <note>oats</note>, some *bromos*, the Romans *abena* [oats]." And soon after regarding *bromos*: "some call it *siphonion*, some *akropaphela*, the Romans *abena*."
But to confess the truth, Dioscorides' *aegilops* does not seem to be counted among the grain-bearing plants, since it is only described in the fourth book, whereas he had included all grains in the second. Yet truly *Siphon* <note>identified here as a type of oat</note> is clearly categorized with grains by the Jews; from which even Paschal unleavened bread can be made (Tractate Pesachim II. 5) and from whose dough the priest's portion <term>Challah</term> <note>the portion of dough set aside for the priests according to biblical law</note> is to be set aside (Tractate Challah I. 1; Menachot X. 7).

**6** Beans, etc.] To the six names of legumes found here, those six from the list or wall-tablet of Hillel son of Ellem correspond, though they exist in a somewhat corrupted state in the Jerusalem Talmud: <insert>pila, pushna, gilbuna, milicha, sapharvana, sapharva</insert>. Rabbi Nathan <note>author of the Arukh, an 11th-century dictionary</note> presents this passage as follows: <insert>pul, pula, saphir, sapharva, she'atit, pachilta, gulbna, and batit, tzitzirklo, gulban, shuphach</insert>. That is, <insert>pul</insert> is <insert>pula</insert>—perhaps the Egyptian

<column-break/>

*pula* or *pola*? <note>original Hebrew: פּוּלָא or פּוֹלָא</note> i.e., the broad bean; <insert>saphir</insert> is *siphon* <note>original Greek: σίφον</note>, the pea; <insert>parpan</insert> is the vetchling, for the vetchling is called <insert>jilban</insert> <note>Arabic: جلبان</note> in Arabic; *tuphach* is <insert>milicha</insert>, i.e., *meline* <note>Greek: μελίνη</note> or panicum <note>a type of millet</note>; what that might be I do not know, unless perhaps it is a Chaldean form put for <insert>milicha</insert>; the "white bean" <note>Hebrew: פול הלבן</note> is the white bean or <insert>pul sapharva</insert>, perhaps the *ochros* <note>Greek: ὠχρός — yellow pea or vetch</note>; *she'atit* is the kidney bean <note>Latin: phaselus</note>.

Thus he proceeds, matching the six species from the tablet of Rabbi Hillel to those six mentioned in the Mishnah. He adds, however, another quite different interpretation: where <insert>pul</insert> is called *fava* in Italian; <insert>saphir</insert> is the *cicercola*, specifically the black species, the *cicera* of the ancients; *parpan* is the *piso* [pea], the white species; <insert>jilban tuphach</insert>—which word seems corrupt and I suspect is put for the Italian *roviglia*, the *ervilia* [bitter vetch] of the ancients; "white bean" is *fava blanca*; *she'atit* is *vezza* [vetch].
In such great uncertainty regarding these names, one who trusts in a likely conjecture might perhaps deserve pardon; though such a thing does not easily occur in all cases. That <insert>saphir</insert> is the pea is proven to me by the argument that, besides the authority of the Jerusalem Talmud and the Hillelian tablet (where there is no doubt that <insert>pishona</insert> is the pea [*pison*]), Maimonides also, and Rabbi Tanchum after him, use <insert>pishona</insert> for it.
Now, if the Arabic and Persian <insert>mash</insert> <note>Mung bean</note> is not the true pea, it is at least very similar to it, so much so that the inhabitants of Spain, and even Maimonides of Cordoba, took it for the true pea. The testimony of both is found in a remarkable passage of Serapion <note>Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century physician</note>:

> The *mash* is a small grain like a large vetch, green in color, shining, having an eye like the eye of a cowpea, circled with white; its stem is like the stem of the cowpea, and it is contained in pods like those. It is grown in gardens and eaten as legumes are; it has a pleasant taste. It originates from Yemen, where they call it *aktan*, though the people of Andalusia mistake it for the vetchling [*jilban*].

2. The cucumber and the muskmelon are not considered "diverse kinds" relative to each other. Rabbi Judah, however, asserts that they are diverse kinds. Lettuce and wild lettuce; endive and wild endive; leek and wild leek; coriander and wild coriander; mustard and Egyptian mustard; the Egyptian gourd and the <term>ash-baked gourd</term> <note>original: subcineritia</note>; the Egyptian bean and the carob-pod are not considered diverse kinds relative to each other.

3. The turnip and the navew; cabbage and <term>wild cabbage</term>; blite and atriplex are not considered diverse kinds relative to each other. Rabbi Akiba adds: garlic and wild garlic; the onion and the shallot; the lupin and the cowpea are not considered diverse kinds relative to each other.

4. Among trees: pears and <term>Crustumine pears</term>; <term>quinces</term> and service-berries are not considered diverse kinds relative to each other. Apples and <term>medlars</term>; peaches and—

---

The Spanish are mistaken about this, as they take it for a pea. To this is added what Ibn Jazla asserts concerning the <insert>mash</insert> <note>Arabic: ماش — the mung bean</note>: "its substance is very close to the nature of the bean, but it is less flatulent, and it is especially used in the summer." Avicenna says almost the same thing, and in nearly the same words; these were clearly taken from Galen’s description of "peas" <note>original Greek: τῶν πισῶν</note>, who in the first book of *On the Properties of Foodstuffs* speaks of peas thus: 
> They have a nature close to beans in their entire substance, and are eaten in the same ways as them, but they differ in two ways: they are not as gassy as beans, etc. <note>original Greek: πλησίον τι, κατὰ τὴν ὅλην οὐσίαν ἔχουσι κυάμοις, ἐδιώμοὶ τε κατὰ τὰς αὐτὰς τροπὰς αὐτοῖς, ἐν δυοῖν τοῖν δὲ παραλλάττουσιν, ὅτι τε φυσώδεις ὁμοίως οὐκ εἰσὶ τοῖς κυάμοις</note>

As for what is in Galen—"and are eaten in the same ways as them"—you might perhaps wonder why it was expressed so discordantly by Avicenna and Ibn Jazla as "and it is especially used in the summer." But whoever translated Galen’s work into Arabic, from which they got this, read the Greek phrase <note>original: κατὰ τὰς αὐτὰς τροπὰς</note> as "at the time of the same solstices"—specifically the summer ones. Ibn al-Baitar, however, who also applies this Galenic description of peas to the Arabic *mash*, omitted this part as being less understood by him. So much for that. There follows the word <insert>perakin</insert>, which I translate as "vetch" following Rabbi Nathan, although the Italian "cicercula" seems to be the "cicera" of the ancients. Benjamin Musaphia notes on this word that <insert>arkadan</insert> in Greek denotes a type of round legume, but he is mistaken. He seems to mean the *Arachidna* of Theophrastus and Pliny; which, with the Aeolic digamma prefixed, is *Farachidna*. But I hesitate. Concerning the <insert>shauit</insert> I have spoken above, and have nothing to add. I take *shauit* to be the garden cowpea, both because the Hillelian table makes it out to be the 

<column-break/>

*phaselus* [kidney bean or cowpea], and because of Maimonides’ <insert>lubiya</insert> (a word from the Greek *lobos* or *lobion*, which among more recent writers is attributed to this class of "lobes" above others, because it is eaten alone with its pods, as Aetius long ago observed); and also because the derivation of the name fits perfectly, as the garden cowpea, which consists of a remarkable smoothness, would be called *shauit* from the Hebrew word for "smoothness."

1 <term>Ash-baked gourd.</term> A type of bitter gourd which is unfit for eating unless it is first softened by being buried under hot ashes or embers.

2 <term>Wild cabbage.</term> Thus Maimonides explains the Hebrew <insert>turbanuta ha-kerubit</insert> as "a wild cabbage with thin leaves," following the Jerusalem Talmud. Rabbi Nathan explains it in Arabic as <insert>karnabati</insert>; but it should be read <insert>karnabit</insert>. For to the Arabs, <insert>al-karnabit</insert> is the Pompeian cabbage. One must see, however, whether this word has anything in common with the African <insert>gorpath</insert>, which is what they call a radish, according to the spurious works of Dioscorides. The same people call the wild radish <insert>gorpastoudi</insert>; perhaps this is the Hebrew <insert>chorbat sadeh</insert> [waste of the field]. Thus <insert>turbanutor</insert> seems to be made from <insert>chorbat tur</insert>, which would sound like "mountain radish."

3 <term>Crustumine pears.</term> For I believe the word <insert>krustomelin</insert> was deformed from that; unless one prefers "Chrysomela" [Golden Apple]. But in the Tosefta, it is read in the singular as <insert>krustomin</insert>.

4 <term>Quinces.</term> The Jerusalem Talmud calls them <insert>perishin</insert>; erroneously transcribed as <insert>asparaglin</insert>. Rabbi Nathan is more correct. He says "Rabbi Joses (or Josias) explains *perishin* as *asparaglin*." From this, Buxtorf asserted in his study of the Jerusalem Talmud that *perishin* is used for asparagus. But he is most gravely mistaken: for *asparagl* is not asparagus, but the Arabic *safarjal*, meaning a quince.

5 <term>Medlars.</term> Maimonides explains this in Arabic as <insert>azrud</insert>. However, it is the <insert>ayzaran</insert> of Ibn Jazla and Ibn al-Baitar, or the <insert>za'rur</insert>, a species of medlar.
