# Title IV. DIVERSE KINDS.
**H**
<meta>Catchword: thore,</meta>

—and almonds; the jujube and the lotus-tree <note>original: zizyphi & connari</note>, although they are very similar, they are nevertheless of a different kind from one another.

5. The radish and the navew <note>a type of rapeseed or turnip</note>; mustard and charlock <note>wild mustard</note>; the Greek gourd with the Egyptian and the ash-baked gourd, although they are very similar to each other, they are nevertheless of a different kind from one another.

6. The wolf and the dog; the Cypriot dog and the fox; goats and roe deer; ibexes and sheep; the horse and the mule; the mule and the donkey; the donkey and the wild ass; however very similar they are to each other, they are nevertheless of a different kind from one another.

7. They do not <gloss>1</gloss> graft <note>original: superinducunt</note> a tree onto a tree, nor a vegetable onto a vegetable, nor a tree onto a vegetable, nor a vegetable onto a tree. Rabbi Judah permits grafting a vegetable onto a tree.

8. They do not plant vegetables into the trunk of a sycamore; nor do they insert rue into <gloss>2</gloss> white cassia: because that is grafting a vegetable onto a tree. They do not plant a fig-shoot into <gloss>3</gloss> ivy so that it might provide it with shade; nor do they fix a vine-branch into a melon so that it may impart its juice to it: because that is grafting a tree onto a vegetable. They do not insert the seed of a gourd into <gloss>4</gloss> marshmallow <note>original: althaea</note>, so that it may preserve it longer, because this is grafting a vegetable onto a vegetable.

9. <gloss>5</gloss> He who...

---

1 **They graft.** <note>original: Superinducunt</note> In the commentaries of the Rabbis, this is the same as <term>hirkiv</term> <note>original Hebrew: הרכיב</note> and <term>hiknis</term> <note>original Hebrew: הכניס</note>, both meaning "to graft" or "to insert." But, unless I am mistaken, the term <term>hiknis</term> has a much wider scope, being used where there is no actual grafting, and it also encompasses grafting. See below VII. 1.

2 **White cassia.** <note>original: Casiæ albæ</note> Thus they maintain that <term>kiddah</term> <note>original Hebrew: קידה</note> is cassia, although the word <term>ketziah</term> <note>original Hebrew: קציעה</note> is also read in the Psalms. To Dioscorides also, if the passage is free from error, one species of cassia is called <term>kitto</term> <note>original Greek: κιττὼ</note>, which is not far removed from <term>kiddah</term>. Some wish to substitute <term>mauro</term>, or <term>moro</term> from Galen and Arrian; but Ibn al-Bitar also reads <term>qatu</term> <note>original Arabic: قطو</note> from Dioscorides. Ibn Jazla—which is more relevant to our subject—mentions one species of cassia called <term>camphor</term> <note>original Arabic: كافור</note>, which "resembles the flavor of rue" <note>original Arabic: شبه طعم السذاب</note>. And this same thing is called <term>sanabiyyah</term> <note>original Arabic: سنا بية</note> by the Malayan author, or "rue-like kerosia" <note>original Greek: κεροσία πηγανώδης</note>.

3 **Ivy.** <note>original: Hederam</note> Mention of the plant <term>hizra</term> <note>original Hebrew: חיזרא</note> is very frequent in the older books of the Jews. They relate that Joshua described the borders of the tribes with it. They maintain that Noah brought the same into the ark as fodder for the goats. To omit other points. More recent scholars, however, do not know what it is; as is evident from the fact that they explain it as ivy, and at the same time wish it to be a plant that tends straight and deep down with its root, leaning in no direction, and which, being used in the designation of boundaries, would afterwards serve as evidence if someone had moved the boundaries. For that description can in no way fit ivy, as it does not drive its roots either straight or deep. Furthermore, ivy is elsewhere called by the Greek name <term>kissos</term> <note>original Greek: קיסוס</note> in the Mishnah. Elsewhere you may find <term>chalbuz</term> <note>original Hebrew: חלבוץ</note>, as in Abodah Zarah I. 5, which some try to draw into this discussion, but in vain. For that is a species of date-palm, or a "wick-like" vegetable <note>original Hebrew: בוצין</note>. I have retained "ivy" because what else I should put does not easily occur to me. Perhaps, however, the Jews did not understand it as true ivy, but rather a species of bindweed, which the Spanish call *Yedra campana* [Bell Ivy]; surely because it emulates ivy in its leaves and creeping habit, but bears a flower like a bell or a little bell. The Jews may have called the same plant <term>hizra</term> because of the pitcher-like shape of the flower, for <term>hazor</term> means a pitcher. Lest the grafting of a fig onto a vegetable seem strange, here is a notable testimony from the March section of Palladius <note>a 4th-century Roman agricultural writer</note>:
> Some confirm that it is very beneficial if we place a fig plant inserted into a divided squill bulb <note>a sea-onion</note> and held tight with bindings.

<column-break/>

4 **Marshmallow.** <note>original: Althæam</note> Maimonides confesses he does not know what <term>chalmit</term> <note>original Hebrew: חלמית</note> is. However, in the manuscript codex that I use, it is noted in the margin by a more recent hand, "it is said to be althaea" <note>original Arabic: וקיל אנה אלטמיה</note>. Rabbi Tanchum and the Hebrew interpreter follow this. Bertinoro interprets it in Arabic as <term>khubbazi</term> <note>original Arabic: خبازي</note>, i.e., <term>kubzi</term>, which is mallow. Hence Musafia and Cohen de Lara think it is so called by metathesis <note>a switching of sounds in a word</note> for <term>malukhita</term> <note>original Greek/Hebrew: μαλάχη / מלוחית</note>. It may be asked, however, whether <term>chalmit</term> is not the plant which the Arabs also call <term>chalmi</term>, and which, as Asmazo...

# ORDER I. ZERAIM (Seeds)
<meta>catchword: tur</meta>

9. <gloss>1</gloss> One who hides turnips or radishes under a vine, <gloss>2</gloss> if the leaf-tips protrude, do not be concerned about diverse kinds <note>original: "miscellis," refers to the prohibited mixing of species</note>, even in the seventh year <note>the Sabbatical year or Shmita</note>, and regarding tithes; they may even be removed on the Sabbath day. If someone carries a grain of wheat and a grain of barley together, these are considered a mixture of diverse kinds. Rabbi Judah denies they are a mixture unless there is one grain of barley for every two grains of wheat, or two grains of barley for every one of wheat, or wheat, barley, and spelt <note>original: "adoreum"</note> together.

## CHAPTER II.

1. <gloss>1</gloss> When a quarter-measure <note>original: "quadrans," a specific unit of volume for seeds</note> of another kind is present in a sowing-measure <note>original: "fato," referring to a Seah, the standard amount of seed for a specific area of land</note>, it must be reduced. Rabbi Joses wants them to be separated, whether it is of one kind or of two kinds. Rabbi Simeon thinks this was only stated if it is of one kind. But the Sages say: Whatever is of another kind is combined <note>original: "conflatur"</note> to make up the quarter-measure.

2. In what sense are these things said? Concerning grain with grain, and legume with legume; concerning grain with legume, and legume with grain. They truly said: Garden seeds that are not edible are combined to make up <gloss>3</gloss> a twenty-fourth part of what falls into the sowing-measure of a field. Rabbi Simeon says: Just as it was said that it should be added to the burden, so also it should be <gloss>4</gloss> subtracted from it. Flax with grain <gloss>5</gloss> is combined to make up a twenty-fourth part of what falls into the sowing-measure of a field. 3. If

<column-break/>

...thore <note>likely completing "authore," meaning "by the author"</note>, the same is called *covering* <note>original: χῶσις (chosis)</note>. Meanwhile, what is read here about the seed of a gourd of the *mallow* plant <note>original: חלמית (chalmit)</note>, by inserting it so that its fruit may be perceived longer, receives excellent light from the author of the Egyptian nation, Dolo Mendesius, who in Columella <note>a Roman writer on agriculture</note>, Book XI, Chapter 3, Paris Edition page 402, so that the fruit of the cucumber might persist even in winter, *prescribes in a sunny and manured place to have fennel-stalks sown in alternating rows with brambles in the gardens, then to cut them a little below the earth at the equinox, and with a wooden stylus, having loosened the pith of either the bramble or the fennel, to put in manure, and thus insert the seeds of the cucumber, which by their growth will unite with the brambles and fennel. For thus they are nourished not by their own root, but as if by a maternal root: and thus the grafted stock provides cucumber fruit even in the cold.*

<gloss>1</gloss> *He who hides.*] Burying them so as to preserve them longer. This is different from sowing. Therefore, diverse kinds can be buried, even in the seventh year in which all sowing is forbidden; and things thus buried are immune from tithes, which must be paid from sown crops.

<gloss>2</gloss> *If they protrude.*] If the leaf-tips protrude, they can be taken up or removed on the Sabbath day. This is how the Interpreters explain this passage.

<gloss>3</gloss> *A twenty-fourth part etc.*] And if they make up a twenty-fourth part, and are mixed into the 

<column-break/>

sowing-measure of grain, they must be reduced. For since garden seeds are usually much smaller than grain, a much smaller quantity of them will suffice for sowing a measure of a field. Therefore, if it is in the sowing-measure of grain, not a twenty-fourth part of the sowing, or a quarter-measure of garden seeds, but as much as suffices for sowing a *Beth Rova* <note>a "quarter-measure area," roughly 100 square cubits</note> in a field that holds a quarter-measure of wheat seed or legumes—that is, a twenty-fourth part of a sowed field—it must be remedied by reduction. Let me be permitted to use the terms "field-measure" and "field-quarter" for *Beth Seah* and *Beth Rova*, while I understand that specific measure of a field which takes a sowing-measure or a quarter-measure of grain.

<gloss>4</gloss> *Subtracted.*] In the case of a larger garden seed, of which a greater quantity is required for sowing a field-measure than is required of wheat. Such is flax, of which three *sata* <note>measures</note>, as the Jews hold, are equal to one of wheat, and are for sowing an equal measure of field. Columella, however, assigns about twice as much flax as wheat to a *jugerum* <note>an ancient Roman acre</note>. Therefore, if three quarter-measures of flax are in a sowing-measure of grain, which suffice for sowing a field that holds a quarter-measure of wheat, only then is the work of reduction necessary.

<gloss>5</gloss> *Is combined.*] Thus the manuscripts read with great consensus *mitztarfin* <note>original: מצטרפין, a Hebrew legal term for different items joining together to reach a minimum quantity</note>. This is also how all the Interpreters I have seen read it. Perhaps it would be more correctly read—

# Title IV. KIL'AYIM (Diverse Kinds)

3. If a man, whose field has been sown with wheat, changes his mind and wishes to re-sow it with barley, he must wait until the wheat <note>original: "prorumpat," literally "breaks forth" or "bursts through," here referring to the seed's decay or the first sign of growth</note> breaks down, turn the soil over, and then re-sow. If it has already grown into greenery, let him not say, "I will re-sow and then turn the soil over"; rather, he must turn the soil over first, and then re-sow. To what extent is he required to plow? In the manner of <note>original: "fulcorum pluvialium"</note> rain furrows. Abba Saul says: he must plow to the extent that he does not leave behind a quarter-measure <note>a "quadrans," or a quarter-kav</note> of the original sowing per area.

***

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>The text <note>original: "מתמעטת"</note> is diminished, so that the words sound thus: Flax mixed with grain is diminished if it makes up a twenty-fourth part, etc.</margin>

1 *Breaks forth.* ] Thus I interpret the Hebrew word <term>hatliah</term> <note>original: "התליע"</note>. Maimonides interprets it as "to be corrupted" and "to rot." Rabbi Nathan says, "when grain is sown, it first rots and creates worms, and afterwards it sprouts." They are looking at the meaning of the word <term>tole'ah</term> <note>original: "תולעת"</note>, which means "worm." But all these are mere trifles, born of a gross ignorance of the Hebrew language. In the difficulties by which that language is currently constrained, the related Arabic language comes to our aid; in which the word corresponding to our Hebrew verb <note>original: "اتلع" and "ذلع"</note> signifies "to stick out one's head or neck," or "to stretch out," or "to peer out with the head." Thus <note>original: "اتلعت الظبية"</note> is said of a gazelle stretching its neck out of its hiding place, as noted by the scholars Jauhari and Zamakhshari. We have an example of this in a most elegant verse by the poet Dhu'r-Rumma:
> As the gazelles poke their necks out from under the *arta* <note>a type of desert shrub</note> of the sands at the whisper of a voice.
Therefore, the word means "to push out a part of oneself" or "to emerge"; and the Hebrew <term>hatliah</term> means the same: regarding recently sown grain (as in this passage of the Mishnah), it refers to the first protrusion of the germ or bud. The same thing happens in grain as when a bean "nauseates" <note>a Roman agricultural term for the first sprouting</note>, as Festus says. Concerning this same word, but taken in another sense, see our notes on Midrash II. 5. Meanwhile, the first emerging sprout does somewhat resemble a small worm; so if anyone insists the word is derived from "worm," provided they admit our meaning, I should not strongly object.

2 *Rain furrows.* ] Regarding what these <term>talmei ha-revi'ah</term> <note>original: "תלמי הרביעה"</note> or "rain furrows" are, Maimonides teaches in a way that does not entirely satisfy me. However, I will set down his words because they support, at least in part, our opinion which I provide below. He says: "Since he is forced to turn the land, it is added that he is not obliged to break it all up with

<column-break/>

4. If
perfectly contiguous furrows, so that neither a little nor a lot remains unworked; rather, he is held to plow in the manner that one plows before the rain, so that the falling rain penetrates deeper into it; this is done with a light furrow, and not one driven deep." In contrast, Rabbi Samson, whom Bertinoro copies, says: "These are the furrows that men are accustomed to plow after the rain has fallen, when they make even larger furrows." But these explanations, as I said, do not satisfy me at all. I believe this is indicated in the Mishnah: that in this turning of the soil (or "un-plowing") under discussion, frequent and touching furrows are not required, with no unplowed ridge between them as in a proper plowing; rather, more scattered furrows are used, such as are typically used to channel rainwater through gutters into ditches. For I believe "rain furrows" are the kind of furrows that Festus teaches are called *porcae* <note>ridges or balks</note>. *Porcae* are the name for scattered furrows driven for the sake of diverting water. They are called this because they "prevent" <note>original: "porcent"</note> the water from harming the grain. More frequent furrows are called *limi*. Festus says this, though not entirely in the spirit of the better authors like Varro and Columella. Certainly, those Masters whose opinion is praised in the Jerusalem Talmud thought only a more scattered furrow was required: "Once he has set his mind to plowing, even if he has not made the furrows continuous, it is sufficient." Abba Saul says in the same place: "He is not to be forced to plow finely, but only in the manner of rain furrows." You may best understand the kind of plowing required in this turning of the soil from the words of Rabban Simeon, son of Gamaliel, in the same Talmud: "Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel asserts that this kind of plowing is called a 'horse's tail,' when the edge of the soil moved by one pass touches the edge of the next, and the edge of that one touches another again." He is describing an undulating continuation of furrows with wedge-shaped ridges between them, which I can represent by no better figure than the Greek letter $\Sigma$.

# Order I. ZERAIM (Seeds)

<columns>2</columns>

4. If a man changes his mind and wishes to plant trees in a field previously used for grain, he should not say, "I will plant them first, and then turn over the soil"; rather, he must turn over the soil first and then plant. If he changes his mind and wishes to return an orchard to a grain field, he should not say, "I will sow the seeds first, and then uproot the trees"; rather, he must uproot them first and then sow. If he prefers, he may cut the trees down to less than a palm’s height <note>The "palm" or handbreadth is a standard Rabbinic unit of measurement, roughly 3–4 inches</note>, sow the field, and later uproot the stumps.

5. If a man’s field was sown with hemp <note>original: "cannabo"</note> or arum <note>a genus of flowering plants; original: "aro"</note>, he must not sow over them again, even though they do not produce fruit until after three years. If perennial woad <note>original: "isatis restibilis"; a plant used for blue dye</note> springs up among the grain, or if different species sprout in the soil of a threshing floor, or if various herbs grow within fenugreek <note>original: "foeno Graeco"</note>, the authorities do not compel him to weed them out. However, if he does weed or cut them, they command him to uproot everything except for one species.

6. If a man wishes to divide his field into long individual beds for different species, the School of Shammai <note>original: "Sammaeani"</note> believe he should place three <term>furrows of first-plowing</term> <note>original: "sulcos proscissionis"; the initial deep breaking of the soil</note> between them. The School of Hillel <note>original: "Hillelaei"</note> require a space the width of a Sharonian yoke <note>A specific agricultural measurement used in the Sharon plain of Israel</note>. Indeed, the opinion of the latter closely approaches the opinion of the former.

The ancient *Tosefta* <note>A collection of Jewish oral laws from the same era as the Mishnah</note>, from which these matters were transferred into the Gemara, is found in the three editions I have seen to be most faultily written: <note>original Hebrew: "אין מחייבין אותו להיות חורש דק אלא התלמי כל שקה מנהא תלם של פתיח מענה חורש וחריש נמי בתלומי הרביעיה רבן שמעון אומר וזנב הסוס היתה נקרית סוף עפרה"</note>. Reconstruct it thus: *He is not compelled to plow minutely; but a rougher furrow should be drawn, such as are the rain-furrows. Rabban Simeon says: it was called a "horsetail" when etc., as above.*

1 *Hemp.*] Thus all printed editions have it as <note>original: "קנבוס"</note>. Rabbi Yom-Tob, in his edition prepared at Kraków, notes that some read here <note>original: "קרכוס"</note>, which he himself approves. If I am not mistaken, he understands this as *crocus* <note>saffron</note>. But crocus is not called *karkos*, but *karkom* <note>original: "כרכום"</note>. The manuscript has <note>original: "קרבס"</note>, as does Maimonides <note>The 12th-century philosopher and legalist</note> in his commentary, where he explains it in Arabic as *karawya* <note>caraway</note>. Rabbi Tanchum, following Maimonides' reading and interpretation, has the Arabic *karawya*. Arabic physicians use *karawya* or *karawya* for what the Greeks call *kyminon* <note>cumin</note> or *kareon* <note>caraway</note>, as is clear from Jazlaide, Ibn al-Baitar, Ibn al-Khabath, and most clearly from Serapion. However, the word <note>original: "קרבס"</note> in sound comes closer to the *carbasum* <note>fine linen or cotton</note> or *carpesium* of the ancients.

2 *Even though.*] Thus the manuscript: <note>original Hebrew: "אף על פי שאינו"</note>. The printed editions do not recognize that "even though," so it would be translated "because they do not produce fruit."

3 *Fenugreek.*] The word <note>original: "תלתן"</note> comes from the Greek *telis* <note>original: "τῆלις"</note>, but from the oblique case, as is often done.

<column-break/>

4 *Furrows of first-plowing.*] Maimonides is clearly trifling in this place when he comments thus: *When the earth has been thoroughly soaked, it gaps open with wide cracks, and each of these cracks is called* <note>original: "פתיח"</note> *or "furrows of opening."* I interpret <note>original: "תלמי של פתיח"</note> as "furrows of first-plowing," relying on the passage in Isaiah: *Does he always plow to sow? Does he "open" and "break" his ground?* (Isaiah 28:24). For the Hebrew words *shadad* <note>to harrow/break clods</note> and *patach* <note>to open/plow</note> seem to be opposed just as the Latin *proscindere* <note>to break up soil for the first time</note> and *offringere* <note>to break the clods of a plowed field</note>. Varro, in *On Agriculture* I.32, says: *When you have broken the soil (proscideris), it ought to be "offringed," that is, repeated, so that the clods are broken; for in the first plowing, large clods are cut out from the earth.* First-plowing, with a wider furrow, raises up large clods and tears away vast sods, which a more frequent repetition breaks and diminishes. See the same Varro, I.29. Meanwhile, I know that in the ancient Tosefta, in place of "furrows of opening," it says *three furrows passing through the whole field from one end to the other.*

5 *Pointed vertex.*] Maimonides says: *The earring which women hang from their ears is called* "Tor" <note>original: "תור"</note>, *as in the Song of Solomon 1:11, "We will make you earrings of gold," etc. Its shape is triangular, in this manner:* <image-desc>a small downward pointing triangle</image-desc>. *Therefore they call the sharp corner of any shape a "Head of a Tor" (Rosh Tor).* Anyone can see how tasteless and utterly ridiculous these remarks are; and yet Bertinoro, being destitute of better explanations—

3. If a pointed corner of a garden bed planted with vegetables extends into another field planted with vegetables, it is permitted, because it is seen as the boundary of the field. Rabbi Akiba requires a furrow six handbreadths long and just as wide. Rabbi Judah requires it to be as wide as the sole of a foot.

4. If one plants two rows of cucumbers, two of gourds, and even two of Egyptian beans, it is permitted; but a single row each of cucumbers, gourds, and Egyptian beans is not permitted. One row of cucumbers, one of gourds, one of Egyptian beans, and then another of cucumbers: Rabbi Eliezer permits this, but the Sages forbid it.

5. It is permitted to plant a cucumber and a gourd in the same pit, provided that the latter is leaned in one direction and the former in the other. [<gloss>3</gloss> Moreover, let the leaves of this one be turned to this side and the other to that side; because whatever is forbidden by the Sages was decreed for no other reason than <gloss>4</gloss> for the sake of outward appearance.]

6. If someone whose field is planted with onions wishes to plant rows of gourds in the same field, Rabbi Ismael is of the opinion that they should uproot two rows and plant one, then leave two rows of onions standing, uproot another two rows, and plant one. Rabbi Akiba is of the opinion that for every two rows uprooted, they should plant two, leave two rows of onions standing, and then for the next two uprooted, plant two. The Sages say: unless there are <gloss>5</gloss> twelve cubits between the rows, they must not allow the intermediate crops to grow.

7. A gourd among vegetables follows <gloss>6</gloss> the rule for vegetables: if it is with grain, an interval of a quadrant <note>a *rova* or quarter-measure of land</note> is left. If someone whose field is sown with grain wishes to plant a row of gourds in it,

1 **Rather large.**] A type of chickpea called *apyonim gamlunin* <note>original: **אפונים גמלונין**</note>, as if you were to say "of camels." It is common to call anything that excels in its kind for its size *gamluni* <note>original: **גמלוני**</note> from *gamal* <note>original: **גמל**</note>, a camel, just as the Greeks are accustomed to prefix *ba-* <note>original: βᾶ</note> from "ox" in *batyos* and similar words. Thus, elsewhere *gamlunitha* <note>original: **גמלוניחא**</note> is a dung beetle, that is, a very large one. It is possible, however, that the species of chickpea is named after a place, such as Gamala.

2 **One on this side.**] In the margin.

3 **Let them be bent, etc.**] The text included in brackets is absent from the manuscript. It has also been noted as absent from several codices in both Amsterdam editions of the Mishnah,

and in the Cracow edition of Yom Tob. They certainly seem to have originated from a marginal explanation.

4 **For the sake of outward appearance.**] Lest the field appear from a distance to be sown with a mixture.

5 **Twelve cubits between.**] Eight cubits for the intermediate crops, and two empty cubits left on each side between the intermediate crops and the single rows newly planted on each side. For they assign four cubits to each row. Thus, if a new row occupies the middle space of two uprooted rows, two empty cubits will be left on each side.

6 **The rule for vegetables.**] Meaning that an interval of six handbreadths should be left between them.

1. <gloss>2</gloss> The "baldness" of a vineyard <note>an empty patch or clearing within the rows of vines</note> according to the *Shammaites* <gloss>3</gloss> must be twenty-four cubits; according to the *Hillelites*, sixteen. The "enclosure" of a vineyard, according to the *Shammaites*, must be sixteen cubits; according to the *Hillelites*, twelve. What, then, is the "baldness" of a vineyard? A place in the middle of the vines that is empty. If it is smaller than sixteen cubits, no seed shall be sown there. If it is sixteen cubits, <gloss>4</gloss> the cultivation space is given to the vineyard, and the remaining space may be occupied by crops.

2. What is called the "enclosure" of a vineyard? The space between the vines and the outer wall. If it is less than twelve cubits, no seed shall be sown there. If it is twelve cubits, the cultivation space is given to the vineyard, and the remaining space may be occupied by crops.

3. *Rabbi Judah* considers this to be nothing other than the wall of the vineyard. What, then, is called the "enclosure" of a vineyard? The space between two vineyards. <gloss>5</gloss> What constitutes a wall? Ten palms high. A ditch? Ten high <note>meaning ten palms deep</note>, and four wide.

If a wall is broken through for a space of ten cubits, it is considered like a gateway; beyond that measurement, <note>meaning if the gap is wider than ten cubits</note> opposite the broken part <gloss>7</gloss> it is forbidden to sow. Likewise, he compares the **watchtower** <term>shumrah</term> with the "tower" <note>Greek: "πύργῳ"</note> in the same passage, which I indeed commend.

-># Title IV. FORBIDDEN MIXTURES <note>original: "Chilaim," referring to the Hebrew tractate Kil'ayim</note><-

**§ 5.** Anyone who plants a vegetable in a vineyard, or allows one to grow there, renders **forty-five vines** forbidden <gloss>1</gloss>. When does this apply? When they are planted at intervals of four or five cubits <note>a cubit is roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note>. But if they are planted at six or seven cubits, he renders forbidden whatever vines are within sixteen cubits in every direction, measured in a circle rather than a square.

**§ 6.** If a man sees a vegetable sprouting in his vineyard and says, "When I reach that spot, I will pull it up," it is permitted. But if he says, "I will pull it up when I return," and in the meantime the plant grows by **one-two-hundredth part** <note>the legal threshold for a mixture to become forbidden</note>, it is not permitted.

**§ 7.** If, while someone is passing through a vineyard, seed accidentally falls; or if it was carried there with dung or with water; likewise, if while sowing, a storm blew the seed <gloss>2</gloss> backward <gloss>3</gloss>, it is permitted. However, if the storm blew the seed forward [into the vineyard], Rabbi Akiba maintains that while it is still grass, it must be turned over with a plow; if it has formed a stalk, it must be broken up; and if the grain has ripened, it must be burned.

**§ 8.** If someone allows thorns to grow in a vineyard, Rabbi Eliezer considers them forbidden. The Sages do not consider them forbidden unless they are the kind of plant that people usually choose to preserve. Iris, ivy, the royal lily, and all species of seeds are not considered a "different kind" <note>heterogeneous species</note> from the vine. Regarding hemp, Rabbi Tarphon says it is not considered a different kind. The Sages believe it should be counted as a different kind. The artichoke is considered a different kind from the vine.

---

### CHAPTER VI.

1. What is a **trellis** <note>original: "pergula," an arbor or structure for climbing vines</note>? It is where <gloss>4</gloss> a row of five vines is placed against a wall ten palms high <note>a palm or handbreadth is about 3-4 inches</note>, or against a ditch ten palms deep and four wide; they grant the vines their own **cultivation area** <note>original: "cultum," the space around the plant that must remain clear</note> of four cubits. The House of Shammai believe the four cubits should be measured into the field from the roots of the vines; the House of Hillel want them measured from the wall into the field. Rabbi Jochanan ben Nuri thinks those who report the law in this way are in error; rather, if there is an interval of four cubits between the roots of the vines and the wall, they should be granted their <gloss>5</gloss> cultivation area, and the remainder may be sown with seed. How large is the cultivation area of a vine? Six palms in every direction. Rabbi Akiba believes it is three palms.

2. Regarding a trellis extending from a mound, Rabbi Eliezer son of Jacob says, if he who...

<columns>2</columns>

1 **Forty-five.** This refers to how many vines are enclosed in the path of a circle which, drawn from the vegetable as the center, falls just within the corners of a square consisting of seven rows of seven vines each. See figure 5. Maimonides <note>the 12th-century scholar Moses Maimonides</note> argues quite subtly on this point.

2 **Backward.** Behind the person who is scattering seed in the field, toward the vineyard.

3 **Permitted.** That is, to allow it to grow and thus gather the 

<column-break/>

fruit.

4 **Is placed.** Understand this to mean "and the trellis is erected."

5 **Their cultivation area.** Six palms, the same as for a single vine. For he does not believe a single row should be considered a "vineyard," even if the trellis is erected against a wall. He therefore thinks the remaining space between the roots and the wall can be fully utilized.

# Order I. SEEDS <note>original: "Zeraim"</note>

...who stands on the ground and can harvest the whole vine, he renders four cubits into the field forbidden for sowing. If he cannot reach it all, he only renders forbidden the area directly beneath the vine. Rabbi Eliezer adds: Even when one row is planted on the ground and another is on a mound, if the mound is ten palms <note>about 30 inches or 75 cm</note> higher than the ground, the two rows are not joined together. If the height is less than that, they are joined <gloss>1</gloss>.

**3.** If someone suspends a vine over a portion of a set of withered branches <gloss>2</gloss>, he must not sow seed under the remaining part of those branches. If he does sow there, however, it is not legally considered "sanctified" <note>in this context, "sanctified" means forbidden for use and subject to being burned as a forbidden mixture</note>. Nevertheless, if the new growth of the vine spreads over them, it becomes forbidden. The same applies if one raises a vine over part of a barren tree.

**4.** If someone suspends a vine over part of a fruit-bearing tree, it is permitted to sow seed under the rest of the tree. If the foliage of the vine spreads further, he must pull it back. **A Case:** Rabbi Joshua went to Capharazizum to visit Rabbi Ishmael. Ishmael showed him a vine suspended over part of a fig tree and asked: "Am I permitted to sow seed under the rest of the tree?" Joshua replied that it was permitted. From there, Ishmael took him to Bethmagania and showed him a vine suspended over one part of a beam; that beam was actually the trunk of a sycamore tree into which many other beams had been fixed. Joshua told him that sowing under that specific beam was forbidden, but under the others, it was permitted.

**5.** What is considered a "barren tree"? Any tree that does not bear fruit. Rabbi Meir believes all trees should be considered barren except for the olive and the fig. Rabbi Joses maintains that any tree species that people do not typically plant in entire fields should be categorized as barren.

**6.** The gaps in a trellis are eight cubits or more. In all the measurements concerning vineyards handed down by the Sages, the phrase "or more" does not apply, except in the case of these trellis gaps. These gaps occur when the middle part of a trellis is removed or dies away, leaving five vines remaining on either side. If this gap measures eight cubi-

1 *They are joined.*] And thus they together constitute a vineyard.

To him, <term>apipirot</term> here means <note>original: "אילן שעושה פירות הרבה"</note> *a tree which produces abundant fruit*.

<column-break/>

But Musaphias, more correctly using the Greek language, interprets it as a tree *which no longer produces fruit, being worn out by old age or for another reason.* In my opinion, this is an excellent interpretation, matching Hesychius's term <term>apophora</term> <note>original: "ἀπόφορα"</note>, that is, <term>trees not bearing fruit</term> <note>original: "δένδρα μὴ φέροντα καρπόν"</note>. Nor should we listen to Cohen de Lara, who, rejecting Musaphias's explanation, contends that <term>apipirot</term> is a mistake for <term>apophyades</term> <note>original: "ἀποφυאַδες"</note>. That would be a clever point if it were true, as he adds <note>original: "כי הוא סמוך אפיפירות, אל גפן וממנו הוא"</note> *that they are joined to the vine and born from it*. For such are <term>the offshoots</term> <note>original: "αἱ ἀποφυάδες"</note>. But this is far from the truth, as is abundantly clear from the authority of this one Mishnah alone. It would be foolish to believe that a vine could be trellised and suspended upon its own shoots. Therefore, we should read it as <term>apophora</term> <note>original: "ἀπόφορα"</note>.

[If the space] is [less than four] cubits <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches or 45 cm</note>, it is not permitted to bring seed there. If it is eight cubits or more, once the space for cultivation is assigned to the vines, the remainder may be filled with sowing.
**7.** If a trellis <term>pergula: a structure for climbing vines</term> projecting from a wall stops short of the corner, its assigned cultivation space is granted to it, and the rest may be sown. Rabbi Joses says that unless there is a vacant space of four cubits, he denies that seed can be brought there.
**8.** If someone neglects to prune the poles extending beyond the trellis, it is permitted to sow beneath them. But if he set them up for the purpose of allowing the vine wood to spread across them, it is not permitted.
**9.** They evaluate the vine wood flourishing beyond the trellis by hanging a sort of plumb line <note>to determine the vertical boundary</note>, so that whatever lies beneath is considered forbidden for sowing. Similarly, with a suspended vine, if someone extends a vine-shoot <term>tradux: a vine branch trained to grow from one support to another</term> from tree to tree, whatever is beneath it is considered forbidden. <gloss>1</gloss> If he has continued the connection with a rope or a reed, what lies beneath that supplement is considered permitted. But if he used it for the purpose of letting the vine wood spread along it, it is forbidden.

## CHAPTER VII.

**1.** He who has layered a vine <term>propagaverit: the practice of layering, where a branch is buried to form a new root</term> flat on the ground must not sow seed over it unless it is covered with soil to a depth of three palms <note>about 9 inches or 22 cm</note>, not even if it is pressed down through a gourd or a <gloss>2</gloss> small pipe. On a rock, however, provided the soil on top does not exceed three fingers <note>about 2.25 inches</note> in depth, it is permitted to sow seed over it. As for the measurement of the bend of the layered branch in a vine, the measurement is taken from no other point than the second root.
**2.** If someone presses down layered branches from three vines so that the roots are visible, Rabbi Eleazar son of Zadok considers them <gloss>3</gloss> to be united, provided there are between four and eight cubits between them; if less, they are not united. his son reports in his name, that even only that which lies over the buried vine is illicit, yet it does not cause it to be consecrated <note>original: "sacrare." In the context of these laws, "consecrating" a crop means it becomes forbidden for any use or benefit because it was grown in violation of the Mixed Species law.</note>.

**3.** These things make a crop illicit, but do not make it sacred: the remainder of a "bald patch" in a vineyard, the remainder of the vineyard's border, the remainder of the gaps in a trellis, and the remainder of withered branches. But whatever lies directly under the vine, the cultivation area of the vine, and the four cubits of the vineyard—these certainly make the crop sacred.

**4.** He who extends his vine over another person’s crops <note>The Latin text uses "fata," likely a transcription of "sata" (crops/sown fields).</note> has made them sacred, and he is bound to pay for the damages. Rabbi Joses and Rabbi Simeon think that no one can make something sacred that is not his own.

**5.** Rabbi Joses reports a case regarding a certain man who sowed seed in his vineyard in the seventh year <note>The Sabbatical year (Shmita), when the land must lie fallow and its produce is considered ownerless.</note>. When the matter was brought before Rabbi Akiba, he replied: "No one can consecrate a thing that is not his own."

**6.** If a robber <term>praedo: an illegal occupant or usurper</term> forcibly sows someone else's vineyard and then abandons it, the owner should see to it that it is harvested, even on a festival day. How much is he bound to give to the workers? Up to a third <note>of the crop's value</note>. If more is demanded, let him harvest slowly as he is able, even after the festival. From what time is he called a "robber"? From the moment he has become "firmly entrenched" <note>original: "penitus inhaeserit," translating the Hebrew term *mishaka*.</note>.

**7.** If a storm knocks vines down onto the crops, they must be pulled back immediately.
->But if<-

<column-break/>

<margin>Regarding the phrase "to place crops," Maimonides correctly explains the Hebrew *tzemer* as <term>cotton</term>; however, he interprets the passage about cotton or wool-bearing trees not being planted in a vineyard incorrectly, if I see things right. I interpret it as saying other seeds should not be sown next to cotton bushes because of the similarity they bear to vines.</margin>

**1. The remainder of the bald patch of a vineyard.]** If a vineyard becomes "bald" in its middle part to the extent that the baldness occupies a square of sixteen cubits, once four cubits are left on all sides for the cultivation of the vineyard, it is permitted to bring seed into the inner square of eight cubits (as mentioned above in IV. 1). Now, if the baldness falls short of this measure, as if the part required for the full measure were missing, it is called the <term>residuum calvitii vineae: the remainder of the vineyard's baldness</term>. This does not mean what exceeds the proper measure, but the baldness itself when it is "incomplete" <note>original Greek: "ἐλλιπες"</note> or falling short of the required size. The same applies to the "remainder of the border" and the "gaps."

**2. Of the vine.]** That which flourishes beyond its cultivation area.

**3. Which is not his own.]** Namely, in the seventh year, no one has a private right to the produce of his field, but it is of common right.

**4. Bound to give.]** Meaning they are willing to perform the work on a festival for the proper payment.

**5. A third.]** Some understand this as a wage increased by a third; others as a third of the value of the vineyard and its produce.

**6. Firmly entrenched.]** That is, from the time when the good-faith owner has been terrified and driven away, and the robber possesses the estate as his own and is "sunk" into it. This is how I interpret the word <term>mishaka</term>. For that word signifies to be fixed deeply or to stick within.

<column-break/>

Lest I deceive the reader, I will not hide the interpretation of the Jews. Thus says Bertinorius: <gloss>From what time is he called a robber? That is to say, from what time is the vineyard called by the name of the robber, to be considered his so as to forbid sowing in it? From the time the name of the owner is "submerged" <note>Hebrew root *shaka*</note> from the vineyard and it is called by the name of the thief; from that hour the vineyard will be regarded as his, and whatever is sown in it becomes sacred.</gloss> For Bertinorius, then, *mishaka* is the point from which the name of the legitimate owner is submerged, abolished, or deleted. Maimonides interprets it differently: <gloss>And what is said, *mishaka*, means: from the time the owner of the vineyard turns his back [despairs] on his property due to the fear of the robber who threatens him with violence.</gloss> Both relate the word to the owner who suffers the violence. I prefer to relate it to the one who inflicts the violence. I confess, however, that the Jerusalem Gemara <note>The Palestinian Talmud</note> contains things that support Maimonides' opinion.

**7. Retracted.]** Yom Tob <note>referring to the commentator Tosafot Yom Tov</note> notes three variations in the reading: *yigror* according to Rabbi Samson, *yigrad* according to Rabbi Obadiah (which Rabbi Samson also mentions), and *yigdor* according to Maimonides, although most editions—except for the small folio edition—have *yigror* in Hal. Chil. V. To these I add a fourth, *yigrar*, which is found in the Manuscript and in Maimonides' Arabic commentary, which I believe is the most correct.

If force has prevented it, ¹ it is permitted. Crops bent down under the vine are pulled back, and likewise for vegetables; yet they do not make the crop sacred <note>The term "sacred" or "consecrated" here refers to the crop becoming "Asur"—forbidden for any use or benefit because it was grown in violation of the laws against mixing species.</note>. From what time does grain become sacred? From the time it has grown to a ² third of its size. Grapes? As soon as they equal a white bean in size. Grain that has dried sufficiently, and grapes that have ripened as much as necessary, are thereafter not made sacred.

**8.** A perforated pot in a vineyard makes the crop sacred; one not perforated does not make it sacred. Rabbi Simeon considers both to be illicit, but neither to make the crop sacred. To carry a perforated pot through a vineyard, such that in the meantime it increases in growth by a two-hundredth part <note>A tiny fraction of growth that occurs during the passage through the field.</note>, is illicit.

## CHAPTER VIII.

**1.** It is illicit to sow or allow a mixed vineyard <note>A vineyard containing mixed species.</note> to grow, or even to derive profit from it. It is illicit to sow or allow a mixed sowing <note>Likely referring to hybrid plants or seeds of different species sown together.</note> to grow; however, it is permitted to eat them; ³ and much more so to derive profit from them. Mixed garments <term>shatnez: clothing made of both wool and linen</term> are permitted for every purpose, except that they are illicit to wear. ⁴ Mixed-breed cattle may be reared and maintained; and nothing else regarding them is illicit, other than practicing cross-breeding. It is not permitted to yoke mixed-breed cattle together.

**Technical Vocabulary:**
*   **Mixed Species (Chilaim/Kil'ayim):** The biblical prohibition against mixing different seeds, animals, or fibers.
*   **Mishna:** The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions.
*   **Maimonides:** A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.
*   **Jerusalem Talmud:** A collection of rabbinic notes on the Mishna compiled in the Land of Israel.
*   **Moses of Coucy:** Author of the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol* (Smag).
*   **Tosefta:** A secondary compilation of Jewish oral law.
*   **Babylonian Gemara:** The part of the Talmud consisting of rabbinical analysis and commentary.
*   **Mixed (Miscella):** Referring to hybridity or prohibited combinations.

4 Libyan Ass.] So in the Babylonian Gemara <note>The commentary portion of the Talmud</note>, Shabbat 51b, the word *Luvdakos* <note>original: לובדקס</note> is explained as a Libyan ass <note>original: המרא לובא</note>. From this, Maimonides says, "An ass in the land of the Libyans that resembles a camel." The word itself, as tends to happen with such things, is written in many ways. For besides *Levdakos* or *Luvdakos*, which is found in both Talmuds, in the Rabbinic commentaries, in the Lexicons of Nathan <note>Author of the Aruch</note> and Tanchum, and in the manuscript, and *Luvdakim* or *Luvkeram*, which is seen in many editions of the Mishnah, it is read in the ancient *Tosephta* and in Isaac Fessanus, and the commentaries on him by Rabbenu Nissim as *Lunbarken*. In the small Asherian Constitutions, it is *Dulbaki*. Finally, in Genesis 32:15, where the Hebrew has *Ayirim* <note>foals</note>, the Jerusalem Chaldean paraphrase <note>Targum</note> reads *Lurin Karen*, or *Velerin Dakin*, or *Velerin Dakin* in three editions (London, Hanau, and Venice). In the Pseudo-Uziel paraphrase (which is the same as the Jerusalem one to older writers), it is *Valadin Rakin* in the Venice and London editions, but *Luvandakin* in the Hanau edition. From the Jerusalem paraphrase, it is cited as *Levadkin* by Nathan, Tanchum, and Philippe d'Aquin (the lexicographers), and as *Leberkin* by Elias in the Chaldean Lexicon. However, Rabbi Samson in his commentaries has *Luvaskin*: all of which seem to be errors <note>original Greek: "σφάλματα"</note> of the same word. Indeed, doubt about the true reading of this word is not recent; a variant reading was noted long ago in the Jerusalem Gemara: "There is a teacher who teaches... and not the *Libdakos* or *Niverkos*. He who says *Libdakos* uses a name derived from a place <note>original: "paronymicum"</note> after the name of the Libyans and Ethiopians who are in his company. He who says *Niverkos* means *Abhatos*. What is *Abhatos*? A sterile ass." This is how it is read in the Gemara of *Kil'ayim* for this Mishnah; but for Shabbat 5:1, where the same words recur, it is slightly different: for instead of *Niverkos*, it is read twice there as *Lanirakos*, and *Ambatos* instead of *Abhatos*; those words about the name of Libya are also omitted (where "Libyan" is a mistake for "Company," that is, a name derived from a gloss that seems to have crept in). These same things are cited by Rabbi Nathan in his Lexicon, who likewise omits them, and has *Nivdakos* twice for *Niverkos*, and *Abhatos* for *Ambatos*. Cohen de Lara <note>A 17th-century Sephardic scholar</note> judges this reading to be better; he observes that it

<column-break/>

easily happens that scribes, when the letters *Nun* (נ) and *Bet* (ב) merge, write a *Kaph* (כ), especially in exotic words; and thus he recognizes the Greek word for "ass" <note>original Greek: "ὄνος"</note> at the end of the word. Beyond that, he despairs. As for me, I have no doubt that *Abhatos* is much more correct than either *Ambatos* or *Abhatam*. However, I wonder that the usual quick-wittedness <note>original Greek: "ἀγχίνοιαν"</note> of Cohen failed him here, so that he did not see that a slight further change was needed, which even that error *Abhatos* could have suggested: that instead of *Abhatos*, one should read *Anatos*, that is, a mule <note>original Greek: "ἡμίονος"</note>. Thus I translate the passage: "Neither the *Luvdakos*." There are those who read *Nivdakos*. He who says *Luvdakos* (which is a derived name) says it from a proper name: (as in Daniel 11:43) "the Libyans and the Ethiopians shall be at his steps." He who says *Nivdakos* understands it as a mule. What is a mule? A sterile ass. And so much for those views. By what reasoning *Libdakos* could be derived from the Libyans, or in what way *Nivdakos* signifies a mule, I confess, is hidden from me. I once doubted whether instead of *Nivdakos* we should refer to *Nemadikos*, with the *Nun*... that is *Abhatos*, that is *Nomadicos* <note>Nomadic/Numidian</note>, and by that understand that third species of camels which the nobler Arabs of Numidia and the Libyan Africans are accustomed to use, as we find in Leo Africanus. He asserts they are called *Raguahil*. But it should be read *Raguahil*, that is, "traveling camels" <note>original Arabic: "رواحل"</note>. However, I decide nothing on this. Regarding the other word *Luvdakos*, or as Elias has it *Leberkin*, Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a famous 17th-century orientalist</note> suspects it should be rewritten as *Ludarkin*; and he interprets that as "asses from the land of Lud." Bertinoro says the same in express words for this Mishnah and for Shabbat 5:1. For he says *Bennos* is an African word for an ass, which the Cyrenians received from the Libyans. Hesychius says: "Bennos: an ass among the Cyrenians; foreign." But I am most averse to such word-compositions, in which Bochart almost always indulges, as they are plainly foreign to the genius of the Oriental languages. If the *Luvdakos* of the Mishnah and the *Leberkin* of the Paraphrast are to be sought in *Bennos*, I would recognize that very word as it is written in Elias, *Leberkin*, as legitimate. Only the Arabic article *Al* <note>original: "ל" representing "ال"</note> is prefixed; for the first element, which is used in purer Arabism, is not essential and is omitted by others, according to the distinguished Arabic grammarian Sibawayh. Thus *Leberk* would be "The Bennos" <note>original: "ὁ Βεννὸς"</note>. Both, as I indeed think, are the same as *The Buraq* <note>original Arabic: "البراق"</note> in purer Arabism. It is moreover

# Title IV. MIXED SPECIES <note>original: Chilaim</note>

...the entire offspring of mares, even if sired by a father ass, may be rightly joined; and similarly, the entire offspring of she-asses, even if sired by a father horse, may be rightly joined. However, the offspring of mares may not be lawfully joined with the offspring of she-asses.

<margin>
† Mules of ambiguous origin.] These are those for which it is not certain whether they are mules <note>offspring of a male ass and a female horse</note> or hinnies <note>offspring of a male horse and a female ass</note>. For a mule is produced from a mare and an ass; conversely, a hinny comes from a horse and a she-ass, as Varro states in *On Agriculture*, II. 8. For the Jews explain the word *frotiyot* <note>original Hebrew: פרוטיות</note> in this way. Maimonides says: "The name *frotiyot* falls upon those species which are produced from..."
</margin>

5. Mules of ambiguous origin are joined together illicitly, but it is licit to join bur-

...the **Buraq**, the beast upon which the Muslims write that their Prophet was carried to heaven during his night journey. Bochart <note>original: Bochiarius</note>, that famous compiler of Muhammadan traditions, asserts that it was "a beast larger than an ass and smaller than a mule" <note>original Arabic: دابة فوق الحمار ودون البغل</note>. And this is the case if the reading of Elias is accepted. But since the reading in the Talmud is instead *le-vurdakos* <note>original: לבורקס</note>, that word seems to be of Greek rather than Arabic termination. Of Greek words, as far as I know, none comes closer than *lepargos* <note>original: λεπάργος</note>, which most closely expresses the reading of the Tosefta, *le-prakim*. *Lepargos* is indeed an adjective applied to an ox or any other animal that has white <note>that is, *argas*</note> flanks <note>original: λαπάρας</note>, as is clear from Hesychius in his entry for *lepargesos*—where one should read *lepargo boos*—and from Eustathius on the *Odyssey*, Book II. This same word is also used as a noun for an ass because of the whiteness of its loins or abdomen, as in the description of the thirsty ones in Nicander, where weary mortals, placing the gift of youth recently received from Jove upon a slow ass, are miserably robbed of it.

->For the gifts were brought by a slow, weary lepargos<-
->Gifts.<-

Where the commentator explains: "By *lepargos* they mean the ass, because it has white flanks." From this passage, the Etymologist should be corrected, who, citing the same verse of Nicander under *amorbeuo* but erroneously, explains *lepargos* as "the ass, because it is white along the belly." To this is added what is permitted in Tractate Shabbat V. 1: that on the Sabbath day, the *lubdakos* may go out with a *phrombeia* <note>original: הלוברקים בפרומביא</note>, that is, the *lepargos* with a halter or bridle. The scholars of the Gemara, and the commentators following them, ridiculously take *phrombeia* there to be a kind of iron muzzle by which a fierce and stubborn animal might be better restrained. But a *phrombeia* is the simplest halter by which an ass, a slow and dull beast of burden, can be safely enough led; indeed, Lucian attributes the *phrombeia* to the ass.

<column-break/>

"...a mixture of an impure species and a pure species, however the mixing happened." The name *frotiyot* denotes a genus of animal that is procreated from any mixture of the equine and asinine genus. These words of Maimonides—a man exceedingly devoted to the books of Aristotle and the Peripatetics—seem to have been taken from Aristotle's *On the Generation of Animals*, Book II: "And from the horse and the ass comes the mule, from both combinations of male and female." Buxtorf translates this very poorly: "*Frotiyot*: Mules, a special species of mules, lacking signs of purity or impurity." For, I ask you, what signs of "purity" could there be in mules? <note>Mules are inherently "unclean" animals in Jewish law as they are cross-bred</note>. He did not understand Rabbi Samson or Bertinoro, who understand such mules to be the "ambiguous" ones I mentioned, which you cannot distinguish by signs as to whether they were procreated from she-asses or mares as mothers. Those signs are touched upon in the Jerusalem Gemara: "If its mother was a she-ass and its father a horse, the ears are small; if its mother was a mare and its father an ass, they are large." Rabbi Jonas says: "Whichever has small ears, its mother is a mare and its father an ass; if large, its mother is a she-ass and its father a horse." Maimonides in *Laws of Mixed Species* <note>original: Halachot Chilaim</note> IX: "Therefore, whoever wishes to mate a mule with a mule, or use joined mules for pulling, must judge by the signs of the ears, the tail, and the voice. If they are similar to each other, it is known that their mothers were of the same genus, and they are lawfully joined." Nor is this stated rashly; for even Columella (VI. 37) says: *Those who are conceived and generated from a horse and a she-ass, although they take their name from the father because they are called hinnies, are in all respects more similar to the mother.* Damiri, the Arab, also says:

->If the father is an ass, it will strongly resemble a horse; but if the father is a horse, it will strongly resemble an ass.<-

However, as far as the ears are concerned, what Varro asserts in the place just cited seems different: "The one called a hinny is from a horse and a she-ass; it is smaller in body than a mule, usually more reddish, with ears like a horse's, and a mane and tail like an ass's." These are the signs about which Buxtorf hallucinates not slightly. *Frotiyot*, however, are mules which cannot be distinguished by these signs, according to their view. But Rabbi Nathan in his Lexicon wants them to be the mules which the Greeks and Italians call *monomi*. So it appears in most editions. But in the Basel edition, it is *muli* (mules); incorrectly, unless I am much mistaken. The word *monomi* is indeed faulty, but...

# Order I. SEEDS <note>original: Zeraim</note>

### ¹burdones. ² Wild little men are reckoned among the beasts. R. Joses says—

...but a very light little bee. For one should read *mosmoni* <note>original Hebrew: מוסמוני</note>, that is, the Greek *mosmones* and the Italian *musimone*. The *mosmones* are properly a type of sheep in Sardinia which is covered with goat-like hair instead of wool, as is clear from Strabo. From this comes the *musimo*, a hybrid animal from a ram and a goat, the opposite of the *tityrus*, just as the *hinny* is to the *mule*. Regarding this, there is an ancient epigram:

->*The Tityrus is born from sheep with a goat as a parent;*<-
->*The Musimon is sired by a ram from a goat mother.*<-

Yet the *musimo* is not found only among sheep and goats, but also among asses and horses. Nonius Marcellus says: "*Musimones* are asses, mules, or short horses." Lucilius in book 6: "He pays the price, who sells a *musimon* horse." Cato in *On the Destruction*: "An ass, or a *musimon*, or a ram." R. Tanchum asserts that *mules* are explained as *baghal al-frutiyot* <note>original Arabic: באגאל אל פרוטיות</note>; by others as *aghadish*; or as read in other codices and in the Epitome, *akhadish*. What that might be, I do not know; unless perhaps it should be read as *gahash* <note>original Hebrew: גחש</note>, as if the plural of a plural *agahash*, which is a young ass according to the lexicographers Jauhari and Phiumio, and frequently used by Arabic translators of the Bible. These men are essentially strangers to Greek and Latin literature. To me, the word *protiyot* <note>original Hebrew: פרוטיות</note> seems to be sought in those languages. I do not interpret them as asses or mules, but as *Epirot* horses <note>horses from Epirus, a region of Greece/Albania</note>. The fame of Epirot horses is quite celebrated among the poets, Virgil <note>original: Maro</note>, Faliscus, and others. Vegetius also says: "You should not look down upon Epirot or Sicilian horses, if beauty does not fail their character." The author of our Mishnah had heard something of these, and as is the custom of those men, he seized upon a new word—though not yet fully understood—and summoned it into his law. So it seems to me regarding this word, and the word *leptorgo* <note>original Greek: λεπτοργῷ, meaning "fine-worked" or "thin"</note> mentioned above, and several others about which I will speak when the occasion arises. They mean, therefore, that Epirot horses, being animals of a different kind, should not be mated with common horses or even the noble ones known to them; though they acknowledge this is permitted in the case of the *burdon* <note>a hinny, the offspring of a horse sire and an ass dam</note>. However, in the translation, I decided to retain the common interpretation of the Jews, lest I seem to peddle my own conjectures too rashly.

1. **Burdones**.] The word *remek* <note>original Hebrew: רמך</note> also occurs in the Bible in Esther 8:10. However, its meaning is not sufficiently known; and if we are unable to grasp it, we deserve an excuse, since the Jews themselves—not just the recent ones, but even the ancient scholars of the Gemara <note>the commentary portion of the Talmud</note>—bring this very passage as an example of a thing that cannot be understood. The passage is in Megillah 18a, where regarding that Mishnah II.1: "A barbarian who has heard the scroll of Esther in Syriac has fulfilled his duty," it is objected in the Gemara that the barbarian does not understand what is being read. Rabina retorts: "Do even we know what *the ahasteranim, the sons of the ramakim* <note>original Hebrew: האחשתרנים בני הרמכים</note> means? And yet the reading is commanded, and the miracle is to be publicized; so too here

<meta>The text transitions from the difficulty of translating specific Persian/Hebrew terms in the Book of Esther to a philological analysis using Arabic to define types of horses.</meta>

<column-break/>

the reading is commanded, and the miracle is to be publicized." Truly, since Abenezra <note>a 12th-century scholar</note> observes that *ramakim* are mares, and that the word signifies this in the Arabic language, it would be the mark of a lazy man not to call upon that language for help. The Arabic *ramlah* <note>original Arabic: رملة</note> indeed signifies a mare, though not just any, but "the female of the *burdhon* kind," as the lexicographers Jauhari and Phiumio say, and Damiri in his *History of Animals* citing Jauhari. Now indeed, *burdhon* <note>original: برذون</note> (Greek: *bordōn*, Latin: *burdo*) signifies a cheaper kind of horse to the Arabs, which yields in nobility to the Arabian horse. Mutarrizi says: "The *burdhon* is of the horse kind, but the opposite of the Arabian." Damiri says: "He is called by the nickname *abu 'l-achtal* <note>'father of the flabby-eared'</note>, so named because of the flaccidness of his ears, which is the opposite of the ears of the Arabian horse." Hence the proverbs: "The *burdon* has become a noble horse" <note>said when an inferior person gains status</note>. "Slower than a *burdon*, more harmful than a lizard." These are found in Zamakhshari, which you would seek in vain in the large collection of Midani. From this also comes the verb *bardhana*: "he rode a *burdon*, or he rode upon a cheaper horse"; as in the same author: "I met so-and-so riding a noble horse, and his brother riding a *burdon*." Likewise, "he was slow like a *burdon*": as in, "I asked a certain thing of him, but he was slow to grant it." Finally, to exhaust Zamakhshari, not without benefit to the reader devoted to Arabic studies, the same verb also signifies actively to make a noble horse dull and slow like a *burdon*, as in that verse of Phala:

->*By God, the noble horses of which you are the groom,*<-
->*You have made them like burdons, though they have white markings on their legs and forehead.*<-

## TITLE IV. FORBIDDEN MIXTURES <note>original: Chilaim</note>

God cares for those noble horses of which you are the leader. You would turn them into hinnies <note>original: burdones; a cross between a horse and a donkey</note>, even if they are distinguished by the whiteness of their feet and forehead. You see how the Arabs distinguish between the horse and the hinny, to which this verse excellently pertains:

->*I saw that if the horses made a turn with you,*<-
->*They carried you on a hinny of no great worth.*<-
<note>original Arabic: أريت ان اجالت بك الخيل جولة وأدت على بردونة غير طايل</note>

You showed yourself off, while horse-drawn circles were made around you, and you yourself ran in a circle, though you were carried by a short hinny. If these Arabic accounts are true, Rabbi Tanchum is certainly greatly mistaken, as he interpreted the word <term>remach</term> <note>original: רמך</note> as noble horses, and did so following Arabic usage. Nor does he follow his master Maimonides here. For Maimonides says: "<term>Remach</term> is a certain species of noble horse, and as I believe, a wild one, for there are also wild horses." The Hebrew translator did not grasp this. But the passage in Esther led Rabbi Tanchum into error. He thought that "sons of the <term>remachim</term>" <note>original: בני הרמכים; Esther 8:10</note> there specifically meant the foals of noble mares. But perhaps "the <term>remachim</term>" there means nothing other than what the lexicographer Phiruzabadius calls <term>ramaka</term> <note>original Arabic: رمكة</note>, namely "mares or female hinnies destined for procreating offspring." Or perhaps they are Armenian mares, from the Persian <term>ramak</term> meaning "a herd," in the plural <term>ramakan</term>. A deformed, degenerate, and base kind of horse could be called <term>remach</term>, either from a lean and thin body—from the word <term>armak</term> <note>original Arabic: ارملك</note>, which means to have that habit of body—or from a duller color, as <term>ramaka</term> denotes a color "darker than dust-color," as Phiumius says, or, as Zamachsharius puts it, "a dust-color mixed with black." This is clearly a sooty color, as can be understood from the very witty verse of Rudba:

->*And young boys like smoke, sooty,*<-
->*Mixed with musk, they are made into Succon.*<-
<note>original Arabic: وصبية مثل الدخان رمكا يخلط بالمسك فتجعل سكًا</note>

Meaning the youths are sooty like smoke, and when musk is added, the scent called *Succon* is made. *Succon* is a perfume composed of a dark aromatic called <term>ramak</term> <note>original Arabic: رامك</note> and musk. The poet alludes to that composition and mockingly attacks the ugly and dark-skinned youths who nevertheless took delight in the use of musk and perfumes. Why indeed should the use of the word not be extended to horses,

<column-break/>

since in the case of camels, the lexicographers Jauhari, Zamachsharius, Phiumius, and Phiruzabadius mention "a male and female camel of a sooty color" <note>original Arabic: ناقة & جمل ارمك</note>? In the Jerusalem Talmud, Rabbi Immaus, in the name of Rabbi Lazarus, explains <term>ramachah</term> <note>original: רמכה</note> as <term>kalinos</term> <note>original: כלינס</note>? Is it perhaps "unbridled"?

2. **Wild little men.** <note>original: Homunculi agrestes</note>] Regarding the "Lords of the Field" <note>original: אדני השדה; Adney ha-Sadeh</note>, Maimonides says: "The <term>Adney ha-Sadeh</term> is a species of animal resembling a human; the authors of chronicles report that it speaks much, never falling silent, and its speech is like human speech; its name (among the Arabs) is the <term>Nefnas</term> <note>original Arabic: אלנסנאס</note>; many descriptions of it are found in books." Rabbi Tanchum says almost the same. In the printed Hebrew codices, <term>Al-Nas</term> is mistakenly written for <term>Al-Nefnas</term>. And regarding the <term>Nefnas</term>, it is true that many Arabic fables exist. Damirius collected them from various authors. Bochartus took not a few from him, but he hallucinated in many places, as is his habit with Arabic matters. Truly, in that whole heap of Damirius's, there is no description that fits with the <term>Adney ha-Sadeh</term> found in the Jerusalem Talmud. The Arabic *Nefnas* is a half-human, wandering and swift. The "wild little man" of the Mishnah grows from a root; it is both animal and plant, restrained by an umbilical cord and tied to one place. For in the Talmud it says: "It is a mountain man who lives by his umbilicus; if the umbilicus is cut, he no longer lives." <note>original Aramaic: בר נש דטור הוא והוא חיי מן טיבוריה ייה איפסיק טיבורייה לא חיי</note> Bochartus, citing these same things from Jarchius (though he should have said Rabbi Samson, for what he attributes to Jarchius is taken from Samson's commentary), translates it very poorly as: "It is a wild beast from the navel down, but the part above the navel is not a wild beast." But the words sound as I have stated. Hence, in the Talmud, the reason why Rabbi Joses judges that this animal pollutes a tent <note>original: referring to ritual impurity</note> is sought from Numbers 19:16; as if what is written there—"And whoever touches one slain with a sword in the open fields"—he had interpreted as: "And whoever touches that which grows upon the face of the field," namely, this <term>zoophyton</term> <note>original Greek: ζωόφυτον; an animal-plant</note>. Rabbi Moses, son of Calonymus of Speyer, thinks this same monster is called by another name, <term>Yidua</term> <note>original: ידוע</note>, and he describes it thus (as Rabbi Samson reports his opinion): "Like a kind of large rope..." etc. A certain large cord comes out of a root which is in the earth, from which that animal lives, which is called <term>Yidua</term>, clearly in the manner of cucumbers and gourds. Yet its form completely resembles a human: in its face, body, hands, and feet. From the navel, however, it is connected by a cord growing from the root; and no one is able to approach within the length of the cord, because it seizes and kills everything all around. As far as the cord extends, it grazes on everything. When they hunt it, no one dares to approach...

# Order I. ZERAIM (Seeds)

[The creature mentioned previously] is capable of **polluting a tent** like a human being. <note>original: tentorio polluere; refers to the Jewish law where a corpse makes everything under the same roof ritually impure.</note> ¹ The hedgehog and the ² **bush-weasel** are counted among the wild beasts. The bush-weasel, as Rabbi Joses reports the opinion of the Shammaites, pollutes by its being carried if it is the size of an olive, or by touch if it is the size of a lentil.

6. The wild ox is of the cattle kind; but Rabbi Joses thinks it should be counted among the wild beasts. The dog is of the wild kind; but Rabbi Meir counts it among the cattle. The pig is of the cattle kind; the wild ass is of the wild kind; the elephant and monkeys are counted among the wild beasts. A man joined to any of these [is forbidden] to ³ **plow or pull.**

### CHAPTER IX.

1. **N**othing else is considered forbidden under the ⁴ name of **mixed fabrics** <note>original: miscellorum; referring to the law of Shatnez</note> except wool and linen. Nor is anything else ⁵ **defiled by leprosy** <note>original: lepra; referring to the biblical plague of tzara'at which could infect clothing</note> except wool and linen. Nor are the Priests clothed in anything else for their sacred service, so that they may perform the holy rites—

[The commentary continues below:]

...[The creature] does not yield, but they seek the cord with arrows; once it is cut, it dies immediately. These are his words; and the things that Bertinorius says regarding Sanhedrin VII. 7 are not from any other source, where he adds that in the dialect of the Sages it is called בר נש דטור <note>original: Bar Nash de-Tur</note> **"Mountain Man"**; looking back, without a doubt, to the passage of the Talmud just cited. Therefore Maimonides, and Bochart following him, wrongly compare the Mishnaic אדני השדה <note>original: Adney ha-Sadeh; Lords of the Field</note> with the Arabic *Dinasnas*. These are fables on both sides, but of different kinds. Although the Rabbis seem to have strained every nerve in forging fables, perhaps they are to be excused here, and should not be thought to have invented a lie themselves so much as followed Josephus (a most weighty author, as it seems to some). Certainly, what he relates through the whole of Chapter 23, Book VII of the *Jewish War*, concerning the root βααρας <note>original: baaras</note>, which usually grows in a place of the same name in the valley surrounding Machaerus from the north, are such that you may recognize the origin of this fable there. The human form is indeed missing; all other things are present that fill out the description. Hence, for *baaras* one should read *baras*, that is, the Talmudic *Bar Nash*. And so what is missing from the description is sufficiently indicated by the name itself. And regarding these *Adney ha-Sadeh*, I add this one thing: in the Jerusalem Gemara, contrary to the faith of all editions of the Mishna and the manuscript codex, אבני <note>original: Abney; stones</note> is read instead of אדני <note>original: Adney; lords</note>; so that you do not believe this was done by chance, look at Job 5:23, where it is said, *Because you have entered a covenant with the* אבני השדה **"stones of the field"**; Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] comments thus: אבני השדה מין אדם הן, **"The stones of the field are a kind of human being"** that is spoken of here.

1 *Polluting a tent.*] Numbers 19.
2 *Bush-weasel.*] חולדת הסנאים <note>original: chuldat ha-sana’im</note>, **"bush-weasel"**, and the weasel that lives in the hiding places of houses, seem to be 

<column-break/>

opposed in the same way as the **wild weasel** <note>original: γαλέη ἀγρία</note> and the **house weasel** <note>original: γαλέη οἰκίδιος</note> are among the Greeks. However, in the Gemara, chapter 80. a., the bush-weasel is numbered among the semi-domesticated wild beasts which it is permitted to feed for this reason, שעושים לנקר את הבית, **"because they are suitable (not for digging through the house, as Bochart translates, but) for cleaning the house"**; namely, from mice, as Rabbi Solomon explains. But perhaps it should be read לנקיות הבית, that is, **"for freeing the house from mice."** Cohen de Lara wants the *chuldat ha-sana’im* to be the Chinese weasel rather than the Scythian one, and asserts that in Spanish it is called *marta zebelina* (**sable**). To the same point belongs what Musaphia notes regarding the word גלאקסונין <note>original: galaxonin</note> (a word which Rabbi Nathan derives from the *Bereshith Rabba*, and which he wants to be composed from the Greek γαλέη [weasel] and ἔχις [viper]), meaning a very valuable weasel skin originating in Northern lands); he notes that this same weasel is the one which is called the *chuldat ha-sana’im* in the Mishna of the Title *Chilaim*.

3 *Plow or pull.*] Almost all printed editions have "to plow and to lead," or "to plow, and to lead," using the same words as above in section 2, but with the order changed. But in the Jerusalem Talmud, it says "to plow and to pull." This is also the case in the manuscript codex I use, and the old parchments praised by Yom-Tov. It is also cited this way in the passage of Shabbat 54. a. in the Babylonian Gemara. And I follow this reading. For that word *lead* <note>original: נהיג; nahig</note> cannot have a place here.

4 *Mixed fabrics.*] Regarding garments.
5 *Is defiled.*] Or "defiles." A garment infected with leprosy is defiled and defiles [others]; and depending on the different vowel pointing, the word תטמא <note>original: titamei / tetamei</note> expresses either sense. The passive meaning is more approved by me. See *Negaim* XI. 2.
