## Title IV. MIXTURES (CHILAIM).

...in the Sanctuary, than wool and linen. ^1 Camel wool and sheep wool mixed together, if the camel wool is the greater part, ^2 they are **permitted**; but if the sheep wool prevails, they are **forbidden**; and if they are mixed in equal parts, they are forbidden. The same applies to linen and hemp mixed together.

2. The prohibition against mixtures does not apply to ^3 **silk** and ^4 **sea-fleece**; and therefore these may be safely used for linings and mixed into other garments.

---

^1 *Camel wool*.] <gloss>Thus they call <note>original Hebrew: צמר ארנבים</note> "rabbit wool," and <note>original Hebrew: צמר עזים</note> "goat wool."</gloss>

^2 *Permitted*.] These are correctly mixed with linen in the same garment.

^3 *Silk*.] In the Babylonian Gemara (Shabbat 20b), a distinction is clearly made between *shiraya* <note>original Hebrew: שירייא</note> and *serikon* <note>original Hebrew: סיריקון; silk</note>; and the same distinction is made there by Rabbi Nathan. However, they seem to be distinguished more by dialect than by the actual substance. Therefore, in Revelation 18:12, the Syrian translator uses for the Greek *serikon* (silk) the word <note>original Arabic: وهــذا</note> which is our *shiraya*. Added to this is the Arabic word <note>original Arabic: سـيـرا, *sira*</note>, which the lexicographer Jauharius interprets as <note>original Arabic: بـــرد فـيه خطـوط صــفر</note> "a cloak with yellow stripes." Phiumius follows him in this. But if Jauharius had no other authority than the verse of Nabega which he cites, I do not hesitate to call that interpretation into question. For what Jauharius interprets in Nabega as "yellow like a cloak painted with yellow stripes," I would rather interpret as "yellow like silk." For a yellowish hue—or a color very close to yellow—is almost natural to silkworm cloth. I believe I have discovered not only the error, but the occasion of the error itself. The Arabic word *siyar* refers to a segment drawn out lengthwise, and because of this similarity, it means a "stripe" in a garment. From this, they call a striped garment *musayyar*. Hence Jauharius wished to interpret *sira* this way. You will see this is true if I provide the words of Zamachsharius, which are quite excellent on this matter:

> From the word for "stripe" (*siyar*), a striped garment is called *musayyar*, as its stripes are similar to long segments. From this it is also said, "he is clothed in a garment of *sira*," referring to a specific kind of silk cloak.

You see Zamachsharius making the same error—though for a clearer reason—by referring the word *sira* to the stripes rather than the material in a garment he himself acknowledges is silk. Indeed, I have no doubt that "a garment of *sira*" should be explained as "a garment of silk." That Arabic word is the same as the Mishnaic *shira* <note>original Hebrew: שירא</note>, and in Chaldean [Aramaic] the same *shiraya*, as seen in [references]. I believe in both places we should read *phrygianum*, that is, "excellent Phrygian silk" <note>Ancient Phrygia was famous for high-quality textiles and embroidery</note>. Thus I interpret *shira pargada* (Sota 48b) as "wavy silk"; for *farand* to the Arabs refers to the "wavy shimmer of a sword." Unless, of course, someone prefers to take *pargada* as a geographical name. Indeed, Jauharius mentions *Fardan* as the name of a place.

^4 *Sea-fleece*.] Regarding the material called *kelach* <note>original Hebrew: כלך</note>, Maimonides writes in the *Yad*, Laws of Mixtures, Chapter 10: <note>original Hebrew: ויש בכרכי הים...; quoting Maimonides' Mishneh Torah</note> "In the coastal cities, there is something like wool that grows on the stones in the salt sea, bearing the appearance of gold, and it is very soft. Its name is *kelach*. It is forbidden [to mix] with linen because of its appearance, for it resembles sheep's wool; likewise, silk and *kelach* are forbidden because of their appearance." From this description, compared with the description of "sea-fleece" or <term>pinna-wool</term> <note>also known as sea silk or byssus, a fiber produced by Mediterranean pen-shells</note> which the scholar Salmasius collected from various Greek and Latin authors, the most learned Bochartus judges that the pinna-wool and the *kelach* of our Mishnah are the same thing. He adds that *kelach* is named after the Colchians—not those of the Black Sea... but the Colchians of the Indian trading post within the Ganges, and the adjacent "Colchic Gulf," where Ptolemy and Arrian recognize a notable fishery for the pinna mussel. He argues this with his usual great sharpness. Meanwhile, the reader might consider whether the Jews did not derive their word *kelach* from the Greek word *kochlos* <note>original Greek: κόχλος; a spiral shell or shellfish</note>, by using <term>apheresis</term> <note>the dropping of a sound or syllable from the beginning of a word</note> so that the same letter wouldn't be doubled at the start, which the Hebrew language rarely allows. For *kochlos* is used not only for a shell, but specifically for the wool or fleece growing on it. Basil, in his *Homily to the Rich*, says: "Where are your flowers of the sea, the pinna-fleece? The purple? The beryl? The wool of the pinna-mussels?" And these things are so, if Maimonides' description is true. Others explain *kelach* as...

### Order I. SEEDS (ZERAIM)

...mixed fabrics; however, they are forbidden because of their outward appearance <note>To avoid the impression that one is violating the law, even if the use is technically permitted.</note>. The prohibition against mixed fabrics does not apply to mattresses and pillows, provided that the body does not come into contact with them <note>This implies that a heavy coverlet or sheet must be placed between the person and the mixed fabric.</note>. Not even the temporary use of mixed fabrics is permitted; for no one should put on a mixed garment even over ten others, nor even for the purpose of evading the custom-house <note>original Latin: "telonium"; a place where tolls or taxes on goods were collected. This refers to the practice of wearing clothes to avoid paying import taxes on them as cargo.</note>.

2. The prohibition against mixed fabrics does not apply to hand-towels, ^1 barbers' cloths, or bath-towels. Rabbi Eliezer, however, forbids mixed fabrics even in these. ^2 Book-covers are also forbidden under the category of mixed fabrics.

4. The prohibition against mixed fabrics does not apply to burial shrouds or to a donkey's saddle-cloth. However, no one should place such a saddle-cloth upon their shoulder, not even for the purpose of carrying out dung <note>Because the cloth would then be serving as a garment/protection for the human shoulder, which is forbidden if it is a mixture.</note>.

5. Clothing merchants ^3 sell garments in their usual manner; however, they must not wear them to protect themselves from the sun in summer or the cold in winter. Those who are more scrupulous, however, hang the garments on a staff behind their back.

6. Tailors sew in their usual manner; however, they must not wear the garments to protect themselves from the sun in summer or the cold in winter. Those who are more scrupulous, however, sew while sitting on the ground <note>rather than letting the garment rest on their lap or shoulders</note>.

7. It is permitted to wear ^4 birruses <note>hooded cloaks</note>, bardiacs <note>Gallic-style cloaks</note>, dalmatics <note>wide-sleeved tunics</note>, and ^5 shoes made of coarse wool.

---

<note>The following notes provide philological analysis of the terms used above.</note>

Maimonides and others explain <note>original Hebrew: פסולת של משי</note> "silk waste" as the dross of silk; and <note>original Hebrew: אותן קליפות שנשארו מן המשי שמוציאין התולעין ואין נוחין לטוות</note> "those husks which remain from the silk which the worms produce and are not easy to spin." So says Rabbi Nathan. However, where it says <note>original Hebrew: שמוציאים</note> "which they produce," I would prefer to read—by slightly rearranging the letters—<note>original Hebrew: משוציאים</note> "after the worms emerge." For silkworm cocoons (as Golius asserts regarding the word <note>original Arabic: خز</note> *khazz*), once broken open by the butterflies, are boiled with a little soap to soften them, and the sticking parts are drawn into threads by women using a spindle. Whether this is the <note>original Hebrew: אנביג קיסריי</note> "Caesarean Anbig" which is read in the Jerusalem Gemara on this passage, or simply <note>original Hebrew: אנביג</note> "Anbig" as read in the same Gemara on Shabbat II.1, let others decide. I only note that *Anbig* is used several times in the Pseudo-Uzielide <note>Targum Jonathan</note> on Genesis 44 for Pharaoh’s cup; a broken silkworm cocoon does not poorly resemble a cup or chalice. However, I hold the other opinion of Maimonides to be better. For it is established that such wool was used for garments from Procopius' *On the Buildings of Justinian* (III.1), where among the insignias of the Satraps of Lesser Armenia is listed a cloak made of "pinna-wool." <note>original Greek: χλαμυς ἐξ ἐρίων πεποιημένη, οὐχ οἷα τὰ περιβάτιον ἐπίφυκεν, ἀλλ' ἐκ θαλάσσης συνειλεγμένων, πίννας τὰ ζῶα καλεῖν νενομίκασιν, ἐν οἷς ἡ τῶν ἐρίων ἔκφυσις γίνεται.</note> "A cloak made of wools, not such as grows on sheep, but gathered from the sea; they are accustomed to call the creatures 'pinnas,' in which the growth of the wool occurs." Silk waste seems unsuitable for use as lamp-wicks, so for that reason <note>original Hebrew: כילך</note> *Kilach* (in Shabbat II.1) must be something else.

1 *Barbers’*.] The word <note>original Hebrew: ספרים</note> (*S-P-R-Y-M*), depending on how it is vocalized, signifies either "books" or "barbers."

<column-break/>

In the first instance, the Jews understand it as "books," in the second as "barbers"; and in the manuscript, I find points applied to express this. However, in my judgment, "barbers' linens" are more correctly grouped with hand-towels and cloths than with the coverings of the Law. And this is the punctuation found in the Amsterdam Mishna.

2 *Book-covers*.] A cloth <note>term: mappa</note> is spread under the Law-book <note>Torah scroll</note> in the Synagogue, and after each reading, the book is covered with it until another reader <note>term: anagnosta</note> is called up to approach. Such cloths are called <note>original Hebrew: מטפחות הספרים</note> "wrappings of the books."

3 *Sell*.] They carry garments around to be sold.

4 *Birruses*.] Maimonides confesses his ignorance regarding these words; however, he thinks they are types of socks. Rabbi Nathan reads <note>original Hebrew: בורסין</note> for *birros*, and counts both that and the following term among bedding. He adds, however, that others explain <note>original Hebrew: ברסין</note> in the vernacular as <note>original Latin/vernacular: "lina"</note> "wool," and <note>original Hebrew: ברסין</note> as seamless woolen garments. I would venture to affirm this opinion as closer to the truth. In the text outside the body of the Mishna called *Semachot* (Chapter IX), Rabbi Judah says: <note>original Hebrew: קורע את הברסים ואת הבררסים</note> "He who tears birruses or bardiacs, etc. [in mourning] does not fulfill the duty." I do not think anyone would be so foolish as to want to tear socks or bed-coverings in mourning to satisfy the commandment of tearing one's garments. Rather, I believe the words themselves are derived from the Latin terms I have used.

5 *Shoes made of coarse wool*.] Obadiah of Bertinoro rightly explains: <note>original Hebrew: מנעל שעשות מפסולת הצמר</note> "A shoe which they make from the refuse of wool." For the word <note>original Hebrew: פיוון</note> (*pivon*) is the Greek <note>original Greek: πίννον</note> (*pinnon*); a word which signifies filth, specifically of wool; hence <note>original Greek: πινώδη & πιναρὰ ἔρεα</note> "filthy and squalid wools" in Hippocrates, or coarse wool.

# Title IV. KILAIM (Forbidden Mixtures)

...to [re]sell is not permitted, unless an inspection has been made. Rabbi Jose asserts that there is no need for inquiry regarding items that come from the coast or from a maritime province, because in those places the presumption is that they are made of hemp <note>Hemp was commonly used in maritime regions for ropes and heavy cloth, and unlike linen, it does not create a forbidden mixture when combined with wool</note>. The prohibition against mixed fabrics does not apply to a **foot-sock** <note>original Latin: *soccum pedulem*; a type of soft slipper or liner worn inside a shoe</note>.

8. Nothing else is forbidden under the name of mixed fabrics except what is spun and woven; for it is said (Deuteronomy 22:11), *You shall not wear* **sha'atnez** <note>Hebrew: שעטנז; the biblical term for forbidden wool-and-linen mixtures</note>, namely a thing that is **combed** <note>Hebrew: שוע (*shua*)</note>, **spun** <note>Hebrew: טווי (*tavui*)</note>, and **woven** <note>Hebrew: נוז (*nuz*)</note>. Rabbi Simeon Elea-
->zari<-

***

¹ **Foot-sock.** <margin>Maimonides: A slipper for the foot which is placed under the sole of the foot; one walks with it upon carpets and floor-coverings.</margin> It is called a *pedule*—a lining for the sole of the foot, used for walking on carpets and couches, as is the custom in the East. Rabbi Tanchum says: A *zarab* slipper; it is also called *vabar* by transposition, and also *zarad*; and it means the same thing. According to the view of some commentators, these are the boots worn by soldiers and such people. Maimonides, however, in his exposition of the Mishnah, maintains that the foot-sock is to be worn under a boot, so that when the boot is removed, one walks upon the rugs and such with this; since it is clean, being worn under the boot, neither mud nor dust nor other filth reaches it. These are his words in the excellent Pococke manuscript <note>Referring to the collection of Edward Pococke, a 17th-century English Orientalist</note>. In others it is different; but the discrepancy is of little concern for us to note. In these matters, the reader will observe that Tanchum mistakenly substitutes *al-khuff* <note>Arabic script: الخف</note>—the boot—for Maimonides' *kaf al-rijl* <note>Arabic script: كف الرجل</note>—the sole of the foot. What I should determine regarding the word *zarab*, or *vabar*, or *zarad*, as it is variously written, is not immediately clear. If *zarab* is correct, as it appears in the manuscript and the Jerusalem Talmud, it seems not far removed from the Arabic *jawrab* <note>Arabic script: جورب</note>, which also means a foot-sock or stocking.

² **Combed.** Maimonides explains this as "smoothed," and understands it as the final task in cloth-making, by which already finished cloths are polished. We follow the opinion of others who understand it as the first task in cloth-making, that is, carding or combing; which, besides felting, is the only process used in felted items, so that this opinion is confirmed by the following paragraph.

³ **Woven.** Some explain the word *nuz* as "woven," others as "twisted." But the word is purely artificial, devised to support an

<column-break/>

absurd etymology. Maimonides indeed thinks it should be sought from the Armenian language. <gloss>Maimonides' Arabic: "And *nuz* is that it is woven joined together... from the language of the Armenians, and its meaning is joining and union."</gloss> He says *nuz* is used when the fabric is made from both wool and linen together, namely from the language of the Armenians, among whom that word signifies joining and union. Rabbi Tanchum says almost the same. But why do they not seek the origin of the Hebrew word from the Chinese language with equal right? For there is no word in the Armenian language similar to this that means such a thing. Maimonides adds that no garment is to be considered a mixed fabric according to the Law <note>Meaning biblical law as opposed to later rabbinic decrees</note>, <gloss>Maimonides' Arabic: "unless these three qualities are all combined in it; and if it is otherwise, it is only a mixture according to the words of the Scribes [Rabbinic law], and this is a certain and correct decision about which there is no doubt..."</gloss> unless these three meet in it. That which is otherwise is a mixed fabric only by the decrees of the Scribes. This is the true decision, of which there is no doubt, since it is the very text of the Talmud. If, however, you have noticed anyone thinking otherwise, do not doubt that he has forgotten that text proposed in the Gemara of tractate Nidda. These things are found in the same way in the Hebrew version of Rabbi Judah al-Harizi. However, in the Arabic manuscript which I use by the kindness of a most excellent man, I find the style reversed and everything after the word "Scribes" deleted, and this substituted: <gloss>Arabic: "So some of the Geonim mention. But this seems to me not at all true. Indeed, each one of them is a mixture according to the Law. The text cited from the Gemara Nidda is not a text of the Talmud, but a gloss."</gloss> The passage of the Gemara is Nidda 61b, where Mar Zutra interprets *sha'atnez* as *shua*, *tavui*, and *nuz*—a thing combed, spun, and woven; but Rav Afes contends it can be explained as "either combed, or spun, or woven," so that any one of them would suffice. It is added: "The law follows the opinion of Mar Zutra, because God expressed those three in a single word."

# Order I: SEEDS (ZERAIM)

...the son of Eleazar says: <margin>1</margin> ¶ He turns away, and makes his Father who is in heaven turn away from him.

9. Felted garments are forbidden because they are combed. A woolen hem with a linen cloth is forbidden, because they are woven back and forth in the manner of a web. Purple bands <margin>2</margin> are forbidden, because <margin>3</margin> once they are sewn they are fastened tight. No one shall tie a woolen and a linen strip together to gird his loins with them, not even with a leather strap intervening in the middle.

10. The marks of weavers and fullers <note>Fullers were craftsmen who cleaned and thickened cloth.</note> of various kinds are forbidden. A single stitch of a needle does not effect <margin>4</margin> a joining; nor does it violate the prohibition concerning mixed fabrics; and he who undoes it on the Sabbath is considered guiltless <note>Because it is not considered a permanent "work" of sewing.</note>. If both ends of the thread are on the same side, a joining is made; and there the prohibition of mixed fabrics applies; and he who undoes it on the Sabbath is guilty.

***

<margin>1 He turns away.]</margin> Rabbi Simeon wants the last part of the word <term>Sha'atnez</term> <note>original: שעטנז</note> to be formed from *lun* or *lunen* <note>original: לון</note>, which has the meaning of turning away or rebelling, because whoever uses a mixed garment turns away as a rebel against God and religion. This is most foolish. <note>The translator here dismisses the Rabbi's creative etymology.</note>

<margin>2 Forbidden.]</margin> Understand this as: for strengthening a linen cloak.

<margin>3 Sewn.]</margin> Maimonides explains the word <term>mollel</term> <note>original: מולל</note> by the Arabic word *fatala* <note>original: فتل</note>, which means to twist. In Hebrew, this is called *shazar*. However, the Arabic language teaches us much more certainly what *malal* means in this passage. To the Arabs, *mal* <note>original: مل</note> means to sew a garment with a first and rougher stitch, so that it may finally be sewn more neatly. Al-Jawhari <note>A famous 10th-century lexicographer.</note> says, "you *mallalta* the garment," when you sew the garment the first time before the *kaff* <note>original: كف</note>, or the legitimate and proper sewing. The same author says regarding *kaff*: "I *khafaqtu* the garment, that is, I sewed its hem, which is the second sewing." He says: "the garment was *khafaqta* after the *al-mall*," when you sew the edge of the garment (which is doubled) again, which is the second stitch after the *al-mall*. Al-Zamakhshari <note>A 12th-century scholar.</note> says: "The tailor *malla* the garment and then *kaffahu* [hemmed it]." He sewed the garment with the first stitch, then finished it. And shortly after he explains *al-mall* as the "first sewing." To these same Arabs, *shall* <note>original: של</note> is used

<column-break/>

in a sense not much different. For Al-Jawhari says "I *shallaltu* the garment" when you sew the garment lightly. You will understand that these things apply perfectly to our passage if I add one or two *Baraitas* <note>External traditions of the Jewish oral law not included in the main Mishna.</note> from the tractate Moed Katon, page 26, regarding the re-sewing of garments torn in mourning, where both *mollel* and *shollel* occur in this sense. *The Rabbis taught: For all torn garments, it is permitted to stitch them lightly, to baste them, to gather them, or to make them like ladders, but not to mend them seamlessly.* <note>The "ladder" stitch leaves a gap like the rungs of a ladder, showing the garment was once torn in grief.</note> Another *Baraita* in the same place: *The Rabbis taught: He who tears a garment in the part that was lightly basted, or basted, or gathered, or in the ladder-stitch, has not fulfilled his duty of mourning; but if he tears it in the part that was seamlessly mended, he has fulfilled his duty.* Therefore, *melilah*, *shelilah*, *lakitah*, and *sulamot* <note>original: מלילה, שליקה, לקיטה, סולמות</note> are four types of sewing and mending, all distinct from *ihui* <note>original: איחוי</note>. *Ihui* is, as the author of the *Tosafot* <note>Medieval commentators on the Talmud.</note> says from the Jerusalem Talmud on the cited passage, "any mend whose place is not recognizable." In English, we call this **Fine-drawing** <note>A technique of invisible mending.</note>. Rabbi Samson explains *mollel* here in this sense, and following him, Bartenura does as well, which I believe is best. No one would want to use purple bands of great value for girding a cloak unless they were sewn on, lest they be lost if they came loose. However, it is forbidden to sew a woolen band onto a linen cloak.

<margin>4 A joining.]</margin> So that the pieces of cloth so connected might be considered as one; and thus if one part becomes ritually defiled, the other is also defiled; or vice versa, if purification water is sprinkled on one, the effect passes to the other.

### Title IV. FORBIDDEN MIXTURES (CHILAIM)
L
<meta>catchword: TITLE.</meta>
<warning>Page contains significant ink bleed-through from the verso side, obscuring parts of the paper.</warning>

...Rabbi Judah denies it, unless it is threaded through a third time. <margin>Sack and basket</margin> Sack and basket are combined regarding the law of forbidden mixtures <term>miscellorum</term> <note>The Latin 'miscellum' refers to the forbidden mixture of wool and linen, known in Hebrew as Sha'atnez.</note>.

---

<margin>Sack and basket.] Maimonides. And his words:</margin>
<note>original Judeo-Arabic: והשק והקופה מצטרפין... וצאר להא נוע מן אלאתצאל וצארה כלאים...</note> And what he said, "the sack and the basket combine for forbidden mixtures," he meant by it: if one gathers a garment of wool and linen and joins them with a piece of sack or a basket, he has added them to the sack or the piece of sack, joining them to each other so that they have acquired a type of connection, and it becomes a forbidden mixture; it is not permitted for a person to wear that garment as a load gathered together.

What he says, however—that *the sack and the basket are combined with regard to the law of mixed fabrics*—is understood thus: if someone connects a woolen and a linen garment together by means of a piece of sack or basket, so that the sack or basket joins them to each other, and thus they are united in some way, this becomes a forbidden mixture, and the garment thus composed cannot be lawfully worn by a person. This is what Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note> wrote, and it is how Rabbi Judah Harizi <note>original: R. Juda Harizius. A 12th-century translator and poet known for translating Maimonides' works into Hebrew.</note>, the Hebrew translator, read it in his version, although he did not understand it. Moreover, in the best manuscript of Maimonides just

<column-break/>

praised, whether Maimonides himself or someone else, having deleted those words <insert>and joined them with a piece of sack</insert>, wrote back instead, <insert>in a single load</insert>; and instead of those <insert>wearing that garment</insert> wrote again <insert>for a person</insert> <insert>carrying the whole collection</insert> <insert>meaning that this load or basket is on the back of a person</insert>.

The words sound thus: "if someone has joined a woolen and a linen garment in the same bundle or basket, so that the sack or basket joins them to each other, and they are thus united in some way, it becomes a mixture, and such a bundle or basket cannot be lawfully carried on a person's back." Bertinorius <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro, a 15th-century Italian rabbi and commentator on the Mishnah.</note> explains the passage differently, like this: *if a piece of woolen cloth is added to a sack, and a piece of linen cloth to a basket, they are combined, and thus become a mixture.* I have great doubt about the soundness of this passage.

<summary>This page analyzes a passage from Maimonides regarding whether carrying wool and linen in the same sack or basket constitutes a violation of the laws against forbidden mixtures. The translator compares different manuscripts and translations, specifically highlighting a correction that shifts the focus from "wearing" a mixture to "carrying" it as a load.</summary>

# TITLE V. SHEBIITH.
### OR
## CONCERNING THE LAW OF THE SEVENTH YEAR.

->Regarding the cessation of agricultural work in that year, Exodus 23:10, 11;<-
->Leviticus 25:1, 2, etc. and the remission of debts, Deuteronomy 15:1, 2, etc.<-

# CHAPTER I.

1. **HOW LONG** is it permitted to plow a field planted with trees <gloss>1</gloss> in the year before the seventh? As long as it benefits the fruit, according to the opinion of the Shammaites <note>The school of Shammai, known for a stricter interpretation of Jewish law.</note>. The Hillelites <note>The school of Hillel, usually more lenient than the Shammaites.</note> believe it is permitted until <gloss>2</gloss> Pentecost. And the opinion of the latter closely approaches the opinion of the former.
2. What constitutes a field planted with trees? Any field that has three trees within the space required to sow a *seah* <note>A dry measure of volume; here referring to the area of land required to plant that amount of seed.</note> of grain. If those trees can produce sixty Italian minas of pressed fig cakes, the whole sowing-space of the field may be plowed for their sake; if less, one may not plow further beyond the tree than the space required for the fruit-picker and his basket. <meta>catchword: 3. This-</meta>

---

<columns>2</columns>

1 *In the year before the seventh.*] Just as in the week of days, the sixth day is called by the Jews *Erev Shabbat* <note>original: ערב שבת</note>, "the eve of the Sabbath," or in Greek *Sabbaton* <note>original: σάββατον</note>, "before the Sabbath," and the first day of the week is called *Motzaei Shabbat* <note>original: מוצאי שבת</note>, "the exit of the Sabbath"; so in the week of years, the sixth year is called *Erev Shebiith* <note>original: ערב שביעית</note>, as if you were to say (if I may use a harsher metaphor) the "Sabbatical-eve year," or the "pre-Sabbatical year": and the first year of the following seven-year period is called *Motzaei Shebiith* <note>original: מוצאי שביעית</note>, "the exit of the seventh year."

2 *Pentecost.*] The word *Atzeret* <note>original: עצרת</note> is used in Holy Scripture for the final day of the Passover assembly and the Feast of Tabernacles, as noted by common lexicographers; and this is for the reason that on those days more celebrated sacred assemblies of the people are held. For this is the true meaning of this word, as is clearly evident from a single passage in Jeremiah 9:2. There, the seventy-two translators [the Septuagint] use *synodos* <note>original: σύνοδος</note> [assembly] for *Atzeret*, the Chaldean [Targum] uses *kenishata* <note>original: כנשיתא</note>, the Syriac uses *kenushya* <note>original: ܟܢܘܫܝܐ</note>,

<column-break/>

and Jerome uses *coetus* [company], all with the same meaning. For assemblies consist of the mutual pressing and close crowding of people, which is the meaning of the word *Atzeret*. This is better than what Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval biblical commentator and grammarian.</note> suggests: that a festive solemnity is called *Atzeret* because on it "the people are restrained and held back from performing work" <note>original Hebrew: נעצרים ונמנעים העם בו מעשות מלאכה</note>. As for his addition that the eighth day of the Feast of Tabernacles is called by this name specifically above other festivals, while I might grant this as true regarding the use of the word in the sacred text (where it is also attributed to the seventh day of Passover), certainly, if we look at the usage of his countrymen in the most ancient times around and shortly after the time of Christ, it must be flatly denied. For in the Mishna, it is very frequently used for Pentecost, of which you have very clear examples in *Bikkurim* 1.6 and *Bekhorot* 9.5; and Josephus expressly states in *Antiquities* 3.10: "The Hebrews call Pentecost *Asartha*" <note>original Greek: τὴν πεντηκοστὴν δὲ ἑβραῖοι ἀσαρθὰ καλοῦσι</note>. *Asartha* is the Aramaic *Atzarta* <note>original: עצרתא</note> in the dialect of the people returning from Babylonia.

3. The same rule applies to both non-fruit-bearing and fruit-bearing trees; they are valued as if they were fig trees. If they are capable of producing sixty Italian <term>minas</term> <note>A unit of weight; an Italian mina was roughly 325 grams.</note> of <term>palatha</term> <note>original: "massae palathae," a cake of dried figs.</note>, the entire sowing-area of the field may be plowed for their sake; if less, they plow only as much as is necessary for the tree.

4. Whether a single tree can produce that mass of pressed figs and two others produce nothing, or whether two can produce it and a third produces nothing, one may not plow for them more than is necessary, up to a ratio of nine trees per <term>seah-space</term> <note>The area required to sow a seah of seed, approximately 2,500 square cubits.</note>. If there are ten or more trees, whether they can produce the weight or not, the entire sowing-area of the field is plowed for their sake. As it is said in the Law (Exodus 34:21): $^1$ *In sowing time and in harvest you shall rest.* There was no need for this to be commanded regarding the sowing and harvest of the seventh year itself <note>Since all work is already forbidden in the seventh year.</note>. Therefore, it pertains to the sowing in the year *before* the seventh, which carries over into the seventh, and to the harvest of the seventh year, which carries over into the end of the seventh <note>referring to the transition periods at the start and end of the Sabbatical cycle</note>. Rabbi Ismael speaks thus: What kind of sowing is meant? That which is done by choice; therefore, the harvest meant is also that which depends on choice; this exempts the $^2$ harvest of the first-fruits <note>original: "praemetii messis." This refers to the Omer, the mandatory offering of the first grain.</note>.

5. If three men own three trees in one plot, they are combined so that the entire sowing-area may be plowed for their sake. But how much space must there be between them? Rabban Simeon, son of Gamaliel, judges it should be as much as allows a passage for oxen with their farming implements.

6. If ten young plants are positioned without a specific order within a sowing-space, the entire area is plowed for their sake until the beginning of the Sabbatical year. If they are arranged in a line, or curved in the manner of a crown, one should not plow more than what they necessarily require.

7. Young plants and gourds may be combined within a sowing-space. Where there are ten gourds within a sowing-space, Rabban Simeon, son of Gamaliel, judges that the entire sowing-area can be plowed until the beginning of the Sabbatical year.

8. Until what age are they called "young plants"? Until they $^3$ are profaned <note>This refers to the "fourth-year" fruit (Revai), which must be redeemed or "made common" before it can be eaten by anyone.</note>, as Rabbi Eleazar son of Azariah pleases. Rabbi Joshua suggests seven-year-old saplings are treated as such...

---

$^1$ *In sowing etc.*] They interpret this text as referring to the cessation of work in respect to the seventh year. However, Rabbi Ismael interprets it differently and much more soundly: as the cessation of work on the Sabbath day, even during the seasons when sowing or harvesting is done. From the fact that no sowing exists that is not voluntary, he concludes that the precept should only extend to that harvest which is also voluntary. Thus, the harvest of the first-fruits, which is not voluntary but commanded by divine law, may be performed on any day, and as they say, it even overrides the Sabbath itself.

$^2$ *First-fruits.*] I use this term <note>original: "Praemetium"</note> for that sheaf which those about to begin the harvest were bound to offer, harvested on the day after the Passover Sabbath, and waved formally before God (Leviticus 23:10, etc.). 

<column-break/>

The Romans used the word *praemetium* for the sacred offering to Ceres, which was harvested beforehand for the sake of a preliminary offering, as is clear from Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a Roman grammarian.</note>.

$^3$ *Are profaned.*] After the completion of four years of growth. Maimonides adds: or during the fourth year itself, after they are redeemed by a valuation of money; I do not approve of this. He indeed draws this from the Jerusalem Talmud, where we read: <note>original Hebrew: מהו עד שיחולו עד שיפרו או עד שיעשו חולין מאליהן</note> "What is this 'until they are profaned'? Until they are redeemed, or until they become common of their own accord." But there it immediately follows that Rabbi Abba the son of Jacob, in the name of Rabbi Johanan, reports: <note>original Hebrew: כיני מתניתא עד שיעשו חולין מאליהן</note> "Such is the sense of the Mishnah: Until they become common of their own accord." Truly, that action of redeeming the fruit makes the *fruit* common; it in no way affects the trees themselves.

to be called thus. Rabbi Akiba says, whatever is known by that name is called a plant. A tree that has been cut down to below a palm’s breadth <note>A handbreadth or "tefach," about 3-4 inches.</note> in height, and has produced a shoot, is considered a plant; if it is above a palm’s breadth, it is considered a tree. So says Rabbi Simeon.

## CHAPTER II.

1. How long is it permitted <gloss>1</gloss> to plow a "white field" in the year before the seventh? As long as the sap does not fail—that is, for as long as people are accustomed to plow for the purpose of sowing cucumber and gourd patches. Rabbi Simeon says: You have left this to each person's own judgment. However, the limit for a "white field" is Passover, and for a field planted with trees, it is Pentecost <note>Shavuot, the festival of weeks, occurring fifty days after Passover.</note>.

2. It is permitted to fertilize and dig in cucumber and gourd patches until the beginning of the [Sabbatical] year; and likewise in <gloss>2</gloss> irrigated gardens.

---

<margin>1 A white field.</margin> That is, the *Sedeh Ha-Lavan* <note>original: "השדה הלבן"</note>. They call a grain field or a field prepared for sowing by this name because it lacks shade, as some would have it. Perhaps it is better to say it is because the ripening crop turns white for the harvest. See John 4:35.

<margin>2 Irrigated gardens.</margin> Nowhere does the carelessness and dullness of the Jews in interpreting their own Mishnah appear more clearly than in the fact that they explain *Beit Ha-Shelahin* <note>original: "בית השלהין"</note> as a "thirsty field," as if it were exhausted and fainting with dryness. The Babylonian Gemarists <note>The authors of the Gemara, the commentary that makes up the Talmud along with the Mishnah.</note> lead the way in this opinion in the tractate *Moed Katan* (1:1), where they talk nonsense in these words: *What does this Beit Ha-Shelahin mean? The notion of "dryness" belongs to it. For it is written (Deuteronomy 25:18): "when you were weary and worn out," which the Chaldaic translation renders as "faint and weary."* <note>original: "מאי משמע דהאי בית השלהין לישנא דצחותא היא דכתיב ואתה עיף ויגע ומתרגמי' ואת משהי ולאי"</note> — Anyone can see that these are the most trifling arguments. The words *Hashelahin* and *Mashlei* <note>the word for "faint"</note> are entirely different; nor are the notions of "weariness" and "dryness" any less different. And yet, the Jewish legal interpreters rush blindly into this opinion. Even Maimonides, in the very ancient Huntington manuscript, sometimes has *Shalachim* for *Shelahin*. There he also confuses it with "Baal-land" <note>Unirrigated land dependent on rain</note>, about which we will speak soon in question 9: *Beit Ha-Shelahin is the same as Baal-land, that is, thirsty land.* <note>original: "בית השלהים ארץ בעל... וחי בארץ טעטשאנר idem est ארץ בעל, id est terra siticulosa."</note> Here the Hebrew translator omits that mention of "Baal-land," being more prudent than faithful to the text. Rabbi Tanchum also follows Maimonides here. But in the Mishnah itself, *Beit Ha-Shelahin* is clearly distinguished from a "Baal-field" in *Baba Batra* (3:1). Perhaps these things could be tolerated if this sense satisfied the meaning of the Mishnah wherever this word oc-

<column-break/>

curs. But truly, there are places in the Mishnah where this meaning absolutely cannot stand. Such is the case in *Baba Batra* (4:7): *When a city is sold, the houses, the cisterns, the wells, the caves, the baths, the dovecotes, the oil-presses, and the* Beit Ha-Shelahin *are sold.* Here it is clearly evident that it refers to something considered part of a city. In the same work (3:1), it is numbered among those things that produce fruit continually. Therefore, the Gemarists are forced to retreat from that other interpretation in the earlier passage; there they explain it as "little gardens" and "pleasure grounds" <note>original: "גנוניתא & באגי"</note>; those who wish to place a difference between these terms are looking for a knot in a reed <note>A Latin idiom meaning to look for a problem where none exists.</note>. For *Bagi* is the Persian word *Bagh* <note>original: "باغ"</note>, which sounds the same as the Chaldean *Ganunita*. Both signify a garden or a pleasant green space. The Persian *Bagh* is explained by someone as a "pleasant place" or "place of recreation" <note>original: "تفرج گاه"</note>. The Royal Garden at Babylon seems to be specifically called this in the writings of Pliny: *The most famous of all, which they called "Royal" out of honor because they were reserved only for the Kings of Persia, were born at Babylon in the single garden of Bagou.* Pliny uses the name of a eunuch, "Bagou," there. To me, it seems it was rather called the "Royal Garden" [Bagh], which the following words of Pliny confirm: *That garden was never anything but the court of the ruler.* Therefore, I would wish to correct the passage in Theophrastus, from which Pliny took this: *almost in the middle of the old Bagh garden... near Babylon.* <note>original: "σχεδόν τι ἐν μέσῳ τῷ Βάγω κήπῳ τῷ παλαιῷ ... πεרὶ Βαβυלῶνα"</note> In common editions, it is read as "Bato." From here the name was transferred to other gardens. Bertinorius, therefore, in that Mishnah, explains *Beit Ha-Shelahin* as "gardens and paradises that belong to the city" <note>original: "גנות ופרדסין השייכין לעיר"</note>; even though elsewhere he always takes it to mean a thirsty field. And this seems to me to be the true meaning of *Beit Ha-Shelahin*.

# Title V. SHEBIITH. <note>The Sabbatical Year</note>

1. It is permitted to remove knots from trees <note>original: "abnodare"</note>, to prune, to stir the dust [around the roots], and to use smoke [to kill pests] until the beginning of the [Sabbatical] year. Rabbi Simeon asserts that even stripping leaves from grapevines is lawful during the seventh year.

3. It is permitted to clear stones from the soil until the beginning of the year. It is permitted to trim, prune, and clean <gloss>2</gloss> trees until the beginning of the year. Rabbi Joshua assigns the same standard for pruning and cleaning in the sixth year as is done in the fifth year <gloss>3</gloss>. Rabbi Simeon says: "As long as I am permitted to cultivate a tree, I am also permitted to clean it."

4. It is permitted to coat plants with mud <note>Likely "sordibus oblinere," a practice of protecting plant wounds</note>, to bind them, to sprinkle them with ash <gloss>4</gloss>, to protect them with cages, and to water them until the beginning of the year. Rabbi Eleazar, son of Zadok, considers it lawful to water the foliage during the seventh year itself, but not the root.

5. Early figs <term>Grossi: small, unripe figs that often remain on the tree through winter</term> may be rightly oiled and scraped <gloss>5</gloss> until the beginning of the year. Early figs of the year preceding the seventh that remain into the seventh year, and those of the seventh year that remain until the end of the seventh, are neither oiled nor scraped. Rabbi Judah says: "Where they are accustomed to oiling, they do not oil, because that is considered cultivation. Where they are not accustomed to oiling, it is permitted to oil." Rabbi Simeon permits this for the tree <gloss>6</gloss>, because cultivating the tree is permitted.

6. Not

<column-break/>

**Shelahin** <note>original: "שלחין"</note> denotes a garden field that is exceptionally cultivated and constantly irrigated; hence also in the Talmudic tractate *Baba Metzia* IX. 2, a perennial spring is required for such a field to be watered. We find this linguistic usage in the Sacred Text: **"Your plants are a paradise of pomegranates"** (Song of Songs 4:13), where Rabbi Baruch Aben-Jaiis—a brilliant commentator printed in Constantinople but not yet well known—explains **shelachayich** <note>your plants</note> as **gardens** <note>original: "גנות"</note>; asserting also that **shelahim** refers to the "Irrigated House" (*Beit ha-Shelahim*) in the Talmud. David Kimchi and, following him, Aben-Melech, hold much the same view. Hence also the pool next to the royal garden is called the **Pool of Shelah** <note>original: "Piscina horti"</note> (Nehemiah 3:15). This sense is consistent everywhere. It is especially clear in the passages cited from *Baba Batra* and in Title II. 13 of the same, where a tree hanging over into another’s field is ordered to be trimmed back so a plowman can swing his goad freely; unless that field becomes a **shelahin**, or is considered an irrigated garden. Finally, this passage can, and perhaps should, be punctuated differently: *And so in pleasure gardens, to remove knots, etc.*

1 *To remove knots.*] I translate the word **movlin** <note>original: "מובלין"</note> thus. However, what is read in its place in the *Gemara Moed Katan* 3a—**mochlin**—taken from this Mishnah, is an error. Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] nonetheless includes it in his commentaries and explains it as if it were hay. The same error appears in the *Siphra* and in Aaron's commentary there. But the manuscript of the *Siphra* reads **movlin**. This is also found in the *Pesikta Zutarta* and the *Questions of Ahai Gaon*.

<column-break/>

2 *To clean.*] By pruning away old and dead branches. Here too, in the same passage of *Moed Katan*, instead of **mipsalin**, we read **mipsagin**, which Rabbis Solomon and Nathan recognize there; and which, according to their view, means to support a tree with a prop when it is sinking into the ground due to excessive growth. Rabbi Aaron Aben-Chayim also says this in his commentary on the *Siphra*, although **mipsalim** is read there in the *Siphra* itself, both in print and in manuscript, as well as in the *Pesikta Zutarta* and the *Questions of Ahai Gaon*.

3 *Of the fifth year.*] Or any other common year. One does not usually apply that level of cultivation right up until the start of the new year in a standard common year.

4 *To sprinkle with ash.*] This is how some interpret **kotmin** <note>original: "קוטמין"</note>. Others prefer "to top" or to break off small branches, just as a sprout or willow is said to be **plucked at the head** <note>original: "נקטם ראשו"</note> (*Sukkah* III. 1). But concerning all these words, see the synopsis by Rabbi Nathan under the entry **zabal** <note>fertilizer</note>.

5 *Oiled and scraped.*] See what we wrote above regarding *Demai* I. 1.

6 *For the tree.*] Even if the tree is still laden with fruit produced in the seventh year after that year has passed. Rabbi Simeon permits oiling and scraping such fruit, not so that the fruit can be harvested sooner, but to care for the tree; for the sooner a tree is relieved of its burden, the faster it recovers its strength to produce new offspring. And this is what is read in the *Siphra*: **"Even though the Sabbatical year has ended, although its fruits are still subject to Sabbatical law, you are permitted to perform labor on the body of the tree itself, even if its fruits are forbidden, until the 15th of Shevat."** <note>The New Year for Trees</note>

### Order I. ZERAIM <note>Seeds</note>

6. A tree is not planted, nor layered <note>bent over to root a branch</note>, nor grafted in the year before the seventh within thirty days of the new year. If it has been planted, layered, or grafted [within that window], it must be pulled up. Rabbi Judah asserts that any graft which does not take within three days will never take. Rabbis Joses and Simeon say this takes two weeks.

7. Rice, millet, poppy, and sesame that have taken root before the beginning of the new year are tithed $^1$ according to the rate of the past year, and $^2$ may be lawfully gathered in the seventh year. If they have not [taken root], they are gathered unlawfully in the seventh year, and they pay tithes according to the rate of the following year.

8. Rabbi Simeon $^3$ of Sezor <note>Sezorita</note> maintains the same condition applies to the Egyptian bean sown for seed from the start. Rabbi Simeon maintains the same condition for the large chickpea. Rabbi Eleazar says: "The large chickpea [is included], if it has formed a pod before the beginning of the $^4$ year."

9. $^5$ "Eunuch" onions <note>onions that do not produce seed</note> and Egyptian beans from which water has been withheld for thirty days before the beginning of the year are tithed according to the rate of the past year, and may be lawfully gathered in the seventh year. If not, they are gathered unlawfully in the seventh year, and pay tithes according to the rate of the following year. $^6$ However, for those grown in a "dry-field" <term>Baal: a field relying on rain rather than irrigation</term>, from which water is withheld—

<column-break/>

<margin>At the end of the seventh year, although the fruits are still subject to the laws of release, you are nevertheless permitted to work on the tree itself, even if its fruit remains forbidden until the fifteenth day of the month of Shebat.</margin>

1 *According to the rate of the past year.]* For instance, if the past year in which they took root was the third or sixth of the seven-year cycle, they should pay the "Poor Man's Tithe," even if they only ripen in the fourth or seventh. If it was the first, second, fourth, or fifth year, they pay the "Second Tithe." See our notes on Peah VIII. 2.

2 *Lawfully gathered in the seventh.]* Since the preceding year was a common year <note>not a Sabbatical one</note>.

3 *Sezorita.]* This name is a derivative of "Sezor." Now Sezor—or as the Arabs write it, <note>original Arabic: "Shayzar"</note> Shayzar—is a town situated on the southern bank of the Orontes river between Epiphaneia and Antioch. This is the account of the Arab geographers Idrisi and Abulfeda. Maimonides is therefore mistaken when he writes in his Preface to the commentaries on the Mishnah (which our celebrated Pococke published) that this Simeon earned his surname from the trade he practiced, namely the twisting of silk <note>original Latin: "serici contorsione"</note>. To such an extent are these men blind to their own affairs.

4 *Beginning.]* Supplement from the previous paragraph: *it is tithed according to the rate of the past year, etc.*

5 *Eunuch onions.]* The Jerusalem Gemara <note>Rabbinic commentary</note> calls them "onions of..." or "green onions," a Cyprian onion which does not bear seed. Perhaps they are rather Ascalonian onions <note>shallots</note>, of which Theophrastus says: <note>original Greek: "Its nature is unique. For it alone is used as if sterile from the root. Furthermore, in these cases it is weak and does not increase. Therefore they do not plant it, but sow it."</note> Hist. Plant. VII. 4. Hence Pliny says in XIX. 6: *The nature of Ascalonian onions is peculiar. For they become sterile, as it were, from the root, and for that reason the Greeks ordered them to be sown from seed, not planted.*

<column-break/>

6 *In a dry-field, etc.]* And here again the Jewish legal interpreters, at least the more recent ones, are stumbling. For they do not know what a *Baal* field is, though the term recurs very often in the Mishnah. Rabbi Solomon says it is a field <note>original Hebrew: "which is satisfied by rainwater"</note> that subsists on rain and is not irrigated from elsewhere. Regarding the Sukkah, he says it is <note>original Hebrew: "land that does not need irrigation, for the rain of heaven is enough for it."</note> This is not entirely wrong, though it is clear even from this Mishnah that a *Baal* field is one where at least some irrigation is practiced. But these definitions led Rabbi Samson and his copyist, Bertinoro, into a foul error. To them, *Baal* is <note>original Hebrew: "a field in a valley, marshy, which therefore does not need to be irrigated."</note> Nothing could be said more contrary to the meaning of this word. Maimonides, if possible even more foully, confuses *Baal* with an irrigated field <note>original Hebrew: "Beth ha-Shalchin"</note>, when they are clearly distinguished in the Mishnah itself. However, Rabbi Tanchum in his Lexicon...

# Title V. SHEBIITH <note>The Sabbatical Year</note>

10. Cu-

describes it much better, **Baal** <note>original: **בעל**; a term for rain-fed land</note> as it were **the land** <note>original: **ארץ**</note>
**that is thirsty, not irrigated from elsewhere than from the rain, which it drank in winter.** <note>original Arabic: **טעטעאנה אתי לא תסקי גיר מא תשריבה פאשתא מן המטר**</note>
Indeed, I will teach the meaning of this word much more certainly both from the Mishnah <term>Terumot X. 11</term> <note>Terumot concerns the "heave-offering" or portions of the harvest given to the priests</note> and from its use in the Arabic language. In that passage of the Mishnah, we have the opposites **Shakya** <note>original: **שקיא**; irrigated land</note> and **Baal**, plainly as the "dry-fields" and "irrigated fields" in Columella <note>a Roman writer on agriculture</note>. **Baal cabbage** <note>original: **כרוב של בעל**</note>, or **an irrigated field with Baal cabbage**, <note>original: **שקיא עם כרוב של בעל**</note> meaning irrigated fields along with cabbage from a dry-field, or a dry-field. Bertinorius <note>a 15th-century commentator on the Mishnah</note> explains **Shakya** at this passage as **arid land that needs irrigation** <note>original: **ארץ יבשה שצריך להשקותה**</note>; and on the contrary, he interprets **Baal** as **moist land that does not need irrigation at all.** <note>original: **ארץ לחה שאין צריך להשקותה**</note>
Namely, so that **Baal** may be moist soil, he even turns the very well-known word **Shakya** away from its certain and proper meaning. But **Shakya**, for a place naturally well-watered, occurs a hundred times in the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> Paraphrasts <note>the Targums</note>. I bring an example from Onkelos, Genesis XIII. 10: *he saw the whole plain of the Jordan* **because the whole place was well-watered.** <note>original: **ארי שקיא כוליה בית**</note> From here also the ancient and excellent anonymous Syrian Glossary
> **an irrigated field, for the land of Al-Saqy** <note>original Syriac/Arabic: **ܚܩܠܐ ܡܫܩܝܬܐ ܠܐܪܥܐ ܐܠܣܩܝ**</note>
signifying that **an irrigated field** <note>original: **ܚܩܠܐ ܡܫܩܝܬܐ**</note> is so called. I know, however, that **Shakya** and **Beit Shakya** among the Chaldeans, and likewise the Syriac **field** <note>original: **ܚܩܠܐ**</note>, are used not only for soil naturally well-watered but also for that which is irrigated by art. It signifies, therefore, a place well-watered in any manner. Now, then, **Baal**, being its opposite, will be dry-field soil. Columella II. 17 says: *Therefore we notice two kinds of it, of which one is dry-field, the other irrigated. And above in chapter 2: Concerning dry-fields and irrigated ones, we have not found which are more numerous.* This appears more clearly from the Arabic language, where **Baal** <note>original: **بعل**</note>, according to the explanation of Mohammed Phiruzabadius <note>a famous 14th-century lexicographer</note>, is:
> **Higher land rained upon once a year; likewise whatever palms, trees, and crops are not irrigated at all, or only by the heavens.** <note>original Arabic: **الارض المرتفعة تمطر في السنة مرة وكل نخل وشجر وزرع لا يسقى او ما سقتها السما**</note>
Where, besides being attributed to un-irrigated land, it is also attributed to palms, trees, and crops that are not irrigated, plainly as the Atinian elms of the dry-fields are opposed to the irrigated ones

<column-break/>

in Pliny XVI. 17. To this also belongs what Ismael Jauharius <note>an 11th-century lexicographer</note> explains as **Baal**:
> **The palm tree which attracts moisture with its roots and is not in need of irrigation.** <note>original Arabic: **النخل الذي يشرب بعروقة ويستغني عن السقي**</note>
He adds, moreover, that Abuamrum and Asmaeus (or as it is read from him in Phiumius, Azharaeus) disagree about the meaning of the word **Baal**. The former contends that **Adhi** <note>original: **عذى**</note> and **Baal** are used synonymously for whatever is watered by heaven. The latter puts this difference between them: **Adhi** is said of whatever is watered by heaven; **Baal** is that which is nourished neither by heaven nor from elsewhere, but by its own roots alone. But what clearly pertains to our subject is that verse of the Poet praised by Jauharius, and his note upon it. The verse is thus:
> **When we overcame the back of a wide-extending Baal-field.** <note>original Arabic: **اذا ما علونا ظهر بعل عريضة**</note>
Where Jauharius notes that **Baal** does not signify just any field, but **higher land, which neither a flowing river nor a flood ever reaches.** <note>original Arabic: **ارض مرتفعة لا يصيبها سيح ولا سيل**</note> But as our Mishnah speaks of the irrigation of a **Baal** field, a thing which seems to fit neither the **Baal** of the Arabs described thus far, nor the dry-fields of Columella; (For Columella also plainly excludes irrigation in the words cited before, of which one is dry-field, the other irrigated, subjoining these: *In a lush and fat plain a flowing stream is not required, and hay is considered better which is produced in soil naturally succulent than that which is drawn out by waters being irrigated.*) this must be understood as irrigation done by hand, not through channels led into the field, which the higher situation of the field, such as the verse praised above expresses, does not even allow.
Moreover, that the **Baal** of the Arabs admits of another kind of irrigation may be recognized even from this verse of Abdalla, son of Ravaha:
> **Here I do not care for the watering of the palm nor the Baal-field, however much it may increase the yield.** <note>original Arabic: **هنالك لا ابالي سقي نخل ولا بعل وان عظم الاتا**</note>

# Order I. ZERAIM <note>Seeds</note>

10. Gourds that are kept for seed, if they have hardened before the beginning of the year, and thus have become unfit for human consumption, may be lawfully kept in the seventh year; but if not, they are kept unlawfully in the seventh year. The blossoms of the same are considered unlawful in the seventh year. It is permitted to sprinkle <note>1</note> a whitening clod <note>likely referring to a method of marking or preparing the soil</note> according to the opinion of Rabbi Simeon. Rabbi Eliezer, the son of Jacob, forbids it. It is permitted to soak rice in the seventh year <note>2</note>. Rabbi Simeon adds <note>3</note>, but not to weed it of grass.

->C H A P T E R III.<-

1. **A**t what time is it permitted to carry manure out to the dung-heaps? From the time when farming <note>4</note> has ceased to be practiced. So says Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Judah says <note>5</note>, from the time when the sap has dried up. Rabbi Joses says, from the time when the soil begins to crumble.
2. How

---

<columns>2</columns>

Others here read for *nakhl* <note>original: **نخل**; palm tree</note>, *saqiy* <note>original: **سقي**; irrigated</note> so that it ought to be rendered thus: *Here I do not care for the irrigated palm, nor the dry-grown one, etc.* so that in this verse of the Arabic poet, **Saqiy** and **Baal** <note>original: **בעל**; rain-fed land</note> are opposed in the same way as **Shakya** <note>original: **שקיא**; irrigated</note> and **Baal** in the cited passage of the Mishnah. And from these things it is clear enough what **Baal** is; namely, a field or dry plain, so positioned by its nature that it can enjoy only rain-fed growth rather than irrigation.

<note>1 Sprinkle.]</note> Water distributed more sparingly. Thus, according to Columella <note>a Roman writer on agriculture</note>, nurseries of elms ought to be *sprinkled* rather than irrigated. Here, however, a variation in the reading is noted in the Jerusalem Talmud, with these words interposed: "it is permitted to sprinkle in the seventh year, but not on a festival," <note>original: **בשביעית אבל לא במועד**</note> according to the opinion, etc.

<note>2 To soak, etc.]</note> Here Maimonides <note>the renowned 12th-century Jewish scholar</note> compares the word *memarsin* <note>soaking</note> with the Arabic *marasa* <note>original: **مرس**</note>, meaning to macerate in water. And it is certainly established that rice grows with difficulty unless it is thoroughly soaked, and if it does grow, it bears either no crop or a hollow one. Also, that word *kassach* <note>original: **כסח**</note>, which elsewhere sounds to him like "to cut down" or "to prune," here signifies *achnakia* <note>original Arabic: **אחנקיה**</note>, "to clear of harmful weeds," specifically by cutting them down. Others take it for a certain pruning of the rice itself, so to speak, by which its superfluous leaves are cut away and removed. But this is trivial. Another thought occurs to me—whether it will please everyone I do not know, but I do not think it superfluous to bring it forward. The same Arabic verb, but in the fifth form, *tamarrasa* <note>original: **تمارس**</note>, signifies "the tree was gnawed at intervals." 
*And he grazed upon it from time to time,* <note>original Arabic: **وياكلها وقتا بعد وقت**</note> as Zamachsharius <note>a medieval Persian scholar of the Arabic language</note> says. We have an example of this in the 

<column-break/>

Sunnah <note>the traditional law of Islam</note>, or the "Mohammedan Mishnah":
*It is a sign of the approaching end of the world that a man diminishes his religion by gnawing it away bit by bit, just as a camel diminishes a tree by repeatedly gnawing upon it.* <note>original: **من اقتراب الساعة ان يتمرس الرجل بمدينته كما يتمرس البعير بالشجرة**</note>
Where it must be especially observed, that this verb is constructed with the letter *b* <note>a Hebrew and Arabic preposition</note> in the same way as *memarsin* is in the Mishnah. Now, if we attribute the same meaning to the Hebrew *maras*, the words of the Mishnah would yield this sense: *It is permitted to occasionally crop the rice in the seventh year as opportunity arises; but it is not permitted to cut it all down at once.*

<note>3 Rabbi adds.]</note> So it is read in most editions and in the manuscript, "Rabbi Simeon says." <note>original: **ר' שמעון אומר**</note> But in the Jerusalem Talmud it is "The words of Rabbi Simeon," <note>original: **דברי ר' שמעון**</note> so that the passage ought to be read and punctuated thus: "it is permitted. So says Rabbi Simeon. But not, etc."

<note>4 Farming being practiced.]</note> That is, when it is already contrary to the logic of rural affairs to spread dung through the fields. However, I follow the reading of the Jerusalem Talmud, which I see is also approved by Yom-Tob <note>a reference to a commentator, likely Yom-Tob Lipmann Heller</note>. Others instead of "those who practice" have "transgressors," <note>original: **עוברי עבירה**</note> that is, from when it has ceased among the transgressors. So the manuscript, Maimonides, etc. These words are correctly read at the beginning of the next chapter, and seem to have been substituted here for the other words.

<note>5 From the time when the sap has dried up.]</note> It was easy here to recognize the most trifling interpretations of the Jews. To attain the correct one is not so readily at hand. In all the books it is "from when the sweet has dried up" <note>original: **משיבש המתוק**</note> or "from when it shall bind"; Rabbi Joses says "from when it shall bind" <note>original: **משיקשור**</note>. In the Jerusalem Talmud, "from within" is "the colocynth," <note>a bitter desert plant</note>

2. How many manure heaps may they make? Up to three for the space of a *seah* <note>a unit of land area, roughly 500 square cubits</note>, each heap consisting of ten baskets, with each basket holding a *half-kor* <note>about 120 liters</note>. It is permitted to increase the number of baskets in a heap, but not the number of heaps. Rabbi Simeon, however, maintains that even the number of heaps may be increased.

3. Anyone is permitted to arrange three manure heaps throughout his field for every *seah* of land. According to the opinion of Rabbi Simeon, even more are allowed. But the Sages forbid this, unless the manure is placed in a spot hollowed out three handbreadths deep, or raised three handbreadths high. It is permitted to gather dung into a storehouse. Rabbi Meir forbids this unless it is in a spot three handbreadths deep or three handbreadths high. If a person has only a small amount of manure, he may add to it bit by bit. Rabbi Eleazar, son of Azariah, forbids this unless it is placed in a spot three handbreadths deep, or three handbreadths high, or unless he places it upon a rock.

4. He who stables his cattle in the field <note>to naturally fertilize the soil</note> may make a fold for a space of two *seahs*. Then, having removed three sides of the enclosure, <gloss>2</gloss> he may leave the middle section standing. In this way, he will be found to have stabled the cattle over a space of four *seahs*. Rabban Simeon, son of Gamaliel, says over a space of eight *seahs*. If the entire field is exactly four *seahs*, one must leave a certain part unfertilized for the sake of appearances <note>to show he is not intentionally preparing the whole field for planting in the Sabbatical year</note>. However, one may place manure brought out from elsewhere in the field in the manner of those who normally fertilize.

5. No one shall open a stone quarry in his field for the first time unless there are three <gloss>3</gloss> piles already there, each three cubits square, so that they contain twenty-nine stones. 6. If...

---

To Maimonides and others, this refers to the <term>bitter gourd</term> <note>original: colocynthis</note>, so called by "antiphrasis" <note>a figure of speech where a word is used to mean its opposite—calling something bitter 'sweet'</note>, if it please the Gods. The word **משיישה** is the same as **משיישר**, that is, **קשרין קשרין**, meaning "it abounds in knots." To this, Rabbi Ananias adds: **מכיון שנתקשר בו קשר, העליון מיד הוא יבש**, "as soon as it is tied with a knot at the top, it immediately withers." Thus the passage should be translated: *From the time the bitter gourd has withered.* Rabbi Joses says: from the time it abounds in knots. But it is plainly ridiculous that they explain **מתוק** <note>sweet</note> as <term>bitter gourd</term>, and I do not know if anyone can truly understand what they add regarding the knots. Therefore, Rabbi Samson, and Bertinoro following him, take **מתוק** here to mean the manure itself, which brings the fruit to maturity and sweetness; and Bertinoro explains **משיישר כשמתחיל להתיבש** thus: when the dung begins to dry out, it thickens and becomes, as it were, full of knots. But it is not likely that manure is called "sweet" here, since it was called **זבל** <note>dung/manure</note> just before in this same Mishnah. The phrase **משיישר** occurs again below in Chapter IX, 6, and it seems to mean what I have set down, which also fits this passage well. Rabbi Judah maintains that manure can lawfully be exported in the seventh year when the moisture has already completely dried up, whether of the fruits or the earth, and there is no longer any hope that it can be of any use this year for producing a more abundant crop. Rabbi Joses orders that one need not wait so long, but permits it to be exported...

<column-break/>

...when it is **משיישר**: a word which produces difficulty, and if I see rightly, should be changed to **משייקד**, that is, from the time when the sap of the fruits, or the prolific power of the earth, is not entirely dried up, but frozen as it were and blunted, cutting off all hope of an increased return.

<gloss>1</gloss> **Even more are allowed.**] I read **יתר מכך מותר**, as does Jomtob. Or simply **יתר מכך** as in the Manuscript. For that word **מחזיק** <note>holding/containing</note>, which is seen in some editions, seems foreign to this place.

<gloss>2</gloss> **Middle.**] Between the old demolished fold and the new one to be placed next to it on the other side.

<gloss>3</gloss> **Piles.**] The word **מורביות** <note>Murbiot</note>, which nearly all editions, the old Manuscript, the *Tosefta*, and the commentators recognize here, elsewhere signifies the longer branches of trees (as in *Sukkah* IV. 5 and *Tamid* II. 3), a meaning which cannot apply here. This word, to my knowledge, occurs nowhere else with a different meaning except in this passage. Here, however, it is clear from the Mishnah itself that an orderly pile of stones is meant. Therefore, I am not afraid to replace **מורביות**, an ancient error, with **מרבנות** <note>Marbanot</note> or **מרבגים** <note>Marbagim</note>, in which sense **מרבג של אבנים** <note>a pile of stones</note> was formerly read in *Oholoth* III. 7 according to Rabbi Nathan; where modern codices have either **מרבך** or **מרבך**; and in the *Gemara* of *Sukkah* 20b, where the same Mishnah is cited; and *Shabbat* 125b, where the same point is indicated. Modern codices read **מרבך**.

6. If there are ten stones in a stone wall <note>Latin: *maceria*</note> that are each a load for two men, they may be lawfully removed. The measure of a wall is ten handbreadths. If it is smaller than that, it is considered a quarry <note>Latin: *lapicidina*</note>, and it is permitted to cut it out from the ground even below the height of a handbreadth. How are these things to be understood? This refers to one's own land. But from another person's land, one may remove whatever one pleases. How is this to be understood? This applies when the work had not yet begun in the year before the seventh. But if the work had already begun in the year before the seventh, then whatever one pleases may be lawfully removed.

7. Stones that the plow has turned up, or those that are uncovered after being buried—if among them there are two that are each a load for two men, one may remove them. He who clears a field of stones should remove the upper ones but must leave those that are touching the ground. Likewise, regarding a heap <gloss>1</gloss> of pebbles or a mound of stones: once the upper ones are removed, those touching the ground should be left. If there is bedrock or stubble underneath them, they may also be lawfully removed.

8. <gloss>2</gloss> It is not permitted to surround ponds with embankments in the year before the seventh after the rains have ceased, because this constitutes preparing them for the seventh year. However, in the seventh year itself, after the rains have ceased, it is permitted, because this is preparing them for the conclusion of the seventh year. This should not be done with <gloss>3</gloss> piled earth, but with <gloss>4</gloss> masonry work <note>Latin: *opere cæmentitio*</note>; and any stone that can be reached with an outstretched hand may be taken.

9. <gloss>5</gloss> Shoulder-stones may be brought from anywhere. <gloss>6</gloss> A contractor <note>Latin: *Redemtor*</note> may also bring them from anywhere. Those stones are called "shoulder-stones" which cannot be lifted by a single hand. This is the opinion of Rabbi Meir. But Rabbi Jose contends that shoulder-stones, according to the meaning of the name, are those which are carried by twos or threes on the shoulder.

<gloss>6 Contractor.]</gloss> One who undertakes the work. Not someone who holds the field by the right of a sharecropper, as Maimonides and others following him would have it.

## CHAPTER IV.

1. In ancient times they used to say: one may gather wood, stones, and grass from one’s own field, just as from another’s—namely, the larger pieces. But after law-breakers became more frequent, it was ordained that anyone might gather from another’s field, and the other from his, without any return of favor. It is unnecessary to add that they should not agree on providing food <note>In the Sabbatical year, fields are meant to be open to all; this rule prevented people from "paying" for the privilege of gathering from someone's field, which would violate the spirit of the year.</note>.

2. A field cleared of thorns may be rightly sown at the end of the seventh year. A field that has been cultivated <gloss>2</gloss> or enriched by folding livestock <note>The practice of letting animals graze and manure a specific patch of land.</note> shall not be sown at the end of the seventh year. The School of Shammai <note>A stricter school of Jewish law.</note> thinks that the crops of a cultivated field in the seventh year should not be eaten. The School of Hillel <note>A generally more lenient school of Jewish law.</note> thinks they may be eaten. The Shammaites say the crops of the seventh year should not be eaten with a return of favor. The Hillelites believe they may be eaten both with and without a return of favor. Rabbi Judah <gloss>3</gloss> counts the reversal of this opinion among those cases where the Shammaites take the more lenient view and the Hillelites the more severe.

3. It is permitted to rent fallow land from Gentiles in the seventh year, but not from an Israelite. It is permitted to assist <gloss>4</gloss> Gentiles in the seventh year, but not an Israelite. One may also offer them a greeting of peace for the sake of maintaining harmony.

4. If someone thins out his olive trees, the Shammaites say he should cut them down; the Hillelites say he should uproot them. They agree that one who strips the trees must cut them down. Who is he who "thins"? He who removes one or two trees. Who "strips"? He who removes three in a row. How are these things to be understood? This applies if someone is working his own land. But if it is on another's land, even the one who strips them may uproot them.

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>1 *For his own benefit.*]</margin> So that it may benefit him as a substitute for manure. Other interpreters explain this differently. Bertinorius <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro (c. 1450–1515), a famous commentator on the Mishna.</note> says: **He can pile it in the public domain, but afterward, having removed it, he shall restore the public place to its former state.** <note>original Hebrew: צוברו ברשות הרבים ואחר כך נוטלו משם ומתקן את רשות הרבים כמו שהיה</note> This is a very weak interpretation. Yet he speaks the mind of the others. But the word **tikkun** <note>original: תקן</note> denotes not only to restore and repair, but also to improve.

<column-break/>

<margin>2 *Cultivated.*]</margin> Repeatedly tilled, if we trust the Jewish interpreters. But they are talking nonsense. Understand "cultivated" as referring to the seventh year, when all agriculture is forbidden.

<margin>3 *The reversal of this.*]</margin> This occurs in the tractate Eduyot, Chapter V, Section 1.

<margin>4 *To assist.*]</margin> While they are engaged in farming. However, the Jewish interpreters claim this means assisting not by doing work, but only by offering a prayer for their success. Sharp-witted men! See 2 John 10-11.

It also outlines how to interact with Gentiles during the sabbatical year to maintain social harmony.</summary>

Order I. SEEDS

## CHAPTER V.

1. The seventh year for **white** figs falls into the second year of the next cycle, because they only complete their fruit every three years. Rabbi Judah adds: $^2$ for Persian fruits, the seventh year falls at the end of the seventh year, because they complete their fruit in two years. It was said to him: that rule was not stated regarding any others except white figs.

2. If someone wishes to store buried arum <note>A genus of plants, including the cuckoo-pint, often grown for its edible starchy roots.</note> during the seventh year, Rabbi Meir commands him to bury at least two seahs <note>A biblical unit of volume, approximately 7 to 13 liters.</note> three palms deep, with one palm of soil cast over it. But the Sages instruct him to bury at least four cabs <note>A smaller unit of volume; four cabs are equal to two-thirds of a seah.</note> one palm deep, with one palm of soil cast over it. He should bury it in a place where people frequently walk.

3. Regarding arum that remains after the seventh year has passed, Rabbi Eliezer judges thus: If the poor have gathered the leaves, let it be. If not, a $^3$ settlement should be reached with the poor. Rabbi Joshua judges thus: If the poor have gathered the leaves, let it be. If not, the poor cannot demand a settlement.

4. Concerning...

---

1 *White figs.* ] There is frequent mention of <term>benot shuach</term> <note>original: בנות שוח</note> figs in the books of the Jews. Likewise of the <term>benot sheva</term> <note>original: בנות שבע</note> or <term>shua</term> <note>original: שוע</note> figs, as in Maaserot II. 8. and elsewhere. Rabbi Tanchum wishes these to be the same, differing only in pronunciation. The author of the *Tosephot* to Aboda Zara 14. *a.* also brings a passage from *Bereshith Rabba* <note>Genesis Rabbah, a collection of ancient explanations of the book of Genesis.</note> to prove this. <note>original: "תאנים שאכל אדם הראשון איכא דקרו להו בנות שוח לפי שגרמו שוח לאדם ואיכא דקרו להו בנות שבע שגרמו שבע אבילות לאדם" — "The figs which the first man, Adam, ate: some call them 'daughters of depression' because they brought depression [shoo-ach] to man; others call them 'daughters of seven' because they caused the seven days of mourning for man."</note> Truly, this cannot be proven from this passage. For nothing prevents different types of figs from being designated by those names; and different authors may have held different opinions about the type of fig through which Adam sinned. Similar points are made in the commentary on Shebuot 12. *b.* In the Jerusalem Talmud, <term>benot shuach</term> is explained as <term>pitoria</term>, in Rabbi Nathan as <term>pitoriaia</term>, and in Rabbi Samson as <term>pitria</term>—that is, without any notable discrepancy. Rabbi Nathan thinks this is Greek. But among the Greek names for figs, I find none, unless perhaps it is a corruption for <term>phithelea</term> <note>original: φιθελεα</note> or <term>philaleia</term> <note>original: Φιλαλεα</note>.

2 *Persian fruits.* ] Musaphias thinks the word <term>persa'ot</term> <note>original: פרסאות</note> is made from the Greek, as if it should be understood as <term>the last year's figs</term> <note>original: τὰ πέρυσι σύκα</note> or <term>the last year's fruits</term> <note>original: οἱ πέρυσι καρποί</note>. Rabbi Nathan interprets it as <term>Persian dates</term> <note>original: תמרי פרסייתא</note>,

<column-break/>

referring to the *Persian* variety, looking to a passage in Shabbat 29. *a.* where <term>Syrian and Persian dates</term> <note>original: ארמיאתא & פרסייאתא</note> are contrasted. Just as also the <term>Syrian palm</term> and <term>Persian palm</term> <note>original: דקלא ארמיא & דקלא פרסא</note> are mentioned in Baba Kama 59. *a.* It is commonly a type of fig that only completes its fruit in the second year, which Rabbi Nathan himself mentions. I have no doubt that <term>persa'ot</term> are *Perseae*, a type of tree peculiar to Egypt. They agree not only in name but in fact. Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note> says of the Persea in his *History of Plants* IV. 2: <note>original: "καρπὸν δὲ φέρει πολὺν καὶ κατὰ πᾶσαν ὥραν πεπαίνει. ἐπικαταλαμβάνει δὲ ὁ νέος ἀεὶ τὸν ἔνον" — "It bears much fruit and ripens at every season. The new fruit always overtakes the old."</note> However, it must be admitted that this is explicitly denied regarding <term>persa'ot</term> in the Tosephta. For it reads there at the beginning of the fourth chapter: <note>original: "רבי יהודה אומר הפרסאות שביעית שלהן מוצאי שביעית שהן עושין לשתי שנים אמר לו הרי הן אצל טבריא ואינן עושות אלא בנות שנתן" — "Rabbi Judah asserts that for Persian fruits, the seventh year falls at the end of the seventh year because they produce fruit over two years. It was said to him: 'Behold, they are near you in Tiberias, and they do not produce any fruit except that which belongs to their own year.'"</note>

3 *Settlement.* ] So that the leaves grown in the seventh year go to the poor, and the new ones to the master of the house. In this Mishnah, Rabbi Eliezer follows the opinion of Rabbi Judah, who gives the crops of the seventh year only to the poor after they have been handled improperly. But Rabbi Joshua follows the opinion of Rabbi Jose, who allows them equally to the poor and the rich. See below, IX. 8.
