# Title V. SHEVIIT <note>The Sabbatical Year</note>

4. Concerning arum <note>A starchy root plant</note> from the year before the seventh that has grown into the seventh, and likewise regarding summer onions, and madder <note>A plant used for red dye</note> grown in richer soil: the School of Shammai believe these should be uprooted with wooden stakes; the School of Hillel allow metal axes. They both agree that regarding "angular" madder, it may be uprooted with metal axes.

5. From what time is it permitted to purchase arum after the seventh year has ended? Rabbi Judah believes it is allowed immediately. However, the Sages say only from the time when the new crop becomes available in sufficient quantity.

6. A craftsman is not permitted to sell these tools during the seventh year: a plow with all its equipment, the yoke, the winnowing fan, and the plowshare. But he is permitted to sell a hand-sickle, a harvest-sickle, and a wagon with all its equipment. This is the general rule: anything whose specific use tends toward a violation of the law <note>i.e., tools used exclusively for forbidden agricultural work</note> is sold illegally; but if it can be used for both forbidden and permitted tasks, it is sold legally.

7. A potter is permitted to sell five oil-jars and fifteen wine-jars; because it is customary to collect this amount from communal property. If someone acquires more than this, it is permitted; and he may sell to Gentiles within the land of Israel or outside the land.

8. The School of Shammai forbid selling a plowing cow during the seventh year. The School of Hillel permit it, because the cow could be intended for slaughter <note>and thus for food, which is permitted, rather than for plowing, which is forbidden</note>. One person may sell produce to another at the time of sowing; and one may lend a *seah* measure <note>A unit of volume</note>, even if he knows the borrower has a threshing floor; and one may exchange money, even if he knows the person has laborers to pay. All these things, if they are **explicitly named**, are illegal.

9. $^4$ Any woman may lend to another who is suspected of violating the seventh year laws...

---

<columns>2</columns>

1 *Richer soil.*] In Gittin 5:1, there are three recognized differences in the quality of land: *Idit* <note>original: עידית</note> for the most excellent soil, *Benonit* <note>original: בינונית</note> for mediocre soil, and *Ziburit* <note>original: זיבורית</note> for lean and poor soil. The same word *Idit* is read with the same meaning in the Aramaic Translation of Psalm 83:13 and Lamentations 2:2. The origin of the word, which Jewish scholars seek in vain, is suggested to us by the Arabic language, in which the word *azzi* <note>original: عزي</note>, when used of soil, signifies that it has become soft and fat. From this comes the word for such soil, *adhat* or *adhiyah* <note>original: عذاة & عذية</note>, which is clearly our *Idit*. Zamakhshari provides an example: *They settled in valleys encompassing very wide meadows.* Where he explains *the good lands* as *soils of noble plants*, meaning soil of wide extent and very rich yield. Another example from a Poet: *In a most fertile land, whose clear mornings are pleasant.*

<column-break/>

But a verse by Dhur-Rumma surpasses all elegance, in which he uses this word in such a way that it leaves no doubt about its meaning:
-> In a land of fine soil, the moist earth of spring, <-
-> most fertile, from which saltiness and the sea are far away. <-
To these add what we said above regarding *azzi* at the word *Baal*. Rabbi Nathan wants the names *Idit* and *Tzelaot* and the word *Pe'ah* to refer to the specific nature of the locations. Unskillfully so.

2 *Angular.*] For Maimonides correctly explains *puah* <note>original: פואה</note> as *madder of the ribs/angles* <note>original: פוה של צלעות</note>, that is, the madder of Dioscorides, of which *the stem is square* <note>original Greek: ὁ καυλὸς τετράγωνος</note>. He adds that it is fixed deep in the earth, and therefore is uprooted with difficulty without iron tools.

3 *Explicitly.*] As if he should say: "Sell me produce so that I may sow it," "lend me a measure so that I may measure grain," or "exchange money for me so that I may pay wages to laborers."

4 *Any woman.*] This paragraph recurs in Gittin 5:9.

Order I. ZERAIM <note>Seeds</note>

...she may give a coarse sieve, a fine sieve, a mill, or an oven. However, she may not sift or grind with her <note>This refers to an observant woman assisting the wife of a common person who might not observe the Sabbatical laws or tithing strictly</note>. The wife of a Fellow <note>A Chaver, one who is scrupulous in observing ritual purity and tithes</note> may lend a coarse sieve or a fine sieve to the wife of a common person; she may even sift, grind, and winnow flour with her. But once she has poured water [on the flour], she must no longer approach it; for one must not assist those who violate the law <note>The addition of water makes the flour susceptible to ritual impurity according to Jewish law</note>. All these things are permitted only for the sake of maintaining peace <note>To prevent social friction and maintain neighborly relations</note>. It is permitted to help Gentiles during the seventh year <note>Sabbatical year</note>, but not Israelites. It is also permitted to greet them with "Peace" <note>the Hebrew greeting 'Shalom'</note> for the sake of maintaining peace.

## CHAPTER VI.

1. <gloss>1</gloss> The land is divided into three parts regarding the laws of the seventh year. In all the territory that the people returning from Babylonia occupied—from the land of Israel as far as Ecdippa <note>also known as Achziv</note>—crops may not be harvested, and the land may not be cultivated. In all that territory which those who came out of Egypt occupied, beyond Ecdippa as far as the river and Amana <note>likely Mt. Hor or the Amanus Mountains</note>, crops may be harvested, but the land may not be cultivated. From the river and Amana further inland, crops may be harvested and the land may be cultivated.

2. Once the crops have been detached from the soil in Syria, it is permitted to work with them, but not with those still attached to the ground; such as threshing, winnowing, treading grapes, and binding sheaves; but one may not reap, harvest grapes, or pick olives. Rabbi Akiba states a general rule: <gloss>2</gloss> whatever is legally permitted in the land of Israel may also be done in Syria.

3. Onions that have sprouted due to soaking rains: if the leaves turn black, they are considered forbidden; if they are green, they are permitted. Rabbi <gloss>3</gloss> Ananias, son of Antigonus, says they are forbidden <gloss>4</gloss> if the leaves can be pulled away without bringing the bulb with them; on the other hand, at the end of the seventh year, they are permitted.

---

<columns>2</columns>

1 **The land is divided into three.** Lightfoot, in his *Chorographical Century* LXV, interprets this passage very poorly: *Three regions [namely, Judea, Galilee, and Perea] are bound to the law of the seventh year.* That division into Judea, Galilee, and Perea does indeed occur elsewhere, as seen below in IX. 2. But here a different matter is addressed. The nature of this division is sufficiently shown by what follows in the Mishnah and by similar passages in Challah IV. 8.

2 **Whatever is legally permitted.** One might wonder at this rule, which seems so irrelevant. But Bertinorius <note>Obadiah of Bertinoro, a 15th-century commentator</note> provides the supplement: *Whatever is legally permitted;* that is, by the sole force of the Biblical law, without the additional decrees of the Teachers; such as working with detached crops. Or: Whatever is legally permitted in the land of Israel regarding communal property, the same is permitted in Syria even in private and guarded property.

3 **Ananias.** חנניא. Others read חנינא Hanina, as often happens in these names.

<column-break/>

4 **If the leaves can be pulled away.** Both Talmuds and several editions of the Mishnah read אינם יכולין להתולש בעלין שלהן *if they cannot be pulled away by their leaves*. But in the Babylonian Gemara, Nedarim 58a, where this Mishnah is cited, the negative particle *inam* or *inan* is omitted; and this is how Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> reads it there. Rabbis Samson and Obadiah also read it this way here. Consequently, it is omitted in the Krakow edition of Yom-Tov and in both Amsterdam editions. In the Manuscript, it is read as אם היו יכולין להתולש בעלין שלהן, *if their leaves can be pulled away*. That is, according to Maimonides' interpretation, <note>original Judeo-Arabic: "ان اعقلت ورقها وبقيت هي لا ترتفض مع وورق"</note> *if the leaves are pulled, the onion bulb itself remains and is not lifted up together with the leaves.*

# Title V. SHEBIITH <note>The Sabbatical Year</note>

4. From what time is it permitted to purchase vegetables at the end of the seventh year? From the time that a vegetable of the same kind has produced its new growth. If the early crop has already produced growth, the late-ripening crop is permitted. <gloss>1</gloss> Rabbi permitted the purchase of vegetables immediately once the seventh year has concluded.

5. It is not permitted to export <gloss>2</gloss> oil for burning <note>ritually impure oil designated for fuel</note> or the fruits of the seventh year from the land of Israel to a foreign land. Rabbi Simeon said: I have received a specific tradition that it is permitted to export to Syria, but not to a foreign land.

6. It is not permitted to bring First Fruits <note>Bikkurim</note> from a foreign land. Rabbi Simeon said: I have received a specific tradition that they may be brought lawfully from Syria, but not from a foreign land.

---
->### CHAPTER VII.<-
---

**A** great rule is handed down regarding the seventh year: Whatever serves as food for man, or for cattle, or is of the kind used for dyeing, and does not remain perennial in the earth, is subject to the law of the seventh year and to the laws governing its price <note>meaning money used to buy it must be treated with Sabbatical sanctity</note>; the law of removal <note>the requirement to clear produce from the home once it is no longer available in the field</note> applies to it and to its price. What exactly are these? Surely the leaves of the wild arum, mint leaves, chicory, leeks, purslane, and <gloss>3</gloss> spurge. And food for cattle, such as thistles and thorns. And what is used for dyeing, such as woad and <gloss>4</gloss> biennial safflower.

<columns>2</columns>

<gloss>1</gloss> *Rabbi.*] Thus, as is the custom of the Jews, he is called by this title with his name suppressed; he is Rabbi Judah the Holy, the compiler of the Mishnah. Whether it is probable that an author would set forth his own opinion in this manner, the reader shall judge. Elsewhere in the Mishnah, mention is made of the sons of this same Rabbi Judah, such as in Makkot 3:15, where the opinion of Rabbi Simeon, son of Rabbi, is cited. And in Aboth, Chapter 2, where after the opinion of Rabbi is cited in the first paragraph, the opinion of Rabbi Gamaliel, son of Rabbi Judah the Prince (who is the same Rabbi Judah the Holy), is immediately added in the second.

<gloss>2</gloss> *Oil for burning.*] This refers to the First Fruit oil <note>Terumah</note> that has become ritually impure, which cannot be used for any other useful purpose except for lighting lamps.

<gloss>3</gloss> *Spurge.*] Maimonides <note>original: <term>נץ החלב</term></note> interprets the Hebrew "Flower of Milk" <note>original: <term>פסקרונס</term></note>. Among the Arabic herbalists Ebn al-Kabati and Beitar, this is "Maqdunis" <note>original: <term>مقذونس</term></note>, which is the "Petroselinum" <note>rock-parsley</note> of Dioscorides. Dioscorides says: *Celery which is also called rock-celery; this grows in Macedonia.* <note>original Greek: Σέλινον τὸ κἀι πετροσέλινον, τῦτο φύεται ἐν Μακεδονίᾳ</note>. According to Ebn Jazla, "Maqdunis" <note>original: <term>مقذונש</term></note> is "Greek celery" <note>original: <term>الكرفס الرومى</term></note>. I prefer the other opinion, which explains "Flower of Milk" <note>original: <term>נץ החלב</term></note> as a plant that pours out milk when cut, such as the spurge <note>original: tithymalus</note>.

<gloss>4</gloss> *Safflower.*] Maimonides says that "Kotza" <note>original: <term>קוצה</term></note> is a certain 

<column-break/>

dye-plant, and is explained by some as "Usfur" <note>original: <term>עצפיר</term></note> or safflower. From this, I detect a gap in Nathan's Lexicon <note>The Aruch</note> that needs to be filled under the entry "Istim" <note>original: <term>אסטם</term></note>. There it reads as follows: *The explanation of Istim is Indigo; in the Arabic language it is "nil," and in the Syriac language "murika." Another explanation is that it is the rose [flower] of the safflower, and it has another name in the Holy Tongue, "cakes of dung," and in the Syriac language "murika," and in the Arabic language "usfur"; they dye linen and cotton cloth with it for brides to decorate the bridal chamber.* The word "Istim" <note>original: <term>אסטים</term></note> signifies Indigo (in Italian), "nil" in Arabic <note>original: <term>نیل</term></note>, and "murika" in the Syriac language <note>original: <term>מוריקא</term></note>. Alternatively, it is explained as the flower of the safflower <note>Carthamus tinctorius</note>, which has another name in the Holy Tongue, such as "safflower cakes" <note>original: <term>חלות הריע</term>, cf. Oketzin 3:9</note>, "murika" in Syriac <note>original: <term>מוריקא</term></note>, and "usfur" in Arabic <note>original: <term>עصفر</term></note>. With this, they dye linen and cotton fabrics to decorate the bridal chamber for brides. In these words of Rabbi Nathan, if I see correctly, all those words—"and in the Syriac language murika," "This also is Kotza," and "not Istim"—are clearly redundant in the first part; and in their place, another explanation of the word "Kotza" seems to have fallen out, by which he had explained "madder," as is very clearly gathered from the same Rabbi Nathan under the entry "Puah" <note>original: <term>פואה</term></note>, where...

# Order I. ZERAIM <note>Seeds</note>

...is applicable. To these belongs the law of the seventh year, and to their prices: and to the same belongs the removal <note>The law of *Bi'ur*, requiring produce to be removed from the home once it is no longer available in the field for animals</note>, and to their prices.

2. Furthermore, another rule is handed down: $^1$ Whatever is not food for man nor for cattle, or is in the category of dyeing agents, but remains perennial in the earth, the law of the seventh year applies to it, and to its price. However, the law of removal does not apply to it, nor to its price. What indeed is that? Specifically, the root of the wild arum, and of mint, $^2$ scolopendrium <note>hart’s-tongue fern</note>, $^3$ peplis <note>water purslane or a type of spurge</note>, $^4$ baccharis <note>an aromatic plant used in medicine and perfumes</note>. And from the category of dyeing agents, madder and $^5$ radicula <note>literally "small root," likely soapwort or a similar plant</note>.

---

...where he refers the reader to this place. Being destitute of manuscripts, I cannot fill the gap; however, I would dare to affirm for certain that Rabbi Nathan here explained *kuẓẓah* <note>original: קוצה</note> as madder; then added another explanation, which signifies safflower <note>original: *cnicum*</note>. In a similar way, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> wavers, for whom sometimes *kuẓẓah* is *chalbezin* <note>original: חלבצין</note>; which in the Gemara <note>Niddah 62a</note> is to be read as *worsha* <note>original: וורשא</note>, as in Pesachim 56b, that is, *guesde* <note>woad</note>, or *guede* <note>original: גוודא</note>, in Latin *glastum* or *guastum*. I approve of that last explanation of Rabbi Nathan's. I already said above at Kilaim II, 8, that *kuẓẓah* is safflower. Its heads, or the spheres from which the flowers unfold, are called *kuẓẓah*, and that indeed because of the prickly scales with which they are armed, and of which they mostly consist; for *kuẓ* <note>original: קוץ</note> means a thorn. Let the reader consider whether the Chaldean Paraphrast <note>Targum</note> on Proverbs 3:11 looked to this, who renders the Hebrew word *takuẓ* <note>original: תקוץ</note> as *kuẓẓah*. Certainly *kuẓẓah* to the Syrians and Chaldeans is *moriqa* <note>saffron or safflower</note>.

1 **Whatever &c.**] This passage in the manuscript is thus:
> Whatever is not food for man, nor for cattle, 
> nor of the category of dyeing agents, and does not remain in the earth.

Maimonides also reads it this way, and twists himself much in eliciting the sense. In the Jerusalem Talmud, the negative particle is omitted twice. In the first place, instead of "which is not," it is read "which they ate"; in the second, instead of "remains," it is read "and remains." So that the passage is translated: *Whatever is food for man, or cattle, or of the category of dyeing agents, and remains in the earth.* But those which are listed next do not serve as food for men or cattle. Therefore, in the first place, I retain the negative with most editions.

2 **Scolopendrium.**] *Aqraban* <note>original: עקרבן</note> is the Arabic *aqruban* <note>original: عقربان</note>, by which name the Spanish Arabs call scolopendrium, or the *asplenon* of Dioscorides, as the authors Ebn-al-Cabatius and Beitarides testify.

3 **Peplis.**] In the Jerusalem Gemara *bitzi netz chalab* <note>original: ביצי נץ חלב; literally "eggs of the hawk of milk"</note> is explained as *chalbezin* <note>original: חלבצין</note>.
Rabbi Nathan: *The explanation: seed like eggs, which is from the giant fennel.* Maimonides confesses his ignorance regarding this and the following word. Rabbi Tanchum denies that he has anywhere found an explanation of this word,

<column-break/>

although he not infrequently praises Rabbi Nathan. It seems, however, that Nathan's explanation is fused from two: from that of the Jerusalem Talmud, and from another by someone who had read *chalbinin* <note>original: חלבינין</note> instead of *chalbezin*. Thus, what in Gemara Niddah 62a is *chalbezin*, in Shabbat 90a is *hachalbanon*. He who read it thus easily imagined the galbanum-bearing fennel. To me, *chalbezin* seems to be the Arabic *helbiet* <note>original: حلبيتة</note>, by which name Beitarides describes the *peplion* of Hippocrates and the *peplis* of Dioscorides. To the author of the *Malajessa*, the name is *dawa yatui* <note>original: دوا يتועי</note>, a medicinal herb of the spurge <note>milkweed</note> genus. And the *chalbon* <note>original: חלבון</note> of Jarchius <note>Rashi</note> at Shabbat 90a supports this, i.e., in French *Lactieron* <note>sow-thistle</note>.

4 **Baccharis.**] Maimonides confesses he does not know what *bakhria* <note>original: בכריא</note> is. Rabbi Nathan, and after him others, Rabbi Tanchum, Bertinoro, etc., explain it as *kababi* <note>original: כבבי</note>. *Kankar* <note>original: کنکر</note> to the Persians, and thence to the Arabic physicians, is a type of thistle or artichoke <note>scolymus</note>. Yet Rabbi Nathan did not know that, to whom *kababi* is a species of colocynth <note>bitter cucumber</note>. He who first explained it thus, if I see anything, did not say *kababi*, but *kabkabi*. Certainly, in Jarchius's commentary on Shabbat 109b, instead of *atna* <note>original: אתנא</note>, which is read faultily in the Gemara there, I find *kabkabi* twice. But Rabbi Nathan brings *kababi* from there. Therefore, I hardly doubt that it should be read *kabkabi*, that is, *kankhry* <note>original: κάγχρυ</note>. Now *kankhry* or *kankhrys* <note>original: κάγχρυς</note> is the fruit of the fruit-bearing rosemary. Thence also the shrub itself is called *kankhrys* by Hippocrates, as Galen is the authority in his Glosses; and from the crushed element *gamma*, it is *cachrys* to Pliny. Therefore it seems that he who explained it thus read not *bakhria* but *kakhria* <note>original: ככריא</note> in this Mishnah. If anyone approves of this, let him put *cachrys* in place of *baccharis* in our version.

5 **Radicula.**] Inexpertly (as it seems to me), Maimonides explains *rabkah* <note>original: רבקה</note> as a dye <note>original: צבעא</note>, and Rabbi Tanchum followed him in this. From the Herbals of the Arabs, it is established that *al-baqqam* <note>original: البقم</note> is a rather large tree with almond-like leaves, or rather the wood of that tree, which grows in India and Ethiopia, as Beitarides reports from Abuhanifa, or in the islands of the Indian and Zinj seas as the author of *Malajessa* says, the decoction of which is used for dyeing. Edrisi also and Abulfeda, the Arabic geographers...

# Title V. SHEBIITH <note>The Sabbatical Year</note>

To these belongs the law of the seventh year, and to their prices. But to these the removal <note>original: *polluctura*; the Hebrew law of *Bi’ur*, requiring that Seventh-Year produce be removed from the home once it is no longer available in the field for animals</note> does not apply, nor to their prices. Rabbi Meir asserts that their prices must undergo removal until the beginning of the following year. It was said to him: "If the law of removal does not apply to the items themselves, much less does it apply to their prices."

3. Pomegranate peels and its flower, walnut shells and kernels—both the items themselves and their prices are bound by the law of the seventh year. A dyer may dye for himself <note>For personal use only</note>, but not as a hired laborer. For it is not permitted to conduct trade with the fruits of the seventh year, nor with firstborn animals, nor with first-fruits, nor with animals that died of natural causes, nor those torn by beasts, nor with abominable things or creeping creatures. Nor is it permitted to gather wild vegetables and sell them in the market. However, any man may gather them, and his son may sell them on his behalf. If he gathered them for his own use and some remain, those may be sold legally.

<margin>1</margin>
4. If someone has purchased a firstborn animal <note>Referencing a blemished firstborn animal which could be eaten but not sacrificed</note> for his son's wedding or for a solemn feast and no longer has need of it, he is permitted to sell it. Hunters of wild beasts, birds, or fish, who by chance happen upon unclean species, may sell them legally. Rabbi Judah adds: Even he to whom such a thing happens by chance on the road may take it and sell it, provided he does not make it his regular trade. But the Sages forbid this.

<margin>2, 3</margin>
5. The shoots of palms and their offshoots <note>original: *filiarumque*, literally "daughters"</note>—both they and their prices are bound by the law of the seventh year; both they and their prices must undergo removal. However, regarding the shoots of the oak, the 2 pistachio, and the 3 buckthorn <note>original: *rhamnus*</note>, the law of the seventh year applies to them and their prices, but the removal does not apply to them or their prices. Their leaves, however, must undergo removal because they fall from the trunk.

<margin>4</margin>
6. For roses, henna, balsam, and 4 ladanum <note>original: *ledo*; a resin from the Cistus plant</note>, both for themselves and their prices, the law...

---

<columns>2</columns>
...some report that this tree grows on the island which he—following Birunium and Pharafum—calls *Lameri* <note>original Arabic: لامر ي</note>, toward the east from *Sarandibo* <note>modern-day Sri Lanka</note>, or Taprobana. From these things it is sufficiently clear that the exotic tree *rakam* <note>original: رقم</note> has absolutely nothing in common with the Mishnah’s *rakpah* <note>original: רכפה</note>. However, Rabbi Nathan is even more unskilled here, and some following Rabbi Tanchum explain *rakpah* here as *bachur maryam* <note>original: בחור מרים</note> or *shagar maryam* <note>original: שגר מרים</note>, names by which the Arabs understand the cyclamen—a plant clearly alien to the use of dyeing, which for that reason cannot have a place here. The Arabic word *rakhaf* <note>original: رخف</note> comes close to *rakpah*, which according to Jauhari is "a certain kind of dye" <note>original Arabic: ضرب من الصبغ</note>. I have proposed "radicula" <note>little root</note> until someone brings forth something more certain. I understand it to be "the Syrian flower, which they call *rhizion*" <note>original Greek: τοῖ Συριακῷ ἀνθῷ, ὁ καλᾶσι ῥίζιον</note>; concerning which see Salmasius’s *Plinian Exercises*, page 1162.

1 **Firstborn animal.**] Meaning one affected by a blemish <note>Since an unblemished firstborn belongs to the priest and cannot be sold</note>.

<column-break/>

2 **Pistachios.**] So say Maimonides and Rabbi Tanchum. It is added that Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>, regarding Genesis 43:11, notes that a certain Rabbi Machir, the glossarist, explains *botnim* <note>original: בטנים</note>—which is read there—as *pistachios* <note>original: פישטקא"ס</note>. Nor do only the Jews interpret it thus, but the Samaritans do as well. The Chaldean-Samaritan text has <note>Samaritan script characters</note>, and the unpublished Arabic Samaritan version has *fustuq* <note>original: فستق</note>. This is also how it should be read in Erpenius's interpreter instead of *qust*. The Septuagint’s "terebinth" <note>original Greek: τερέβινθος</note> also points here. For the pistachio tree is very similar to the terebinth, though its fruit is different, which is why not a few of the ancients call it a terebinth.

3 **Buckthorn.**] This matches Dioscorides' note on the buckthorn <note>original: *rhamnus*</note>, "a decoction of thorns" <note>original Greek: Ἄφεψις ἀκανθῶν</note>. That is clearly our *atadin* <note>original: אטדין</note>.

4 **Ladanum.**] The printed editions have *lot* <note>original: לוט</note> here, and thus the Chaldean Paraphrasts translate *lot* in Genesis 37:25 and 43:11. The Syrian Metaphrast also has *ladana* <note>original: ܠܕܢܐ</note> in the latter place and *ladanya* <note>original: ܠܕܢܝܐ</note> in the former.

# Order I. SEEDS <note>original: ZERAIM</note>
A 4
<meta>catchword: 1 Solu-</meta>

...is subject to the law of the seventh year. Rabbi Simeon denies that the law of the seventh year applies to balsam, because it is not a fruit.

7. If a "new" rose <note>grown in the Seventh Year</note> is preserved in "old" oil <note>grown in a previous year</note>, the rose must be removed; if a "new" item is preserved in "old" oil, it must be treated with the law of removal <note>original: *polluceri*; refers to the Hebrew *Bi'ur*, the requirement to remove or declare produce ownerless once it is no longer available in the fields</note>. If "new" carobs <note>original: *siliquæ*</note> are preserved in "old" wine, or "old" carobs in "new" wine, they must be subject to the law of removal. This is the general rule: Whatever imparts flavor when mixed with a different species is subject to the law of removal; if mixed with the same species, even the smallest amount [triggers the law]. Produce of the seventh year, in any amount, makes another thing of its own kind forbidden; if it is of a different kind, it is forbidden only if it imparts flavor.

## CHAPTER VIII.

1. A great rule is handed down regarding the seventh year: Whatever is specifically for human food shall not be made into a poultice <term>malagma: a medicinal plaster or paste applied to the skin</term> for a person; and there is no need to add that it cannot be used for a beast. Whatever is not specifically for human food may be made into a poultice for a person, but not for a beast. Whatever is specifically for neither man nor beast—if it is nonetheless intended as food for both man and beast—the most stringent conditions for both human and animal food are imposed upon it. If it is intended for use as wood <note>fuel</note>, it is treated as wood, such as savory, hyssop, or thyme.

2. Produce of the seventh year may be used for food, for drink, and for the use of anointing; that which is fit for eating should be eaten, and that which is fit for anointing should be rubbed on the skin. Wine or vinegar shall not be used for anointing, but oil may be used for anointing. The same applies to first-fruits and the second tithe. However, the condition of seventh-year produce is more favorable than theirs, for it may even be used for lamps <note>as fuel for light</note>.

3. Fruits of the seventh year are not sold by measure, weight, or number. Neither figs by number, nor vegetables by weight. The Shammaites <note>original: *Sammæani*</note> add: nor even in bundles. The Hillelites <note>original: *Hillelæi*</note> allow that which is usually gathered into bundles <gloss>1</gloss> to be brought home; they even allow it to be gathered into bundles to be brought to the market, such as leeks and spurge <note>original: *tithymalum*</note>.

---

->Lotem <note>original Hebrew: לוטם</note><-
This word is the same as the Chaldean. Some interpret this *Lotos* <note>original: לוטוס</note> of ours as a chestnut, for no other reason (I believe) than because Rabbi Saadias, in his version, put *ashtabelut* <note>original Hebrew: אשתבלוט</note>—which is what the Arabs call a chestnut—in place of *Lot* <note>original Hebrew: לוט</note>. In Kimchi’s Lexicon, that word is incorrectly read as *shir belut* <note>original Hebrew: שיר בלוט</note>. Abenezra, in his commentary on Genesis 2:10, notes and sharply attacks Saadias's rashness in these botanical matters. I am much pleased by the opinion of Junius on Genesis 37:25, that both *Lot* and *Lotos* are a species of rockrose <note>original: *cisti*</note>, which

<column-break/>

4. they call *ledon* <note>original Greek: ληδον; the source of labdanum resin</note>. See also Ludovicus de Dieu on the same passage. However, in the manuscript it is read as *Lotus* <note>original Hebrew: לוטס</note>, both in the Mishnah and in Maimonides' commentary, as well as in Nathan’s Lexicon, which seems to be *lotius*. But because it is joined here with *kataf* <note>original Hebrew: קטף; balsam sap</note>, just as in the Chaldean Paraphrasts, I think nothing should be changed. It is common for the Jews to confuse the final *m* <note>ם</note> and *s* <note>ס</note> in foreign words.

1 *To be brought home.* In the manuscript, it reads "to the market and to the house" <note>original Hebrew: לשוק & לבית</note>, which is better than "in the house and to the market" as found in the printed editions.

<meta>This page continues the eighth chapter of the tractate Shebiith (The Sabbatical Year), which details how produce grown during the fallow seventh year—which is considered holy and ownerless—must be handled, sold, and used. It specifically addresses the restriction on using Sabbatical year funds for commercial debts or non-essential purchases.</meta>

# Title V. THE SABBATICAL YEAR <note>original: SHEBIITH</note>

4. If anyone says to a laborer: "Here is this small coin <term>assarium: a Roman copper coin of low value</term> for you; now, gather some greens for me today"; his wage is considered "released" <note>footnote 1: meaning it is permitted under the law of the seventh year because the money was given as a gift or for labor, not as a direct purchase price for the produce</note>. [But if he says,] "Gather greens for me today **in exchange for** that [coin]"; the wage is "bound" <note>footnote 2: the Hebrew word *bo* (in it/for it) indicates the greens were sold for that coin; this creates a commercial transaction which is restricted</note>. If someone receives a loaf of bread worth two small coins <term>dupondius: a Roman coin worth two asses</term> from a baker [having promised thus]: "When I gather wild greens, I will bring them to you," it is permitted. But if he simply received it from him <note>without a specific arrangement</note>, he may not pay him with money from the seventh year. For it is not permitted to pay off debts <note>original: *nomina*; referring to personal debts or credit accounts</note> with money from the seventh year.

5. It is likewise not permitted to give [this money] to a well-guard, a bath-attendant, a barber, or a ship’s captain. However, one may give it to a well-guard in exchange for water to drink. To anyone, one may also give it as a free gift.

6. It is not permitted to spread out figs of the seventh year on a drying-frame <note>original: *tabulato*</note>, but it is permitted on a flat, cleared space. It is not permitted to tread grapes in a [large] wine-press, but it is permitted in a small trough <note>original: *mactra*</note>. It is not permitted to process olives in a [commercial] mill and press, but it is permitted to crush them and place them under a small press. Rabbi Simeon permits one to even grind them in a mill and place them under a press.

7. It is not permitted to cook greens of the seventh year in "first-fruits" oil <note>oil of the highest quality from a previous year</note>, lest it lead to the oil being wasted <note>or "depraved," as the holy status of the greens might make the oil unusable once the greens must be removed</note>. Rabbi Simeon permits it. Every item exchanged for seventh-year produce is subject to the law of the seventh year <note>footnote 7: the "sanctity" of the Sabbatical year transfers to the object of exchange</note>, and the fruit itself also remains "bound" by the law.

8. It is not permitted to purchase slaves, fields, or ritually unclean animals <note>such as camels or donkeys</note> with money from the seventh year; and if someone has made such a purchase, he must spend an equal amount on food and consume it [according to the Sabbatical laws]. It is not permitted to bring the "nests" <note>pairs of birds/pigeons used for purification offerings</note> for men or women with discharges, or for women after childbirth, using money from the seventh year; and if one has brought them, he must spend an equal amount on food. It is not permitted to anoint vessels with oil from the seventh year; and if one has anointed them, he must spend an equal amount on food.

9. If someone has anointed a leather hide with oil from the seventh year, Rabbi Eliezer commands that it be burned. The Sages say that an equal amount must be spent on food. It was said in the presence of Rabbi Akiba that Rabbi Eliezer had ordered a hide anointed with seventh-year oil to be burned. He replied: "Be silent; I will not tell you what Rabbi Eliezer [really] commanded concerning that matter."

10. Furthermore, they said in the presence of Rabbi Akiba that Rabbi Eliezer equated one who eats the bread of the Samaritans <note>original: *Cuthæorum*; literally "people from Cuthah," a term used in the Talmud for Samaritans</note> to one who eats the flesh of a pig. To which he replied: "Be silent; I will not tell you what Rabbi Eliezer thought about that matter."

---

1. **Released.** <note>Lege anni septimi</note> Regarding the law of the seventh year.
2. **In exchange for it.** The word *bo* [Hebrew: in it] indicates for that coin the greens were sold. For it is the same as if he had said: "Gather as much as is worth [the coin]." There is a linguistic difference between a hirer and a merchant.
3. **Having promised thus.** One should understand or supply in the Mishnah the words "and he said to him," which are found in the *Tosaphta* <note>a collection of Jewish oral laws from the same era as the Mishnah</note>.
4. **To give.** In exchange for an agreed-upon wage.
5. **Drying-frame.** The *mokzeh* is a tool for spreading figs so they may dry,

<column-break/>

prepared for this purpose. See the description, if you like, in Columella’s *On Agriculture* XII. 15.
6. **In a mill.** The Jerusalem Talmud reads *be-beit chavar* instead of *be-beit ha-bad*, that is, in the house of a "Friend" <note>an associate who is trustworthy in matters of tithes and purity</note>.
7. **The latest thing.** If produce of the seventh year is exchanged for another thing, and that for another, and so on, the original fruit does not change its status, and the most recent of those items becomes subject to the law of the seventh year.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the laws regarding produce grown during the Sabbatical Year—the seventh year in the agricultural cycle when the land in Israel was left to rest. # Order I. SEEDS <note>original: Zeraim</note>

...is subject to the law of the seventh year. Rabbi Simeon denies that the law of the seventh year applies to balsam, because it is not considered a fruit <note>Simeon argues that since balsam is a resin or sap rather than a consumable fruit, it falls outside the standard Sabbatical restrictions.</note>.

7. If a "new" rose <note>grown in the seventh year</note> is preserved in "old" oil <note>from a previous year</note>, the rose must be removed. If "old" produce is mixed with "new," it must be cleared <note>original: *polluceri*; referring to the Hebrew concept of *bi'ur*, the requirement to remove or destroy Sabbatical produce from one's home once it is no longer available for animals to forage in the fields</note>. If new carobs <note>original: *siliquae*</note> are preserved in old wine, or old ones in new wine, they must be cleared. This is the general rule: Whatever imparts its flavor to a thing of a different kind makes it subject to the clearing requirement, no matter how small the amount; but for things of the same kind, even the slightest mixture [obligates it]. Produce of the seventh year, in any amount, makes a mixture of its own kind forbidden; if mixed with a different kind, it only becomes forbidden if it is enough to impart its flavor.

## CHAPTER VIII.

A great rule is handed down concerning the seventh year: Whatever is specifically for human food may not be made into a poultice <note>original: *malagma*; a soft, medicinal plaster or ointment</note> for humans, and there is no need to add that it cannot be used for animals. Whatever is not specifically for human food may be made into a poultice for humans, but not for animals. Whatever is not specifically food for either humans or animals, if it is nonetheless designated for the food of both, the strictest conditions of food for humans and animals are imposed upon it. If it is designated as wood for fuel, it is treated as wood—such as savory, hyssop, and thyme.

2. The yield of the seventh year may be used for food, for drink, and for anointing; that which is fit for eating should be eaten, and that which is fit for anointing should be used as an ointment. One should not anoint oneself with wine or vinegar, but oil may be used for anointing. This is similar to the rules for first-fruits and the second tithe. However, the produce of the seventh year has a more favorable status than those, for it may even be used for lamps <note>meaning it can be burned as fuel for light, whereas some other holy tithes have stricter disposal rules</note>.

3. The crops of the seventh year are not to be sold by measure, weight, or number. Figs are not sold by number, nor vegetables by weight. The followers of Shammai <note>original: *Sammæani*</note> add that they should not even be sold in bundles. The followers of Hillel <note>original: *Hillelæi*</note> permit things that are usually gathered in bundles <gloss>1</gloss> to be taken home in bundles, and also to be brought to the market in bundles, such as leeks and spurge <note>original: *tithymalum*</note>.

<columns>2</columns>

...contains the word *halta*, but there also it should read *lotam* <note>original: לוטם</note>. This word is the same as the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note>. Some interpret our word *lotum* <note>original: לטום</note> as "chestnut," for no other reason (I believe) than because Rabbi Saadias, in his version, placed *shahbalut* <note>original: שאהבלוט</note>—the Arabic word for chestnut—in place of *lot*. In Kimchi's Lexicon, that word is erroneously read as *shaikh balut*. However, Ibn Ezra <note>original: Abenezra</note>, in his commentary on Genesis 2:10, notes and sharply criticizes Saadias’s boldness in these matters. I much prefer the opinion of Junius on Genesis 37:25: that both *lot* and *lotam* refer to a species of rockrose <note>original: *cisti species*</note>, which

<column-break/>

they call *ledon* <note>original: ληδον</note>. See also Louis de Dieu on the same passage. However, in the manuscript, it reads *lotis* <note>original: לטיס</note> both in the Mishnah and in Maimonides' commentary, as well as in Nathan’s Lexicon, which seems to be "lotus." But because it is joined here with *kandros* <note>likely an artichoke or thistle species</note>, just as in the Chaldean Paraphrasts <note>the Targums</note>, I think nothing should be changed. It is common for Jews to confuse the final *m* and *n* in foreign words.

4. If...

It is not permitted to bring the bird-nests of those with discharges <note>Referring to the ritual offerings of "Zabim" or "Zabot," men and women with specific bodily discharges</note> or of women who have given birth using coins of the seventh year; and if someone has brought them, he must spend an equivalent amount on food and consume it. # Order I. SEEDS
<meta>catchword: Sun</meta>

**7.** If a new rose <note>i.e., from the seventh year</note> is preserved in old oil <note>from a non-Sabbatical year</note>, the rose must be removed; if old [roses are preserved] in new [oil], it must be treated as Sabbatical produce <note>original: "polluceri debet." This refers to the legal status where the mixture takes on the "sanctity" of the Sabbatical year, requiring it to be consumed according to specific laws or removed/destroyed at a certain time.</note>. If new carobs are preserved in old wine, or old ones in new, they must be treated as Sabbatical produce. This is the general rule: whatever imparts flavor to a thing of a different kind when mixed makes it subject to the Sabbatical restriction; but for a thing of the same kind, any amount [of Sabbatical produce] makes it restricted. Produce of the seventh year, in any amount, makes another thing of its own kind forbidden; if it is not of its own kind, it becomes forbidden only as much as it imparts flavor.

## CHAPTER VIII.

**1.** A great rule is handed down concerning the seventh year: Whatever is set aside specifically for human food, a poultice <term>malagma: a medicinal plaster or poultice applied to the skin</term> shall not be made of it for a person; and there is no need to add, nor for an animal. Whatever is not set aside specifically for human food, a poultice may be made of it for a person, but not for an animal. Whatever is set aside as food for neither humans nor animals, yet if it is intended for the food of both humans and animals, the strictest conditions of food for humans and animals are imposed upon it. If it is intended for firewood, it is treated as firewood, such as savory, hyssop, and thyme.

**2.** The produce of the seventh year is used for food, for drink, and for the use of anointing; so that what is suitable for eating is eaten, and what is suitable for anointing is applied to the skin. Wine or vinegar shall not be applied to the skin, but oil may be applied. The same applies to first fruits and second tithes. The condition of the seventh-year produce is more favorable than theirs, for it may even be used for lighting lamps.

**3.** The fruits of the seventh year are not sold by measure, weight, or number. Not figs by number, nor vegetables by weight. The Shammaites <note>The School of Shammai, known for stricter legal interpretations</note> add: nor even in bundles. The Hillelites <note>The School of Hillel, usually more lenient</note> [permit] that which is usually gathered into bundles <note>1</note> to be carried home, to be gathered into bundles also to be brought to the market, such as leeks and spurge <term>tithymalum: a plant of the Euphorbia genus</term>.

# Title V. SHEBIITH.
### 101

**4.** If anyone says to a worker: "Here is an *assarion* <note>original: "affarium" (Greek: assarion), a small Roman copper coin</note> for you; now, pick some greens for me today"; his wage is considered released <note>original: "soluta." This means it is viewed as a gift rather than a commercial transaction, which is permitted with Sabbatical funds.</note>. But if he says: "Pick greens for me today *in exchange* for this"; his wage is bound <note>original: "nexa." This creates a commercial contract or debt, which is forbidden to be settled using Sabbatical money.</note>. If anyone receives bread worth two *dupondii* <note>a Roman coin worth two 'as' coins</note> from a baker on this promise: "When I have gathered wild greens, I will bring them to you," it is permitted. But if he simply receives it from him without a specific promise, he may not pay him using coins from the seventh year. For it is not permitted to discharge debts using coins of the seventh year.

**5.** It is likewise not permitted to give these [coins] to a well-keeper, a bath-attendant, a barber, or a ship-master. However, one may give them to a well-keeper in exchange for water to drink. It is also permitted to give them to anyone as a free gift.

**6.** It is not permitted to spread out figs of the seventh year on a drying-floor <note>original: "tabulato." A specific rack or structure for drying fruit commercially.</note>, but it is permitted in a clearing. It is not permitted to tread grapes in a wine-press, but it is permitted in a kneading-trough <note>original: "mactra." A smaller vessel, indicating private rather than commercial use.</note>. It is not permitted to process olives with an oil-mill or a beam-press, but it is permitted to crush them and place them under a small press. Rabbi Simeon permits even grinding them with an oil-mill and placing them under a beam-press.

**7.** It is not permitted to cook greens of the seventh year in first-quality oil <note>original: "oleo primitio," likely referring to high-grade or non-Sabbatical oil</note>, lest it lead to its degradation. Rabbi Simeon permits it. Every latest thing <note>This refers to the "law of exchange" where the sanctity of the Sabbatical year transfers to the item for which it was traded.</note> is subject to the law of the seventh year, and the fruit itself remains bound by the restriction.

**8.** It is not permitted to purchase slaves, lands, or unclean animals <note>animals not fit for sacrifice or food</note> with coins of the seventh year; and if someone has purchased them, he must spend an equal amount on food in their stead. One may not bring the offerings for those with a discharge <note>referring to ritual impurities described in Leviticus</note> or for women after childbirth using coins of the seventh year; and if someone has done so, he must spend an equal amount on food in their stead. It is not permitted to anoint vessels with oil of the seventh year; and if someone has done so, he must spend an equal amount on food in his place.

**9.** If someone anoints a hide with oil of the seventh year, Rabbi Eliezer orders that it be burned. The Sages say an equal amount must be spent on food. It was said before Rabbi Akiba that Rabbi Eliezer ordered a hide anointed with seventh-year oil to be burned. He replied, "Be silent; I will not tell you what Rabbi Eliezer ordered regarding that matter."

**10.** Furthermore, they said before Rabbi Akiba that Rabbi Eliezer compared one who eats the bread of the Cutheans <note>Samaritans</note> to one who eats the flesh of a pig. He replied to them, "Be silent; I will not tell you what Rabbi Eliezer thought regarding that."

**1** *Released.*] Read as: of the seventh year.

**2** *In exchange for it.*] The word *bo* [in Hebrew] for "in exchange for it" indicates that the greens were sold for that coin. For it is the same as if he had said, "Pick as much as it is worth." There is a difference in phrasing between a hirer and a merchant.

**3** *So promised.*] One must understand or supply in the Mishnah the words "and he said to him," which are found in the Tosephta <note>a supplemental collection of Jewish oral law</note>.

**5** *Drying-floor.*] *Muktzeh* <note>original: מוקצה</note> is a tool prepared for spreading out figs so they may dry in it.

**6** *Oil-mill.*] The Jerusalem Talmud uses the phrase "in the house of the Habad" instead of "the house of the Bad," that is, in the communal house of the association.

**7** *Every latest thing.*] If the fruit of the seventh year is exchanged for something else, and that thing for another, and so on, the fruit itself does not change its status, and the latest of those items becomes subject to the law of the seventh year.

# Order I. SEEDS (ZERAIM)
### 102

If a bath has been heated with straw or stubble from the seventh year, it is permitted to bathe in it. But one who is of a more honored rank <note>likely referring to scholars or those who observe the law with extra piety</note> should not bathe in it.

### CHAPTER IX.

**R**ue, amaranth <note>original: "blita"</note>, wild asparagus <note>original: "corrudæ"</note>, wild purslane, mountain coriander, river celery, and meadow rocket are exempt from tithing; and they may be lawfully purchased from anyone in the seventh year, because these sorts 

<column-break/>

<margin>1. Amaranth, wild asparagus.</margin> Maimonides <note>a famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and physician</note> notes that this is called *yirbuz* <note>original: ירבוז</note> in Arabic. Rabbi Tanchum also calls it *yirbuz*, a vegetable similar to orache or spinach, but with a larger leaf. The Arabic herbalists recognize both, as well as *yarburuz* and *jurmuz*, and they maintain it is the same vegetable they call the "Yemeni herb" <note>original: "olus Jamanense"</note>, that is, the herb of Arabia Felix <note>the "Fortunate Arabia," or southern Arabian Peninsula</note>, which is what they call the amaranth. Serapion <note>a 9th-century Christian physician from Damascus</note> says: "In the dialect of the Syrians, *yarburuz* is the Yemeni herb." Furthermore, from the Alexandrian excerpts of Galen’s book *On Simple Medicines*: "In the Arabic language, *yarburuz* is the name for the Yemeni herb, which is called *blitum* <note>amaranth</note>." Amaranth is a vegetable quite similar to orache and spinach, which agrees well with the descriptions of Rabbi Tanchum and the Arabs. Even today, the Poles call amaranth *jarmuz* <note>usually referring to kale or similar greens today</note> in their own language, which is the *jurmuz* of the Arabs. Therefore, I have used "amaranth," although I am aware that elsewhere in the Mishnah amaranth is called *tardin*. Perhaps they differ in the same way that amaranth and spinach do. Or perhaps *yirbuz* refers specifically to the wandering and wild variety. But let others look into this. As for what is read here as "wild amaranth" <note>original: "והירבוזין השוטים"</note> in all the printed editions—except for the Jerusalem Talmud, which reads *haribuzin* with one letter transposed—the manuscripts, Maimonides, and Rabbi Tanchum also have it. Instead of this, in the Gemara <note>the commentary portion of the Talmud</note> of Sukkah 39b where this Mishnah is cited, it is read as *ha-rabuzin*, which is also how Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the 11th-century commentator</note> reads it. He interprets *yerbuzin* in German as "hemp-like" <note>original: הנפלש (henflesh?)</note>, or in the vernacular as "wild asparagus" <note>original: אווילד שטים (O-wild-schtim)</note>; he

<column-break/>

takes it as a name for a vegetable and explains it as *asparagi*, "asparagus." This is also how Rabbi Nathan <note>author of the Arukh, an 11th-century Talmudic dictionary</note> used to read it, not only in that passage of the Gemara but also in our Mishnah. This is evident because he explains the first word as "garden asparagus" and the latter as the "wild" kind, or perhaps "fennel." However, today’s codices—here, as well as in other sections and regarding "purslane"—erroneously give us "wild amaranth" <note>original: הירבוזין השוטים</note> three times, which goes against his intended meaning. Therefore, the less familiar word *hashutim* should be restored here, as it was changed to the more common word for "wild" or "foolish" <note>original: shutim</note> by the recklessness of scribes.

<margin>2. Wild purslane.</margin> Previously we had *regila*, which is the Arabic *rijla*, or purslane. Here the word is *haluglugit*, which is also purslane, but a different species. At one time, people did not know what this word designated, until some went to the house of the Rabbi <note>Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah</note> to inquire. There they saw a certain person carrying his purslane in his cloak, and they fell out. His servant girl said to him: "Rabbi, Rabbi, your *haluglugot* have been scattered!" <note>The text provides the anecdote in Hebrew and then Latin translation</note>. From this, it became known to them that *haluglugot* are purslanes, the same as *parpahinin*, a word used by both Syrians and Arabs to denote purslane. The Arabs call it *farfakhin* or *farfakh*, not *farfajin* as Golius <note>a 17th-century Dutch orientalist</note> incorrectly has it. In the excellent codex of Ibn Jazla, I find it written as *farfakh* twice, even with a note added to confirm it is the correct spelling, and once with the letter "kha" clearly dotted. I also see it written this way in the very elegant and high-quality codex of Al-Jawhari.

It includes a famous Talmudic anecdote where the meaning of the word for purslane was recovered by listening to the speech of a servant girl in a rabbi's household.</summary>

# Title V. SHEBIITH (The Sabbatical Year)
### 103

...kinds of vegetables are not usually guarded <note>Referring to "custody," or plants that are not fenced in or cultivated, which affects their status during the Sabbatical year</note>. Rabbi Judah declares self-sown mustard <note>original: "sinapi restibile"</note> to be permitted, because those who would violate the law are not suspected of doing so with this plant. Rabbi Simeon declares all self-sown crops permitted, except for self-sown cabbage, because no such variety is found among wild vegetables. The Sages, however, judge all self-sown plants to be forbidden.

**2.** The land is divided into three regions regarding the law of removal <note>the "biur" law, which requires Sabbatical produce to be removed from the home once it is no longer available to animals in the fields</note>: Judea, Perea <note>the region east of the Jordan River</note>, and Galilee. Each of these is further divided into three. Galilee consists of the Upper, the Lower, and the Valley. The Upper Galilee includes everything above Kfar Hananiah where sycamores <note>original: "sycomoros," the sycamore fig tree</note> do not grow; the Lower Galilee is everything below Kfar Hananiah that produces sycamores; the Valley is the territory of Tiberias. Judea is divided into the mountainous region, the plain, and the <insert>80</insert> valley. <insert>81</insert> The plains of Lydda <note>modern-day Lod</note> are equated to the <insert>82</insert> plains of the south, and its mountains to the mountain of the same southern region.

<margin>Purslane and farqah <note>Arabic: رجلة & فرقח</note></margin>
...to my [herbarium]. Although *purslane* and *farqah* <note>Arabic: "rijla" and "furqah"</note>, as far as I can see, are merely synonyms among the Arabic herbalists, we must still make a distinction for *haluglogah* <note>original Hebrew: הלוגלוגיה or הלו גלוגה</note>. Maimonides <note>a 12th-century Jewish polymath</note> says: "*Haluglogah* is a species <note>original Hebrew-Arabic: גני מן הלוגלוגיה</note> with broad leaves and longer stalks, which is called the 'foolish vegetable.'" You clearly have the "wild purslane" of Dioscorides <note>a Greek physician of the 1st century</note>, which fits this passage perfectly. If Maimonides intended that only this species be called "the foolish vegetable" <note>Arabic: البقلة الحمقا, "al-baqla al-hamqa"</note> in Arabic, he is greatly mistaken; for besides the authority of the Arabic herbalists, it is well known from the proverb "More foolish than purslane" <note>Arabic: احمق من رجلة</note>. The scholar Midanius notes the origin of this proverb is that the Arabs call purslane—that is, the other species—the "foolish vegetable."

<insert>80. Valley.]</insert> In most printed editions, this reads "and the southern region" <note>Hebrew: והנגב, "ve-ha-negev"</note>. But the manuscript and Maimonides have "and the valley" <note>Hebrew: והעמק, "ve-ha-emek"</note>. Yom-Tov <note>Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller, a 17th-century commentator</note> also published it this way; and it is clear from the Tosefta and the Jerusalem Talmud that it should be read thus. The valley they designate is clearly not to the south of Judea, but rather to the northeast, extending from Ein Gedi to Jericho.

<insert>81. The Plains of Lydda.]</insert> You might rightly wonder here at the dullness of the Jewish interpreters, who place the plains and mountains of Lydda—as well as the region from Beth-horon to the sea—in Perea (Transjordan), and claim this is the three-part division of Perea. Who has ever heard of Lydda or Beth-horon being in Perea?

<column-break/>

...both of which are quite famous in Judea. Our Mishnah says that Judea is divided for this purpose into the mountain, the plain, and the valley. The territory of Lydda, which is part of Judea, cannot be strictly assigned to any one of these due to its uneven terrain; rather, its plains follow the rules of the "plain" region, and its mountains follow the "mountain" region, or the "royal mountain." The division of Perea, which was omitted in the Mishnah, is supplied by the Tosefta <note>a companion collection of Jewish oral law</note>, from which it also passed into the Jerusalem Gemara. But in both places, there are very serious errors, as the Jews are quite careless in the publishing of their books. The corrected passage of the Tosefta—though I do not know if it is yet fully sound—reads as follows: <note>original Hebrew: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר אומר איזהו הר שבעבר הירדן...</note> "Rabbi Simeon son of Eleazar says: What is the mountain of Perea? Namely, the mountains of Machaerus and Gador and their neighbors. Its plain is Heshbon with all its towns in the level land, such as Dibon, Bamoth-baal, and Beth-baal-meon. Its valley is Beth-nimrah, Beth-haran, and their neighbors." In the printed editions, instead of "the mountains of Machaerus" <note>Hebrew: הרי מכור</note>, there are "mountains of Haris and Gabuy" <note>Hebrew: הריס וגבוי</note>, which are monstrous names <note>implying they are linguistic corruptions or fictional places</note>. Then, for "Beth-haran" <note>Hebrew: בית הרן</note>, it reads "Beth-nimrah Ramatha." But since I find Beth-nimrah and Beth-haran mentioned together in the book of Numbers (32:36), and the same appear in the Jerusalem Gemara as if from the Tosefta (though in reverse order), I did not hesitate to restore these cities to the Tosefta. You would think Maimonides and others were dreaming when, though they had these facts at hand, they preferred to carry Lydda and Beth-horon across the Jordan, tearing them from their proper places.

<insert>82. To the plains of the south.]</insert> That is, of Judea; for Judea is very frequently called "the South" <note>Hebrew: דרום, "Darom"</note> when it is contrasted with Galilee.

# Order I. ZERAIM (Seeds)

...to the royal mountain. From Bethhoron to the sea $^{83}$ is a unique region.

**3.** For this reason it was said: the land is divided into three parts $^{84}$ so that one may eat the fruit of each part only as long as the last of that fruit remains available in that specific region. Rabbi Simeon denies that this three-part division applies to any region other than Judea; he argues all other regions follow the conditions of the "Royal Mountain." All are considered the same regarding the Sabbatical status of olives and dates.

**4.** One may eat fruits $^{85}$ because of those left openly exposed in the fields, but not because of those kept by guards <note>Private gardens that are fenced off do not count toward the "available in the field" rule</note>. Rabbi Joses permits eating even because of guarded fruits. One may eat because of $^{86}$ late-ripening and twice-bearing fruits, but not because of winter fruits. Rabbi Judah permits it, provided that the earlier fruits ripened before the summer had ended.

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>83 A unique region.</margin>
$^{83}$ And yet, in the Jerusalem Talmud, a certain Rabbi Johanan says: 
<note>original: "עוד היא יש בה הר ושפלה ועמק מבית חורון ועד אמאום הר מאמאום ועד לוד שפלה מלוד ועד הים עמק"</note> 
*Even this region is divided into mountain, plain, and valley. From Bethhoron to Emmaus is mountain; from Emmaus to Lydda is the plain; from Lydda to the sea is the valley.* From this, one can clearly determine the locations of Bethhoron and Lydda, which are assigned the same positions here as they are in Josephus's *The Jewish War*, Book II, Chapter 37.

<margin>84 So that one may eat &c.</margin>
$^{84}$ That is to say, if someone has stored the crops of the seventh year <note>the Sabbatical year</note> in their home, they may lawfully use and eat them as long as the same kind remains in the field. However, when they are no longer available in the field, it is no longer permitted to keep them; rather, one is bound to <term>biur</term> <note>Hebrew: לבער, meaning "to clear out" or "remove"</note> or "publicly expose" them. This is the <term>biur</term> (the ritual of public exposure) of the seventh-year crops that I must explain here. According to the law in *Leviticus 25:7*, the crops of the seventh year were to serve as food for cattle and wild animals as well as humans. Hence the Masters, whose decrees allowed seventh-year crops to be stored at home for use, concluded in the *Siphra* <note>a legal commentary on Leviticus</note> that it is not permitted to keep them stored at home longer than that same species lasts in the fields, exposed to cattle and wild animals. Afterward, it is necessary that they be "exposed"—that is, brought out into the open to become the property of anyone who finds them. Even the master of the house who had stored them could reclaim them, and once reclaimed, he could lawfully eat them until they were finished. This is the opinion of the *Tosefta*, Chapter VIII: 
<note>original: "מי שיש לו פירות שביעית והגיע שעת הביעור... ויאמר אחינו בית ישראל כל מי שצריך ליטול יבוא ויטול"</note>
*He who has seventh-year fruits when the moment for public exposure arrives, let him distribute part of them to his neighbors, relatives, and acquaintances; let him carry out the rest and place them before the doors of his house, and say:*

<column-break/>

->ISRAELITES, WHOEVER AMONG YOU HAS NEED OF THESE, COME AND TAKE THEM.<-

*Once this was done, it was permitted to store them at home again and eat them until they were gone.* This was the ritual of exposure according to the *Tosefta*, one or two errors of which we have corrected with the help of the *Additaments* (called *Tosephtoth*) on *Pesachim 52b*, Moses of Coucy’s *Positive Commandments 147, 148*, and Joseph Karo’s commentary on Maimonides' *Laws of the Sabbatical Year, Chapter VII*, all of whom cite this *Tosefta*. Maimonides, however, feels very differently about this ritual in the cited passage. *For he says:* 
<note>original: "היו לו פירות מרובין"</note> 
*If someone has an abundance of fruit, let him distribute enough for three meals to each person. After the exposure, neither the poor nor the rich may lawfully eat them. If he finds no one to eat them when the time for exposure arrives, he must burn them in a fire, or throw them into the Salt Sea, or destroy them in any way possible.* Here, Rabbi Abraham ben David <note>known as the Ra'avad</note> rises up sharply against Maimonides, asserting that he did not understand what <term>biur</term> was. Indeed, Maimonides was deceived by a corrupt reading, which we note soon in paragraph 8. But even Abraham does not escape criticism; Joseph Karo accuses him of equal ignorance in this matter for inventing a "double exposure," and the studious reader will find this entire matter disputed there. Thus, <term>biur</term> consisted of this: that crops gathered at home, at the time when their kind no longer existed in the fields, were brought out into public and exposed to those who would take them. For this reason, I believe I have rightly called it "Public Exposure" <note>original: "Pollucturam"</note>.

*They are harder grains among the types of grain and legumes, which* <note>Maimonides' Arabic text describes a naturally occurring, hardy species similar to a wild barley</note>

# Title V. SHEVI'IT (The Sabbatical Year)

**5.** If anyone has pickled three kinds of vegetables in the same jar, Rabbi Eliezer holds that they may be eaten only as long as the first of those kinds remains in the field <note>The earliest-disappearing vegetable dictates the deadline for all three</note>; Rabbi Joshua says they may be eaten until the last of them remains. Rabban Gamaliel commands that each kind, as it disappears from the field, must be removed from the jar. [And the Law is according to his opinion.] Rabbi Simeon maintains that all garden herbs are considered equal regarding the requirement of removal. One may eat purslane until the artichokes <note>original: "cinaræ"</note> disappear from the valley of Beth Netophah.

**6.** One who has gathered green herbs may use them until their moisture has dried up. One who has gathered dry herbs may use them until the second rainfall. One who has gathered the leaves of reeds or vines may use them until they fall from their stem. One who has gathered dry leaves may use them until the second rainfall. Rabbi Akiba says of all things: they may be used until the second rainfall.

**7.** Similarly, if someone leases a house to another "until winter," this is understood to mean until the second rainfall. If someone is forbidden by a vow from receiving benefit from another "until winter," it is understood to mean until the second rainfall. Until what time do the poor have the right to enter the orchards? Until the second rainfall. From what time is it permitted to use and burn the straw and stubble of the seventh year? From the time the second rainfall has fallen.

**8.** One who possesses Sabbatical year fruits when the time for removal arrives should distribute the food for three meals to each person. Even after the time of removal, the poor may eat them, but the rich may not. This is the opinion of Rabbi Judah. Rabbi Joses holds that the poor and the rich have an equal status in this matter.

...they are not sown, but grow spontaneously. They remain in the soil for a long time because of their dryness and hardness, and in this regard, they are the same as other species, such as the <term>Qurtuman (Safflower/Wild Barley)<gloss>original: قرطمان</gloss></term>, which is called *Sufin*, as we have mentioned several times above. And concerning this, let his word be trusted. See also what we said above regarding *Pe'ah* VI, 7. Meanwhile, in the Tosefta, the word is read as *Sefihiyov* instead of *Sefihim*, which is perhaps better. This passage illustrates our text, and it is as follows:

<note>original: "אין אוכלין על הספיחים שבעכו..."</note>
*One does not eat based on the spontaneous growths of Acre. Rabbi Joses says: One may eat based on the spontaneous growths of Acre and on the twice-bearing trees, but not on the winter crops. Rabbi Judah says: Even on the winter crops. Rabbi Joses says: Regarding a twice-bearing tree that ripened before the summer ended, one may eat based on it.*

The word for "winter crops" <note>original: "shifuniyot"</note> should be read twice as *takhuniyot*. Where the text says "until it ends," it should be read as "unless." The words so amended yield this sense: One is not permitted to eat fruits because of the thistles of Acre. Rabbi Joses permits eating because of the thistles of Acre and because of twice-bearing trees, but not because of winter crops. Rabbi Judah permits it even for winter crops. Rabbi Joses permits eating because of a twice-bearing tree that produced early fruit before the end of summer.

In the parchment manuscripts of the *Siphra*, I find *Sandariyot* from the valley of *Beth Netophah*. 9. If anyone possesses fruits of the seventh year which came to him by right of inheritance or were given as a gift, Rabbi Eliezer commands that they be given to those who wish to eat them. But the Sages say that no one should be hired to commit a sin; therefore, they should rather be sold to those who wish to eat them, and the proceeds should be distributed to everyone. # C H A P T E R X.

1. The seventh year cancels a loan whether it is secured by a handwritten document <term>chirographum; a written bond of debt</term> or not. A shopkeeper’s credit is not cancelled; but if it is turned into a loan, it is cancelled. Rabbi Judah <note>original: "R. Juda"</note> believes that each initial item <note>of the shop credit</note> is cancelled. A laborer’s wages are not cancelled; but if they are turned into a loan, they are cancelled. Rabbi Joses states that the wages for work that must be suspended during the seventh year are cancelled; however, wages for work that is not suspended during the seventh year are not cancelled.

2. If someone slaughters a young cow and distributes the meat at the beginning of the year <note>The transition from the sixth to the seventh year</note>, if the month was intercalated <note>meaning an extra month was added to the calendar, extending the year</note>, the debt is cancelled; but if not, he is not bound to cancel it. Fines for one who commits rape or seduction, or one who slanders another’s reputation, and finally all judgments of the Sanhedrin <note>original: "Synedrii"; the high court</note> are not cancelled. One who gives a loan upon a pledge, or one who delivers his legal bonds to the Sanhedrin, is not compelled to cancel the debt.

3. <note>original: "Judicialis cautio"; referring to the Prosbol</note> A judicial safeguard is not destroyed by the Sabbatical year. This is one of the things instituted by Hillel the Elder. When he saw that the people were becoming alienated from lending to one another, and thus that which is written in the Law (Deuteronomy 15:9)—*Be careful that there be not a wicked thought in your heart, etc.*—was being violated, Hillel instituted the judicial safeguard. <meta>catchword: 4. Ju</meta>

It is omitted in the printed and handwritten *Siphra*, where this Mishnah is cited (Section *Behar*, Chapter 1). It is also omitted in the *Tosefta*, the *Tosafot* to *Pesachim* 52b, and in Moses of Coucy. This passage led Maimonides into the error of saying that "removal" <note>pollucturam</note> refers to the time when fruits naturally and completely disappear from the environment.

belongs to the seventh, those who received the portions of the cow cannot be sued for payment.

<sup>94</sup> *Judicial safeguard.*] Thus I interpret the word *Prosbol* <note>original: "פרוזבול" or "פרוסבול"</note>, about which the Jews speak foolishly, and others torment themselves greatly. For a *Prosbol* is a safeguard "before the councilors" <note>original Greek: "πρὸς βουλευτὰς" (pros bouletas)</note>, to be placed before the judges. This is the meaning of that famous etymology of Rabbi Hisda in the Gemara (*Gittin* 36b), where he explains *Prosbol* as *pros bouli ve-buti*. Those words were badly joined and equally badly separated. I have little doubt that Rabbi Hisda said *pros boul* and *buti*, that is, "before the councilors." Rabbi Joseph meant the same: *bula* and *buti* are the "councilors" <note>original Greek: "βουλευταί" (bouleutai)</note> among the Jews. However, Samuel views it differently, suggesting *Prosbol* means "a grievance and judges," signifying that the *Prosbol* was a forceful legal device of the judges by which they bypassed the divine law—that is, an "application" <note>original Greek: "προσβολήν" (prosbole)</note>.

## Title V. SHEBIITH

4. This is the formula for the judicial caution <note>original: "judicialis cautio"; the *Prosbul*, a legal document that transferred debts to a court so they would not be cancelled by the Sabbatical year</note>: **I HAND OVER TO YOU, N. AND N., JUDGES OF THE PLACE N., THAT WHATEVER DEBT IS OWED TO ME, I MAY COLLECT IT AT WHATEVER TIME I PLEASE.** The judges then sign below, or the witnesses.

5. A judicial caution <gloss>95</gloss> is held valid with back-dating <note>original: "prochronismo"; dating the document earlier than it was actually written</note>, but invalid with forward-dating <note>original: "metachronismo"</note>. Debt records with back-dating are invalid, but with forward-dating are valid. If one person accepts a loan from five people, a judicial caution must be written for each individual. If five people accept a loan from a single person, a single judicial caution is written for him on behalf of all.

6. A judicial caution is not to be written unless land is pledged as collateral. If the debtor does not have any, the creditor may grant him a right to even the smallest portion of his own field. If the debtor has a field pledged in a city, the judicial caution is written based on that. Rabbi Hoshaiah <note>original: "R. Hospithes"</note> considers it appropriate to write the caution based on the pledged assets of the debtor's wife, or for orphans based on the pledged assets of their guardians.

7. <gloss>96</gloss> Rabbi Eliezer considers a beehive to be regarded as land, so that a judicial caution may be written when it is pledged; it follows that, being fixed to the place, it does not receive ritual uncleanness, and anyone who removes honeycombs from it on the Sabbath becomes liable for a sin offering <note>Because removing honey from a hive attached to the ground is legally equivalent to harvesting crops</note>. But the Sages deny that it is held as land, and thus a judicial caution is not written when it is pledged, it does receive ritual uncleanness even while fixed to the place, and finally, he who removes honeycombs from it on the Sabbath shall be exempt from punishment.

8. If someone wishes to repay a debt in the seventh year, the creditor should say to him, *I remit it* <note>original: "Remitto ego"</note>. If the debtor responds, *Even so, accept it*, the creditor may take it. For it is said (Deuteronomy 15:2): *And this is the <gloss>97</gloss> word of remission.* Similarly, a manslayer who has retreated to a city of refuge, if the inhabitants of the city wish to advance him to honors, let him say to them, *I am a manslayer*. If they respond, *Even so, accept it*, he may. For it is said (Deuteronomy 19:4): *And this is the word of the manslayer.*

9. If someone returns a debt in the seventh year, it is a matter very pleasing to the Sages. One who has accepted a loan from a proselyte <note>A convert to Judaism</note> whose children [converted] together with 

---

<gloss>95 With back-dating</gloss>] Because in this way the creditor's case is made worse, which happens differently in debt records. For a judicial caution is not valid except for those debts which were made before its delivery to the Sanhedrin <note>The high court</note>. Those made after it was delivered, no matter if a caution was interposed, are destroyed by the seventh year regardless of the previous one. Therefore, if anyone interposes a caution with back-dating, it results in his own loss. On the contrary, if debt records err by back-dating, they are held invalid, because in that way the creditor's case would be made better to the loss of another. For if a time is written in the legal instrument which precedes the time of the actual debt 

<column-break/>

by a space of six months, the creditor would then have the right of eviction against a "good faith" purchaser who bought the debtor's field within that six-month window—that is, before the debt was actually bound.

<gloss>96 Beehive.</gloss>] This occurs again in Oketz III. 10.

<gloss>97 Word of remission.</gloss>] The cause, reason, or manner of remission and <term>seisachtheia</term> <note>a Greek term for the "shaking off" of debts</note>. This is what <term>Davar HaShemittah</term> <note>the Hebrew phrase for "the matter of the release"</note> signifies. But because *Davar* also means "word," the somewhat foolish Masters <note>The translator's critique of certain rabbinic interpretations</note> argue from this a necessity of remitting at least in word, however much the debtor may be prepared to repay.

# TITLE VI. TERUMOTH,
