## ON THE FIRST-FRUITS.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>1.</margin> FIVE classes of people shall not set aside the **first-fruits** <term>primitiae: here referring to Terumah, the "heave-offering" or portion of the harvest designated for the Priests</term>, and if they have set them aside, that which is designated is not considered valid first-fruits: the deaf-mute, the mentally incapacitated, the minor, he who sets aside from that which is not his own property, and the foreigner <note>original: "alienigena"; a non-Jew</note> who sets aside from the property of an Israelite, even if acting upon the Israelite's command. That which is set aside by these is not considered valid first-fruits.

<margin>2.</margin> 2. A deaf person who speaks but does not hear shall not set aside [as a matter of law]; but if he has done so, that which is set aside is considered valid first-fruits. The "Deaf person" of whom the **Sages** <note>original: "Sapientes"; the rabbinic authorities</note> speak everywhere is he who neither hears nor speaks.

<margin>3.</margin> 3. Regarding that which is set aside by a minor who has not yet produced two hairs <note>a physical sign of puberty and legal adulthood</note>, Rabbi Judah considers it to be valid first-fruits. If he set them aside before he reached <gloss>1</gloss> the age for making vows, Rabbi Jose says it is not considered valid first-fruits; but if it was after he reached the age for making vows, he considers it valid.

<margin>4.</margin> 4. One must not set aside first-fruits of oil from olives, nor first-fruits of wine from grapes <note>meaning one should not designate unprocessed fruit as the offering for the processed product</note>. And if anyone has so set them aside, the **Shammaites** <note>original: "Sammaeani"; the followers of the school of Shammai</note> acknowledge the first-fruits of the fruits themselves are contained within them. The **Hillelites** <note>original: "Hillelaei"; the followers of the school of Hillel</note> deny that what is set aside in this manner is considered valid first-fruits.

<margin>5.</margin> 5. First-fruits are not taken from the **gleanings** <note>original: "spicilegio"; ears of grain dropped during harvest</note>, the **forgotten sheaf** <note>original: "praetermisso"</note>, the **corner of the field** <note>original: "angulo"; the portion of the field left for the poor</note>, or from common property. Nor from the **first tithes** <note>original: "decimis primis"</note> from which the [priestly] first-fruits have not yet been removed, nor from **second tithes** or consecrated things that have not yet been redeemed. Not from what is bound <note>liable for tithes</note> on behalf of what is exempt, nor from what is exempt for what is bound. Not from what is plucked on behalf of what is still attached to the ground, nor from what is attached to the ground for what is plucked. Not from the new [crop] for the old, nor from the old for the new. Not from the fruits of the Land [of Israel] for foreign fruits, nor from foreign fruits for fruits of the Land. And that which is so set aside is not considered valid first-fruits.

<margin>6.</margin> 6. Five—

---

1 *The age for making vows.*] In males, twelve years and one day besides; in females, eleven years and one day besides. <note>original: "In maribus duodecim annos & insuper diem unum ; in foeminis undecim & insuper diem unum."</note>

# Order I. SEEDS

6. Five [additional classes of people] shall not set aside the **first-fruits** <term>primitiae: referring to Terumah, the portion of the harvest given to the Priests</term>; but if they have done so, that which is set aside is considered valid. The mute, the drunkard, the naked, the blind, and the one suffering from a bodily discharge <note>original: "fluxum passus"; a state of ritual impurity</note> shall not set aside the offerings; but if they have done so, that which is set aside is considered valid.

7. First-fruits are not set aside by measure, weight, or number [as a primary ritual]. However, they may be set aside from produce that has already been measured, weighed, or counted. One should not take them using a basket or a crate that serves as a standard measure. However, they may be taken using half-sized or third-sized containers. They shall not be taken using a half-seah <note>original: "fato dimidio" / "sato dimidio"; a seah is a dry measure of about 7.3 liters</note>, because the half-seah is itself a standard measure.

8. One should not set aside oil as first-fruits for olives intended for crushing, nor wine for grapes intended for treading. If they are so set aside, they are valid first-fruits, but another offering must be taken subsequently. The first of these <insert>2</insert> separately render the rest forbidden <note>original: "inficiunt"; meaning they cause the whole batch to become "meduma," or restricted for priestly use only</note>, and they require the addition of a <insert>3</insert> fifth <note>a penalty of 25% added to the value if eaten by a non-priest</note>. However, this does not apply to the second offering.

9. One may set aside oil as first-fruits for olives intended for pickling, and wine for grapes intended to become raisins. Indeed, if someone sets aside first-fruits of oil for olives intended for food, or from olives for other olives intended for food; or of wine for grapes intended for food, or from grapes for other grapes intended for food; and later changes his mind and wishes to press them, it is not necessary to set aside first-fruits again.

10. First-fruits must not be set aside from a finished product <note>original: "re elaborata"; produce that has completed its processing, like oil or wine</note> for a product not yet finished, nor from an unfinished product for a finished one, nor from one unfinished product for another unfinished product. But if they are so set aside, they are considered valid first-fruits.

1. First-fruits must not be set aside from that which is ritually clean for that which is ritually unclean; but if they are so set aside, they are valid. The same applies to a bundle of vegetables or a heap of grain. If there are two fig cakes, two bundles, or two heaps—one unclean and the other clean—the offering of one must not be taken from the other. Rabbi Eliezer maintains that the offering for the unclean may rightly be set aside from the clean.

2. First-fruits must not be set aside from the ritually unclean for the ritually clean; but if someone has set them aside unintentionally, that which he set aside is considered valid;

3. He who immerses vessels in water on the **Sabbath** <note>to ritually purify them</note>, if done by mistake, let him use them for work; but if done on purpose, he must not use them. 4. First-fruits of any kind must not be set aside from one species for another kind; and if they are so set aside, they are not considered first-fruits. All kinds of wheat are considered as one; and all kinds of figs, dried figs, and pressed fig-cakes are considered as one, so that first-fruits may be set aside from one for the other. Where a Priest is present, the first-fruits should be set aside from the better quality; where the Priest is absent, from that which lasts longer. Rabbi Judah always commands that first-fruits be plucked from the better quality.

5. For the first-fruits, a small whole onion is separated rather than half of a larger onion. Rabbi Judah denies this, commanding that a half of a larger onion be separated instead. In the same way, the same Rabbi Judah asserts that first-fruits are set aside from onions received from country-folk for the sake of city-dwellers, but not from city-dwellers for country-folk, because the former are the **food of the city-folk** <note>original: "Politicorum esca"; likely referring to the more refined or "civilized" palate of urbanites compared to rural farmers</note>.

6. First-fruits are also taken from oils for pouring for the sake of preserved oils, but not from preserved oils for those meant for pouring; and from unboiled wine for boiled wine, but not from boiled for unboiled. This is the general rule: whatever is considered a mixture with another, first-fruits shall not be taken from the one for the other, not even from the better for the worse. If, however, something is not a mixture with another, one may take first-fruits of a worse quality for the better, but not of the better for the worse; but if first-fruits are indeed taken from the worse for the better, they are held to be valid first-fruits: except, however, in the case of **darnel** <note>original: "lolio"; a weed often found in wheat fields</note> for wheat, because that is not edible. # First Order: SEEDS <note>original: "Ordinis I. ZERAIM"</note>

6. Five types of people shall not set aside the offering; but if they have set it aside, that which is offered is considered valid first-fruits <note>In this context, "first-fruits" refers to the *Terumah*, the heave-offering given to the Priests</note>. The mute, the drunk, the naked, the blind, and those suffering from a bodily discharge <note>referring to a *Zav*, someone in a state of ritual impurity</note> shall not set aside the offering; but if they have done so, that which is offered is considered valid first-fruits.

7. First-fruits are not to be set aside by measure, weight, or number <note>The offering was intended to be a gift of "generous eye" rather than a strictly calculated tax</note>. However, they may be set aside from produce that has already been measured, weighed, or counted. One should not take the offering from a basket or a crate that serves as a standard measure. However, they may be taken from those same vessels if they are half-filled or a third-filled. They shall not be taken using a half-**seah** <term>satus: a Hebrew measure of volume, approximately 7.3 liters</term>, because a half-seah is itself a fixed measure.

8. First-fruits should not be set aside from oil produced while crushing olives, nor from wine produced while treading grapes <note>referring to the liquid that escapes before the formal pressing process</note>. But if they are so set aside, they are valid first-fruits, though a second offering must be set aside afterward. The first of these ^2 **render the whole batch forbidden** <note>original: "seorsim inficiunt"</note> and require the ^3 **added fifth**. This does not apply to the second offering.

9. However, first-fruits are set aside from oil intended for preserving olives, and from wine intended for making raisins. Indeed, if someone has set aside first-fruits from oil intended for olives to be eaten, or from olives for other olives to be eaten; or from wine for grapes to be eaten, or from grapes for other grapes to be eaten; and then he changes his mind and decides to press them, he does not need to set aside the first-fruits a second time.

10. First-fruits should not be set aside from processed produce for produce that is not yet processed, nor from unprocessed produce for processed produce, nor from unprocessed produce for other unprocessed produce. But if they are so set aside, they are considered valid first-fruits.

Rabbi Eliezer maintains that first-fruits for unclean produce may be rightly set aside from clean produce.

<meta>This page continues the translation of the first order of the Mishnah, Seeds (Zeraim), specifically the third chapter of the tractate regarding Heave-Offerings (Terumoth). It builds on the previous page's discussion of the legality of intention and the species of offerings.</meta>

# Order I. SEEDS <note>original: "Zeraim"</note>

## C H A P T E R III.

<margin>1.</margin>If anyone sets aside a cucumber as **heave-offerings** <note>original: "primitias", referring to the *Terumah* portion given to the priests</note>, but it is found to be bitter; or a melon, and it is found to be rotten; they remain heave-offerings, but he must set aside others once again. If anyone sets aside a jar of wine as heave-offerings, and it is found to be vinegar: if it can be established that it became vinegar before the separation, it is not considered a heave-offering; if it became vinegar after the separation, it is considered a heave-offering; if it is doubtful, they are heave-offerings, but he must set aside others once again. The former ones do not contaminate common produce separately, nor do they require the **added fifth** <note>the *homesh*, a penalty of an additional 20% paid if a non-priest accidentally eats holy offerings</note>. Likewise, neither do the second ones.

<margin>2.</margin>If one of these falls into common produce, it does not contaminate it <note>rendering the whole batch forbidden to non-priests</note>; and if the second ones fall into another batch elsewhere, they do not contaminate that either. If both fall into the same batch, they contaminate it <gloss>5</gloss> according to the measure of the smaller of the two.

<margin>3.</margin>If partners set aside heave-offerings one after the other, Rabbi Akiba deems that what was set aside by both is considered heave-offerings. But the Sages recognize only what was set aside by the first as heave-offerings. Rabbi Joses says: if the first of them separated the required amount, that which was set aside by the second is not considered heave-offerings; but if the first did not separate the required amount, that which was set aside by the second is considered heave-offerings.

<margin>4.</margin>How are these matters to be understood? Provided it was not done against his command. But if one commands a steward, a male servant, or a female servant to set aside heave-offerings, that which is set aside is considered heave-offerings. If the mandate is revoked: if it was revoked before the separation, what was set aside is not considered heave-offerings; if he revoked it after the separation, it is considered heave-offerings. Laborers do not have the power to set aside heave-offerings, except for winepressers, because they would otherwise immediately <gloss>6</gloss> pollute the winepress.

<margin>5.</margin>If someone should say, *"The heave-offerings of this pile shall be in that part of it, the tithe of the same shall also be in that part, and the heave-offering of those tithes <note>the 'tithe of the tithe' given by the Levite to the Priest</note> shall be in that part":* Rabbi Simeon asserts that he has designated them by name. The Sages deny this, unless he specifies whether it is from the north or from the south. Rabbi Eleazar Hasma says: if someone should say, *"The heave-offerings of this pile shall be from the pile itself for its own sake":* he has already designated it by name.

---

<note>5 According to the measure etc.] Heave-offerings that fall into common produce which does not exceed them by a hundredfold contaminate the whole mass, as we have said. Now, if it is doubtful which of these are the true heave-offerings, and both fall into the same common produce, they indeed contaminate it, but only under this rule: if the common produce does not exceed a hundred times the quantity of the smaller amount.</note>

<note>6 Pollute.] As soon as the must (grape juice) flows, the winepress, being wet, is susceptible to ritual impurity. For this reason, winepressers are given the authority to remove the heave-offerings as quickly as possible, lest any impurity during the ongoing work should contaminate the whole batch.</note>

# Title VI. HEAVE-OFFERINGS <note>original: "Terumoth"</note>

...designated it. Rabbi Eliezer son of Jacob says: if someone should say, "Let the **tithe of these tithes** become the **heave-offering of the tithe** <note>original: "Decima harum decimarum pro illis fiat decimarum primitiæ"; this refers to the portion a Levite gives to a Priest from the tithe he received</note> for those," he has already designated it by name.

**6.** If someone presents the **first-fruits** <note>original: "primitivis"; refers to *Bikkurim*, the very first of the harvest brought to the Temple</note> before the **heave-offering** <note>original: "primitiis"; the *Terumah* for the priests</note>, or the heave-offering before the **first tithe**, or the first tithe before the **second tithe**, the act is legally valid, although he has violated a divine prohibition. For it is written (*Exodus* 22:29): ⁷ *You shall not delay the offering of your mature and abundant crops.* <note>original: "Maturas & opimas fruges tuas non dabis præpostere"</note>

**7.** On what basis is it established that first-fruits must be presented before heave-offerings, since both are called ⁸ **offering** <note>original: "delibatio"</note> and ⁹ **beginning** <note>original: "principium"</note>, and these others are also called ¹⁰ **offering** and ¹¹ **beginning**? Truly, the first-fruits must come first because they are the "first-fruits of all things"; the heave-offerings before the first tithes, because they are called "the beginning"; and the first tithes before the second tithes, because in them ¹² the "beginning" is also found.

**8.** If someone intended to say "**Heave-offerings**," but said "**Tithes**" instead; or meant "**Tithes**" and said "**Heave-offerings**"; or meant a "**Burnt offering**" <note>original: "Holocaustum"</note> and said a "**Peace offering**" <note>original: "Salutaris hostia"</note>; or meant a "**Peace offering**" and said a "**Burnt offering**"; or meant "I will not enter **this** house" but said "**that one**"; or "I will receive no benefit from **this** man" but said "**that one**"—it is not considered as if he has said anything at all, until his mouth and his mind are in agreement.

**9.** The heave-offerings of **foreigners** <note>non-Jews</note> or **Samaritans** <note>original: "Cuthæi"; descendants of settlers placed in Samaria by the Assyrians</note> are considered true heave-offerings, their tithes are true tithes, and what they consecrate is truly consecrated. Rabbi Judah says: if an Israelite receives the fruit from ¹³ a **fourth-year vineyard**...

<columns>2</columns>
⁷ *Your mature crops, etc.*] That is, the first-fruits which come from the mature crops, and the heave-offerings which come from the abundance. These words should be translated here in a way that satisfies the meaning of the *Mishnah*. The Hebrew words are: *mle’atekha v’dim’akha lo te’acher* <note>original Hebrew: מלאתך ודמעך לא תאחר</note>. Regarding these words, I read in the *Mechilta*: *By 'mle’atekha' is understood the first-fruits, which are taken from the full harvest; by 'dim’akha' is understood the heave-offering. 'Lo te’acher' (you shall not delay) means you shall not put the second tithe before the first, nor the first tithe before the heave-offering, nor the heave-offering before the first-fruits.* This is found in the manuscripts, though in the Venice edition those words are missing, likely by error; for both the author of the book *Yalkut* and Moses Nachmanides assert they belong to the *Mechilta*. *Mle’ah* signifies mature crops, and here they wish to use it for the first-fruits to be taken from there. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> explains *mle’atekha* as: *the debt incumbent upon you when your produce is fully matured and ready to be cooked, which are the first-fruits.* Concerning the term *dema* (juice/tears), I spoke of it above regarding the tractate *Demai* (1.3). The same Rabbi Solomon explains *lo te’acher* with these words: *You shall not change the order of their separation by delaying that which should be earlier and advancing that which should be later: namely, that the heave-offering should not be moved ahead of the first-fruits, nor the tithe ahead of the heave-offering.*

...that the fourth-year fruit <note>Referring to the fruit of a tree in its fourth year of growth, which held special sanctity</note> does not apply to a foreigner. The Sages, however, maintain that it does apply. The first-fruits of a foreigner cause impurity and require the payment of an additional fifth <note>A penalty for eating sacred food unintentionally</note>. Rabbi Simeon¹⁴ excuses this.

## C H A P T E R IV.

**1.** One who separates a portion of the first-fruits or tithes should take the first-fruits¹⁵ for that portion from the same batch, not from another item elsewhere. Rabbi Meir permits taking the first-fruits or tithes even from another item in a different location.

**2.** A man who has grain in a granary: if he has designated a portion¹⁶ for the Levite and another portion for the poor, he may subsequently separate eight other portions and eat them. This is the view of Rabbi Meir. But the Sages forbid separating them unless it is done according to the proper proportion¹⁷.

**3.** This is the proportion for the first-fruits: He who gives most generously <note>original: "largissime"</note> gives a fortieth part, though according to the School of Shammai <note>original: "Sammæanos"</note> it is a thirtieth; he who is average gives a fiftieth; and he who is stingy <note>original: "parcissime"</note> gives a sixtieth. If someone sets aside a sixtieth part as a consecrated offering, it is considered a valid first-fruit, and there is no need to set more aside; but if he adds anything later, that addition must be tithed. If he sets aside—

---

perceives it, without regard to the law of the fourth-year vineyard.

14 *Excuses.*] He who eats the first-fruits of a foreigner through oversight is excused from the payment of the additional fifth beyond the principal amount.

15 *For that.*] For a portion so separated that is too small to be considered a proper first-fruit or tithe, and therefore must itself have first-fruits or tithes paid upon it. I read the word "portion" <note>original: "מקצת" (miktzat)</note> twice here, as it appears in the Jerusalem Talmud, and as it clearly appears to have been read formerly in the Gemara <note>The commentary on the Mishnah</note> of that same Talmud. Maimonides <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>, contrary to the intention of other interpreters and the Talmud itself, reads "portion" twice, whence according to him the whole passage must be understood in a completely different sense. 
> *One who separates a portion of the first-fruits or tithes, take the first-fruits of that same portion from itself, not from elsewhere. Rabbi Meir says even from elsewhere, etc.*

16 *Levite.*] To the Levite for the Tithes of the Levites, and to the poor for the Tithe of the Poor—namely in the third or sixth year of the seven-year cycle. You have here the First Tithe and the Second Tithe taken at the same time, contrary to the opinion of Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a renowned Renaissance scholar</note>, which we refuted above at Pea VIII. 2.

17 *According to the proportion.*] Namely, for the quantity of the portion not yet consumed from the batches he gave to the Levite and the poor; for instance, if half of them remains, he is allowed to separate only four batches; if a quarter, two. So says Maimonides. Others interpret it differently.

18 *Most generously.*] Literally, *with a good eye, a medium eye, and a bad eye*. Thus Proverbs 22:9, "a good eye" <note>original: "טוב עין" (tov ayin)</note> 

<column-break/>

is used to mean the liberal and munificent; and Proverbs 23:6, "an evil eye" <note>original: "רע עין" (ra ayin)</note> for the stingy and mean. In the Gospels, an "evil eye" <note>original: "ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρὸς" (ophthalmos poneros)</note> is used several times for greed and stinginess, to which a "single eye" <note>original: "ὀφθαλμὸς ἁπλοῦς" (ophthalmos haplous)</note> is opposed in Matthew 6:22. Once this is noted, the sense and coherence of that passage will be clear, which is otherwise not plain enough. In verses 19, 20, and 21, Christ forbids the worry over earthly wealth and kindles the minds of men to store up heavenly riches. Then, taking the opportunity from the fact that in the dialect of his countrymen, liberality is called a "good eye" or "single eye," while greed is called an "evil eye," he reasons thus: 
> The lamp of the body is the eye: if therefore your eye is single—that is, if you are not greedy—your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil—that is, if you are greedy and mean—your whole body will be dark, etc. 

Thereafter, until the end of the chapter, he pursues the argument against greed and excessive anxiety about worldly things. These words from our Mishnah are clearly identical to what Jerome <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his Bible translation</note> wrote regarding the Hebrew tradition of first-fruits in his commentary on Ezekiel 45: *“The first-fruits for him are what we call first-fruits; he speaks thus.”* 
> But truly the first-fruits which they offered from the crops were not defined by a specific number, but were left to the discretion of the offerers. We have received the tradition of the Hebrews—not commanded by law, but established by the discretion of the teachers—that he who gave the most gave a fortieth part to the priests; he who gave the least, a sixtieth; and between the fortieth and the sixtieth, they were permitted to offer whatever they wished.

### Title VI. HEAVE-OFFERINGS <term>Terumoth; the portion of the harvest dedicated to the Priests</term>.

...if he has set aside a sixty-first part, it is considered a valid heave-offering, but he shall set it aside again so that he may know it better, <sup>19</sup> by measure, weight, or number. Rabbi Judah adds: even from <sup>20</sup> that which is not nearby.

4. If anyone says to an agent, "Go and separate the heave-offering," he must separate it according to the mind of the master of the house; and if he does not know the mind of the master of the house, he should separate the average proportion, which is one-fiftieth. If <sup>21</sup> he errs by a denarius <note>A small silver coin used here as a unit of value/measure</note> in deficiency or in excess, what he has separated is still considered a valid heave-offering. If <sup>22</sup> he intentionally tried to increase it by even a single part, the separation is not valid.

5. If someone wishes to separate a more generous heave-offering, Rabbi Eliezer permits it up to a tenth part, the same as the tithe of the tithes. Beyond this measure, he orders it to be made a heave-offering <sup>23</sup> for something else in another place. Rabbi Ishmael permits it if half is ordinary food and half is heave-offering. Rabbis Tarphon and Akiba permit it as long as some portion of ordinary food remains.

6. At three intervals of time they estimate the measuring basket: <sup>24</sup> at the first ripening, at the end of the harvest, and in mid-summer. <sup>25</sup> He who counts the fruit deserves praise; he who measures it is more praised than him; and he who weighs it is the most praised of the three.

7. Rabbi Eliezer asserts that the heave-offering <sup>26</sup> "emerges" <note>Meaning it is neutralized or nullified when mixed with ordinary food</note> from one hundred and one parts; Rabbi Joshua says from one hundred parts and "something more." This "something more" has no fixed measure. According to Rabbi Jose, son of Meshullam, that "more" must equal a *kab* <term>A measure of volume, roughly 1.4 liters</term> above the aforementioned hundred—specifically a sixth of the particle that caused the mixture.

8. Rabbi Joshua thinks that dark figs <sup>27</sup> "bring out" <note>Neutralize the sacred status in a mixture</note> white ones, and white ones bring out dark ones; large rounds of pressed figs bring out small ones, and small ones even bring out large ones; rounds of...

---

19 *Measure, weight.*] It is forbidden to separate the heave-offering by measure, weight, or number (as seen above in I. 7). But afterward they estimate what portion of the whole the separated heave-offering makes up, and if it does not make up a sixtieth, an addition is added later, and that is taken by measure, weight, or number. Such clever men!

20 *Not nearby.*] But the heave-offerings themselves should be separated <note>original: "min ha-muqaph"</note>, that is, as Maimonides says <note>original: "mimma hasala tahta ihata mouda wahid"</note>, *from that which is gathered together in the same place.*

21 *By a denarius.*] By a denarius in deficiency if he took a sixtieth, or in excess if he took a fortieth instead of a fiftieth.

22 *By even a single part.*] As if he wished to take a forty-ninth part instead of a fiftieth.

23 *For something else.*] Both Talmuds say, *but not for something else.* The manuscript and other interpreters say otherwise.

24 *At the first ripening.*] At the time when the first fruits are ripened. At the end, at the time when—

<column-break/>

25 *He who counts the fruit.*] Specifically in separating the tithes of the heave-offerings.

26 *Emerges from one hundred and one.*] That is, if a portion of heave-offering falls into one hundred parts of ordinary food, it is sufficient for it to "emerge," or be drawn out—namely, that the one-hundred-and-first part of the total mass (which is exactly how much fell in) be removed. Thus, the whole mass is not so "infected" <note>Consecrated or made forbidden to commoners</note> that it is bound by the laws of heave-offerings. Rabbi Joshua thinks it "emerges" even if it falls not into a hundred, but only into ninety-nine and a little bit more. If it falls into only ninety-nine or fewer, everyone agrees the whole mass is "infected," so that no one except the Priests may lawfully eat it. The son of Meshullam contends that this "little bit more"—by which the ordinary food must exceed the particle of heave-offering more than ninety-nine times—must necessarily equal a sixth part of that particle, just as a *kab* is a sixth of a *seah* <term>A larger dry measure</term>; otherwise, the whole mass is infected.

27 *Bring out.*] To make "emerge" in the sense we just described.

...round cakes [of figs] neutralize blocks, and blocks [neutralize] round cakes. <note>The Latin *elicere* (to draw out/elicit) corresponds to the Hebrew concept of "raising" or neutralizing a mixture. If a small amount of sacred food falls into a large amount of ordinary food, the majority "lifts" the minority into a status where it can be eaten.</note> Rabbi Eliezer considers this forbidden. Where it is known which kind fell in, Rabbi Akiba thinks they do not neutralize one another; where it is not known which kind fell in, they do neutralize one another.

9. How so? For example, if a black fig falls into fifty black ones and fifty white ones, the black ones become forbidden <note>Because they are of the same kind and the ratio is only 50:1, which is insufficient for neutralization</note>, but the white ones remain permitted. If a white fig falls in, the white ones are forbidden, but the black ones are permitted. Where it is not known which kind fell in, they neutralize one another. And in this matter, Rabbi Eliezer takes the stricter view, while Rabbi Joshua takes the more lenient view.

10. However, in this [other] matter, Rabbi Eliezer takes the more lenient view and Rabbi Joshua the stricter view: namely, concerning one who has pressed a pound <gloss>28</gloss> of dried figs <note>original: *aridarum ficuum*</note> into the top of a certain jar, and it is not known into which jar. Rabbi Eliezer wants them to be considered <gloss>29</gloss> as if they were separated, and thus the [ordinary figs] below neutralize the [sacred figs] above. Rabbi Joshua says they are not neutralized unless there are a hundred jars.

11. If a *seah* <term>satum; a dry measure of about 12 quarts</term> of the heave-offering <note>original: *primitiarum*; refers to the portion of the harvest dedicated to the Priests</note> falls onto the top of a storehouse and is spread across the surface, Rabbi Eliezer thinks that provided there are a hundred *seahs* in the spread-out portion, it is neutralized by the hundred and one. Rabbi Joshua says it will not be neutralized. If a *seah* of heave-offering falls on the top of the storehouse, let it be scraped off from the top. If so, why is it said that the heave-offering is neutralized by a hundred and one parts? Namely, if it is not known whether they have been mixed or not, or in which part they fell.

12. If there are two baskets, or two storehouses, and a *seah* of heave-offering falls into one of them, but it is not known into which it fell, they neutralize each other. Rabbi Simeon adds: even if they were in two different towns, they neutralize each other.

13. Rabbi Joses said: A case was brought before Rabbi Akiba concerning fifty bundles of vegetables among which fell one such bundle that was half composed of heave-offering; and I said before him that it ought to be neutralized; not because the heave-offering is neutralized by fifty-one parts, but because there were a hundred and two half-portions. <note>In Jewish law, Terumah is usually neutralized in a 1:100 ratio. By counting the bundles as half-portions, R. Joses reaches the necessary mathematical threshold.</note>

## CHAPTER V.

**1.** **I**F a portion <note>original: *fatum*; likely referring to a *se’ah*, a biblical unit of dry measure</note> of impure first-fruits falls into less than a hundred [parts] of profane <term>Chullin; ordinary food with no sacred status</term> matter, or of the first tithes <term>Ma’aser Rishon; given to the Levites</term>, or of the second tithes <term>Ma’aser Sheni; eaten by the owner in Jerusalem</term>, or of a consecrated thing, whether they be impure or pure, they are allowed to rot. If that portion was pure, they are sold <gloss>30</gloss> to the Priests according to the value of first-fruits, minus the price of that portion. And if it falls into the first tithes, they are designated <gloss>31</gloss> by the name "first-fruits of the tithes" <term>Terumat Ma'aser; the ten percent of the tithe that the Levite gives to the Priest</term>. If it falls into the second tithes or a consecrated thing, these must certainly be redeemed <gloss>32</gloss>. If, however, the profane crops themselves were impure, they are eaten dry <gloss>33</gloss>, or roasted, or kneaded with fruit juice, or distributed into cakes so small that no single one is equal to the size of an egg <note>According to Jewish law, food smaller than an egg-bulk cannot convey ritual impurity</note>.

**2.** If a portion of impure first-fruits falls into a hundred [parts] of pure profane crops, Rabbi Eliezer commands it to be removed and burned; for I would say, he says, that the same portion that fell in is the one that has emerged. But the Sages <term>the majority of Rabbinic scholars</term> permit the crops to be eaten after the portion is extracted, provided they are dry, or roasted, or worked with fruit juice, or distributed into such small cakes that none of them equals the size of an egg.

**3.** If a portion of pure first-fruits falls into a hundred [parts] of impure profane crops, once the portion is extracted, they may be eaten dry, or roasted, or worked with fruit juice, or distributed into such small cakes that none of them equals the size of an egg.

**4.** If a portion of impure first-fruits falls into a hundred portions of pure first-fruits, the School of Shammai <note>original: *Sammæani*</note> forbid them to be drawn out, but the School of Hillel <note>original: *Hillelæi*</note> permit it. The School of Hillel said to the School of Shammai: "Since pure [offerings] are considered forbidden to laypeople, and impure ones are forbidden even to the Priests themselves, just as the pure are raised <note>original: *emergunt*; neutralized by the ratio</note>, so also should the impure be raised." To which the School of Shammai replied: "By no means! For if ordinary crops, which are of a lighter condition and permitted to laypeople, allow pure [offerings] to be remitted; should first-fruits, which are of a weightier condition and forbidden to laypeople, therefore remit the impure?" After this was conceded, Rabbi Eliezer ordered the extracted portion to be burned.

---

<columns>2</columns>
30 *They are sold.*] The crops into which [the portion] fell. It is added *according to the value of first-fruits*, for first-fruits, which only Priests may lawfully eat, are sold for less than profane matter, which is permitted to all and thus more easily finds a buyer.

31 *They are designated by the name etc.*] Understand [this to mean], *and thus they are sold to the Priest with the price of the missing portion and the first-fruits of the tithes deducted.* So says Maimonides. Obadiah of Bertinoro <note>A 15th-century commentator on the Mishnah</note> says otherwise, holding that the whole of the crops thus affected should be established as the first-fruits of the tithes for

<column-break/>

other crops by the Levite.

32 *They are redeemed.*] Understand here also, that once redeemed they are sold to the Priest.

33 *Dry etc.*] So that the mixed-in first-fruits do not contract pollution <note>ritual impurity</note>. Food is not made susceptible to pollution except by the pouring on of one of the seven liquids: water, dew, oil, wine, honey, milk, or blood; nor can the food be polluted once made susceptible unless it is at least the size of an egg.

<meta>This page continues the Latin translation of the Mishnah tractate Terumoth (Heave-offerings), Chapter 5. It continues the legal debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding the "neutralization" of sacred offerings when mixed with ordinary food, specifically focusing on the ratios required to make the food permissible for common use again.</meta>

<page-num>118</page-num>
<header>Order I: SEEDS <term>Latin: Zeraim; the first division of the Mishnah dealing with agricultural laws</term></header>

...commanded. But the Sages think it is nullified by its own smallness <note>This refers to a small amount of sacred food being "canceled out" by a much larger quantity of common food</note>.

**5.** If a portion <note>original: *fatum*; likely referring to a *se’ah*, a biblical unit of dry measure</note> of first-fruits <term>Terumah; the portion of the harvest given to the Priests</term> that fell into a hundred [parts of common food] is removed and then falls elsewhere, Rabbi Eliezer thinks it renders the new mixture forbidden just as certain first-fruits would. The Sages say it only renders it forbidden <gloss>1</gloss> according to the proportional calculation.

**6.** If a portion of first-fruits falls into less than a hundred [parts], so that the whole mixture becomes forbidden, and some of that forbidden mixture falls elsewhere, Rabbi Eliezer thinks it renders the new mixture forbidden just as certain first-fruits would. The Sages, however, deny <gloss>2</gloss> that a forbidden thing makes another mixture forbidden except according to the proportional calculation; or <gloss>3</gloss> that a leavened mass leavens another mass except according to the proportional calculation; or <gloss>4</gloss> that drawn water spoils a ritual bath <term>Mikvah; a bath used for ritual immersion</term> except according to the proportional calculation.

**7.** If a portion of first-fruits falls into a hundred parts, and after it is removed another falls in, and after that is removed another falls, the mixture remains permitted as long as the first-fruits <note>the total amount of sacred offerings added</note> do not exceed the quantity of the profane crops.

**8.** If a portion of first-fruits falls into a hundred parts and could not be removed before another portion falls in, it is removed unlawfully. Rabbi Simeon considers it permitted.

**9.** If a portion of first-fruits falls into a hundred parts and they decrease in volume when ground together, just as the profane crops are diminished, so the first-fruits are seen to be diminished, and they are removed lawfully. If a portion of first-fruits falls into less than a hundred parts and they increase when ground together, just as the profane crops are increased, so the first-fruits are considered increased, and it is not lawful to remove them. But if it is clear that the profane wheat was of better quality than the first-fruits, it may be lawfully removed. If a portion of first-fruits falls into less than a hundred parts, and later other profane crops are mixed with them—if this happens by accident, it may be removed; but if it was done intentionally, it is not permitted.

->CHAPTER<-

---

<gloss>1</gloss> **According to the proportional calculation.**] That is, according to the ratio of its hundredth part, or less than a hundredth.

<gloss>2</gloss> **A forbidden thing making another forbidden, etc.**] For example, if a portion of first-fruits falls into twenty parts of a profane substance and thus makes them forbidden; then some of that forbidden substance falls into other crops; it does not make those crops forbidden even if they are a hundred times greater, not because of the whole forbidden mixture that fell in, but only because of the twenty-first part of that mixture; that is, according to the ratio of the original forbidden particle to the profane substance it first affected.

<column-break/>

<gloss>3</gloss> **A leavened thing leavening, etc.**] If a mass of profane material swells because of leaven prepared from first-fruits, that whole mass is forbidden for common use and belongs to the Priests by the rite of first-fruits. If a further mixture of that mass leavens another mass, that second mass does not belong to the Priests like the first, unless by a calculation it is established that enough of the original first-fruit leaven was present to leaven that second mass.

<gloss>4</gloss> **Drawn water.**] See Mikvah <note>Latin: *Micva*; the tractate of the Mishnah regarding ritual baths</note> IV. 4.

### CHAPTER 6

1. Anyone who eats first-fruits <term>Terumah; the portion of the harvest designated for the Priests</term> by mistake is required to pay back the principal and an additional fifth. This applies whether one eats them, drinks them <note>such as wine or oil</note>, or uses them for anointing <note>a common use for oil in the ancient world</note>. It is also the same whether the first-fruits were ritually pure or impure; the person is still required to pay the fifth, and even a "fifth of the fifth" <gloss>1</gloss>. Furthermore, he must not pay this restitution from other first-fruits, but from common produce that has been properly prepared <note>meaning the tithes have already been removed</note>. That replacement food then takes on the status of first-fruits <gloss>2</gloss>, as does any compensation for it. A Priest, no matter how much he may wish to do so, cannot waive this payment.

2. If the daughter of an Israelite <note>a non-priestly Hebrew</note> eats first-fruits and later marries a Priest, and the first-fruits she ate had not yet been assigned to a specific Priest, she may pay the principal and the fifth to herself <note>since as a Priest's wife, she is now entitled to eat Terumah</note>. However, if the first-fruits she ate had already been assigned to a specific Priest, she must pay the principal to that owner, but may keep the fifth for herself. For it is said: *If anyone eats first-fruits by mistake, he shall pay the principal to the owner, but the fifth to whomever he wishes.*

3. If someone serves first-fruits to his laborers or guests to eat, he himself is bound to pay the principal, but they must pay the fifth. This is the opinion of Rabbi Meir. However, the Sages believe that the guests are bound to pay both the principal and the fifth, while the host must pay back the guests for the value of the meal he provided.

4. Whoever stole first-fruits but has not yet eaten them must pay a double penalty <note>based on the law of theft in Exodus 22</note> according to the value of the first-fruits. If he has eaten them, he must pay a double principal and a fifth: one principal and the fifth from common produce, and the second principal according to the value of the first-fruits. If he stole and ate first-fruits that were already consecrated <note>dedicated to the Temple treasury rather than just the Priest</note>, he must pay two fifths along with the principal, since the law of double penalty does not apply to consecrated property.

5. It is not permitted to pay restitution using the gleanings, the forgotten sheaves, the corner of the field <note>these are various portions of the harvest left for the poor</note>, or shared property. Nor may it be paid from "first tithes" from which the priestly portion has been taken, nor from "second tithes" or consecrated items that have been redeemed, because a sacred thing cannot be used to redeem another sacred thing. This is the view of Rabbi Meir. But the Sages allow restitution to be made from these <gloss>3</gloss> items.

---

<columns>2</columns>

¹ **A fifth of the fifth.**] If he accidentally eats the fifth that was already paid as restitution.

² **Compensation for the same.**] If he eats the produce paid in place of the first-fruits, he is bound to compensate for it just as he was for the original first-fruits, and that compensation follows the legal status of first-fruits. This is the common interpretation of this passage. However, regarding the preceding words, *and they become heave-offerings* <note>original Hebrew: והם נעשין תרומה</note> and these words *and the compensation for them becomes heave-offerings* <note>original Hebrew: ותשלומי תרומה</note>,

<column-break/>

I believe they denote exactly the same thing; one is likely an explanation of the other and has mistakenly crept into the text from a marginal note. See Chapter 7, sections 1, 3, and 4.

³ **These.**] The last items mentioned: first tithes, second tithes, and consecrated property. So say the commentators. But in the *Siphra* <note>an ancient legal commentary on Leviticus</note>, section *Emor* VI. 5, it is expressly read: *But the Sages assert that it is permitted to pay from all of them.*

It also clarifies who receives the payment in cases of marriage or theft, and what types of produce can be used for repayment.</summary>

6. Rabbi Eliezer permits one to make restitution from one species for another, provided that a superior species is given for an inferior one. However, Rabbi Akiba forbids making restitution from anything other than the same species; to the extent that if someone ate cucumbers from the year before the seventh <term>the Sabbatical year, or Shmita, when the land lies fallow</term>, he must wait for cucumbers from the year after the seventh, and pay his debt from those. Furthermore, from the very same passage where Rabbi Eliezer derives a more lenient opinion, Rabbi Akiba maintains a stricter one; namely, from that which is said in Leviticus 22:14: *and he shall give the holy thing to the Priest.* <note>original: "et sacrum Sacerdoti reddet"</note> According to Rabbi Eliezer's mind, this means whatever is fit to become a "holy thing." But according to Rabbi Akiba, it means a "holy thing" of the same kind as that which he ate.

### CHAPTER VII.

1. He who eats first-fruits <term>Terumah; the portion of the harvest set aside for the Priests</term> with deliberate intent is bound to pay the principal <note>original: "sortem"</note>, but not the additional fifth <note>original: "quintam"</note>; furthermore, that compensation is considered common <term>Chullin; ordinary, non-sacred food</term>: and if the Priest so wishes, he may forgive the debt.

2. If the daughter of a Priest is married to an Israelite <note>a non-priestly Hebrew</note> and later eats first-fruits, she is bound to pay the principal, but not the fifth; and if she is guilty of a capital crime <note>such as adultery</note>, she is punished by being burned alive. If she should marry any of those with whom marriage is not legally contracted, she is bound to pay both the principal and the fifth, and if guilty of a capital crime, she is punished by strangulation. This is the opinion of Rabbi Meir. The Sages, however, judge that in both cases they must pay the principal, but not the fifth, and if guilty of capital crimes, they are to be punished by being burned alive.

3. If someone feeds first-fruits to minor children, or to servants—whether they are adults or minors; or if he himself eats first-fruits from foreign crops, or a quantity of first-fruits less than the size of an olive, he is bound to pay the principal, but not the fifth; that compensation is considered common food; and if the Priest so wishes, he may forgive the debt.

4. This is the general rule: Whenever both the principal and the fifth must be paid, the compensation is regarded as first-fruits <note>it becomes sacred</note>, and the Priest, even if he greatly desires to do so, cannot waive the payment. However, whenever the principal must be paid but not the fifth, the compensation is reckoned as common food, and if the Priest so wishes, he may waive the debt.

5. Where two baskets exist, one full of first-fruits and the other full of common crops; if a portion of first-fruits should fall into one of them, but it is not certain into which one, I would certainly say it fell into the first-fruits. If it is also unknown which of them contains the first-fruits and which contains the common crops, he who eats one of them is exempt; but the other must be used as if it were first-fruits, and he is bound to the <unclear>sacred thing</unclear>. This is the opinion of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Jose exempts him from the <unclear>sacred thing</unclear>. If someone else <note>catchword for the next page: "quispiam"</note>

## CHAPTER VIII.

1. If a woman, while eating first-fruits, is told by a messenger: *“Your husband has died,”* or *“Your husband has divorced you”*; and likewise if a servant, while eating first-fruits, is told: *“Your master has died,”* or *“An Israelite has bought you,”* or *“He has given you as a gift,”* or *“He has set you free”* <note>In these cases, the woman or servant loses their legal right to eat the Priest's food</note>; and likewise if it becomes known to a Priest, while he is eating first-fruits, that he was born to a mother who was a divorcee, or who had undergone the "removal of the shoe" <term>Halizah; a ritual where a widow releases her brother-in-law from the duty of marrying her</term> <note>Children of such marriages were disqualified from the priesthood</note>; Rabbi Eliezer holds him liable for the principal and the additional fifth <note>the standard penalty for a layperson eating sacred food</note>: Rabbi Joshua acquits him. If it becomes known to the Priest while he is standing at the altar performing sacrifices that he was born to such a mother, Rabbi Eliezer thinks all the offerings he presented at the altar are rendered useless; Rabbi Joshua considers them valid. But if it is established that he had a physical defect <note>original: "vitio affectum"</note>, his worship is rendered invalid in either case.

2. Regarding all of these people, if they have first-fruits in their mouth [when they hear the news], Rabbi Eliezer commands them to swallow, but Rabbi Joshua commands them to spit it out. If someone is told: *“You have become unclean,”* or *“The first-fruits have become unclean,”* Rabbi Eliezer commands to swallow, but Rabbi Joshua commands to spit it out. *“You were already unclean some time ago,”* or *“The first-fruits were already unclean”*; or if it is clear that the thing he is chewing is untithed <note>original: "illibatam"</note>, or consists of first tithes from which the heave-offering has not yet been taken, or second tithes or consecrated items not yet redeemed, or if he perceives the taste of a bedbug in his mouth—in these cases, he shall spit it out.

3. If someone, while eating a grape, enters from the <gloss>2</gloss> garden into the courtyard, Rabbi Eliezer permits him to finish eating it, but Rabbi Joshua forbids it. If the shadows of evening fall and the Sabbath night begins, <gloss>3</gloss> Rabbi Eliezer permits him to finish eating it, but Rabbi Joshua forbids it.

# Order I. SEEDS

4. Wine of the first-fruits <term>Terumah; sacred offerings given to priests</term> which has remained uncovered must be poured out <note>This is due to the danger that a snake may have drunk from it and left venom behind</note>. It is not necessary to say the same regarding common <term>non-sacred</term> wine. Three liquids become forbidden due to exposure: water, wine, and milk; all others remain permitted. How long must they remain uncovered to become forbidden? Long enough for a reptile to crawl out from a nearby hiding place and drink.

5. Regarding uncovered water <gloss>1</gloss>, it must be of such a volume that any venom diluted within it would be neutralized. Whatever the amount in a vessel, Rabbi Joses considers it forbidden; but in large reservoirs <note>literally: "on the grounds"</note>, it is permitted up to forty *seahs* <term>a standard Jewish unit of volume, approx. 300 liters</term>.

6. Figs, grapes, cucumbers, gourds, melons, and watermelons that have been hollowed out by gnawing <gloss>2</gloss>—whether they are as small as a jar or whether they are large or small, whether plucked or still attached to the ground—provided they contain moisture within, they are forbidden to eat. And likewise <gloss>3</gloss> anything bitten by a serpent is forbidden because of the danger to life.

7. A wine strainer becomes forbidden if it is left uncovered. Rabbi Nehemias considers it permitted.

8. A jar of first-fruits about which a doubt of impurity has recently arisen: Rabbi Eliezer, if it had been placed in an impure place, believes it should be moved to a ritually clean place; and if it was open, it should be covered. Rabbi Joshua, if it was placed in a clean place, wants it moved to an impure place; and if it was covered, it should be uncovered. Rabban Gamaliel forbids making any change at all.

9. When a jar is broken in the upper part of the wine-press and the lower part is polluted, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua agree that if a quarter-measure <term>a log; approx. 0.3 liters</term> can be rescued from it while maintaining its ritual purity, it must be rescued. But if not, Rabbi Eliezer says it is allowed to flow away and be polluted; <gloss>4</gloss> but do not pollute it with your own hands.

10. And likewise, if a jar of oil is spilled, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua agree that if a quarter-measure can be rescued in purity, it must be rescued. But if not, Rabbi Eliezer says it is allowed to flow away and be absorbed; but one should not act with one's hands to ensure it is absorbed.

11. Regarding both of these, Rabbi Joshua says: These are not the first-fruits about which I was warned "do not pollute," but rather "do not eat them." However, the prohibition against polluting <gloss>5</gloss> is as follows. If someone traveling from place to place, carrying loaves of first-fruits, is commanded by a foreigner <term>a non-Jew/gentile</term>: *"Give me one of those so that I may pollute it, for if you do not, I will pollute them all,"* Rabbi Eliezer prefers that all be polluted rather than handing over one to be polluted. Rabbi Joshua commands that he should lay one out before him upon a rock <note>This avoids the act of handing it over directly, which would be an active participation in the pollution</note>.

# Title VI. FIRST-FRUITS <term>Terumoth</term>

## CHAPTER IX.

1. If someone unintentionally sows first-fruits <term>Terumah; sacred produce reserved for priests</term>, he must plow it under <note>turning the soil to destroy the crop</note>. If he did it intentionally, he may let it grow. If the crop has reached one-third of its growth, whether he sowed it unintentionally or intentionally, he may let it grow. However, if one intentionally sows flax <note>from which first-fruits were also taken</note>, he is required to plow it under.

2. Furthermore, the resulting crop is subject to the laws of gleaning <term>spicilegium; ears of grain dropped during harvest</term>, forgotten sheaves, and the corner of the field <term>Peah; the portion of the field left unharvested for the poor</term>. Both poor Israelites and poor Priests may gather these. However, the poor Israelites must sell what they have gathered to the Priests at the lower value of first-fruits <note>sacred food is cheaper because its market is limited to Priests in a state of purity</note>, and the proceeds belong to them. Rabbi Tarphon forbids anyone other than poor Priests from gathering these, lest they accidentally put the food to their mouths <note>eating sacred food while in a state of ritual impurity</note. Rabbi Akiba said to him: “If that is so, then only those who are ritually pure should be allowed to gather.”

3. The crop is also subject to tithes and the tithes of the poor, which poor Israelites and poor Priests may take together. Again, the poor Israelites sell their portion to the Priests at the value of first-fruits, and keep the money. It is best to thresh the grain with whips; however, if one prefers to use an animal for threshing, how should he proceed? He should hang baskets around the animal's neck and fill them with grain of the same kind <note>non-sacred grain</note>. In this way, he neither muzzles the ox <note>violating the biblical law against muzzling a treading animal</note> nor allows the animal to eat the sacred first-fruits.

4. That which grows from first-fruits is considered first-fruits; and what grows from that in turn is considered common <term>profanum; non-sacred food</term>. However, what grows from untithed produce, from first tithes, from the aftergrowth of the seventh year <term>Shevi'it; the sabbatical year</term>, from the first-fruits of foreign crops, or from produce mixed with first-fruits, is considered common. What grows from consecrated property or from second tithes is also common, but these must be redeemed <note>exchanged for money to be spent in Jerusalem</note> at the time of sowing.

# TITLE VI. HEAVE OFFERINGS <term>Terumoth</term>

3. If someone should place hot bread, just taken from the oven, over the mouth of a jar of wine from the first-fruits <note>Heave Offering or Terumah, which only priests may eat</note>: Rabbi Meir considers it forbidden <note>because the bread absorbs the vapor and flavor of the sacred wine</note>; Rabbi Judah holds it to be permitted; Rabbi Joses recognizes it as permitted if it is wheat bread, but forbidden if it is barley bread, because barley attracts moisture.

4. If an oven is heated using cumin from the first-fruits, and bread is baked within it, the bread is considered permitted, because it does not possess the flavor of the cumin, but only its aroma.

5. If fenugreek falls into a vat of wine, whether it be from the first-fruits or from the second tithes, it must be calculated whether there is enough of its seed to impart flavor, but not also the stalk <note>the stalk is not usually considered to impart a food-flavor</note>. If it is from the crops of the seventh year <term>Sabbatical year</term>, from the mixed seeds of the vineyard <term>Kilayim</term>, or from a consecrated thing, it must be calculated whether there is enough in both the seed and the stalk to impart flavor.

6. If someone possesses bundles of fenugreek from the mixed seeds of the vineyard, they must be burned. If he has bundles of untithed <note>original: "illibatae," referring to Tevel, produce from which tithes have not yet been taken</note> fenugreek, he should crush them and calculate how much seed they contain, and set aside the <insert>portion for the</insert> seed ¹; however, it is not necessary to set aside the stalk. If he has already separated them, he may not say: "I will crush them and take the stalk for myself, and give the seed <insert>to the priest</insert>"; rather, he must give the stalk together with the seed.

7. It is not permitted to preserve common olives with first-fruit olives, whether they are crushed common olives with crushed first-fruits, or crushed common olives with whole first-fruits, or in the brine of first-fruits. However, it is permitted to preserve whole common olives with crushed first-fruits.

8. If an unclean <note>ritually forbidden</note> fish is preserved together with clean fish in any jar that holds two *sata* <term>a dry measure, roughly 13 liters</term>, and there is a weight of ten Judean drachmas ²—which are equivalent to five Galilean tetradrachms—of the unclean fish, then its brine is considered forbidden. Rabbi Judah thinks this is the case if it makes up a quarter-log <note>a small liquid measure</note> out of the two *sata*; Rabbi Joses says it is forbidden if it makes up one-sixteenth part.

9. If unclean locusts are preserved together with clean ones, they do not spoil the brine. ³ Rabbi Sadocus testified concerning the brine of unclean locusts, that it is clean <note>ritually permitted</note>.

10. Whatever things are ⁴ preserved together are permitted, except for anything preserved with a ⁵ bulb. If a common bulb is preserved with a first-fruit bulb, or common greens with—

<meta>catchword: num</meta>

---

¹ **Separate the seed.** Just as much as is needed for the tithe of the tithes.

² **Judean, which [are equivalent to] five Galilean etc.** Since the value of Judean currency was double that of Galilean currency. See Ketubot V. 9.

³ **Testified.** See Eduyot VII. 2.

⁴ **Preserved.** Since this Mishnah seems contrary to those in Shebiith VII. 7 and IX. 5, Jomtobus <note>Rabbi Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller, a 17th-century commentator</note> prefers to read "boiled" <note>original: "elixantur"; Hebrew: nishlakim</note> instead of "preserved" <note>original: "condiuntur"; Hebrew: nichbashim</note>, and he thinks the authority of the Jerusalem Talmud pertains to this.

<column-break/>

⁵ **Bulb.** What the Hebrew term *chasith* <note>original: חסית</note> is, the Tosefta on Terumot IX teaches us: *These are the species of "chasith": arum, garlic, onions, and leeks. Rabbi Judah says: you have no species of "chasith" except for the leek alone.* <note>original: אלו הן מיני חסיות : הלוף. והשום והבצלים והקפלוטות ר' יהודה אומר אין לך מיני חסיות אלא קפלוט בלבד</note> The word *chasith* therefore denotes solely the leek according to Rabbi Judah. According to others, it is extended to all other bulbs which are commonly considered edible.

11. Rabbi Joses declares that whatever is boiled with beets is to be considered forbidden, because the beets impart their flavor. Rabbi Simeon thinks that cabbage from an irrigated field <note>original: "agri rigui"</note> boiled with cabbage from a dry field <note>original: "siccanei campi"</note> is forbidden, because the former attracts moisture. Rabbi Judah considers anything cooked together to be permitted, unless it is cooked with meat. Rabbi Johanan ben Nuri asserts that the liver renders another thing forbidden <note>by imparting its flavor</note>, but the liver itself does not become forbidden, because it excretes moisture but does not absorb it.

12. If an egg is seasoned with forbidden spices, even the yolk is considered forbidden because it absorbs the flavor. The broth in which first-fruits have been boiled or seasoned is forbidden to laypeople <note>those who are not from the priestly families</note>.

## CHAPTER XI.

1. It is not permitted to put a date-cake <note>original: "Palatham"</note> or dried figs into brine, because the brine consumes them. However, it is permitted to put wine into brine. It is not permitted to season oil with spices; but it is permitted to make honey-wine <note>original: "œnomeli"</note> from wine. It is not permitted to boil down wine of the first-fruits because this diminishes its quantity. Rabbi Judah permits it, because he believes it improves the wine.

2. Regarding date-honey, apple-wine, vinegar from winter grapes, and all other juices of first-fruit produce: Rabbi Eliezer makes one liable for the sacred portion and the additional fifth <note>the penalty paid if a non-priest eats sacred food accidentally</note>. Rabbi Joshua exempts them from this penalty. Rabbi Eliezer also asserts that these juices can become ritually unclean in the same manner as liquids. But Rabbi Joshua says: The Sages did not list the seven liquids in the same way they usually list spices <note>meaning, they were very specific and did not intend to include all fruit juices</note>; rather, they said: "Seven liquids are capable of becoming impure; all other juices are considered pure."

3. It is not permitted to make honey from dates, nor wine from apples, nor vinegar from winter grapes; indeed, it is not permitted to change any other fruits from their natural state if they are first-fruits or second tithes, except for olives and grapes alone. They do not suffer the punishment of forty lashes on account of fruits...

### Title VI. TERUMOTH <term>Heave-Offerings</term>

Nor is it permitted to bring in liquids as first-fruits <note>original: "primitiva"</note>, except for what is extracted from olives and grapes. Nor does anything else cause impurity by reason of being a liquid, except for that which is made from olives and grapes. 4. The stems of figs and dried figs, <gloss>1</gloss> wild figs <note>original: "caprifici"</note>, and carob pods <note>original: "siliquae"</note> which are from the first-fruits are considered forbidden to laypeople <note>Non-priests are forbidden from eating the portion of the harvest dedicated to the priestly class</note>.

5. The seeds <note>original: "nuclei," referring to pits or stones</note> of first-fruit crops, if someone wishes to keep them, are considered forbidden; if he has thrown them away, they are permitted. And likewise, the bones of sacred sacrifices: if someone wishes to keep them, they are judged forbidden; if he has thrown them away, they are permitted. Chaff is permitted. The husks <note>original: "furfures"</note> of new grain are forbidden, but those of old grain are permitted. Furthermore, it is permitted to handle the first-fruit grains <gloss>2</gloss> in the same manner as common <note>original: "profanas," meaning non-consecrated</note> grain. He who has set aside one or two cabs <term>cabum: a measure of volume, roughly 1.4 liters</term> of flour from the sowing must not let the remainder be destroyed; rather, it should be stored in a clean place.

6. If someone has removed first-fruit wheat from a storehouse, he is not obliged to be overly scrupulous or to pick up the grains one by one. Truly, it is enough to sweep in the customary way, so that he may put common grain in that same place.

7. And likewise, if a jar of oil is spilled, he is not obliged to be scrupulous or to wipe it up by hand. Truly, he ought to conduct himself just as he would in a common matter.

<columns>2</columns>

1 **Wild figs** <note>original: "Caprifici"</note>.] What is read here and in [Tractate] Oketzin I. 6, as **הכלוסין** or **הכלוסים** <note>original Hebrew: "ha-kelusin"</note>, Maimonides <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and scholar</note> thinks denotes a certain kind of fig. One might suspect the Greek word to be **ἄκυλοι** <note>original Greek: "akyloi"</note>. Now, an *akylos* is an acorn from the holm-oak or cork-oak. And so it would be the same as that which is read with an **א** <note>the letter Aleph</note> prefixed in the Babylonian Gemara <term>Gemara: the component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis</term>, Avodah Zarah 14a: **אכלוסין באכלוסין, ואיצטרובילין ומוכססין** <note>Hebrew/Aramaic: "aklusin among aklusin, and pinecones, and muksisin"</note>, just as *akyloi, strobiloi, and moxea*. For so it should be read; not **אלכסין** <note>original: "alexin"</note>, as in the common books, or **מכססין** <note>original: "makhsasin"</note>, as in the Tosafot <note>Medieval commentaries on the Talmud</note> to Shebuot 12b. Nathan’s Lexicon <note>The Arukh, a famous 11th-century dictionary</note> has **אכלסון** <note>original: "aklason"</note> from there, which comes very close; and the order of the letters clearly confirms our reading. But since I read in the Babylonian Gemara, Chullin 67b: **את הזיזין שבעדשין ואת היתושין שבכליסין** <note>Hebrew/Aramaic: "the mites in lentils and the gnats in kelisin"</note>, [meaning] weevils or worms that are in lentils, and gnats that are in **כליסין** <note>original: "kelisin"</note>; I do not hesitate to affirm that the *kelisin* are ancient [figs]. As for the word **כלסין**, I do not doubt it is erroneously written for **בלסין** <note>original: "balasin"</note>. Certainly, I find **بلس** <note>Arabic: "balas"</note> among the Arabian physicians for a certain species of fig. It is also explained by Jauhari <note>An important Arabic lexicographer</note> as **شي يشبه التين يكثر باليمن** <note>Arabic: "something resembling a fig, abundant in Yemen"</note>. To the Ethiopians, the same word denotes the common fig. From this also comes **بلس**, the plural of **برلس** <note>Arabic: "barlas"</note> according to the same Jauhari in that Arabian prayer: **اراديك السلم علي البلس** 

<column-break/>

: **بلس** *As a suppliant I fix my face upon You, O God, for* **غراير كبار** <note>Arabic: "large sacks"</note> if he explains it well, it signifies **من مسوح يجعل فيها التين** <note>Arabic: "sacks made of haircloth in which figs are stored"</note>. Golius <note>A 17th-century Dutch orientalist</note> wrongly reads here in his book **التبن** <note>Arabic: "al-tibn," meaning straw</note> instead of **التين** <note>Arabic: "al-tin," meaning figs</note>. He admitted the same error in the word **غرارة** <note>Arabic: "gharara," a large sack</note>. He explains it from Jauhari as: *A large sack in which they are accustomed to carry straw.* For he was reading "straw." But here, in my excellent and most ancient manuscript, it is correctly read as **والتين**, which denotes "figs." From this, Jauhari also uses this word **غراير** in the explanation of another term. Yet I fear that Jauhari himself might be deceived in the explanation of that Arabian prayer, where the word **البلس** perhaps denotes not so much the fig-sacks as the figs themselves.

2 **in the same manner as common**.] Namely, it is permitted to sift, and to throw away the husks, which are unfit for eating, just as one does with common grain. So says Maimonides.

# Order I: SEEDS <note>original: "ZERAIM," the first division of the Mishnah dealing with agricultural laws</note>

If three drops follow after a liquid has been poured from one jar to another, one may then put common <note>original: "profanam," referring to non-consecrated, everyday food</note> items into that same jar. However, if the jar is tilted on its side and it releases more liquid, that liquid is still considered part of the first-fruits <note>original: "primitiis," specifically the Heave-offering or Terumah</note>. <margin>1 Of an Octans</margin> What amount must be present in the heave-offerings of the tithes taken from a doubtful matter so that they must be delivered to the Priest? An eighth of an eighth.

If the daughter of an Israelite is married to a Priest and is accustomed to visiting her father, her father may light the lamp in her presence. It is permitted to light such a lamp in a house of wedding, but not in a house of mourning. So says Rabbi Juda. Rabbi Joses says it is permitted in a house of mourning, but not in a house of wedding. Rabbi Meir forbids it in both places. Rabbi Simeon permits it in both.

1 <term>Octans.</term>] A measure which is called the *Sheminit* or "Eighth" in Hebrew; it is the eighth part of a *Log* <note>a liquid measure roughly equal to the contents of six eggs</note>.

2 <term>One who buys a cow in partnership, etc.</term>] Maimonides <note>a famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note> explains the meaning of the word *she-sham* <note>Hebrew: ששם</note> to us in this way: *This means that an Israelite buys a cow from a Priest for a fixed price and agrees with him that the Israelite will feed it until a certain time and then they will both sell it: and whatever is gained above the initial price shall be shared between them.* Bertinoro <note>a 15th-century commentator</note> adds: *An Israelite "who evaluated" [she-sham] a cow from a Priest is one who received a cow from a Priest at a fixed valuation of what it is worth now; the Israelite takes care of it to fatten it, and they divide the profit that exceeds the valuation.* This is similar to the rule in the Laws of Justinian <note>Roman civil law</note>, Book 13, Section 1: *But if I give you a boy to be taught, or a beast to be fed, or a child to be nursed, on the condition that if after a certain number of years...*

<column-break/>

*...he were sold, the price would be shared between us.* I translate the phrase *she-sham parah mi-kohen* as "one who buys a cow from a priest in partnership," following the words of the Emperor Antoninus to A. Muccatraulus in the Code, Book 8: *If it is proved that Apollinaris undertook to feed livestock in partnership (that is, so that their offspring would be divided in agreed portions between the owner and the shepherd).* This is the meaning of the word *sham*, both here and in the Talmudic tractate *Bava Metzia 69a*, where it is written: *He who receives livestock in partnership from another, how long is he bound to care for it?* This was not understood by Buxtorf <note>a famous Christian Hebraist</note> in his entry for *sham*. Whether this is the same type of contract called a "deposit" in Leviticus 6:2, which the Seventy Interpreters <note>the Septuagint</note> translate as "partnership" <note>Greek: κοινώνιαν</note>, the Chaldean Targum as "partnership of the hand," and the Syriac as "association of the hand," I would not dare to say for certain.

3 <term>With the oil of burning.</term>] This is the name for the heave-offering oil that has been defiled; it is normally used by the Priest to light lamps, as it is unfit for eating.

4 <term>Provided he is present.</term>] Or "with his consent." For Maimonides says: *With his permission, so that he allows it to us.* However, the term *hasghat* signifies both presence and obtained permission.

# TITLE VII. TITHES <note>original: "MAASEROTH"</note>,
## OR
# CONCERNING THE TITHES.
### CHAPTER I.

<margin>1.</margin> A general rule is handed down regarding tithes: Whatever serves as food, is guarded <note>referring to owned property as opposed to wild or abandoned crops</note>, and grows from the earth, is liable for the payment of tithes. Furthermore, another rule is also handed down: Whatever is fit for eating both in its early stage and in its final stage—even if it is usually left to grow further to increase the yield of food—is liable both when it is small and when it has grown large. However, that which is not edible in its early stage, but eventually becomes food, is not liable until it becomes fit for eating.

<margin>2.</margin> At what point do fruits begin to be liable for the payment of tithes? Figs, from the time they swell with juice. Grapes and wild grapes, from the time the seeds <note>original: "vinacea," referring to the grape stones or skins</note> become visible. Sumac and mulberries, from the time they turn red. And indeed, all red fruits, from the time they turn red. Pomegranates, from the time they become soft. Dates, from the time they <gloss>1</gloss> scatter leaven <note>an idiom for swelling or softening during ripening</note>. Peaches, from the time they abound with fibers. Nuts, from the time they <gloss>2</gloss> have made a chamber <note>referring to the internal structure of the shell</note>. Rabbi Judah says: Nuts and almonds, from the time they have formed a shell.

<margin>3.</margin> Carobs, from the time they become spotted. And all black fruits, from the time they become spotted. Pears, Crustumine pears <note>a prized variety of pear from the Roman era</note>, quinces, and service-berries, from the time they become smooth. And all white fruits, from the time they become smooth. Fenugreek, when it is already able to grow. Grain and olives, from the time they are one-third ripe.

<margin>4.</margin> Cucumbers and gourds, melons and watermelons among the vegetables, and also apples and citrons <note>original: "mala citrea," likely referring to the Etrog</note> are liable both when they have grown large and 

---

1 <gloss>They scatter leaven.]</gloss> Maimonides: <note>original: Maimonides' Judeo-Arabic commentary</note> *From the time they become sticky and swell like leavened bread; for such is the state of dates when they are small and beginning to ripen.*

<column-break/>

2 <gloss>They have made a chamber.]</gloss> Maimonides: <note>original: Maimonides' Judeo-Arabic commentary</note> *From the time the kernel is separated from the outer shell and lies as if in a <term>magurah<note>a Hebrew word meaning a storage bin or granary</note></term>, that is, in a chest.*
