1 *An eighth*] The measure which is called <insert>**שמינית**</insert> <italic>an eighth</italic> <note>original: "octans"</note> is the eighth part of a *Log* <note>a liquid measure approximately equal to the contents of six eggs</note>.

2 *Who [purchased] a cow in partnership &c.*] Maimonides explains the meaning of the word <insert>**ששם**</insert> <note>original: "she-sham," meaning appraised or partnered</note> for us in this way: <note>original Arabic: "It is when an Israelite buys it from a priest for a known price and agrees with him that the Israelite will feed it until a certain time and then they will sell it, and whatever amount is gained over the price, it is shared between them both."</note> Bertinoro says: <note>original Hebrew: "An Israelite who appraised a cow from a priest: meaning he received a cow from a priest by assessment according to what it is worth now at such-and-such a price, and the Israelite took care of it to fatten it; and whatever value was gained over the assessment, they shall divide between them."</note> This is similar to that rule in the Law of Justinian, book 13, section 1, regarding prescribed words: *But if I give a boy to be taught, or cattle to be grazed, or a child to be nursed, on the condition that if after certain years*

<column-break/>

*it were sold, the price would be shared between us.* However, I translate the phrase <insert>**ששם פרה מכהן**</insert> as "one who purchased a cow in partnership from a priest," following the words of the Emperor Antoninus to A. Muctraulius in book 8 of the Code, regarding pacts: *If it is proved that Apollinaris received partnership cattle to be grazed (that is, so that their offspring would be divided in agreed-upon portions between the owner and the shepherd).* This is what the word **שם** <note>sh-m</note> means, both here, where it is used with the preposition "from," and in the Talmud tractate *Baba Metzia 69a*, where it is used with "to": <insert>**השם בהמה לחברו עד מתי חייב לטפל בה**</insert> *He who receives a partnership animal from another, how long is he bound to care for it?* This was not understood by Buxtorf in his entry on the word "care" <note>original: "tapal"</note>. Whether this is the same as <insert>**פשרא**</insert> <note>original: "peshara," an appraisal</note>, which is called "a matter of the hand" <note>original Hebrew: "teshumat yad"</note> in Leviticus 6:2—which the seventy interpreters <note>the Septuagint</note> translate as *fellowship* <note>original Greek: "koinōnian"</note>, the Chaldeans as "partnership of the hand," and the Syrian as "association of the hand"—I would not dare to affirm.

3 *Oil for burning.*] This is what they call the oil of the heave-offerings that has been defiled, which is usually used by the Priest to light lamps since it is unfit for eating.

4 *Present.*] Or "with permission." For so Maimonides says: <note>original Arabic: "By his authority and he is not a lowly person," meaning with his permission as he allowed it to us.</note> But the word <insert>**רשות**</insert> <note>original: "reshut"</note> signifies both presence and the obtaining of permission.

# TITLE VII. TITHES <note>original: "MAASEROTH"</note>,

## OR CONCERNING TITHES.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>1.</margin>
A **GENERAL REGULAR** is handed down concerning tithes: Whatever serves as food, is kept under watch <note>meaning it is private property rather than wild or abandoned</note>, and grows from the earth, is required to be tithed. Furthermore, another rule is also handed down: Whatever is fit for eating both at the beginning of its growth and at its end, even if it is usually left to grow larger to increase its bulk as food, is liable for tithes both while it is small and when it has grown large. However, that which is not edible at the beginning, but eventually becomes food, is not liable until it becomes fit for eating.

2. At what stage must fruits be taken to be liable for tithing? Figs, from the time they begin to swell with juice. Grapes and wild grapes, from the time they show their seeds. Sumac and mulberries, from the time they turn red. Indeed, all red fruits are liable from the time they turn red. Pomegranates, from the time they become watery. Dates, from the time they <note>1</note> scatter leaven <note>original: "fermentum spargant," a phrase describing the ripening process explained in the footnote</note>. Peaches, from the time they abound in fibers. Nuts, from the time they have <note>2</note> made a chest <note>referring to the internal structure of the shell</note>. Rabbi Judah says: Nuts and almonds are liable from the time they have formed a husk.

3. Carobs, from the time they become spotted. Indeed, all black fruits are liable from the time they become spotted. Pears, Crustumine pears <note>a prized variety of pear from the Roman era</note>, quinces, and service-berries, from the time they become smooth. Indeed, all white fruits are liable from the time they become smooth. Fenugreek is liable from the time it is able to grow to maturity. Grain and olives are liable from the time they are one-third ripe.

<margin>2.</margin>
4. Cucumbers and gourds, melons and watermelons among the vegetables, as well as apples and citrons, are liable both when they have grown large and—

1 *Scatter leaven.*] Maimonides says: <note>original Judeo-Arabic: "מגד : תסתרכי ותדבוא כזבדו אלכתמר לאן כדלך תכון האלה אלתמר ענד אלנצג"</note>. *From the time they become soft and swell like fermented bread; for this is how ripening dates usually appear.*

<column-break/>

2 *Made a chest.*] Maimonides says: <note>original Judeo-Arabic: "מנו ינפצל : טעם מן אקשר אלבראני ויציר אטעם כאנה פי מגורה והי אלמכון"</note>. *From the time the kernel is separated from the outer shell and lies as if in a* <term>megurah</term> <note>a Hebrew word for a storehouse or bin</note>, *that is, as if it lies in a chest.*

If a jar is tilted on its side and the liquid flows back, that liquid is considered a Heave-offering. What is the minimum amount of the "Heave-offering of the Tithe" <note>a portion of a tithe given to the Priest</note> taken from doubtful produce <note>produce where it is uncertain if tithes were paid</note> that must be present to require it to be delivered to the Priest? <gloss>1</gloss> An eighth of an eighth <note>one sixty-fourth of a Log, a standard liquid measure</note>.

An Israelite <gloss>2</gloss> who has entered into a partnership for a cow with a Priest may not feed it with vetch from the Heave-offerings. But a Priest who has entered into a partnership for a cow with an Israelite may feed it with vetch from the Heave-offerings.

If an Israelite’s daughter is married to a Priest and is accustomed to visit her father, her father may light such a lamp <gloss>4</gloss> in her presence. It is permitted to light it in a house of celebration <note>a wedding</note>, but not in a house of mourning. So says Rabbi Judah. Rabbi Joses says it is permitted in a house of mourning, but not in a house of celebration. Rabbi Meir forbids it in both cases. Rabbi Simeon permits it in both.

1 *An eighth*] The measure which is called an **eighth** <note>original Hebrew: "sheminit"</note> is the eighth part of a *Log*.

2 *Who [entered into] a partnership for a cow, etc.*] Maimonides explains the meaning of the word **valuation** <note>original Hebrew: "shum"</note> to us as follows: *It signifies that an Israelite buys a cow from a Priest at a fixed price, and agrees with him that the Israelite himself will feed it for a certain time and then they will both sell it; whatever amount is gained above the initial price is shared between them.* <note>original: "Id hoc significat..." translating Maimonides' Judeo-Arabic commentary</note>. Bertinoro says: *An Israelite who valued a cow from a Priest—that is, who received a cow from a Priest at a valuation according to what it is worth now at such-and-such a price; and the Israelite takes care of it to fatten it; and the profit that accrues above the valued price, they divide between themselves.* Such is that rule in the Law of Justinian <note>Digest 13, section 1, regarding prescriptive terms</note>: *But if I gave you a boy to be taught, or a beast to be fed, or a child to be nursed, on the condition that if, after certain years, he was sold,*

<column-break/>

*the price would be shared between us.* However, I translate the phrase **who valued a cow from a Priest** as *one who entered into a partnership for a cow from a Priest*; following the words of Emperor Antoninus to A. Mucatrauli <note>Codex, Book 8, On Agreements</note>: "If it is proven that Apollinaris undertook to graze livestock on a share-basis (that is, so that their offspring would be divided between the owner and the shepherd in the proportions agreed upon)." This is the meaning of the word **valuation** <note>original: "shum"</note>, both here and in the tractate *Bava Metzia* 69a: *One who receives a beast in partnership from another, how long is he bound to take care of it?*—a point which Buxtorf did not understand in his entry for "care." Whether this is the same agreement called a **deposit of the hand** <note>original: "tishumat yad"</note> in Leviticus 6:2, which the Seventy Interpreters [Septuagint] translate as **fellowship** <note>original Greek: "koinonian"</note>, the Chaldeans as **partnership**, and the Syrians as <term>consociation of the hand</term> <note>original Syriac: "hultana"</note>, I would not dare to affirm.

3 *Oil of burning.*] This is what they call Heave-offering oil that has become ritually impure, which is customarily used by a Priest to light lamps, as it is unfit for eating.

4 *In the presence of.*] Or with his consent. For Maimonides says: *Whenever he permits this to us... with his leave.* The term <note>original: "hashrut"</note> signifies both physical presence and obtained permission.

## CONCERNING TITHES.
### CHAPTER I.

1. A general rule is handed down regarding tithes: Whatever serves as food, is guarded <note>meaning kept under ownership rather than growing wild or abandoned</note>, and grows from the earth, is liable for the payment of tithes. Furthermore, another rule is also handed down: Whatever is edible both at the beginning and at the end of its growth, no matter how much it is usually left to grow so that its food-value increases, is liable for tithes both while it is small and when it has grown large. However, that which is not edible at the start, but eventually becomes food, is not liable until it becomes fit for eating.

2. At what point do fruits become liable for the payment of tithes? Figs, from the time they swell with juice. Grapes and wild grapes, from the time they show their seeds. Sumac and mulberries, from the time they turn red; and indeed, all red fruits from the time they turn red. Pomegranates, from the time they become juicy <note>literally "melt" or "liquefy"</note>. Dates, from the time they <gloss>1</gloss> give off a fermented scent. Peaches, from the time they become full of fibers. Nuts, from the time they <gloss>2</gloss> have formed a hollow space. Rabbi Judah asserts: Nuts and almonds are liable from the time they have formed a husk.

3. Carobs <note>original: "Siliquae"</note>, from the time they become spotted; and all black fruits from the time they become spotted. Pears, Crustuminian pears <note>a famous Roman variety of pear</note>, quinces, and service-berries, from the time they become smooth; and all white fruits from the time they become smooth. Fenugreek, as soon as it is able to sprout. Grain and olives, from the time they have ripened by one third.

4. Cucumbers and gourds, melons and watermelons among the vegetables, and also apples and citrons are liable both when they have grown large,

...and while they are still small. Rabbi Simeon excuses citron apples <note>original: "mala citrea"</note> while they are small. Whatever is required in the case of bitter almonds is considered exempt in sweet ones; and what is required in sweet ones is considered exempt in bitter ones.

5. What is the threshing floor <note>The Hebrew term *goren*, translated here as the Latin *area*, refers to the "completion of work," the point at which produce is ready for use or sale and thus must be tithed.</note> for these same items regarding tithing? For cucumbers and gourds, the stage of completion is from the time their fuzz is rubbed off; and if it is not entirely rubbed off, then from the time they are gathered into a heap. For melons, from the time the down is rubbed off; and if not entirely rubbed off, from the time they are arranged on the shelf. For vegetables usually tied together, from the time they are tied; and if not tied, from the time a vessel is filled; and if a full vessel is not collected, then from the time as much as is needed is gathered. For baskets <gloss>2</gloss>, from the time they are covered; and if not covered, from the time the vessel is full; and if the vessel is not filled, from the time as much as is needed is plucked. In what sense are these things said? Certainly concerning the one who brings them to market. But if someone brings them home, it is permitted to eat them as they are until he reaches the house.

6. For dry pomegranates <gloss>3</gloss>, raisins, and carobs <note>original: "siliquarum"</note>, the stage of completion is from the time they are gathered into a heap. For onions, from the time the stalks <gloss>4</gloss> are removed; and if they are not removed, from the time they are gathered into a heap. For grain, from the time it is winnowed; and if it is not winnowed, from the time it is gathered into a stack. For legumes, from the time they have been shaken through a sieve; if that is not done, from the time they are winnowed. Even when winnowed, one may still take grains pulled from the stack—from those on the sides and from those hidden in the straw—and eat them.

7. The stage for wine is from the time it has been skimmed of foam. However much it has been skimmed, it is still permitted to drink what is taken from the top of the winepress or from the channel. For oil, from the time it flows down into the vat. However much it has flowed, it is permitted to take oil from the basket, or from the press-stone, or from the press-beams and pour it onto a cake <gloss>5</gloss> or a platter, but not into a boiling pot or a cauldron. ---

<columns>2</columns>

¹ **Threshing Floor** <note>original: "Area"</note>] A "threshing floor" belongs properly to grain: but by a metaphorical way of speaking it is also adapted to other fruits, in which sense it signifies the <term>final completion of work <note>original: "gamar melachtan"</note></term> concerning them—the last labor which is usually done in a threshing floor when preparing grain—or the time when they become altogether forbidden to be eaten unless the tithes are first paid. This expression is not only transferred to fruit, but also to livestock, to signify the time when they ought to be tithed. See *Shekalim* 3:1.

² **Baskets.**] Meaning the basket of a fig-picker or an apple-gatherer.

³ **Dry Pomegranates.**] What <term>pered <note>the Hebrew word for separated pomegranate seeds</note></term> is seems to be best established from the *Tosaphta* on Heave-offerings <note>original: "Terumoth"</note>, chapter 3: "He who sets aside Heave-offerings from grapes to make raisins, from figs to make dried figs, and from pomegranates to make <term>pered</term>," etc. Therefore, *pered* is to pomegranates what

<column-break/>

raisins are to grapes and dried figs are to [fresh] figs. In the editions of the *Tosaphta* that we have, the word "fruit" <note>original: "peri"</note> is read instead of *pered*. But it must absolutely be read as *pered*; and so Rabbi Samson reads it there. Rabbi Nathan cites a not dissimilar passage from the *Tosaphta* on the Sabbatical Year <note>original: "Shebiith"</note>: "Separating pomegranates to make *pered*." See *Orlah* 3:8 and *Oketz* 2:6.

⁴ **Stalks are removed.**] Stalks of flax are called *poklin* by Pseudo-Jonathan in Exodus 9:31. From this comes *pakal*, to pluck away or break off stalks or stems, which is the meaning in this passage. What most interpreters claim—that it denotes the same as *pakal* <note>referring to a different spelling/root</note>—lacks authority. What others claim—that it signifies arranging onions on a rope or cord—cannot possibly be true in that other passage, *Oketz* 2:5, where the same word occurs.

⁵ **Cake.**] <term>Maimonides <note>The famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legalist.</note></term> takes the word *hamitah* here to mean a vessel: that is, to use a platter for a cake. See *Tebul Yom* 1:1, 2, and 2:4.

For a round cake of pressed figs, the "threshing floor" <note>The Latin "area" translates the Hebrew "goren," referring to the stage of completion when produce becomes liable for tithing.</note> is from the moment it is smoothed over. ## CHAPTER II.

1. If someone passing through the marketplace shouts, "Take some figs for yourselves," those who eat them are exempt from tithing. However, if they bring them into their houses, they must process them as produce that is certainly untithed <note>Produce that is definitely untithed is called "Tevel."</note>. If the person says, "*Take them, and carry them to your houses*," and they eat them casually on the way, they are not permitted to do so. Accordingly, if they carry them home, they are not bound to treat them as anything other than doubtful produce <note>original: "rem dubiam," referring to "Demai," produce where it is uncertain if the previous owner tithed it.</note>.

2. If while some people are sitting in a gateway or a shop, it is shouted, "Take some figs for yourselves," those eating are considered exempt. But the master of the gateway or shop himself is bound to tithe. Rabbi Judah declares him exempt unless he turns his face or changes his seat.

3. If someone carries produce from Galilee into Judea, or sets out for Jerusalem, he is permitted to eat them casually until he reaches the place where he is going. And it is the same <gloss>3</gloss> on the return. Rabbi Meir thinks it is only until he reaches the place where he must spend the Sabbath. For peddlers who travel around the towns, it is permitted for them to eat casually until they come to the place where they must stay the night. Rabbi Judah's opinion is that the very first house they reach is to be considered as their home.

4. Rabbi Eliezer forbids eating produce casually if the "first fruits" <note>Referring to the "Terumah" or heave offering given to the priests.</note> were taken before the work on them was fully finished. But the Sages permit it, with the exception of a basket of figs. Concerning a basket of figs from which the first fruits <gloss>*</gloss> have been taken, Rabbi Simeon permits it, but the Sages forbid it.

5. If someone says to another, "*Here is a farthing <note>original: "assarium," a small Roman coin of little value.</note> for you; give me five figs for it*," he is not permitted to eat them unless the tithes are paid. So says Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Judah says: if he eats them one by one, he is exempt; if he gathers them together, Rabbi Judah holds him liable.

In the Tosefta <note>A secondary collection of Jewish oral law.</note>, instead of מעגל <note>ma'agel</note>, which follows shortly after, it is read as מעלן <note>ma'alan</note>; that is, "If it is pressed into a jar and put back into the chest."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of exemptions from tithing (Maaseroth). While the previous page focused on when produce is considered "finished" and liable for tithes, this page examines the "worker's right" to eat while harvesting and how commercial transactions or reciprocal agreements trigger tithing obligations.</meta>

# ORDER I. SEEDS <note>original: "Zeraim"</note>
### CHAPTER II (continued)

Rabbi Judah says: This case involves a rose garden that was in Jerusalem, where three or four figs were sold for an *assarium* <note>An *assarium* (Hebrew: *issar*) was a small Roman copper coin of very low value.</note>, and never at any time were the firstfruits or tithes separated from them.

6. If someone says to another: "*Here is an assarium for twenty figs that I shall choose for myself;*" he is permitted to choose them and eat [without tithing]. "*For a grape cluster that I shall choose for myself;*" he is permitted to pick the individual grapes one by one and eat. "*For a pomegranate that I shall choose for myself;*" he is permitted to remove the seeds individually and eat. "*For a melon that I shall choose for myself;*" he is permitted to slice it and eat. However, if he said: "*For these twenty figs: For these two grape clusters: For these two pomegranates: For these two melons;*" he eats them in his usual manner but remains exempt, since he has purchased produce that is still attached to the soil <note>Produce still attached to the ground is not yet "harvested" in a legal sense, so casual snacking remains exempt from tithes.</note>.

7. If someone hires a laborer to spread out <term>ficus pandat|A stage in drying figs where they are spread out in the sun</term> figs, and the laborer stipulates, "*On the condition that I may eat from the figs,*" he may eat and *will be exempt.* "*On the condition that I and my ² son eat, or that my son eats in place of the wages owed to me,*" he himself eats and is exempt; but if the son eats, he is liable [to tithe]. "*On the condition that I eat while spreading them, and after they are spread;*" while spreading them he eats and is exempt; after they are spread, if he eats he is liable, because he is not eating ³ according to the prescription of the law. This is the general rule: One who eats according to the prescription of the law is held exempt; but one who does not eat according to the prescription of the law is liable.

8. One who works with ⁴ wild figs <note>original: "caprificis." These are non-edible figs used to house wasps that pollinate the edible "white" figs.</note> may not eat from the white figs; nor may one who works with white figs eat from the wild figs. However, one is permitted to restrain oneself until reaching the better fruits. If someone enters into a reciprocal agreement with another, ⁵ so that he may eat and the other may eat; or so that he spreads figs and the other spreads figs; or so that he eats and the other spreads figs, he is liable. Rabbi Judah holds that one who enters into a reciprocal agreement to eat is liable; but if it is to spread figs, he remains exempt.

1 *Twenty.*] Others read: *ten.*
2 *My son.*] For the phrase "and my son" [Hebrew: *u-veni*], most manuscripts have "my son and my household" [Hebrew: *beni u-veiti*]. But the Jerusalem Talmud and the manuscript more correctly omit "and my household."
3 *According to the prescription of the law.*] Deuteronomy 23:24. *Baba Metzia* VII 2. <note>Biblical law grants a laborer the right to eat from the crop they are currently harvesting.</note>
4 *Wild figs.*] Because the word is written here twice as *labsin*,

<column-break/>

I have little doubt that it is the same as what is elsewhere written as *balsin*, concerning which see our notes on *Terumot* XI. 4. Certainly Rabbi Nathan, in his Lexicon, does not recognize the word *labsin* at all. I therefore read it as *in balsin*.
5 *So that he may eat.*] Meaning he eats from the other person's figs, and the other person in turn eats from his own.

<meta>This page transitions from the end of Chapter II, which discussed purchasing produce still attached to the soil, to Chapter III, which examines the "worker's right" to eat during harvest and how the location of the produce (such as a courtyard or drying floor) determines when it becomes liable for tithes.</meta>

# TITLE VII. TITHES <note>original: "MAASEROTH"</note>

### CHAPTER III.

1. If someone is carrying figs through a courtyard <note>original: *atrium*</note> in order to spread them out on a drying platform <note>original: *tabulato*; usually a flat roof or raised area used for drying fruit</note>, his children and the members of his household may eat them and remain exempt from tithes. Likewise, laborers who are with him—provided that the employer is not required to provide their food as part of their wages—may eat and remain exempt. However, if the employer is indeed required to provide their food, they may not eat [without first tithing].

2. If he sends laborers into the field, provided he is not required to provide their food, they may eat and remain exempt. But if he is required to provide their food, they may eat figs plucked individually from the tree, but they may not eat from a basket, or a hamper, or from the drying platform <note>Under Jewish law, a laborer has a biblical right to eat from the crop they are harvesting. However, if the food is part of their formal compensation, or if the fruit has been "collected" into a vessel, it may trigger the requirement to separate tithes before eating.</note>.

3. If someone hires a laborer to tend to olive trees, and the laborer stipulates: "*On the condition that I may eat from the olives,*" he may eat them one by one and remain exempt; but if he eats several together, he will be liable [to tithe]. For one who weeds an <term>onion bed|cæpinam</term>, if he stipulates: "*On the condition that I may eat the greens,*" he may pluck and eat individual leaves and remain exempt; but if he gathers several together, he will be liable.

<summary>This page details the specific conditions under which family members and laborers may eat produce without tithing, focusing on the distinction between casual snacking and food provided as formal wages.</summary>
